rules.rule: The repositories that release together and how far each consumer lags the newest shared version are reported; a forced-newest rule is itself a cause.
rules.detail: Release tags per repository joined with the shared-package pins. The unit is the release, never the day, because agent commit rates make day counts meaningless.
rules.why: A many-repo layout rests on pairs of repos not moving together; lockstep deployment signals a misplaced boundary. Independent deployability is what the layout protects.
rules.review_question: Which repositories moved together in the last releases, and is a forced-newest rule the cause?
open: No plant; a measure only. Applies to the multi-repo estate.

rules.rule: A file per service lists the stores and event families it writes and the services each flow includes, compared with a scan of the writers.
rules.detail: The tool compares the file with the writers found by scanning write statements. Measure first, gate once the list exists. An agent cannot infer ownership from the code, so the list is what makes a check possible.
rules.why: Two seam cases of our own were this: no one could say which program wrote a shared store.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a scan of write statements and event publishes compared with the per-service ownership file. Plant: a write to a store not on the service's list fails once the list exists. Control: a listed write passes

open: The list is not yet there and no plant exists until it is built; it extends the rules that a service publishes only the families it owns and that every flow has a journey.

rules.rule: Core code knows nothing it does not own: every connection in or out of a program goes through an interface the core declares and an adapter implements, and the core imports only pure packages.
rules.detail: This is ports and adapters. A connection is a provider, a runtime, the operating system, a store, the network, a child process or a terminal. The core directly imports only the standard library's pure packages, the shared packages that rule data names as pure, and its own core: no OS-specific file, no process-spawning package (os/exec) and no network package (net, matched exactly, so net/url and net/netip stay pure). Only an adapter imports those. Our own domains count the same way (an anti-corruption layer): one domain reaches another only through an interface the caller declares, so any domain of ours can be replaced by an open-source tool or a vendor. In the web stack a provider, data client, engine-specific browser API, analytics, payment or sign-in reaches a screen or feature only through a module we own that the provider's adapter implements, a feature imports no provider package, and a service of ours counts as a provider. A module imports a generated client only for a service its declaration lists; generated types are free. Raw third-party clients are reached only through one shared wrapper. A program need not ship for every OS or provider today, but its shape must leave adding one to an adapter. The rule holds with a single implementation, because the edge is the reason for the interface. A fake adapter is how the core is tested at unmanaged edges, and a managed store runs on the real engine. A shared package that wraps one thing is itself the adapter and declares that.
rules.why: Code that names a vendor or an OS in the core makes every later provider or platform a change across the program. In one repo a Mac port took 151 files, 19 of them in the command layer; in another a second runtime touches 15 files in 3 packages before the index.

unless.reason: a shared package that wraps one thing is itself the adapter and declares that

checks.note: rule data names core paths, pure packages, adapter paths and the domain list; depguard rules generated per core glob with strict list-mode allowing the standard library minus the process-spawning and network packages (with an allow entry for the URL and address packages), the pure shared packages and the core; forbidigo on runtime.GOOS and runtime.GOARCH outside adapter paths, tests included (an OS skip in a core test is a finding); a companion layout test that OS-suffixed files and build-constraint lines sit only under adapter paths; depguard or go-arch-lint independence between domain packages from the domain list. Plant: in a core path an import of the network package and of the process-spawning package are reported, and runtime.GOOS is reported by forbidigo; the same imports under the adapter folder are not reported. Control: the same imports and runtime.GOOS under the adapter path pass

eslint-plugin-boundaries rule boundaries/external restricts provider packages to adapter elements, provider list as rule data, count ratcheted. Plant: importing a provider's package in a feature file fails. Control: the same import in the adapter passes

rules.review_question: Would a second engine or provider have to invent a meaning for any method of the owned module, and which one?
open: In Go the depguard run passed three plants (network and process packages and GOOS) in golangci-lint 2.14.0; domain independence and OS-suffixed-file layout were not run. Denying the network package also hits the URL package unless an allow entry is added in lax mode.
In the earlier trial a depguard config passed all three of its plants, an extended one caught 2 of 3 and a path check caught the third. Reflection on file-system information stays review.
The web rule is vacuous today because neither site imports a provider package; it is held by the network-access rule and the provider-adapter rules in the web part.
The web stack is agnostic at the level of intent, not engine neutrality.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: operator (twin rules in Go and in the web stack); not measured on our web sites

rules.rule: A port the target architecture names is declared before its first adapter, in one interfaces-only port package that the core and every adapter import, one subject per port with a handful of methods, and growth is a new adapter on an existing port; an in-program seam over code the core may already use needs a stated reason.
rules.detail: Platform and edge ports are written up front from the target architecture, not discovered when a second implementation turns up, so moving from a simple adapter to a better one is never a refactor. They live together in one port package per program (slot interfaces may live in their slot package), so the whole platform contract reads in one place and one fake fills it; an interface for a platform or external edge declared beside its user is a finding. A port is a subject (machine, services, peers, storage), with a handful of methods, never one interface per function. The port package holds interfaces, the value types they carry and the absent value of arch.ports.5, and no logic. The limit on speculative seams stays for code inside the program: a wrapper around what the core may already use (a file read, the shared write helper) or a clock port needs a stated reason, and the second implementation or a design names it. Time is passed as a value or tested with the standard synthetic-time helper. A small optional capability a caller tests for by type assertion is not a seam.
rules.why: Three target designs fix their platform ports up front and reject interfaces beside their users, because a port found late is a refactor across every caller. The old limit (an interface only once a second implementation exists) still catches the failure it was written for: one repo has 89 interfaces, 14 with no production implementer, and the true failures were wrappers over pure code.

unless.reason: tested for by type assertion, not injected

checks.note: a layout test: interfaces whose method sets touch an adapter-only import or a port value type are declared only in the port package (or a slot package listed in rule data); the port package holds no function bodies beyond the absent value; method count per port reported with no limit. Plant: an interface over a process-spawning call declared in a command package fails; a function with logic in the port package fails. Control: the same interface in the port package with its adapter under host/<platform> passes

v1 class our-plugin. analyzer iface as a report for in-program seams (union across GOOS, wired implementers by SSA MakeInterface, capability roles and the port package excluded, zero-implementer seams listed) plus golangci-lint iface (identical, unused, opaque) and interfacebloat as config rules. Plant: a wrapper interface over a file read in a core package is listed. Control: a port in the port package with one adapter is not listed

rules.review_question: Is this interface a platform or edge port that belongs in the port package, and if it is an in-program seam, where is its second implementation written down?
open: The in-program seam half is still a report; only the layout test gates.
rules.note: This is the Go form. Related to arch.ports.1, which it shapes, and arch.ports.15, which holds how a port grows.

rules.rule: No dependency-injection framework; wire by hand in the entry point.
rules.detail: The banned list is rule data (the common wiring and container modules), and a module allow file that refuses any module not allowed makes the list not need to be complete.
rules.why: One wiring library is archived and no repo uses one; hand wiring in one place is what makes the composition readable.

checks.note: depguard deny in the shared config for the known dependency-injection modules listed in rule data, plus the module allow file which refuses any module not allowed. Plant: importing a dependency-injection container in a file fails. Control: a file with no such module passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; config only

rules.rule: The entry point is thin and its run function can be tested in process; package-level state exists only as a registry, the machine or the default paths, written once by the entry point before any read or goroutine, and any other mutable package variable is a finding.
rules.detail: A main function under 80 lines (the limit is data in the rule file with its reason, and is a guess) and a test of the run() function. Write-once state is allowed in three forms only: a plug-in registry, the machine value that holds the ports, and the default paths. Each is set by the entry point's files before any read and before any goroutine starts; a second write panics, and a read before the write panics. A test that swaps one restores it in a cleanup. Every other package-level variable that is not a constant, a sentinel error or a compiled pattern is a finding. A library has no main and sets nothing.
rules.why: One repo has 26 init functions. Entry files today are 62, 54, 21, 15 and 15 lines; one outside program has a 934-line main and would fail on day one. Two target designs need a registry and a machine value set at start; allowing exactly those, write-once and loud on misuse, keeps the ban on hidden mutable state without forcing every port through every call.

unless.reason: has no main

checks.note: gochecknoglobals with an allow list of the registry, machine and default-path variables named in rule data, plus an ast-grep rule on main's length, from its current baseline. Plant: a 120-line main fails; an unlisted mutable package variable fails. Control: a 15-line main with a testable run function and a listed registry passes

a test per write-once value: a second set panics, a read before the set panics, and a source test that only files under cmd call the setter outside _test.go files. Plant: a setter called from a command package fails; a second set in a test does not panic and fails. Control: one set in main before any read passes

open: The 80-line limit is a guess; the rule becomes firmer with a fault from a fat main.

rules.rule: An app shell composes modules: one composition file is the only place that imports every module manifest, and the shell holds no module logic.
rules.detail: The shell holds the router, providers, auth screens and the composition file; its module list equals the graph file's list. It reaches a module only through that module's manifest, its pages (from the router folder only) or its public entry. In Go the program's main wires every package by hand in one place and imports no logic of its own.
rules.why: One composition root is the only place that knows every module, so a module can be added or removed in one place.

checks.note: boundary rule allowing only the composition file to import every module manifest, and a check that its list equals the graph file. Plant: a second file importing every manifest fails; a manifest missing from the composition list fails. Control: the composition file importing every manifest passes

open: The Go form is arch.ports.11 and arch.ports.12; no separate Go check is chosen.
Some plants and controls of this rule were written at the merge from the sources' description of the check, and have not been run.

rules.rule: In a program with more than one client, every write from every client goes through one executor and one write port, only that executor and the store adapters import the write handle, and every outcome a caller branches on comes back as a typed result.
rules.detail: Every write is a registered operation (a verb) that the one executor runs through the one write port; a command, a route, an agent tool and a page all call the executor and never open storage for writing. A failure the caller branches on is a typed result value with its exit or status; an exception or panic past the executor means a bug. The import table names the executor package and the store adapters as the only importers of the write handle, so a second writer fails the layer test. A program with one client meets the rule by having one write path.
rules.why: Two writers that each open the store each grow their own checks, and the client that skipped one corrupts the data the other trusted. One executor is the one place a write is checked, logged and undone, whichever client asked.

checks.note: the layer test reads the write handle's importers and fails any package other than the executor and the store adapters; a source test fails a throw or panic that leaves the executor. Plant: a command that imports the write handle and writes directly fails. Control: the same command calling the executor's verb passes

rules.rule: A new library enters only as an adapter on a port that exists, and a new port lands in the target architecture document before its code.
rules.detail: A capability the program does not have yet is a new port, written into the target architecture first with its intended adapter. A new library or tool for a capability the program has is a new adapter on the existing port, so swapping it never touches the core. The change that adds the port's code cites the target document's section; a port in code with no section there is a finding.
rules.why: A library that enters without a port leaks its types into the core, and a port written straight into code has no design anyone agreed; both make the next swap a refactor.

checks.note: a docs test that every port in the port package has a section in the target architecture document, and the import rules of arch.ports.6 that let only the adapter import the library. Plant: a new port interface with no section in the target document fails. Control: a port whose section exists passes

rules.review_question: Which existing port does this library sit behind, and if none, where is the new port in the target architecture?

rules.rule: A plug-in registry is the one place an implementation meets the core, only the entry point's files call Register, a plug-in brings its commands and checks through its port and the command layer mounts them without importing it, and a name clash refuses at start.
rules.detail: Slot packages hold a registry each. Only files under the entry point (cmd/<name>) call Register in non-test code; a test file may register a stand-in. A plug-in contributes commands, checks and routes through its port, and the command layer reads them from the registry, never by importing the plug-in package. Two registrations under one name stop the program at start with both names. A registry is write-once state under arch.ports.12.
rules.why: A plug-in the command layer imports cannot be removed without editing the command layer, and a name clash that one registration silently wins is a command that quietly changes meaning.

checks.note: a source test that Register is called only from files under cmd outside _test.go, a layer rule that the command layer imports no plug-in package, and a registry test that a duplicate name fails at start. Plant: a Register call in a plug-in's own init fails; registering two plug-ins under one name fails at start. Control: main registering each plug-in once passes

rules.rule: The port package declares which ports every platform must fill and which may be absent, and ships one in-memory fake that fills every port so the core's tests run on every operating system; a platform word in the fake is a port finding.
rules.detail: The required set is data on the port package; a platform adapter that leaves a required port absent fails at start and in its test. The fake fills every port, required and optional, and holds no word from any one platform (no tool name, path or OS name); such a word means the port carries the platform's shape. A port is extracted from the existing platform's callers first, and the next platform's adapter is written against the extracted port, not the other way round.
rules.why: Without a fake the core's tests run only on the platform the developer has, and without a declared required set a new platform learns what it must fill from crashes.

checks.note: a test that the fake fills every port, a test per platform adapter that every required port is filled, and a word-list test over the fake with the platform words of arch.ports.4 as data. Plant: a fake that leaves one port nil fails; a tool path literal in the fake fails. Control: a fake with every port filled by neutral in-memory values passes

rules.rule: A consumer decides what to draw or run from the capability list the server publishes, never from a platform name, so a new platform edits one repository.
rules.detail: The server publishes which capabilities this machine has (from arch.ports.5's capability layer). A page, a CLI or an agent shows, hides or disables a feature by reading that list. A platform name may be shown to a person; a branch on it in consumer code is a finding.
rules.why: A consumer that branches on a platform name has to be edited for every new platform, in every repository that reads the server.

checks.note: a source test over consumer code for a comparison against a platform name list in rule data. Plant: a page condition comparing the platform field to "linux" fails. Control: the same condition reading the capability list passes

rules.rule: Data from a less-trusted peer reaches a decision only through fields declared decidable on its type, each naming the one decision it drives, checked by a syntax-tree test over the deciding layer with a planted read.
rules.detail: Every field of a type that carries a less-trusted peer's report is documented either as may decide, naming the one decision it drives, or as display only. A condition in the deciding layer reads only may-decide fields; a display-only field in a condition, a switch or a map key fails. Decoding of such data is strict (an unknown type or field is refused, sizes are capped), which the service and daemon parts hold.
rules.why: A peer that can set a field the core branches on can steer the core. Naming the decision per field makes every new field a choice, not a default.

checks.note: a go/ast test over the deciding packages: every selector on a peer-report type inside an if, switch or map index resolves to a field whose doc comment starts with may decide. Plant: a planted condition on a display-only field fails. Control: a condition on a may-decide field passes

rules.rule: A provider's name and its vocabulary do not appear in the core or command layer, a command reaches a provider only through the port and imports no adapter, and the programs and products a tool manages are named nowhere in its shipped source.
rules.detail: The command layer may import the port package and not the adapter folders. Outside a provider's adapter no identifier, string or JSON field name from the provider's own vocabulary (its name, its plan, quota or account terms) appears in the core or command layer; the check reads tokens, not just imports, and is proved with a planted name. Separately, a program that manages other software names none of it in shipped source: code, comments and help text. A word-list test reads every non-test source file and fails on a listed word; its exception map holds a path and a reason per entry and only shrinks. Tests and fixtures may name the managed software. The word list is data, so a new provider or managed product extends the list and not the rule.
rules.why: One repo has 13 command files importing the runtime adapter directly and 150 lines in 12 packages that name it. A name ban that counts only imports misses the provider's field names and plan words, which tie the core to one provider as firmly as an import, and a product named in a comment or help line is a product the next reader assumes is supported.

checks.note: depguard: the command-layer glob may import port packages and denies the adapter folders; forbidigo or ast-grep count of the provider name in code outside adapter paths, ratcheted. Plant: importing the runtime adapter in a new command file fails. Control: importing the port passes

a word-list test over the tokens of non-test source (identifiers, strings, JSON tags, comments, help text) outside the adapter paths, with the provider vocabulary and the managed-product list as data and a path-to-reason exception map that only shrinks. Plant: a planted provider plan word as a struct field in the core fails; a managed product's name in a command's help text fails. Control: the same words in the provider's adapter and in a test fixture pass

rules.rule: An adapter reads another program's machine format where it has one, and never parses text meant for a person.
rules.detail: Where a program offers structured output (JSON, a stable record format, an API), the adapter asks for it and decodes it. Parsing a program's human text (tables, help text, version banners) is allowed only where no machine format exists, with the reason in the adapter and a pinned sample in its test.
rules.why: Human text changes between releases and locales without notice; a machine format is the part its authors promise to keep. One repo finds a sibling's version by searching its help text.
rules.review_question: Does this program offer a machine format, and if so why is the adapter reading its text?
rules.note: v1 review check (review is not a v2 check class): review of each adapter's decode path; a source test lists adapters that split or regex-match a program's stdout without a recorded reason

rules.rule: A program's entry point only wires: it builds the adapters, fills the ports and calls the core, and holds no logic, no type with behaviour and no direct operating-system work beyond what an adapter's constructor needs.
rules.detail: The entry point is a program's main package or entry file. Reading a flag, an environment variable, a path or the clock, spawning a process and opening a file are adapter work, so each is a port the entry point fills. A type with a method, a loop over domain data or a branch on domain data in an entry point is a finding. The size of the entry point and its run function being testable in process are arch.ports.12's; this rule holds what the entry point may contain.
rules.why: The fleet's own gate grew operating-system calls in its entry point, and no check fired, because the ports rule held the core and said nothing of the file that wires it.
rules.review_question: Does this entry point build adapters, fill ports and call the core, and nothing else?
open: Planned check: a generated layer test of what an entry point may import and declare (its size cap is arch.ports.12's). Plant: an entry point that imports os/exec or declares a method fails. Control: one that builds adapters and calls the core passes. No tool key to bind to: it is the work of gragas#409 to gragas#411, and the rule stays proposed until one gives it a check.

rules.rule: Build, test and gate tooling, scripts and hooks are programs: every rule that holds a program holds them, with ports, one adapter per outside program and no platform literal; a shell step is a thin call or a declared adapter.
rules.detail: A script, a make recipe, a hook and a workflow step that reach the operating system, another program or the network are connections of a program like any other. A shell step is either a thin call to a program the repository builds, or an adapter declared in rule data with the one program it wraps. A platform literal (an operating-system name, a path or a tool flag that exists on one platform) in a shell step outside a declared adapter is a finding.
rules.why: The fleet's own gate grew shell with platform literals and no rule applied, because tooling was not counted as a program.
rules.review_question: Does this script, hook or recipe reach the system through a thin call or a declared adapter, with no platform literal?
open: Planned check: a test over the repository's scripts, hooks and recipes that lists each shell step that is not a thin call or a declared adapter. Plant: a script with a platform literal fails. Control: a script that calls the repository's own program passes. No tool key to bind to: it is the work of gragas#409 to gragas#411, and the rule stays proposed until one gives it a check.

rules.rule: Code that touches an operating system lives only in the host layer, behind ports: no other package imports an operating-system package, reads runtime.GOOS or runtime.GOARCH, or carries an operating-system file name or build tag.
rules.detail: Retired for arch.ports.24, which has no host layer: a ruling moved what the layer held into the platform libraries. The text above is what the rule said while it was active.
rules.why: Each block of the fleet's first programs was built on one operating system and failed on the others, because the operating system was named in every block.
rules.note: Retired with gragas#1683 for arch.ports.24. A product keeps no host layer of its own: a ruling puts the knowledge of an operating system in the platform libraries, so the layer this rule spared is gone and the rule's checks follow the new id.

sources.says: Naming a file dns_windows.go will cause it to be included only when building the package for Windows
As events arrive from the outside world at a port, a technology-specific adapter converts it into a usable procedure call or message and passes it to the application.

rules.review_question: Does any file outside the host layer name an operating system, by import, by runtime.GOOS or by its file name or build tag?

rules.rule: A product names no operating system anywhere: no package imports an operating-system package, reads runtime.GOOS or runtime.GOARCH, or carries an operating-system file name or build tag, and the platform library that covers the need is the way.
rules.detail: A product has no host layer. What differs between systems is the platform libraries' knowledge, and a program reaches it through the library that covers the need, never through golang.org/x/sys, syscall, github.com/gofrs/flock or github.com/shirou/gopsutil, which stay inside those libraries. Three things mark a file of a product as a finding: an import of one of those packages, a read of runtime.GOOS or runtime.GOARCH, and a file whose name go build reads as one system's (_GOOS or _GOOS_GOARCH, before _test), or that ends in _unix or _other by convention, or that carries a //go:build line naming an operating system before its package clause; a Go file that cannot be read as far as that clause, or whose //go:build line go build refuses, is a finding too, never a pass. The register of libraries names the one package of a program that holds each need: its trust package (file-owner-and-mode), its peer package (peer-identity) and the one package of atomic-write, path-lock, app-folders, login-service and unix-socket-listen; machine-facts reaches the machine through the library the register names, in any package. A product's files that stand outside the rule today are rows of its exemptions file, one a file, each with its reason and expiry, and the rows only fall. A lint run reads the files of one system only, so the gate lints each system of its list by GOOS on the one machine it runs on.
rules.why: Each block of the fleet's first programs was built on one operating system and failed on the others, because the operating system was named in every block. A layer inside each product only moved the naming to one more place to keep right; one library owns it once for every product.

sources.says: A product imports no x/sys or syscall at all, the host layer included; that knowledge belongs to the platform libraries.

sources.says: gragas has no host layer: the os-host row spares no folder, and every file that names an operating system is held by a row of its exemptions file or its allowlist.

The file-name and build-line half, the os-files key of the gragas preset, which gragas check computes: each Go file whose name ends in an operating system's suffix, or whose build line names one, and that no live row of the exemptions file names by its path; a folder the os-host row still spares (a project that has not moved its layer yet) is outside the check's reading, as before. rules.review_question: Does any file of this product name an operating system, by import, by runtime.GOOS or by its file name or build tag, or reach a system through anything but the platform library that covers the need?
open: The TypeScript side is held today by the explorer's own lint rows in explorer/eslint.config.js: osProperties (no-restricted-properties), osImports (no-restricted-imports) and osSyntax (no-restricted-syntax). No eslint preset key exists to bind them yet, so no check row names them; a row waits for one.

The file and build-tag half is gragas's own check, not a linter's: no golangci-lint 2.15.0 linter reads a file name or a //go:build line (depguard and forbidigo read the imports and calls of the files the run's system builds, and a file of another system is not loaded at all), and ast-grep has no preset.

The syscall import is held by the no-os-packages row of the shared config, not by a row of its own; a project's files that still import it are excluded by path in its overrides, each with the row that removes it.

rules.rule: The number of files in each package that import a vendor SDK directly is reported, as the price of leaving that vendor.
rules.detail: A report only: counts come from the module's import lists and nothing fails. A commit that adds a provider is read with arch.measures.2.
rules.why: The count is the cost of replacing a vendor, shown before the replacement is wanted.
rules.review_question: Which package has grown its direct vendor imports since the last release, and is the port still the only door?
open: A report with no failure has no plant; only a person reads it.

rules.rule: The core compiles for every operating system in the supported list, shipped or not, and holds no platform path literal and no OS tool name, with no exception list; a new use fails and the fix is a port.
rules.detail: Shipping is a release decision; shape is not. The list is linux, darwin and windows. An adapter path is outside the set. Compiling is not enough, because a path literal compiles everywhere: no non-test file in the core holds a string starting with a system root (/sys, /proc, /run, /opt, /etc), a home-relative system folder, or the name of an OS tool (a service manager, a log reader, a package manager). The path and tool lists are data, so a new platform adds its roots and tools to the list. There is no exception list for this rule: gates.exemptions does not apply, and the fix for a finding is a port. Paths reach the core from the platform's defaults through config. No platform path or syscall sits in the core, and no OS tool name or path outside the OS adapter. go build stops at a failed dependency and so can show a count that rises after a fix, so the check type-checks per OS, continues past failures and counts packages with their own errors, reading the package list from the dependency closure so an adapter reached through the core shows up. It proves compilation only, needs no limit and takes about two seconds.
rules.why: Four core packages of one repo fail on windows (ten over the whole repo); go build showed three of them and hid one. Two other repos have a machine or file package that fails on other systems.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion corecompile: go/packages loaded per GOOS with types, deps and syntax and a type config that continues after errors; core package list from the dependency closure of the core paths in rule data; count of packages with their own errors, ratcheted per GOOS. Plant: a file-lock call from the unix package in a core clock file fails, naming it for windows. Control: a pure core passes

a source test over non-test core files for string literals starting with a listed system root and for listed OS tool names, lists as rule data, with no exception map. Plant: a "/proc/meminfo" literal in a core file fails; a "systemctl" string in a core file fails. Control: the same literals in the Linux adapter pass

rules.rule: The core does not learn the platform from a port: no platform field or name in a port, no core code reads a port's presence as a platform, a missing port is one stated absent value that only the capability layer tests, and a capability the machine lacks is answered by that layer as not on this machine.
rules.detail: No Platform, GOOS or OS-name field or string in a port struct that core code branches on; a platform name may be carried for a health or doctor report only, never for a decision. A port the machine lacks has one absent value, stated on the port package (nil in the machine value, or a named absent type), never a stub that pretends to work. Only the capability layer tests for that value; a nil or absent test on a port field anywhere else in the core is a finding. The capability layer turns an absent port into one answer, not on this machine, that every client shows the same way. A port does not carry the shape of the platform: a method or parameter that means something only on one OS or provider is a finding. A second adapter written before the port is frozen is the cheapest test of its shape. A missing port is nil, not a lying stub, and the port package holds its adapters per OS. The review asks what the port does when no adapter is wired and whether that is stated on the port. In the web stack the owned module's methods are domain verbs carrying domain values, and a failure crosses it as a typed value, never as text to match.
rules.why: One repo has 18 nil tests on port fields outside its port file; its Mac port took 151 files. Agents model the first platform they see.

checks.note: port package list from rule data; ast-grep rules over port paths for a field or parameter named Platform, GOOS or OS and a string literal equal to linux, darwin or windows; a go/analysis analyzer in the companion module counts nil tests on interface-typed port fields outside the capability layer, ratcheted to zero. Plant: a Platform string field in a port struct fails; if m.Services == nil in a command file raises the count. Control: a nil test on a port field inside the capability layer, answered as not on this machine, passes

rules.rule: Every external module and every external program is reached from exactly one adapter package per binary, which declares its binary name, socket, paths, headers, variables and field names, and a test with a shrink-only allow list fails any other importer or caller.
rules.detail: For each binary, one adapter package owns each external module (it alone imports it) and each external program (it alone runs it). Running a program means a name passed to the process-start or path-lookup call, resolved the way the compiler sees it: a literal, a constant, or a variable whose value comes from a constant or from the one adapter; a name from anywhere else counts as unresolved and fails. The adapter declares the program's binary name, socket path, HTTP paths, header names, environment variables and JSON field names, and they appear nowhere else. Names shared between two programs are declared once, in a package both import or in a contract file both check against; a header or path literal in two repos with no shared definition is a finding. The standard library's system-call extension module counts as the standard library. The allow list (module or program to its one package) only shrinks, so a new dependency is one new line and a planted second importer fails.
rules.why: One repo has 41 Go files and 7 site files naming its sibling program outside the adapter, and one finds the sibling's version by searching its help text. A rule that counts only literals lets a program name pass through a variable.

checks.note: a go/packages test per binary: each external module's importers and each process-start or path-lookup call's resolved name (literal, constant or a variable traced to a constant or the owning adapter) compared with the allow list in rule data; unresolved names fail; the allow list only shrinks. Plant: a second package importing an external module fails; a program name passed through a variable from config to the process-start call fails. Control: the same import and call inside the one adapter pass

ast-grep rule, or forbidigo with analyze-types on call arguments, over non-test code outside the sibling's adapter path: string literals equal to a sibling-name list in rule data (binary name, socket path, header and variable names), ratcheted. Plant: a call that spawns the sibling program by name outside the adapter fails. Control: the same call inside the adapter folder passes

rules.rule: A shape crossing a language or program boundary has one source and a consumer-driven contract: the consumer lists the fields it reads, and that list is checked against the provider.
rules.detail: The list is checked against a golden or schema generated from the provider's types. A rename fails and an added provider field passes (a tolerant reader). When a generator lands, the generated type is the list and the check becomes that the generated file is current. The list is derived from the consumer type where possible. It runs when the provider lands, reading the consumer's list. An optional field counts as a miss unless an exception is recorded (66% of the trial list was optional). A list that shrinks without a reason fails, which also catches a shape widened to any. Routes through the consumer's general call path must be on the list, and an empty list on a live consumer fails. Where the consumer is in another language, a generated JSON Schema is the shared file.
rules.why: 193 of one repo's 195 tags and 38 of another's 46 are hand-typed again in TypeScript; names on one side only were 2 and 8. Against the provider the consumer reads 19 routes and 244 fields with 0 required misses and 9 optional ones, none a fault.

rules.rule: Domain modules inside one program import one another only through an interface the calling domain declares, with an independence contract listing the domains as data.
rules.detail: A direct import from one listed domain to another fails, including through the other's public barrel; the allowed route is a file under the caller's ports folder. In the web stack, UI contributed across modules whose host would import upward or sideways goes through a typed slot (home tiles, search providers, shell status, navigation, cache roots, record sections); a direct import is allowed only downward along a declared edge; a dependency marked optional is reached only through slots; typed route links are not imports. Moving the shared piece into a neutral package is the known way round, so a package imported by two domains goes on the review list.
rules.why: A public barrel is a door that the caller did not design and the callee can widen; making the calling side own the shape gives the stricter boundary. It costs more adapters and is weighed against the size of the domains.

checks.note: a dependency-cruiser rule built from a domain list kept as data (not typed per rule) forbids any import between two listed domains except via a file under ports/; typed slots for cross-module UI. Plant: a direct import from one listed domain's barrel into another fails. Control: the same call through a declared port passes

rules.rule: Decision logic is a pure function from values to a decision; the shell reads through ports, calls it and applies the result; functions that take a port and also branch are reported.
rules.detail: Report per module the functions that take a port and also branch. There is no limit.
rules.why: A decision that needs no port shrinks the ports, makes tests need no doubles and stops each decision from growing a store dependency.
rules.review_question: Which function takes a port and also branches, and could its decision be a pure function of values?
open: No plant until built.
rules.note: Plain-value logic is the code an agent can test with no doubles, so it removes a source of fault (an inference). Applies to services with domain logic over a store.

rules.rule: Shared code lives in a small, named set of shared modules with one owner lane, and no other shared module exists.
rules.detail: The set is named in rule data: the shared library modules (for example one for plumbing and one for the terminal look) and any separate private package for design tokens. rules.rule: Every capability that more than one package or program needs is one row in a registry, and the lint bans, the instruction block and the export listing's shared column are rendered from it.
rules.detail: The registry is one file, one row per line, sorted. A row has the capability, the owner package, the export, the shared module's package and export if it has one, the primitives the capability owns, a status (local, shared or later) and the tag since which it is shared. A repository test fails a row whose owner does not exist, a primitive with no rendered ban, a ban with no row, and a shared-module row whose export is not in the pinned tag's package listing. The owner column is held to the owners that the layer table already names, so the two files cannot disagree. A ban nobody can find is not read, and an instruction nobody enforces is not followed; one file is both, and the generator writes the ban rows into the generated part of the lint config and the instruction block into the agents' file. Removing a row narrows a gate, so the registry is a protected path.

rules.detail: The ban is the gate. The shape rule is advice and does not stop a rebuild by itself, because a name search cannot find a copy (copies are called Put, replaceOnce or enqueue). The message names the export to use and old copies stay on a per-file count that only falls. The shape rule has a planted copy under a different name, its known bypasses kept as fixtures (a helper that makes the temp file, a file create call, a root rename, a method-value alias of the rename call, link-then-remove) and its measured rates beside it. Locking, atomic writes, paths and the daemon helper come from the shared module, not a local copy. An export without both halves is planned. A known bypass is a helper in a ban-free package that calls an allowed primitive. In Go the ban rows are not hand-kept: they are generated from the registry of arch.shared.15, one forbidigo or depguard row per primitive with the export in its message, and the exclusion list of each ban is the shrink-only allow list. The bans at adoption are the file-write primitives (rename, temp file, write file, create, open for write) outside the write owners; the digest primitives and the hex encoding of a sum outside the digest owner; the raw stat of a path outside the trust owners; running the version-control program outside its owners; and the golden update flag outside the one golden helper. The shape rule stays advice; the restructured copy it cannot see is made visible by the trailer of agents.discovery.6.
rules.why: 13 hand-written replace-a-file bodies sit outside the owner and 14 production files call flock directly; a name search found none of the copies and a clone detector found 0 clones; the shape rule flagged 1 of 6 planted forms of the atomic write and missed all five restructured copies, so per-export bans are the gate.

checks.note: one forbidigo or depguard ban per primitive outside the owner, generated from the registry of arch.shared.15 with a shrink-only allow list, and one ast-grep 0.51.1 shape rule per export with a planted hit and a clean control; census ratchet. Plant: os.Rename onto a state path fails; a hand-written lock outside the lock package fails. Control: the call through the shared export passes

ESLint no-restricted-imports and no-restricted-syntax generated from the platform export table (primitive banned outside its owner), and ast-grep shape rules per export with planted copies and bypass fixtures, advice only. Plant: a hand-written atomic copy under another name; the ban half fires only on the primitive and the shape half on the renamed copy. Control: the call through the shared export passes

open: The forbidigo half was verified on 5 Nov (selector bans fire on aliases and method forms). Of the 17 exports in the platform list only the write and lock exports have any planted rule today; 0 of 13 web exports have either half.
The ast-grep YAML rules missed cheap restructurings in one trial, so the shape half must carry its bypass fixtures.
The web half is planned; the rule must be written by the person who owns the export.

Proposed until the bans are rendered: the registry and the renderer are step G1 of the shared-code proposal (gragas#513). A ban appears only when its owner exists, so the digest ban comes with step G3 and the write ban with step G4; the bans that already pass land with G1.

rules.rule: Each port and shared package's public surface is listed in one generated file per tag with a stability mark (stable, experimental, internal) on every export, held both ways against the code, and a change to the surface or a mark fails until a reason is recorded.
rules.detail: The listing is regenerated and diffed in the owner repository (for Go, a short doc listing per package); a test that the listing's tag equals the pinned version, and a program reads the listing for the version it pins. A surface is few, typed and closed. Every export carries one mark: stable (kept until a recorded break), experimental (said so at the export site too) or internal (not reachable from outside the package). The register and the code agree both ways: an export with no mark fails, a mark with no export fails, and an internal export reachable from outside fails. For a published web package the surface is its exports map with one subpath per unit, no root barrel on a package with more than one unit, and every entry resolving in the packed tarball. The reason must resolve to a ticket or a second case. Width per part is printed and does not gate because a limit would be a guess. The interface comment is a review question (see code.comments).
rules.why: The shared Go package's surface is 181 lines and 6.9 KB; the list read at the version one repo pins has no UI and no door entry. In the trial, 25 landings in one repo and 11 in another were real port changes. A surface with no stability mark promises everything to every reader; the mark is what lets an experimental export change without a break.

checks.note: a recipe in the shared Makefile fragment: go doc -short listing regenerated per tag and diffed, with a mark column; a test that the listing's tag equals the go.mod version and that every exported name has exactly one mark. Plant: an exported func added without a regenerated listing fails; an export with no mark fails. Control: the regenerated listing with every export marked passes

v1 class our-cli. companion surface: ts-morph 28.0.0 or @microsoft/api-extractor 7.60.1 writes a committed surface file per shared part (exported names, prop names, types and marks); the gate regenerates it and fails when it differs and the change carries no reason (a ticket or decision id in a trailer); publint and are-the-types-wrong run over the packed tarball to prove every exports entry resolves. Plant: adding a prop with no reason fails; an internal export listed in the exports map fails; an exports entry missing from the tarball fails. Control: the same diff with a ticket in the trailer passes

open: The reason is free (nearly every landing names a ticket) so the value is a visible diff, not the judgement. api-extractor is for libraries with declaration files; Astro components need the ts-morph route.
The fingerprint is the reader's inference and the book has no width metric.
rules.note: Shares its engine with the Go listing check and the web surface check.

rules.rule: A new concern lands in exactly one door of a classification table and the change names it; a program cannot grow its own folder for a shared concern.
rules.detail: The doors are an existing module, a new module, a shared package, a design-system part, a generated client, an app-wide concern, a new library and a new check. The change names the door in a trailer. If none fits, the decision record of arch.decisions.2 comes first. The concern table gives one owner per concern. An agent cannot create a plumbing folder in a service, and there is no util or common package.
rules.why: Without a table every agent invents a new place, and shared plumbing grows a private copy in each program.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. commitlint 21.2.4 trailer-exists for a Door trailer at land (body-empty also fires; the rule is machine-read from the commit message) plus the structure check that fails a new plumbing or shared-concern folder in a program; the diff-conditional half (a package file or dependency added needs the trailer) is the land step's check. Plant: a message with no Door trailer exits 1, with one exits 0; a new folder for a shared concern in a service fails. Control: a change with the trailer and a door from the table passes

open: Half the check is commitlint (the message form); the diff condition is ours.
The Go form has no per-change door statement today, only the concern table and the shared-package entry rule.

rules.rule: A fact about a package, an export or a command (what it holds, why it imports what it imports, its stability mark) is written in that thing's own folder, and any central table of such facts is rendered from them.
rules.detail: The fact sits where the thing's own author already edits: what a package holds in its package doc comment, an answer about an import in a file of the package's folder, a mark beside the export or in a per-package file, a command's usage text in the command's own file. The central table, the layer document or the usage page is a generator's output, so a change to one package edits one folder and one generated row. A column of prose in a table that every package change edits is the sign of a fact kept away from its thing. A table row keeps what is true of the layer itself, in one line.
rules.why: Own measure: over three days one layer table was changed in 42 commits, and by changed line the paragraph each package says it holds took 92 lines, more than the lists of what may import what. Each package change edited a prose column that another package change also edited.

sources.says: Build facts about a package live in a build file in that package's own folder, not in one table at the root.
Who owns a directory is a file in that directory, inherited upward.

checks.note: the layer renderer reads each package's doc comment and a test fails a layer-table row that carries a per-package prose field. Plant: a package row with a holds paragraph fails. Control: the same paragraph in the package's doc comment, rendered into the generated table, passes

open: Proposed until the renderer reads package doc comments. That is step 4 of gragas#477 (holds prose moves into package doc comments); it has no tool key to bind to until then.

rules.rule: An extension lands complete in one change: structure, rule, check with its plant, catalogue row, examples and docs.
rules.detail: One change holds the structure (from the generator), the rule rows, each new check with its negative test, the catalogue row, stories and specs, the scope-rules entry, and the rulebook and page update. In Go, growing the foundation is one change record adding the rule, its check, its plant and its grid cell together. A living example per state and a catalogue entry for a part belong to the same change.
rules.why: A rule without its plant or a part without its example is half added, and the half that is missing is the one a reviewer cannot see.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the land check compares the change against the extension checklist (rule row with a check and a plant, a catalogue row, an example, docs) and fails a change that adds one and not the others. Plant: a change adding a rule row without its plant fails. Control: a change adding the row, check, plant and docs passes

open: The checklist check is described by the sources only as one change record; the exact mechanism is to be built.
Some plants and controls of this rule were written at the merge from the sources' description of the check, and have not been run.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Splitting, merging or renaming a module needs a decision, and a move or rename commit changes no behaviour and no baseline count; editing comes in a second commit.
rules.detail: A move commit contains only renames at 100% similarity and import-path and package-clause edits; baseline keys are rewritten and counts left unchanged. A commit that marks itself as a move is checked, other commits are not. A move that lands before any behaviour change is the wanted result.
rules.why: A move mixed with an edit cannot be reviewed as a move, and baselines reset when a rename is not recorded. Not measured in Go; the web rule holds it for the UI.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion move-commit check: a commit whose subject starts with move: may contain only renames at 100% similarity (git diff -M100% --name-status) and import-path and package-clause edits (a diff filter that strips import blocks and package lines leaves empty); other commits are not checked. Plant: a move commit that renames a file and edits a function body fails. Control: a pure rename with updated imports passes

open: Opt-in by the commit subject, so an agent that omits the marker passes; making it automatic needs a rename-detected-with-edit heuristic that fires on legitimate refactors. The must-enforce record asks for detecting a rename with edits from git and blocking until split or answered.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; no fault in our record

rules.rule: A project declares its kind and its one framework and uses the stack the foundation lists for that kind; a package outside the list needs a written exception.
rules.detail: The framework value is read from the project's parameter file. A second framework is refused by the import-side rule in the web part. Which framework per kind follows the foundation's by-kind answer, which is a recommendation: only some project rulings bind their own artefacts.
rules.why: A stack the foundation did not list is a stack nobody maintains; the declared kind is what lets the right pack be applied.

checks.note: companion sync generates the syncpack configuration for the project kind and framework from the stack table; a dependency outside that kind's set is unlisted and fails. Plant: a React dependency in an Astro project fails. Control: the listed Astro set passes

open: Which framework per kind still follows the by-kind recommendation; only the rulings of two projects are ruled, each for itself.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: C for bytes; operator named it

rules.rule: A new module, package or repository names the driver that a folder or namespace cannot meet, because a logical split comes before a physical one.
rules.detail: Before a new package, shared library or repository is created, the change states the driver a folder or namespace inside the existing package cannot meet. A seeded change that creates a package with one importer must be flagged. A required field in the change template can be checked for presence only.
rules.why: Companies reported going back to a coarser split after paying for a physical split they did not need, risking a distributed monolith. New packages are free for an agent to make, so the question has to come from outside.
rules.review_question: What named driver does a folder or namespace fail to meet, so this needs its own package or repository?
open: Review only; a driver-named field in the change template could be checked for presence only.
rules.note: With agents the question has to come from outside (an inference). The new-package case also rides on arch.structure.1.

rules.rule: Things that change together live together, in the same folder shape across a kind of program, and the layout matches the template for that kind.
rules.detail: The folder-shape template for a kind says what folders must exist and which file kinds sit beside which; a missing or extra folder fails. Whether things belong together is judgement; the shape is mechanical. The Go program template is: cmd/<name> for each binary; under internal, core and core/api for the decisions and the operations every client calls; one port package holding the platform interfaces with its fake; slot packages that hold a registry each; adapters under host/<platform> and host/<tool>; door for the network front; config; cli/<group> for commands and cli/ui for terminal output. The import table between these folders is rule data read by the layer test (arch.layers.1), not prose. A new kind of program or a new language adds its own template under the same rule.
rules.why: A census of 20 UI steps found 3 identical and 12 independent; the same shape across a kind is what lets a check and an agent find things. Two Go target designs name the same folders for core, port, adapters and commands, and a template that does not exist (the rule pointed at one) holds nothing.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion shape --kind <kind> compares the tree with the folder-shape template for its declared kind and fails on a missing or extra folder (alternative: eslint-plugin-project-structure 3.14.5 folder-structure). Plant: a feature folder missing its model/ sibling, or a file in the wrong tier of the template, fails. Control: the template shape passes

rules.review_question: Do the things in this folder change together?
open: Built because every rule binds from adoption (decision 19), though the evidence is D; if the operator would rather not build for evidence D this becomes a best practice. Half holds: the shape; belonging together is review.

rules.rule: A package or module is a unit of meaning: no catch-all names such as util, common, helpers, types or misc, and the phrase describing it needs no "and".
rules.detail: The name deny-list holds util and common, the layer-type names helpers, types, models, interfaces and base, and the words other and misc, matched on the whole name. The names adapters, domain and port are the ports model's own and stay off the list. The word "and" in the description stays a review question: Go package names have no word breaks, and a substring match only gives false hits (standin-gate, standdown and ondemand all hit falsely).
rules.why: A run over 190 Go folder names in six repos found one hit, a package named base; the substring test for "and" hit three false names. A catch-all name invites everything.

checks.note: golangci-lint revive rule package-naming (not var-naming, whose package options are deprecated no-ops) with check-extra-bad-name true and user-defined-bad-names listing helpers, types, models, interfaces, base, other, misc; matched on the whole name. Plant: packages named util and helpers each reported by revive package-naming with check-extra-bad-name (run with golangci-lint 2.14.0). Control: a package named lockfile passes

eslint-plugin-check-file 3.3.2 folder-naming-convention with a regex deny-list of layer nouns and catch-alls (util, common, helpers, misc, other, types, models) and ls-lint 2.3.2 for names of non-code files. Plant: a folder named helpers and a file named stuffandthings.ts must each fail. Control: a table-conforming name passes

rules.review_question: Does the phrase describing this package need the word "and"?
open: user-defined-bad-names was not run in the trial; the 'needs the word and' half is review.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; C for the web form (a name lint is cheap and gameable, so the question stays beside it)

rules.rule: A refactor of a path in live use starts only after a merged contract test of what its consumers read, and a refactor that moves code that touches the system (files, processes, the network) behind ports records a transcript of every command's output first, with each step's transcript diff empty.
rules.detail: Before the first refactor commit on a path a consumer reads, a contract test of the fields and answers that consumer reads is merged (arch.ports.7 holds the contract; this rule holds its order). A refactor that moves such code behind ports records, before it starts, the output of every read-only command, the status and health commands and every dry run, and each step of the refactor reruns them and shows an empty diff; a step with a diff is a behaviour change and is split out. The transcripts are committed beside the tests and replaced only by the change that means to change the output.
rules.why: A refactor without a pinned consumer contract finds its breakage in the consumer, after release. A port extraction touches every command at once, and only a recorded transcript shows that nothing a person reads moved.

checks.note: the refactor plan names the contract test and the transcript set; the gate reruns every recorded command and fails on any diff from the committed transcript, and the land review refuses a refactor commit on a live path whose contract test is not already on main. Plant: a refactor step that changes one line of a dry run's output fails the transcript diff. Control: a pure move with every transcript unchanged passes

rules.review_question: Which consumer reads this path, and was its contract test merged before the first refactor commit?
open: The order check (contract test before refactor) is review until the land step can read the plan.

rules.rule: A list that grows by one entry per feature is a folder of one file per entry, joined by a generator and held by gen --check; no feature edits a line another feature owns.
rules.detail: Commands, gate members, planned items, surface marks and the notes an index points at are the usual lists. Adding an entry is a new file, and removing one is a deleted file; the one table the program or a reader needs is rendered from the folder by a generator, sorted by a key in the entries so no order list exists. A cross-cutting rule over the entries ("every entry has two examples") is a test that walks the joined result, not a column each feature edits. A generated join still conflicts as text when two changes add neighbours, and the fix is to run the generator (gates.protection.5). An index is generated too (docs.freshness.1): a person reads it and nobody edits it.
rules.why: Own measure: in one repository a single new command edited a dozen shared files, and the run log of one working day shows each landing sending the queue back through a rebase and a full gate run. Surveyed projects avoid the same by putting each command in its own folder and walking the tree in a test.

checks.note: a repository test that lists each registry folder named in rule data, joins its entries and compares the join with the committed generated file; gen --check holds the file. Plant: a hand-added line in a joined table fails. Control: a new entry file with the join regenerated passes

open: Proposed until a generic folder-join test exists. It is built with the join generator, steps 1 to 3 of gragas#444; the first user is the command folder of cli.commands.29. The count of unresolved checks falls when it lands.

rules.rule: A template per kind lays down configs, scripts and gates, records its answers and version in a file, and a deleted synced file fails the sync check.
rules.detail: One template exists per kind of project. The sync tool writes the version and the source hash to a lock file, so a later update can replay it and so a vendored copy shows where it came from. The tool is one Go command in the same binary as the checks, not an external template engine.
rules.why: A template that does not record its version cannot be updated, and a project that has drifted from it cannot be told apart from one that chose to.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion sync lays down configs, scripts and gates per kind and writes the version and the source hash to a lock file; sync --check compares. Plant: a synced file deleted makes sync --check fail. Control: an untouched synced tree passes

open: Copier is proven for the backend and not for the web; it is a host dependency and was not chosen. Copier, Projen, cruft and template repositories were considered.

rules.rule: A new program, command, package, page, part or surface comes from a generator or golden example, and the gate accepts what it writes.
rules.detail: The generator scaffolds the folder, entry files, registry entry and test stubs, and one reference program is the first file an agent opens. The gate is a self-check that runs the generator into a temporary copy of the repository and then the lint, type check and layer rule over the result, which must pass. Hand-made files are allowed as long as they pass. A hyphenated name is a fixed plant. Come-from-a-generator cannot be forced; the mechanism proves only that the generator's output passes. In Go a scaffold creates a new program, command or package with a thin main and a gate-clean layout.
rules.why: A page generator failed one repo's own gate on a hyphenated page name. There is no Go scaffold or reference program, and an agent copying an old program copies its faults.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion new <page|part|surface> writes from the golden page; a self-check runs the generator into a temp copy and runs lint, type check and the layer rule over it. Plant: generating a page named my-page must produce a tree that passes every gate; a generator edit that breaks the layer rule fails the self-check. Control: the generated tree passes every gate

a test runs the scaffold in a temporary folder and the full gate on its output; the scaffold is a shared template in the shared kit. Plant: a template with a deliberate layer break fails the gate. Control: a clean template passes

open: A hand-written page that also passes is allowed; the web generator has been tried on one page only, and no Go scaffold or reference program exists. The first-file rule for the web side is a separate row owned by the agents part.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: C (the generator failed its own gate on a hyphenated name); practice for Go

rules.rule: The template installer asks exactly three questions (name, version range of the shared package, runtime major) and has no yes or no switches for optional file groups.
rules.detail: Optional file groups are separate kinds, not switches, so two projects of one kind have the same shape. In the ruled Go form the questions become the kind pack and a module path.
rules.why: Each switch doubles the number of shapes a gate must accept.

checks.note: a test of the installer's question list fails when it holds other than three questions or a boolean switch. Plant: a fourth question or a yes or no switch added to the installer fails. Control: the three questions pass

open: The installer is the sync tool of arch.templates.1; the original described a different engine, and the question list may change with the kind pack.
Some plants and controls of this rule were written at the merge from the sources' description of the check, and have not been run.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: On template update, files the repository owns are written once and left alone, managed files are rewritten, and a test checks that no byte-equal file is on the skip list.
rules.detail: The sync tool rewrites managed files and leaves repo-owned local fields; copies that must differ are listed as independent (arch.shared.5). A byte-equal file on the skip list is a managed file that was never updated.
rules.why: An update that overwrites owned files is not used, and one that skips managed files drifts.

checks.note: a test that no byte-equal file is on the skip list, and that an update leaves an owned file's bytes unchanged. Plant: a managed file placed on the skip list fails; an update that rewrites an owned file fails. Control: an update that rewrites managed files only passes

open: Some plants and controls of this rule were written at the merge from the sources' description of the check, and have not been run.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A static Astro project uses no actions and no server islands, because both need on-demand rendering and an adapter.
rules.detail: A test loads the Astro config and fails on an adapter, on an output mode other than static, and on a `src/actions` directory. A lint on `.astro` files fails on a `server:defer` island. A new rendering mode is admitted only with its own pack and a decision.
rules.why: On-demand rendering adds a server and an adapter to a site that was built to be a folder of files. The rule was rated C from the framework's own guides; no site uses either feature yet.

checks.note: a Vitest test that loads astro.config and fails on an adapter, an output other than static or an actions directory, plus ESLint no-restricted-syntax on `server:defer` in `.astro` files. Plant: adding an adapter to the config fails; a `server:defer` island fails; a `src/actions` directory fails. Control: a static config with no adapter and no actions passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: C (the framework's actions and server-islands guides)
rules.note: Static form of the React part's rule that full-stack rendering needs a decision.

rules.rule: The framework generates the script policy, so `script-src` lists hashes and never contains `unsafe-inline`.
rules.detail: The Astro security.csp option is set in the config. A test parses each built page for the policy meta element and fails when `script-src` lacks hashes or holds `unsafe-inline`. Islands stay banned. An unhashed inline script in a template is in no hash list, so the browser refuses it at run time: a loud failure the violation listener catches, not a bypass.
rules.why: A policy that allows inline scripts gives no protection against injected ones. The option was tried on one framework version: four pages built, a policy meta element on the two counted, no script on the plain page and two inline scripts on an island page.

checks.note: v1 class framework. Astro security.csp in the config, read back, and a test that parses each built page for the policy meta element and checks script-src. Plant: the config with security.csp removed fails the built-page parse. Control: the build with the option set passes

open: Trialled on one Astro version; a newer one was out when the source was read and its behaviour is a source read, not run.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: C; trialled on four pages
rules.note: The Astro form of the web part's script-policy rule.

rules.rule: Content a page reads at build time has a schema, and a bad entry fails the build.
rules.detail: Each collection is declared with a collection definition and a zod schema. An entry that is missing a required field, or has a wrong type such as a date, fails `astro build`. The build itself refuses; there is no separate check, and the plant is run once to prove it.
rules.why: Content errors found after deploy are published errors. The rule is rated C from the framework guide; no site uses collections yet.

checks.note: v1 class framework. `defineCollection({ schema })` with a zod schema; `astro build` fails on a schema error. Plant: a content entry with a wrong date type fails `astro build`. Control: a valid entry builds

open: No site uses collections yet; vacuous today.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: C (the framework's content-collections guide)

rules.rule: In an Astro project the inline-script attribute is used only where exempt, and style blocks are linted.
rules.detail: (a) ESLint no-restricted-syntax on the `is:inline` attribute in `.astro` files, through the Astro parser, with a path exemption list. (b) Stylelint with the HTML parser lints `<style>` blocks in `.astro` files with the same rule set as other styles, so a colour literal there fails.
rules.why: Neither hole had a row in the stack list (evidence D). Under the generated script policy an unhashed inline script fails loudly at run time, so the lint is a convenience as well as a net.

checks.note: ESLint no-restricted-syntax on the `is:inline` attribute in `.astro` (astro-eslint-parser) with a path exemption list, and Stylelint with postcss-html for `<style>` blocks (ESLint-only: the Astro parser has no Biome form). Plant: a `<script is:inline>` outside the exemption list fails; a hex colour inside `<style>` in an `.astro` file fails. Control: a hashed module script and a token-based style block pass

open: The attribute selector fired only once written for the namespaced-name node kind; a selector on the plain name matched nothing.
The path-exemption list was not planted.
A donor's earlier text rule for the same hole was unproven (its own self cases did not run in its gate).

rules.rule: No grant uses a wildcard action or a wildcard resource, and a gate that bans wildcards runs in every service.
rules.detail: The gate scans the infrastructure code and the rendered policies for a star in an action or resource position. Allow lists elsewhere (modules, callers) also name entries and a wildcard fails there. In Go, the CI token is read-only and scoped, the daemon callers are checked, and the sandbox comes from a template.
rules.why: A wildcard grant turns any compromise or bug in one function into access to everything the account holds.

checks.note: ast-grep rule over the infrastructure code failing a star ("*") in an action or resource of any policy statement, run in every service gate. Plant: a policy statement with action star or resource star fails. Control: a statement naming exact actions and a resource passes
a test that the CI token is read-only and scoped and that a unit sandbox comes from the template. Plant: a CI token with write scope fails. Control: a read-only scoped token passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Event publishing, invoke and database-connect grants exist only on the declared path: publish only on the shared bus, invoke only through the one internal invoke grant, and runtime database connect only for the service own application role.
rules.why: These three grants are how a unit reaches other services and the data; each must come from one declared place so a reader sees every door a unit has.

checks.note: ast-grep rules over the infrastructure code: a publish grant naming a bus other than the shared bus, an execute-api:Invoke grant not built by the internalInvokeGrant helper, and an rds-db:connect grant for any role but the unit application role (<svc>_app). Plant: a function granted publish on an arbitrary bus fails; a handwritten invoke permission fails; a connect grant for the owner role fails. Control: grants through the declared helpers pass

open: The three exact grant shapes are named from the reference estate and need translating to each product shared constructs.

rules.rule: Concurrency caps come from shared defaults: none in development, none by default in the shared components, and a cap is never used as a queue throttle.
rules.detail: In Go, a daemon bounds its work with request, concurrency and queue caps from one unit template. A queue consumer that needs a ceiling sets the queue maximum concurrency instead; see the consumer rule for outside APIs.
rules.why: A reserved-concurrency cap used to throttle a queue starves the function other triggers need and hides the real limit.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a reserved-concurrency setting outside the shared component defaults and any in the development stage, and a rule on a cap paired with a queue source. Plant: a reserved concurrency on a queue-triggered function fails. Control: a queue maximum concurrency on the event source passes

rules.rule: State-bearing resources are retained on delete.
rules.detail: A resource that holds data that cannot be rebuilt (a database, a bucket with content, a queue holding work) carries a retain-on-delete policy so removing the stack does not remove the data. In Go, a store says whether it can be rebuilt, and state that cannot be rebuilt is append-only and kept; removal keeps user state.
rules.why: Deleting a stack that owns data deletes the data; one command removes it with no recovery.

checks.note: ast-grep rule over the infrastructure code failing a database table, bucket or queue construct without the retain-on-delete setting. Plant: a table declared without retention fails. Control: a table with retention passes

open: In Go, keeping user state on removal or uninstall is a gap with no row yet.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: The retention of imported identity, IAM and DNS resources is the SST rule imported-resources-retained.

rules.rule: Every storage bucket blocks public access (all four flags) and is encrypted at rest, set by the shared component, with no component option that can turn either off.
rules.detail: In Go, a secret is written with its final mode in a private folder and peer credentials are checked. Hosting posture for a static site (public access, encryption at rest) is a gap with no row yet.
rules.why: A public or unencrypted bucket is a data leak by default; removing the choice removes the mistake.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a raw bucket construct, and a unit test of the shared bucket component asserting all four blocks and encryption are always set and no option disables them. Plant: a bucket built without the component fails; a component option that turns public access on fails. Control: the component bucket passes
