rules.rule: A command that writes takes one of two declared forms: it needs an explicit --apply and its dry run writes nothing and ends by naming the apply command, or it writes only into a reviewable draft that a later, separate act makes effective. Its help says which form it has, and the list of writing commands and their form comes from the code, not from a typed list.
rules.detail: A command registry (a walk of the command tree) carries a mutates annotation with the form (apply or draft) set by the command author. The matrix enumerates every command from the tree and runs those without the annotation expecting no write (tree hash equal before and after); an apply-form command run without --apply must leave the hash equal and end by naming the apply command; a draft-form command run once must change nothing a reader of the effective state sees until the separate act runs. A command with no declared form, or with both, fails. A repo-check analyser reports a command that calls a write helper and has no annotation. The reachability half is approximate (call graph through function values); the hash test is the real catch. The help golden must show the form line.
rules.why: Own bugs: a dry run that wrote (9 of 60 sampled bugs in the output-truth class). The goal is that nothing changes without a person seeing the change first: for a tool that edits a machine the dry run is the only way to show it, and for a store with change sets the draft is the dry run, so a second mode there would be code with no reader. Declaring the form per command keeps the matrix test and the help honest.

unless.reason: It has no commands.

checks.note: command registry from the cobra tree walk with a mutates annotation naming the form; matrix hash test per form; go/analysis analyser for a mutating call reachable from a command with no annotation. Plant: an apply-form command that writes in its dry-run path fails the hash test; a draft-form command whose first run changes the effective state fails; an unannotated command calling the write helper is reported. Control: a command annotated mutates with an --apply gate passes, and a draft-form command whose write lands only in the draft passes

open: The registry mutates field and the shared write helper are proposed, not built.

rules.rule: A mistyped command or flag prints the nearest match and the line to type, on stderr, with empty stdout and the usage exit code.
rules.why: Own measure; the command framework supplies suggestions and the test proves they are on. One program prints its version line on stdout after a typo.

checks.note: matrix test with a mistyped command and flag at edit distance one, asserting the nearest name and a usage line on stderr, exit 2 and empty stdout. Plant: a root with suggestions disabled fails. Control: the default passes

rules.rule: A flag has one meaning everywhere: the same name has the same type and shorthand in every command, and one concept has one spelling. Flags are long, lowercase and hyphenated, with short forms only from one short shared list; a closed-set flag lists its accepted values in help and is checked once against them; and a duration or a size is a string with a unit, in flags, config keys and JSON alike, never a bare number.
rules.detail: A helper walks the command tree, groups flags by name and fails when type, shorthand or value kind differ, or two spellings of one concept exist (a list in rule data, such as dry-run and dryrun, json and output-json). It fails a flag name that is not lowercase and hyphenated and a short form not on the shared list (the base list holds -w and -f; a program adds to it only through rule data with a reason). A closed-set flag declares its set once; the parser checks the value against it before the command runs, and the help golden shows the set. A duration or size flag, config key or JSON field is typed as a duration or size and decoded from a string with a unit (15s, 2m, 64KiB); a bare integer is refused at parse time.
rules.why: Own measure; the check proves name and type consistency, same meaning is judgement. A unit on every duration and size stops the oldest config bug (is 15 seconds or minutes), and a short-form list keeps an agent's flags readable.

checks.note: flag matrix helper in the shared test package walking the cobra tree, plus a decode test of the shared duration and size types. Plant: --out as a string in one command and a bool in another fails; a -t short form not on the list fails; a --timeout flag of integer type fails; a closed-set flag given a value outside its set runs the command and fails. Control: consistent long flags with unit strings and a declared set pass

rules.rule: A bare command never hangs: at a terminal it offers a menu of what will work on this machine, off a terminal it prints help and exits with the usage code.
rules.why: Operator rule. Off a terminal a bare call did not do what was asked, so it is a usage outcome and a script can see it. One piped half ran in an earlier trial; the pty half needs a pseudo-terminal helper.

checks.note: pty test (a pseudo-terminal library) starting the binary bare and reading the menu within 2 seconds; bare run with stdin from a pipe asserting help text and exit 2 inside 2 seconds, a timeout kill being a failure. Plant: a bare command that blocks on a stdin read fails the 2-second timeout, and one that prints help and exits 0 fails. Control: a command printing help and exiting 2 when stdin is not a terminal passes

open: The script-test tool's terminal commands do not attach a terminal to stdout, so the menu half needs the pty library (MIT, tagged Oct 2024, pushed 2026).

rules.rule: Work that takes more than 2 seconds shows progress at a terminal and plain lines in a log; a progress line redraws only when the work advances, never on a timer of its own; and a person never waits on a silent screen.
rules.detail: No spinner or bar ticks on its own clock: a redraw follows a work event (an item done, bytes read). Off a terminal the progress is a plain line at most once a minute, and under --json there is no progress on stdout. The test counts redraws against work events with a fake clock that never advances.
rules.why: Operator ruling 4 Nov, practice. A self-ticking redraw wakes the machine for nothing and hides a stall behind motion. Slow steps in the real program are found only if fixtures can slow them.

checks.note: pty test with a slowed fake step (3 s through the fixture); at a pty a progress line within 2 seconds, piped plain lines with no carriage-return spinner bytes; a redraw counter compared with the work events of the fake step, with the clock frozen. Plant: a 3-second step with no output fails the silence check, and a spinner that redraws with no work event fails the redraw count. Control: a step with a progress call per work event passes

open: A program-wide silence watcher is the same test on the real binary.

rules.rule: Every run reads the same way: a heading, what it reads, the work, a dry-run footer when nothing was written, one closing word; the banner shows only in the interactive menu.
rules.detail: The banner is the menu's alone; a command run, --version and --help never print it. Once lessons exist (cli.commands.18) the run also carries a two to four line why from the lesson with a more: pointer on a dry run, and after a write the commands a person can run to check the result without the program; that part binds with cli.commands.18.
rules.why: Operator rule; whether the run reads well is review (cli.commands.16). The banner on every run was a contradiction with the target programs, which show it in the menu only.

checks.note: terminal-test golden per leaf command, plain and role-tagged, with a last-line assertion (a regexp on the last non-empty line against the closing-word list from the shared exit package) and an assertion that no leaf output holds the banner. Plant: a command that ends without a closing word fails the last-line assertion, and a leaf command that prints the banner fails. Control: a frame-compliant command passes

open: The closing-word and dry-run-footer rules are cli.look.5 and cli.look.6.

rules.rule: The main journeys of a CLI (first run, help, menu, one happy path, one refusal) run under a pty at 80 columns as goldens the gate cannot rewrite, and at 60 and 40 columns held to properties against them (tests.journeys.8).
rules.why: Operator rule; scoped by the journey rules of the tests part. A phone over ssh is 40 to 60 columns.

checks.note: pseudo-terminal library plus a terminal emulator package; goldens at 80 columns on the protected-path list, and the properties of tests.journeys.8 at 60 and 40 against them. Plant: a help line wider than 40 columns fails the width property at 40. Control: wrapped help passes

open: Whether the script-test tool can drive a pty is unverified; its docs say the terminal is not attached to stdout or stderr, so a full-screen journey needs the pty library and the emulator package (tagless).
go-internal testscript has ttyin and ttyout commands (source: its doc.go), but its doc says the terminal is not attached to stdout or stderr; whether v1.16.0 has full pty support is unverified.

rules.rule: A new or changed command or menu shows its terminal transcript in the change, and a reviewer judges it.
rules.why: No tool decides that an experience is good.
rules.review_question: Does this change's terminal transcript show an experience a user would find clear, and is it attached?
open: Promotion needs a record paired with a review question that checks its content; the path rule (a command change must change its transcript file) is presence only and is a rule on its own.
Land refuses a changed command with no transcript; the script-test tool can generate it.

rules.rule: The plan a dry run prints and the plan a read answer carries come from one function, a test holds them equal, and no write route or write command takes a dry-run parameter.
rules.detail: The dry-run sentence of a writing command is the plan field of the matching read (CLI --json and API answer). A test runs the dry run and the read on one fixture and compares the plan text byte for byte. A route that writes refuses a dry, dry_run or preview parameter, and an API contract check fails on one.
rules.why: Two code paths for one plan drift: the dry run says one thing and the page another. One function makes the preview a person sees in the terminal and on a page the same fact.

unless.reason: It has no commands or routes.

checks.note: shared test comparing each writing command's dry-run plan with the plan field of its read answer on one fixture, plus a route-contract check for a dry-run parameter on a write route. Plant: a dry run whose sentence is built separately from the read's plan and differs by one word fails; a write route with a dry query parameter fails. Control: both taken from the one plan function pass

rules.rule: Every command that changes the machine has a lesson beside its code with fixed sections, every lesson cites at least one https source read before it went in, --explain prints the lesson before any command runs and writes nothing even with --apply, and a run shows the lesson's why and its check-it-yourself lines.
rules.detail: The fixed sections are: what it is, what was found here, why, what it does, what it does not do, how to undo it or that there is nothing to undo, check it yourself, read more, sources. A test fails on a missing or empty section and on a lesson with no https source. --explain is a shared root flag answered before any command runs; it writes nothing even beside --apply, and a command with no lesson says so in one line rather than printing nothing. A dry run opens on two to four lines of why from the lesson and a more: pointer; an applied run ends, before its closing word, on the commands a person can run to check the result without the program. The same lesson prints from help <topic> and is the source of any generated guide (cli.commands.20).
rules.why: A tool that changes somebody's machine and cannot say what it found, why it acts, how to undo it and where the claim comes from is a tool a person stops trusting. Fixed sections make the lesson generatable and testable, and the sources are the one defence against an agent inventing a tuning.

checks.note: shared lesson test over every command with the mutates annotation (sections present and non-empty, an https source), a matrix test of --explain with --apply asserting no write, and run goldens holding the why and check lines. Plant: a lesson with an empty undo section fails; a lesson with no https source fails; --explain --apply that writes fails the hash test. Control: a complete lesson with one https source passes

open: Binds once the shared lesson generator and its test are built in gragas (R-15 sequencing); until then planned.
--explain joins the shared flags of cli.output.5 when this rule binds.

rules.rule: Every piece setup installs and every way a feature can fail quietly has a doctor line that names the fix when it is missing or wrong, and each subject the program manages has a help topic naming its sources.
rules.detail: Setup declares what it installs in data; a test fails when an installed piece has no doctor check, and when a doctor finding that is not ok has no fix line. Each subject (a managed file, service or setting group) has a help topic, and the topic lists the sources of its lesson.
rules.why: A feature that fails quietly is found by its owner months later; a doctor line per piece is the cheapest place to see it, and the fix line turns a finding into a step.

checks.note: shared test comparing setup's install list with the doctor check list, a fix-line assertion on every non-ok finding, and a topic-per-subject check. Plant: a setup step with no doctor check fails, and a doctor warning with no fix line fails. Control: every installed piece checked with a fix line passes

open: Binds once the shared lesson generator and its test are built in gragas (R-15 sequencing); until then planned.

rules.rule: A command is safe to run twice: the second run changes nothing, or says it has nothing to do.
rules.why: Own measure; shares the fixtures and helper of cli.commands.1, so no extra build. Not measured in Go.

checks.note: matrix test running each mutating command with --apply twice on a fixture and comparing the tree hash after the second run with the first; exit is 0 or the documented nothing-to-do outcome. Plant: a command that appends a line on every run fails. Control: an idempotent write passes

rules.rule: Every command is declared once, in its own package; one registry is assembled from those declarations at build time; and help, help --json, the README's command table, the MCP tool list, the HTTP contract and agent skill text are generated from that registry and held equal by a test.
rules.detail: A declaration carries the summary, the version the command arrived in, what a second run does, and who may run it; a command not yet built is declared in a file of the planned folder instead (cli.commands.9), and the registry joins both. The join of the built packages is generated and held by gen --check (cli.commands.29). help --json describes every command, flag, positional word, exit code and --json field so a UI can be built from it, and is the committed command-tree file of cli.output.4. Generated files say they are generated and are refused when edited by hand (cli.commands.23). A test regenerates every surface and fails on any difference from the committed copy.
rules.why: A command described once and rendered everywhere cannot drift: the agent's skill, the MCP tool and the README are the program because they come from it. All three target programs already generate at least two surfaces from one source.

unless.reason: It has no commands.

sources.says: Each command is built in its own package and the root adds them; no table of the commands sits in one place apart from that join.
The list of commands is data beside the code that runs them.
The command documents are generated from the command tree by a program of the repository's own.

checks.note: shared registry generator with a regenerate-and-compare test over help, help --json, the README table, the MCP tool list, the HTTP contract and the skill text. Plant: a README table row edited by hand fails, and a command added to the tree without a registry entry fails. Control: all surfaces regenerated from the registry pass

open: Binds once the shared registry generator and its test are built in gragas (R-15 sequencing); until then planned.
Reworded on 8 Nov 2026 (A69): the registry is assembled from per-command declarations instead of typed as one table. The rule keeps its id and its status.

rules.rule: A change that can lock the owner out refuses until the new access path is seen to carry an admin, keeps a whole-file undo, and a change to shared network or identity policy that reaches other devices is printed for the owner to apply, never applied by the program.
rules.detail: A lock-out change is one to access control, sign-in, the path a person reaches the machine by, or the identity source. Before writing, the command observes an admin session over the new path (seen recently, within a stated window); without it the command refuses and says what it did not see. It keeps the whole previous file and prints the one line that restores it. A policy that also binds other devices (a tailnet policy, a shared directory) is printed as the change to make, and the program holds no write credential for it.
rules.why: The one change a person cannot undo from outside is the one that removes their way in; a refusal before the write is the only guard that works after it.

unless.reason: It changes no access of its own.

checks.note: test per command annotated as lock-out with a fake access observer reporting no admin on the new path, asserting refusal, no write and a kept whole-file copy on the allowed path; a review of any credential that can write shared policy. Plant: an access switch applied while the observer saw no admin over the new path fails. Control: the switch refusing with what it did not see passes

rules.rule: A writing step reads the machine again after it runs and reports done only when the goal state holds, whatever its commands exited with; a config write is verified on a reloaded copy against the intended change before it replaces the original; and an action that asks another machine is reported by the outcome read back within a stated wait, failed with what was seen otherwise, never as sent or will retry.
rules.detail: The first failed step stops the steps after it. A config write changes only the named table, keeps the rest byte for byte, reloads the result on a copy and refuses unless it equals the old config plus the stated change. An effect that is only a request (a packet, a message to a peer) has one attempt; success is its observed result. A test per writing command plants a step whose command exits 0 but leaves the state wrong.
rules.why: Exit 0 is a claim about a command, not about the machine, and a tool that says done when the state is wrong is worse than one that says nothing. Reading back is cheap, and it is the same check the lesson prints for a person (cli.commands.18).

unless.reason: It writes nothing of its own.

checks.note: shared step helper whose result is a read-back, plus a matrix test per writing command with a fake that exits 0 and leaves the state wrong, and a config-write test with a planted extra change. Plant: a step reported done after its command exited 0 with the goal state unmet fails; a config write that also reorders an untouched table fails the reload comparison. Control: a step that reads back the goal state passes

rules.rule: A command writes every file aside, flushes it, renames it into place and flushes its folder, keeping the old mode and owner; it edits a person-written config only in the lines it owns and keeps comments and order; a change to a file another program ships goes in that program's override or drop-in; and a generated file is marked, refused when edited by hand, and regenerated to resolve a merge conflict.
rules.detail: All file writes go through one shared write helper (a link is written where it points, not replaced). A config edit is a parsed, comment-keeping edit of the owned keys; a test round-trips a commented fixture. A vendor file (a file another package or program installs) is never written; the change goes in the override file or drop-in folder that program reads. A generated file carries a do-not-edit header naming the command that writes it; a check regenerates it and fails on a difference, and a merge conflict in it is resolved by running the command again after the rebase.
rules.why: A half-written config after a power cut and a vendor file overwritten by an update are the two oldest ways a tool breaks a machine; two target programs wrote the same guard. The generated-file half stops a merge from silently un-generating a file.

unless.reason: It writes no files of its own.

checks.note: forbidigo with type analysis on os.WriteFile, os.Create and os.OpenFile with a write flag outside the shared write helper; a comment round-trip test of the config editor; a regenerate-and-compare check on files with the generated header. Plant: os.WriteFile on a config path in a command package fails; a config edit that drops a comment fails the round-trip; a hand-edited generated file fails the compare. Control: a write through the shared helper and an untouched generated file pass

open: The state-file half overlaps store.state-files.2, which holds the atomic write for state files.

rules.rule: Every record a program keeps (run, backup, notification, manifest) carries a version and the same fixed fields whoever did the work, backend detail sits under one passed-through field, and answers are built from the record, never from the tool.
rules.detail: Each record kind has one schema with a version field; the backend that did the work fills the fixed fields and puts anything of its own under one detail field the program never branches on. A status or history answer reads records only; a test runs it with the backend tool absent and expects the same answer.
rules.why: A versioned record with fixed fields is what lets a record written by one backend be read after that backend is replaced.

unless.reason: It keeps no records.

checks.note: schema test per record kind (version and fixed fields present, backend detail only under the one field) plus an answer test with the backend tool absent: an empty PATH (built with filepath.ListSeparator) and the program run through proc.Run. Plant: a record missing its version fails; a history answer that calls the backend tool fails with the tool absent. Control: a record with fixed fields and an answer built from records pass

rules.rule: A run record keeps each changed file's copy and its digest after the run; undo refuses when a file no longer has that digest and names the runs that changed it since; a multi-file undo prints its way back rather than running it; and a batch of independent changes keeps one record and one undo per unit, takes the lock per unit and goes on past a failed unit.
rules.detail: The way back may be a kept timestamped backup and the printed lines that restore it, with no undo command. A batch runs each unit as its own run in turn; one failed unit is reported and the rest still run.
rules.why: The digest check is the difference between an undo and a second accident, and per-unit records keep one bad item from blocking or tangling the rest.

unless.reason: It keeps no run records.

checks.note: undo test that edits a file after a run and asserts undo refuses naming the later run; batch test with one planted failing unit asserting the others ran with their own records. Plant: an undo that restores over a file changed since the run fails; a batch that stops at its first failed unit fails. Control: an undo on an unchanged digest passes, and a batch that records each unit passes

rules.rule: Commands follow [group] verb [noun], with verbs from one shared base list of plain imperatives that a program extends only by declaring its domain verbs in its own single table; each verb has one documented meaning across the tool; ids and names are positional and every other input is a flag.
rules.detail: The shared base list holds the verbs users of common tools already know (for example list, show, add, remove, start, stop, run, logs, status, doctor, help, version); get, make and destroy are refused as command names. A program's domain verbs sit in one table in its own code with a meaning each; no second table exists. A test reads the base list and the program's table against the command tree and fails on a verb in neither, on a verb used with two meanings, and on a positional that is not an id or a name.
rules.why: A shared verb list lets an agent that learned one program drive another without reading its help; the base plus one declared table keeps the list extendable without each program inventing synonyms.

checks.note: grammar test in the shared test package reading the base verb list and the program's verb table against the cobra tree walk. Plant: a command named get fails; a verb in neither the base list nor the program table fails; a second verb table in the program fails. Control: a tree whose verbs come from the base list and the one table passes

rules.rule: A command needing root is registered apart from owner-level ones, and which group a command sits in follows whether it needs root, never the name of the operating system.
rules.detail: Proposed with the privileged-helper design. A test would read the command tree and fail on a root command in the owner group or on a group split chosen by operating system.
rules.why: Privilege is the boundary that matters to a person deciding what to run; an operating-system split puts a root action beside an owner one on the next platform.

checks.note: command-tree test reading a needs-root annotation against the registered group. Plant: a command annotated needs-root registered in the owner group fails. Control: root commands in their own group pass

open: Promoted when part 1 of the daemon's access design merges; the root helper of part 2 is daemon.access.8.

rules.rule: A restore writes into a fresh folder the program makes (owner-only, not existing before, no link, not a served or published folder) and refuses an existing path, a link and a served folder; an in-place restore needs its own flag with a dry run listing every file it replaces; and a restore stops before writing when space is low.
rules.detail: The fresh folder is made with mode 0700 by the program's own account (root for a system service). The space check compares the backup's size with the free space of the target and stops with the numbers. The in-place flag is separate from --apply and its dry run lists every path it would replace.
rules.why: The fresh-folder default is what makes a restore safe to run by reflex; a restore over live data is the one backup action that can destroy what it was meant to save.

unless.reason: It restores nothing.

checks.note: restore test with an existing target, a link target, a served folder and a low-space fake, each expecting refusal and no write; an in-place dry-run golden listing every file. Plant: a restore that writes into an existing folder fails; a restore through a link fails. Control: a restore into a new folder it made passes

open: The scheduled backup behind an interface is daemon.backups.1; backup before migrating is postgres.migrations.5.

rules.rule: Each command family is one package that declares its own row (name, order, summary, two examples, exit words, JSON kind, files written, menu place) next to its command; the root holds no list of commands and reads a generated join; no init function registers a command.
rules.detail: A group of verbs that share a context and a plan screen is one package with a file per verb, not a package per verb. The row is a typed value in the package, exported with the function that builds the command; a package that exports one and not the other does not compile into the join. Order is the command's place in the spec's table and is unique; a command the spec does not name takes a high number and sorts by name. The menu place says which screen leads with the command and at what rank, so no list of leads exists in the root. A generator writes the join from the folders of command packages, sorted by name, and gen --check fails when it is stale. A test walks the joined registry for the cross-cutting rules (two examples, exit words, unique order) instead of a column each builder edits. A command package never sets a run hook that the root owns (the persistent pre-run and post-run, with or without the error return): a package that sets its own replaces the root's, which silently skips the shared refusals and the write claim, and with a join per package no shared line is left to catch it. The registry test walks the joined tree and fails on any command that sets one. A command decided and not built is a file of the planned folder (cli.commands.9).
rules.why: Own measure: in one program every new command edited the registry table, the root help block, the menu lists, four cross-cutting goldens, the README table and two generated command documents, so two builders on two commands collided on the same lines. The fleet's run log of 8 Nov 2026 shows each landing sending the waiting candidates through a rebase and a full gate run. Surveyed command line programs keep a command's code and help in the command's own package, and all but one keep the join by hand; the one that does not registers from init functions, which breaks arch.ports.12 and go.layout.2.

unless.reason: It has no commands.

sources.says: Cross-cutting command rules (examples, help text) are tests that walk the joined tree, not columns each command edits.
The one surveyed program that registers commands from init functions through blank imports.

checks.note: a registry test over the joined tree: every built command has a row with a unique order, two examples and exit words; a name is in the built join or in the planned folder, never both and never neither; gen --check fails on a stale join. Plant: two commands with one order fail; a package that registers itself from an init function fails (go.layout.2); a hand-edited join fails gen --check. Control: the same tree with the join regenerated passes

open: Proposed until the registry test and the join generator exist in gragas. They are built in steps 1 to 3 of gragas#444 (layer patterns, the kit, the join generator and one pilot); the planned folder is step 5. It has no tool key to bind to until then, and the count of unresolved checks falls as they land.
The check for the run-hook clause (a command package never sets a run hook the root owns) lands with the registry test in step 3 of gragas#444 (PR 463).
cli.commands.26 says a program's domain verbs sit in one table; with a row per package the table is assembled from the rows. The wording of that rule is for the rulebook's next pass.

rules.rule: A command serialises its writes through the store's own concurrency (a transaction, an advisory lock or a file lock, declared once per store) taken before its first write, keeps a run record that can be undone, and a destructive step needs the thing's own name, typed at a terminal or given as --confirm NAME without one, which a blanket --yes never answers.
rules.detail: Each store declares its one mechanism in rule data: a database's transaction, an advisory lock, or a kernel file lock through the platform's lock package for a file tree. A two-process test runs a writing command in a child holding the mechanism and starts a second: it must exit with the busy code (or the store must serialise the two with neither write lost), and the first run must be unharmed. An analyser asserts that every command with the mutates annotation acquires the declared mechanism before its first write helper. After a write a run record exists and undo restores the tree hash (record shape and undo discipline: cli.commands.24 and 25). A destructive step is one that removes data the program cannot fetch again (a drive formatted, a store or an owner's file deleted); it carries a destructive annotation. At a terminal it asks for the thing's own name typed out; without a terminal the only answer is --confirm NAME with that exact name. --yes answers only plain yes/no questions (cli.environment.8) and never a destructive step, and no other flag or environment variable answers it. A test drives each destructive command with --apply --yes and no --confirm and expects the refused code, and with a wrong name and expects the refused code.
rules.why: Own bugs: state and concurrency, 5 of 60 sampled. The invariant is that two writers never interleave, and a database transaction holds it better than a file lock beside the database, so the mechanism is the store's. A typed name is the one confirmation an agent cannot answer by reflex; two target programs chose the same shape independently.

unless.reason: It has no commands.

checks.note: two-process test plus a go/analysis check that every command with the mutates annotation acquires the store's declared mechanism before its first write helper; run-record and undo assertions; a destructive-annotation matrix test over --yes, a missing --confirm and a wrong name. Plant: a mutating command that skips the lock lets a second writer succeed and fails the test; a destructive command that runs on --apply --yes alone fails. Control: a command taking the lock gives the second writer the busy exit code, and a destructive command run with --confirm and its exact name passes

rules.rule: Writes stay inside the scope the command names.
rules.detail: Only containment is mechanical: command tests run under a write sandbox with home, XDG folders, temp folder and working directory all inside one scratch root, and any write outside the root fails. Scope the command names is not machine readable. The test also takes a file-system snapshot (a hash of the whole parent of the scratch root) before and after, so a write the sandbox does not deny is still seen; this needs no strace-less tracing.
rules.why: Own bugs: 2 of 60 sampled bugs were a write beyond the command's scope.

checks.note: scratch-root test: the matrix runs each mutating command with every home variable inside one temp root under go-proc's sandbox that denies writes outside it; where the system gives no such block the run is refused by name (sandbox.ErrNoBlock), never made unblocked. Plant: a command that also writes to the user cache folder is denied and the test fails. Control: a command writing only under the root passes

open: Apple's sandbox-exec is deprecated and was not run for this; neither sandbox form was tried.
Proposed split: scope (judgement) from root containment (mechanical).
v1 evidence, not yet a source: own bugs (2 of 60)

rules.rule: A binary never rewrites shared state, and it installs or upgrades by rename, a daemon included; uninstall and removal keep user state unless told otherwise, and a test proves it.
rules.detail: An explicit purge flag is fine. A script test runs install, write, uninstall and looks for the data. Reverting an install is the rollback rule of the supply part.
rules.why: Own bugs. One repo has an install-is-a-rename test; the shared test is proposed.

unless.reason: It installs nothing.

checks.note: install-is-a-rename test (exists in one repo) plus a script test of install, write, uninstall and an assertion that the state remains; shared install helper. Plant: an uninstall that removes the state folder fails. Control: an uninstall that keeps state passes

rules.rule: An operation whose goal state already holds returns success, defined in the callee and documented (delete, stop, close, release, ensure); no caller needs the information.
rules.detail: This defines away operation semantics, never untrusted input or a typo, so the swallowed-error and exit rules stand. Each site that tolerates a not-exist error is counted per package and printed at land, so swallowing dressed as this form shows as drift. Review: does any caller need to know this state was already reached, and is the rule stated on the callee? The analyser requires a double-call test for Delete, Stop, Close, Release and Ensure methods, using one helper. The tolerated sites counted are errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist), errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) and os.IsNotExist.
rules.why: Practice. A count that only falls would punish legitimate idempotent deletes, so there is no number.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. analyser requiring a double-call test for Delete, Stop, Close, Release and Ensure methods through one helper, plus an ast-grep count of not-exist tolerance sites printed at land. Plant: a Delete method with no double-call test fails. Control: a method with a double-call test passes

rules.review_question: Does any caller need to know this state was already reached, and is the rule stated on the callee?
open: The count is a report with no plant.

rules.rule: A multi-step operation that changes more than one thing says which of three it is: it rolls back, it resumes from a mark, or it is documented as having no rollback. A command that changes the machine only for the length of its run has a test that the change is undone after an error, an interrupt and a panic.
rules.detail: Which of the three a multi-step operation is stays review. The temporary-change half is mechanical: a command annotated as changing the machine for its run (an app paused, a service stopped, a setting lowered) is driven by a test three times, once with a planted error in the middle, once with an interrupt sent mid-run (testenv.Binary.Start, then Running.Interrupt, Kill and Wait), and once with a planted panic; after each, the machine fixture must equal its state before the run. No workflow engine is adopted without a decision entry; the module allow file (S-2) refuses a workflow-engine module (temporal, cadence, argo) unless a decision entry is linked.
rules.why: Practice. Which of the three outcomes a function has is semantic, but what is undone after a failure is a fact a test can see, and it is what keeps a program safe to interrupt for its whole life.

unless.reason: It changes no machine of its own.

checks.note: shared undo test helper driving each command annotated as temporary through an error, an interrupt and a panic and comparing the machine fixture with its state before the run. Plant: a command that pauses an app and resumes it only on the happy path fails the panic case. Control: a command that resumes in a deferred step on every path passes

rules.review_question: Which of the three outcomes does this multi-step operation have, and is it tagged?
open: Candidate form for the three-way half: an analyser finds functions with two or more writes through a port, a required tag says which of the three, a model checks the tag.

rules.rule: Help is true and complete: every flag in the documents is registered and tested; every command's help has a one-line summary, usage, flags, two examples and what it writes; help has topics as well as commands; and every pointer in help or in a warning is in one form and resolves.
rules.detail: The command tree is walked and every flag compared with the flag names in the README and docs fenced usage and flag tables; a documented flag not registered or a registered flag not documented fails. The matrix runs each flag once and a repo-check demands a test reference per flag name. Each command's help is parsed into its five parts (summary, usage, flags, examples, writes) and a missing or empty part fails; a read-only command says it writes nothing. help with no word lists commands and topics; help <command> prints the same bytes as <command> --help; help <command> <word> is a topic only when the command names that topic. A pointer has one fixed form (for example "more: <program> help <topic>"), and a test collects every pointer in help, warnings and doctor output and fails on one that names a command or topic not in the tree.
rules.why: Own bugs: help that lies, 9 of 60 sampled. Help with the same parts across every program lets a person or an agent learn one tool and read all of them, and the resolving pointer test keeps help from pointing at a topic that moved.

unless.reason: It has no flags.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. command-tree walk compared with the document extractor, a go/parser scan of test files for the flag literal, a help-part parser per command, and a pointer-resolution test over help, warning and doctor text. Plant: a flag registered with no doc line, a doc line for a removed flag, a command help with no examples, and a pointer to a topic that does not exist all fail. Control: a command with all five parts and pointers that resolve passes

open: Doc extraction is the weak half: it parses fenced blocks only; prose flag mentions are not read.

rules.rule: Output, help and docs say only what the code does. Verbs and options decided but not built are a list in data and absent from the command tree; a refused designed option names what this build has and the design that holds the slot, never a bare invalid; and a stub, placeholder return or not-implemented body in shipped source is reported.
rules.detail: The not-built list is one file per command, internal/cli/planned/<name>.yaml (verb or option, the design that holds it), so deciding a command adds a file and building it deletes that file in the change that adds its package. A name is built or planned, never both and never neither: the registry test fails on a name in both and on a name in neither. A test fails when a listed verb or option appears in the tree, so a stub cannot ship in its place. A refusal for a listed option exits with the refused code and prints the options this build has and the design reference; a matrix test per listed option asserts both. A syntax-pattern rule matches a panic with a not-implemented string and return-only bodies with a TODO, over non-test source; a tier-2 report fails on a rise against the committed count.
rules.why: Own bugs: 9 of 60 sampled bugs say what the code does not do. The list in data keeps the design and the program in step without a stub in shipped code, and naming the built alternatives turns a dead end into a next step. Wording truth cannot be judged by a program.

checks.note: not-built list test against the command tree, a refusal matrix test per listed option, and an ast-grep stub rule with a committed count that may not rise. Plant: a listed verb registered in the tree fails; a refusal that says invalid with no built alternatives fails; a function body that panics with not implemented in shipped code fires and the count rises. Control: the same text in a test file passes, and a listed option refused with the built options and its design named passes

rules.review_question: Does this changed help text say only what the code does?
open: Proposed split: a testable half (the list, the refusal, no stub in shipped source) and a review half (wording truth); the lens is a model comparing changed help text with the code.

rules.rule: Settings come through one declared helper; a program declares which sources it reads (file, environment, flags) and documents them; where more than one source is on they resolve flag, then environment, then file, then default; and a program that runs from a rules file lets the environment name only paths and terminal variables from a short tested list, with a flag overriding only for its own run.
rules.detail: Settings are declared once through the shared config helper (flag name, environment name, file key, default, doc line) together with the program's source declaration; precedence is implemented once with its own test table. A rules-file program (one whose behaviour an owner audits in a file, such as a tool that runs as root) declares the file as its only settings source: the environment may name the config file or the state folder and the terminal variables of cli.config.3, nothing else, and a flag changes only the run it is given to, never the file. A test sets every other environment variable the helper knows and asserts it has no effect. A repo-check bans any other reader: the environment ban (cli.config.3), the flag ban (cli.config.7) and a direct decode of a file into a config type.
rules.why: Practice. A setting that is not in the file of a rules-file program is a setting nobody can audit; a service in a container has no file and reads the environment by design. One helper with declared sources serves both and keeps the precedence table where two sources are on.

unless.reason: It takes parameters instead of reading settings.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. shared config helper with a source declaration and a test table for the precedence, plus the three bans of cli.config.3, 2 and 7. Plant: a setting read by an environment call in a command file fires the environment rule; in a rules-file program, an environment variable outside the tested list that changes a setting fails. Control: the same setting declared in the helper passes

open: A test per setting is proposed; the helper is not built.

rules.rule: A missing config file means the defaults, a config file that exists but cannot be read is an error, never the defaults, and a list key is an allowlist where an empty or absent list allows nothing.
rules.detail: Cannot be read covers permission denied, a parse error and a read error. No key exists whose absence means everything; a program that wants allow-all needs an explicit value naming it.
rules.why: A default used because a file was unreadable, and an absent list that means everything, are two of the places a config reader lies to its owner.

unless.reason: It has no config file.

checks.note: loader test with a missing file, a mode-000 file and a garbled file, plus a list-key test with an empty and an absent list. Plant: a mode-000 config that loads as the defaults fails; an absent allow list that admits a caller fails. Control: a missing file giving the defaults and an unreadable one giving an error pass

rules.rule: A setting that can be implemented more than one way names the implementation with one key and takes its keys in a table named after it, an unknown value is refused naming the implementations this build has, and a key that may grow accepts either its value or a table holding it, both documented as the one shape, so growing it never needs a migration.
rules.detail: For example by = "ntfy" with an ntfy table beside it; a second backend is a new table, not a migration. Both forms of a growable key are read always.
rules.why: This is the config half of ports and adapters: a second backend is one new table, and value-or-table lets a key grow without breaking a file written years before.

unless.reason: It has no config.

checks.note: loader test per implementation key with an unknown value, plus a decode test of both forms of each growable key. Plant: an unknown implementation name accepted or refused without the list fails; a growable key that refuses its table form fails. Control: both forms decoded and an unknown name refused with the list pass

rules.review_question: Can this setting have a second implementation or grow a second field, and is it shaped for that?

rules.rule: A config file whose contents decide what runs as root is refused when anyone but root or the running account owns it, or when group or others can write it, and the refusal gives the fixing line.
rules.detail: The check runs at every load, on the file and on each folder above it up to the root of the filesystem. The fixing line is the chown and chmod to paste.
rules.why: A config writable by a non-root user that a root process runs commands from is a privilege escalation.

unless.reason: It has no config file.

checks.note: loader test with a group-writable file, an other-owned file and a group-writable parent folder. Plant: a group-writable config loads and fails the test. Control: a root-owned 0644 config passes

rules.rule: An unknown config key is refused when a person wrote the file; a renamed or retired key is refused at its file and line with the migrate command and is never read; a kept file of another shape is refused or started fresh and said so, never decoded into the current fields; a message from a peer across a trust boundary refuses unknown fields, and tolerant reading is only for a peer the reader trusts and is stated per decoder; an added field does not raise the schema number.
rules.detail: A person's config refuses unknown keys so a typo is seen. An old key is never read beside the new one, not for a window and not for a release: the loader keeps a list of retired keys with the command that rewrites them and refuses with file, line and that command. A state or record file whose version is not the current one is not decoded into the current type; the program either refuses naming the version or starts a fresh file and says so. Every wire decoder is declared strict or tolerant in code: strict (unknown type or field refused) for a peer the reader does not control (a guest, a route body, an archive), tolerant only for a peer the reader trusts and deploys. The loader decodes a person's file with the undecoded-keys check (or the disallow-unknown-fields option for JSON); forbidigo bans a direct decode into config types outside the loader.
rules.why: Own measure; the planted-key test exists in four repos. Two spellings read at once is the state two target programs measured as the source of silent misreads, and the migrate command in the refusal makes a window unnecessary. Tolerant reading is a courtesy to a peer you trust and a hole for one you do not.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. shared config loader with the undecoded-keys check and a retired-key list, decoders declared strict or tolerant, a version check on every kept file, and a forbidigo ban of direct decodes into config types outside the loader. Plant: a config with an unknown key is refused; a config with a retired key is refused naming file, line and the migrate command; a state file of the previous version decoded into the current type fails; a strict decoder that accepts an extra field from an untrusted peer fails. Control: valid files pass, and a trusted peer's message with an extra field passes a decoder declared tolerant

open: Analyser form proposed; the planted-key test exists in four repos.
The typed trust line (fields declared decidable) is arch.ports.19; archive limits are store.state-files.8.

rules.rule: The environment is read only in the config package, and in the terminal module for the terminal variables (NO_COLOR, TERM, COLUMNS, LESS, PAGER, ACCESSIBLE).
rules.detail: forbidigo with type analysis on the getenv, lookupenv, environ, expandenv and syscall getenv calls outside those two places, through path exclusions, on a one-file-per-entry shrink-only list. Passing the parent environment to a child is legitimate; list those files by path. ACCESSIBLE turns on the accessible mode of forms the same way --accessible does.
rules.why: Own measure; one reader is what lets precedence and the colour decision be tested once.

checks.note: golangci-lint forbidigo with type analysis (analyze-types: true) on the environment-reading calls, path exclusions for the config package and the terminal module. Plant: os.Getenv in an internal store package fails; the same call in an adapter path and in main.go is excluded by path. Control: a read in the config package passes

rules.rule: A secret never comes from a flag and is never printed; it does not reach a child through the environment unless the row that starts the child names why; every secret a program owns sits in one owner-only folder under collision-free names and is referenced by a key ending in _file; and a service receives it through the service manager's credential passing, never through group read.
rules.detail: The keys folder is mode 0700 and each file 0600, owned by the running account (root for a system service). A secret name cannot collide with an id the program makes. A config value is never the secret itself; a key that names a secret ends in _file and holds a path. A planted-secret test runs each command with a fixture secret in the environment and in a file and asserts the secret bytes appear in no stdout, stderr or log; an ast-grep rule flags flags whose name matches token, secret, password, passwd or apikey; a config-key check fails a key that holds a secret value and does not end in _file; a secret scanner runs on staged diffs at tier 1. Which process can read a secret once it is in a child's environment is review.
rules.why: Own bugs. A key in a group-readable file and a token readable from a dump are known leaks; the _file suffix makes a secret reference recognisable in any config.

checks.note: planted-secret test in the matrix, ast-grep flag-name rule, a keys-folder mode test, a _file key check, and gitleaks on staged diffs. Plant: a command that prints the token on error fails the planted-secret test; a --token string flag fires the ast-grep rule; a key api_token holding a value fails; a keys folder of mode 0750 fails. Control: a command reading the secret from a mode-checked file named by a _file key passes

rules.review_question: Which process can read this secret once it is in the environment of a child?
open: Secret file mode is the final-mode rule of the supply and security parts; hashed issued tokens are service.authz.13.

rules.rule: Paths come from one helper filled by the platform's defaults for the program's kind, one key each, overridden only by --config or one environment variable naming a file or folder; the config folder holds only files the owner writes, while history, generated output and state live in their own folders and kept copies are pruned by age and count.
rules.detail: The defaults per kind and platform are rule data: a per-user tool follows XDG on Linux and Application Support on macOS; a system service uses /etc for config, /var/lib for state and /run for runtime files on Linux. A new platform adds a row, not a rule. forbidigo bans the home, config and cache folder lookups outside the shared paths helper, and an ast-grep rule flags string literals that start with ~/ or contain /.config/ or /.local/ in non-test code (the literal list is lint data, in the rule file). History copies go under the state folder (one folder per run, owner-only) and are pruned by age and count; generated files go in their own generated folder.
rules.why: Own measure; hand-built home paths in non-test code today: 19, 4, 1, 3 and 0 across five repos. The folder depends on who runs the program and on which system, and saying so is what makes the helper right on the next platform; keeping history and generated output out of the config folder keeps it readable after a year of runs.

unless.reason: It has no state paths.

checks.note: golangci-lint forbidigo on the folder lookups outside the paths helper, an ast-grep rule for home-path literals, and a helper test table per kind and platform. Plant: filepath.Join(os.Getenv("HOME"), ".foo") fails; os.UserConfigDir() in a command fails; a run writing a history copy into the config folder fails. Control: paths.State() passes

open: The literal rule fires on ~/.foo and /home/x/.config/y and not on a plain string.

rules.rule: Every config key and environment variable has a reader, a default, a doc row and a documented refused-when, and is refused at load naming key and reason; a key spelled in another case is refused naming its spelling; a value that becomes a path, a file name or an argument of a privileged command is held to a closed pattern and never starts with a dash; every boolean switch has a test for its non-default value; and a key meets one more question before it is added: who can pick a better value than the program?
rules.detail: The doc row gives type, default and what refuses the value. Names reaching a path or argv match a declared pattern (for example lower camel case, no leading dash); a URL is https only with no login part. A refusal names the key, the file and line, and the reason. Doctor checks the rest against the machine.
rules.why: Own bugs: one fault in record, a parsed key read by nothing. A silently ignored key and a value that reaches an argv unchecked are two of the places a config reader lies to its owner.

unless.reason: It has no config of its own.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion keys check: collects config fields by tag and environment names from the config helper, counts references in non-test code outside the loader and requires a doc row with a refused-when; each boolean key must have a test reference setting the non-default value; a loader test plants a wrongly cased key and a leading-dash value. Plant: a config field parsed and read nowhere fails; a key written Listen instead of listen loads; a name value -rf reaches an argv. Control: a field read by a command, documented with its refusal, passes

rules.review_question: Who can pick a better value for this key than the program, and does it need to be a key at all?
open: staticcheck's unused rule with field writes as uses false does not help for exported fields (unverified here).
A script comparing declared keys with keys read, and dead-code detection, are the proposed forms.
rules.note: The non-default boolean test overlaps tests.admission.9; the CLI holds its own key list.

rules.rule: Flags are defined in main or the command layer only; a library takes parameters.
rules.why: Practice; libraries that read flags cannot be reused or tested.

checks.note: golangci-lint depguard denying the flag, pflag and command-framework imports in files outside the cmd and command packages, with a shrink-only allow list. Plant: import "flag" in an internal store package fails. Control: the same import in cmd/foo passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A config migration is a dry run first, proves on a copy that the new config means the same as the old before writing, moves across filesystems by copy, sync and rename, leaves no link at an old secret path, and prints its whole way back.
rules.detail: Means the same is checked field by field, for each person's effective permissions, and for every generated unit (rendered again from the new config and compared). The dry run opens on why it migrates. A secret moved to a new path is moved, not linked.
rules.why: The equivalence proof is what makes a migration safe to run on an owner's config, and the printed way back is its undo.

unless.reason: It has no config to migrate.

checks.note: migration test on fixture configs comparing fields, effective permissions and rendered units before and after, asserting no write in the dry run, no link at the old secret path and a printed way back. Plant: a migration that drops one person's permission fails the equivalence check; a migration that symlinks the old secret path fails. Control: a meaning-preserving migration passes

rules.rule: Each setting has one home file; a setting written in two config files is refused at load naming both places; no file overrides another; and everything about one configured thing lives in that thing's own table, with no other file keying a map by its name.
rules.detail: The loader reads every config file, builds the set of keys per file, and refuses a key found in two with both files and lines. A configured thing (a machine, an app, a share) is named in one entry and its settings sit in its table.
rules.why: Override chains between files are the config bug that takes an afternoon to find, and refusing duplicates costs one loop at load. One table per thing keeps it deletable in one place.

unless.reason: It has no config files.
A program with one config file cannot set a key in two.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. shared config loader refusing a key present in two files, plus a schema check that no table is a map keyed by another table's names. Plant: the same key in two files loads; a second file with a map keyed by machine names passes the schema check. Control: each key in one file passes

rules.rule: A screen has one golden per output at the width a person reads, 80 columns for a terminal, updated only by a person reading the diff, and the narrower widths are properties: no line wider than the screen, nothing cut off, the same rows in the same order.
rules.detail: tests.journeys.8 holds the rule for any screen; this line is its terminal form and the member that holds it at push. The 80 column golden is the hand-read oracle. The 60 and 40 column runs check the three properties and keep no file, so an output change is one diff to read, not three. For a web screen a parity check against the generated pages fills the golden. cli.commands.15 and cli.look.8 named goldens at three widths; a ruling replaced the two narrow goldens with the properties, and this rule holds where they conflict.
rules.why: One project kept goldens at 80, 60 and 40 columns; each output change meant three diffs nobody read, and the 60 and 40 goldens went stale on the main branch unnoticed.
rules.review_question: Which width is this screen's golden, who updated it last and did they read the diff, and are the narrow widths checked as properties with no file?
open: cli.commands.15 and cli.look.8 still say three widths of goldens; they are not edited here because their ids carry the pty journey list and the component goldens, and the conflict rows above say which rule holds. A later change retires or rewords them.
Planned check: the journeys member has one golden file per output and the property run for the narrow widths, held by a test over the testdata folder. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A pty journey reads until its expected final frame or the program's exit, never for a fixed time, and the accessible and plain modes have goldens of their own where they differ from the default.
rules.detail: A journey that reads for a fixed time misses its golden under load and passes with time to spare on a quiet host, which is two answers for one tree. It waits on the condition: the frame it expects, or the exit (tests.runners.8, tests.isolation.6). The accessible and plain modes change what is drawn, so each has its own golden where the output differs and shares the default's where it does not.
rules.why: One project's pty control missed its golden under load, at load 76 to 202 on one platform and only under load; the fix was to read until the frame, not longer.
rules.review_question: What does this pty journey wait on, and do the accessible and plain modes have their own goldens where the output differs?
open: Planned check: a scan of journey files for a fixed read time, and the golden list per mode. No tool key is bound yet; the read-until-frame change is gragas#649.

rules.rule: A non-empty NO_COLOR wins over every other setting, even when colour is forced, and so do non-TTY output, TERM=dumb and --no-color; output that is not to a terminal has no escape codes.
rules.detail: The matrix runs every command (help and one real path) with NO_COLOR=1 together with the force variables set, non-TTY, TERM=dumb and --no-color, in a pty and a pipe, and fails on any 0x1b byte in stdout or stderr. The shared terminal module is the one reader of these variables (cli.config.3). One check holds this row, the TERM=dumb row and the pipe row.
rules.why: Own measure: all four CLIs print escape codes with both NO_COLOR and the force variable set (292, 150, 216 and 256 escapes); the module passes and no repo gates on it. This is the fault that earns the matrix helper.

unless.reason: It prints nothing.
A daemon with no terminal has no colour to switch off.

checks.note: matrix in the shared test package with the environment table, driving the pty with a pty library, asserting zero ESC bytes Force variables set are CLICOLOR_FORCE and FORCE_COLOR, together with NO_COLOR=1; the matrix is uitest. Plant: a command printing an escape code directly with fmt.Print("\x1b[31m") fails under NO_COLOR; the four copies fail under forced colour with TERM=dumb. Control: output through the shared module passes

open: Planted in two earlier trials on four copies; the matrix form is not yet run in any repo.

rules.rule: A pager is used only when stdin and stdout are terminals, and a failing pager never loses the page.
rules.why: Evidence S; the test is planned.

checks.note: terminal-test combinations of terminal and pipe, and a failing pager (a Go fake installed by testenv.Binary.Install) asserting the full text still reaches stdout The combinations run through uitest. Plant: a failing pager that swallows the page fails. Control: the text reaches stdout passes

rules.rule: Plain output carries the same facts as coloured output.
rules.detail: Strip test: run a command forced to colour and again plain; strip ANSI sequences from the coloured output with a stripper library and compare byte for byte with the plain output.
rules.why: A status that says ok only by a green colour is invisible without colour.

rules.rule: One documented exit-code table, tested against the code and the built binary, with the estate set 0 done, 1 failed or findings, 2 usage, 3 busy, 4 not ready, 5 refused, 6 declined, in every language; a refused result, a declined one and a failed one never share a code; and a command whose port the machine lacks says not on this machine with the port's name and exits 2.
rules.detail: A test parses the documentation table and the exit constants and fails on any code, name or meaning that differs, and runs the built binary through the matrix for one refused, one failed and one missing-port path and compares the exit status. A refusal is a rule holding and a failure is a bug or an outage: an agent retries one and never the other, so they never share a code. A typed refusal or error maps to its code in one place, by its word or type, never by its message (go.errors.4). A program in another language holds the same seven through its own exit owner. Declined (6) is a plan that was shown, asked for a yes, and not applied because no yes was given, whether the answer was no, no answer or the end of the input: nothing changed and nothing went wrong, and a caller never runs it again unasked, which is why it has a code of its own and does not end done (0), where a script would believe the plan was applied. It is not refused (5), where a rule held against the request, and not failed (1), where the program broke; an agent never retries a declined plan unasked. Failed shares code 1 with findings and is told apart from it by the word and by the kind in the JSON document, so a gate fails on an engine failure while a reader still sees which of the two ended the run. Whether a run that only shows a plan and asks nothing ends done (0) or declined (6) is not set here. A program that never shows a plan never exits 6, yet its table names the code, so a script reads one table across the estate. The set 0 to 5 was ruled 4 Nov (decision 13) and 6 was added on 9 Nov; no meaning of 0 to 5 moved. The change is applied in lockstep: one release of the shared module sets the failed and refused codes and binds the closing word refused to 5, with the programs' tests changed in the same tag (decision 16); every document that maps refused to 1 changes in one commit; the test in each program is the gate that proves it.
rules.why: Own measure. Today one program uses 0, 1, 2, 64, 69, 75 and 78; the shared module uses 0 to 4 with 1 for both refused and failed; three others use 1 for everything; one TypeScript program uses three codes with refusal and bad usage both 1.

rules.rule: --version prints the release tag and the commit stamped at build (a build with no tag says so), the toolchain version, and, for a client of a server, the server's version; version --json gives one JSON document with the same keys plus the API number for a program with an API.
rules.detail: The tag comes from git describe stamped at build time; a build with no tag prints v0.0.0-<commit>. In Go the commit and toolchain are compared with the binary's build information (revision, modified flag, toolchain), built with VCS stamping; another language stamps the same fields at build. A client asks its server for the server's version and prints unknown with a reason when it cannot reach it (cli.output.9). The version line is printed once, also off a terminal, and never with the banner. The matrix runs both forms, asserts exit 0, a non-empty first line and a JSON document with the keys version, commit and toolchain (plus server and api where they apply), and compares them with what was stamped. A repo-check test demands that each program has a test calling the matrix, so a program cannot skip it. The health document of the daemon repeats the same fields (see the daemon part).
rules.why: Own measure: the four CLIs disagree on --version, and it fails in three of them. The version line is the first thing a person pastes into a bug report and the first thing a reader checks against a provider, so it carries the tag, the commit and the API number, the same shape in any language. This rule starts the matrix helper that the output, config, environment and signal rules reuse.

rules.rule: Every CLI that ships to users, in whatever language it is written, takes its look from one shared module by version; exactly one module of the program writes to the terminal or reads from it; and a program holds no copy of a module file.

The seam is the same in every language: one render module is the CLI's only writer to stdout and stderr and its only reader of the terminal (raw mode, size, stdin as a terminal). rules.detail: The program states once, in rule data, the field name and the form (an integer such as 3, or a string such as launcher/3); a removal or a type change raises it and an addition does not. For every leaf command (the list comes from the command tree, never typed) the matrix runs with --json against a fixture, reads stdout fully, decodes it, asserts one document, end of input after it, the version field in the stated form, and empty stdout when the command fails to start; stderr may hold anything. A command annotated as following (logs -f) is read line by line instead: each line is one object with the version field.
rules.why: Own measure: --json exists on 11, 10, 10 and 5 leaves across four CLIs. What a reader needs is one field it can find and compare; whether it holds 3 or launcher/3 is a program's choice stated once. rules.rule: A number is shown no finer than its source resolves, an estimate is marked as one, and what a model cannot explain is its own row, never spread over the measured ones.
rules.detail: Each measured quantity declares its source resolution (whole watts, milliseconds); the formatter rounds to it. An estimate is printed with a mark (≈) and flagged in JSON. The remainder of a breakdown is a row of its own.
rules.why: A number with two decimals from a whole-watt meter is a lie with a straight face, and a remainder spread over the rest makes every row wrong.

rules.rule: A golden records one command's output and lives with that command; no hand-kept golden lists every command, and a listing of all commands is generated output.
rules.detail: A command's help and --json goldens sit in a folder owned by that command (testdata beside its code, and one folder per command for the built binary's journeys). A golden that prints the root help, the menu or the command table of the whole program is not hand-kept: it is a document a generator writes and gen --check holds, so no command change edits a file another command's change also edits. A test walks the golden folders and fails on a golden that names more than one command's own output.
rules.why: Own measure: in one program every new command edited four cross-cutting goldens that each list every command, and each edit of a protected golden bought one reviewer verdict. A per-command golden is reviewed once, with its command. The fleet's run log of 8 Nov 2026 records the cost: each landing sent the waiting candidates through a rebase and a full gate run, and a verdict written on an earlier base was rebuilt.

A struct with json tags in a cli/* package is a finding. TypeScript holds the same seam: result types live in the API module and a verb module declares none.

A wrong summary in one command shows in that document's diff, which gen --check forces into the change that made it.

rules.rule: The command tree (commands, flags with type and default, positional words, exit codes, --json field names) is written to a committed file and compared with the file at the last tag under the program's declared reader mode: with owned readers a removed flag, field or changed exit code fails only when the contract number was not raised in the same change; with independent readers it fails unless the last tag already marked it deprecated a minor release earlier; and an addition always passes.
rules.detail: A program declares its readers once in rule data: owned (every reader ships with it, such as its own page and agents) or independent (a published library, a public API). With owned readers a break raises the contract number in the same change, every reader changes with it, and nothing is kept for an old reader. With independent readers a removal or change of meaning is first marked deprecated for one minor release. Once the command registry exists (cli.commands.20) the committed file is the output of help --json, not a second artefact. A daemon's published route contract is checked the same way: breaking-change diff of the OpenAPI file against the tag under the same declaration, and its error and shape claims against real answers; fuzz is added per route once the walk exists. The file is commands.json; the --json fields it records are the top-level fields of the golden output.
rules.why: Practice. The target programs disagree because they answer for different readers: a program that owns every reader found that a compatibility layer is where its bugs lived, and a program that ships to readers it never sees must not break them. One rule with a declared reader mode keeps the check mechanical. Decision 13 moves every exit code at one program's next minor; a tag diff is how that move is seen to be intended.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion commands-json walks the command tree and writes the file; the release check reads the reader-mode declaration and diffs the file with the file at the last tag; for a daemon, oasdiff breaking on the OpenAPI file against the tag plus a contract fuzzer against the in-process daemon. Plant: with owned readers, removing a flag without raising the contract number fails; with independent readers, removing a flag not marked deprecated at the last tag fails; adding a flag passes in both. Control: an unchanged tree passes, and with owned readers a removal with the number raised passes

rules.rule: Without --json the human answer goes to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, every applied or no-op line names the path it concerns, and a read command's human answer is the content itself, not a count of it.
rules.detail: The render module tags each line as answer or diagnostic and routes it; a matrix test splits the streams and asserts the answer is on stdout. An applied or no-op line has a path field in its constructor. A read command's golden holds the content of a fixture, and a line such as "3 items" with no items fails.
rules.why: Stream discipline is what makes a pipe work in any language, a path on every applied line makes a transcript a record, and content rather than a count is the difference between an answer and a boast.

rules.rule: Every command calls one core operation and reads no store or config file itself; every operation with a route has a command or a named reason; where a command and a route show the same view their answers are one type from one function; and a test walking the route index fails on a route with neither.
rules.detail: What is left to do is computed once and handed out by both surfaces. The exceptions are a list in data with a reason each. A command package that imports a store or the config loader is a finding.
rules.why: Parity is what makes a page, an agent and a person see the same facts, and the walk over the route index keeps it true when a route is added years later. Two target programs wrote the same test.

rules.rule: A state or value the program could not establish is answered as unknown or null with a reason beside it, in text, in --json and in every API answer, never as 0, false, a dash, off, healthy or a default, and it never folds into ok; a field the platform has no such thing as is left out; an answer lists each source it could not read with why and never fills it from an earlier reading; a kept answer carries the time it was read; and a value known only while the program watched is omitted after a restart.
rules.detail: Good news is claimed only for what was checked; an item not checked is listed as not checked. A summary that is ok when one of its inputs is unknown is a finding. A test per answer plants an unreadable source and asserts the null, the reason, the absence of a carried-forward value and a summary that is not ok.
rules.why: This is the property that decides whether a status tool can be believed at 3 a.m. One rule across every surface is cheaper than three and keeps a page from showing fine over an API that said unknown.

unless.reason: It answers no status of its own.

checks.note: answer test per status command and route with a fake source that fails to read, asserting null with a reason, no earlier value, a read time on a cached answer, and a summary that is not ok.
