Control: an unknown with a reason and a not-ok summary passes

rules.rule: Every outward effect goes through a wrapper that records it; each external program and each verb it may run is named in one adapter's closed table; the check resolves a program name through constants and assignments and treats a name from any other source as a finding; and a test fails a program or verb run outside the table.
rules.detail: Runs a program means a name passed to exec.Command or exec.CommandContext (or the equivalent in another language), resolved as the compiler does: a variable counts only when its value comes from a constant or from the one adapter's table. The table lists, per program, its absolute path or lookup rule and its allowed verbs; it may only shrink in the core. forbidigo on exec.Command and exec.CommandContext, and on os.StartProcess and syscall.ForkExec, outside the runner and a test (the import of os/exec is not banned: exec.LookPath starts nothing, returns exec.ErrDot for a hit in the current folder and reads PATHEXT on Windows, so a lookup is std's own and needs no wrapper), and the security analyser's rule for a variable command (gosec G204). x/sys counts as the standard library. A package-import test on net/http. The runner package, proposed, has a context, a timeout, no shell and an output cap (cli.process.2). Counts on macOS, of the former import ban: os/exec appears in 90 production files across seven repositories, and the ban found 24, 20, 11 and 13 in four of them; the call ban spares a lookup.
rules.why: An effect outside the wrapper is invisible to the record and to the journal that precedes effects (the outward-effect journal of the data part, store.consistency.4). One adapter per dependency is the whole value of ports: replacing a tool is one package, not a search. The resolving check and the closed table close the two ways a program name is smuggled past the import rule. Own measure.

unless.reason: It starts no programs of its own.

checks.note: forbidigo with type analysis on exec.Command, exec.CommandContext, os.StartProcess and syscall.ForkExec outside the runner and tests (selector bans, held by the golangci preset, whose comment on forbidigo names this rule), gosec G204, and a go/analysis pass resolving the program name of each exec call against the adapter's table. Plant: exec.Command outside the runner fails; a program name read from a config string and passed to the runner fails the resolving pass; a verb not in the table fails the programs test. Control: the runner package called with a name from the adapter's table passes

rules.rule: An adapter runs an external program by absolute path with a fixed argv, checks each caller value against a closed shape before it enters the argv, caps the program's output and sets a deadline; a port that starts work takes a checked name, never an argv.
rules.detail: No shell, no PATH lookup at run time (the path is resolved once and checked; the child keeps only the variables proc.Needed names for the system), the option terminator before any caller value, a value that starts with a dash refused. The output cap and the deadline are named constants per program; output past the cap is a failure, not a truncation that looks like success. A port's method takes a typed name checked against config, and the adapter builds the argv.
rules.why: Each of these is a known class of bug: PATH hijack, argv injection, a hung child, and a reply that grows without bound. Every program that runs another faces them, in any language.

unless.reason: It starts no programs of its own.

checks.note: runner test with a fake program that sleeps past the deadline, one that writes past the cap, and a caller value starting with a dash; an ast-grep rule for a port method taking a []string argv; a non-absolute path refused by the runner. rules.rule: A child program used as a plug-in gets a bare environment (PATH and LANG only), no secret, a timeout, one versioned request object on stdin, and a size-capped versioned reply that is refused in an unknown version, with its message length-capped and stripped of control characters.
rules.detail: The request and the reply each carry a version field; the parent refuses a reply in a version it does not know and a reply over the cap. Text from the reply that reaches a person goes through the sanitiser of cli.errors.4.
rules.why: A plug-in is code the program did not write, running with the program's authority; a bare environment keeps secrets out of it, and a versioned, capped protocol keeps a new or hostile plug-in from being misread.

unless.reason: It runs no plug-ins.

rules.rule: A comment says why, not what, and none narrates the change; one question judges it.
rules.detail: The question: could someone who never saw the code write this comment from the adjacent lines? If yes it goes. A comment that states an interface contract may be longer than a function body, so the length clause is dropped from this rule. A regular-expression report for change-narrating words (now, no longer, previously, used to, changed, was) was considered and not run; false hits are expected. Agents narrate; the question fails narration without counting words.
rules.why: A comment that restates the line adds a second thing to keep in step with the code. A study of 60 Go bugs found no comment fault, so this is practice and an instruction.
rules.review_question: Could someone who never saw this code write this comment from the adjacent lines?

rules.rule: A TODO, FIXME, HACK or XXX names an issue in one shared pattern; a bare one is refused.
rules.detail: The tracked form is TODO(#123). The first tier is a comment-node pattern check (it catches line and block-comment forms); the second tier checks that the named issue exists and is open. The Go lint runner's godox cannot test the named-issue form and was rejected; in the web stack the core no-warning-comments rule does not read an issue id, so every TODO fails, and the tracked form needs an expiring-todo rule or a small local rule.

rules.rule: Commented-out code is refused, found by a lint check enabled by name.
rules.detail: In Go the check is gocritic commentedOutCode, enabled by name (a stock linter set does not enable it); a two-line commented statement pair beside a nolint line was not reported, so a short group can pass. In the web stack the sonarjs no-commented-code rule fires on some forms and misses others (a commented call chain such as // fetchAll(items.map(x => x.id)); and a commented if block), so it holds only some forms.

rules.rule: Every exported name of a port or shared API has a doc comment stating its contract; elsewhere a doc comment is written only when it says more than the signature, and a comment one could write from the line below is a finding.
rules.detail: On a port, a shared package's surface and any other API a second program or package builds on, every exported name has a doc comment stating, where they apply, units, the meaning of nil, null or absent, ownership, invariants, ordering, what it mutates and what it throws or returns as an error. Presence and form there are a rule: in Go the lint runner's exported check over the port and shared-package paths (with its comments exclusion preset off, so it is not hidden) and the doc-comment form check. Elsewhere an exported name gets a doc comment only when it says something local, non-obvious and with no other home; a comment that restates the name or the line below is deleted. The content is review. A surface change of a shared part or port fails until a reason is recorded (arch.shared.9).
rules.why: Ports are where the reader cannot read the body; a contract that is not written is guessed. A doc comment required on every export elsewhere produces filler that restates the name, which three target repos ban.

Control: an exported helper in a command package with no comment passes
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on godoclint names this rule.

rules.rule: A value specific to one installation comes only from the loaded config: a literal of one in non-config, non-test code fails, and a default is the program's own neutral choice said once, never one installation's fact.
rules.detail: An installation-specific value is a service address, a path on one machine, a port, a container, host, network or household name, or any other fact true of one deployment and not of the program. It comes from the loaded config or is observed on the machine at run time. There is no literal service address or fallback beside the configured one. A default exists only as the program's own neutral choice (a documented port, a path under the platform's standard folders), declared once in the config package. Config is read in one package with a reader, a default and a doc row per key; a secret never comes from a flag. Variables are declared in a typed schema. A word-list check reads non-config, non-test source and the defaults, with the installation's known names, addresses and paths as a list kept outside the repository (supply.secrets.4 holds that list's handling); a hit fails.
rules.why: A hard-coded fallback address sends traffic to the wrong place when the configured one is missing. A default holding one installation's fact works on the author's machine and silently misbehaves on every other.

checks.note: A structural rule flagging a service address literal next to a configured address read. Plant: A literal service address used as a fallback fails. Control: The configured address alone passes.

a word-list test over non-config, non-test source and the config defaults against the installation list kept outside the repository, plus a check that defaults are declared only in the config package. rules.rule: No file nobody imports, no unused export (including in a shared package), no unused dependency and no unused path alias.
rules.detail: In Go the dead-code tool must print nothing, or print only lines on a committed list, because its exit status is 0 even with findings. The dead-code tool and the linter run for each system of the project's list, by GOOS, on the one machine the gate runs on, as one step. Tidying the module file leaves no diff. Both runs are in the local gate. In the web stack the unused-file finder follows the project's entry points (page routes, scripts, test files) with the framework plugins active (else .astro files report false unused), reports unused files, exports and dependencies as errors with a baseline of known ones that only shrinks; the lock holds exactly the declared dependencies. An unused export in a shared package fails.
rules.why: 27 lines of dead exports in one Go repo; 97 and 124 unused exports in two web repos. At the donor the finder caught unused exports at land on two changes. (An earlier version of this rule asked for a run per GOOS because a single run called the other system's code dead; a product now holds none, so one run suffices.)

rules.rule: A project's own Go code has no //go:linkname directive, unless the project lists the file in an exemption with an expiry date.
rules.detail: A linkname binds a name to a symbol of another package by string, past the compiler's export rules and the linker's check of what a package may reach. The scan reads every non-generated Go file of the project's own modules for the directive, in test files too, and a hit outside the exemption list is a finding. The list starts empty; a row names the file, the reason and the date it ends, and a row past its date is a finding. The directive needs an unsafe import, but a scan for that import is not the check: the import has other uses and the directive can sit in a file that gosec passes.
rules.why: A linkname is invisible to the dead-code tool and to the compiler's export rules, and the standard library's linker now refuses new references to its internals, so a binding that builds today can fail on the next toolchain. The gap was found in the review of #650: no rule banned it.

sources.says: The linker now disallows using a //go:linkname directive to refer to internal symbols in the standard library (including the runtime) that are not marked with //go:linkname on their definitions

rules.review_question: Does this directive have an exemption row with a reason and an expiry?
open: Planned check: an ast-grep or text scan for the //go:linkname comment in non-generated Go files outside an exemption list whose rows carry a file, a reason and an expiry date; a row past its date is a finding. Plant: a file with a //go:linkname line and no exemption row fails. Control: the same file with an unexpired row passes. No tool key is bound yet, and a row without one would raise checks-unresolved, a baseline that may only fall. A directive is a comment, so no golangci-lint linter reads it as a call (forbidigo matches calls and selectors); ast-grep has no preset in this repository yet, and the exemption list and its expiry check are not built. It becomes a Hard rule with its row when a key resolves.
Opened as gragas#654, from the review of #650; the finding was that code.deadcode.1 only said linkname may be reported.

rules.rule: Duplicated blocks only fall, measured across packages by a clone detector; no new clone is added inside a repository.

A standalone build of the same detector, pinned in the tool list like the other Go tools and built offline, runs over every non-test file at 60 tokens, so it sees across packages; its clone-group count goes to the measure output and to a shrink-only baseline row, at its count on the day of adoption and then at 0. For TypeScript a clone detector (jscpd) runs over the source roots with generated files ignored, and the clone count and the cloned-block metric are held by a shrink-only ratchet through one ratchet helper; its thresholds are 10 lines and 80 tokens. No Node tool is used where a Go one does the job in the Go gate. A clone found at adoption goes on the baseline.

rules.rule: Size and complexity are watched as a trend and a hotspot list (churn times lines), reported and not gated, with a declared exclusion list and a window by release or ticket, never by days.
rules.detail: A hotspot report uses a declared exclusion list that takes generated files, registers, golden test data and end-to-end files, and states its window and its unit: by release, train or ticket, never by days, because agent commit rates inflate churn and make time windows meaningless (118 commits a day on one repo). After a squash the unit changes little, and splitting a hot file drops it off the list, so a file that leaves it has not shown it got better. A hot file carries a per-file trend (lines and indentation depth over its commits) before and after a refactor, so a fix is checked against history. A ratchet is used only where a number reaches zero in practice, such as files over 1000 lines not rising (code.size.1; one repo's numeric per-file file-baseline already does it). A size distribution (the 90th percentile) is reported as a trend. A diff size (a diff-size ceiling paired with a rework count) is reported beside post-land rework per ticket wherever a small-change rule exists, from the delivery record, with no limit.
rules.why: The top tenth of files by churn times lines took 46.4% of later fix touches in one repo and 30.2% in another, against 9.9% for a random tenth; lines alone gave 34.8 and 36.9, so the product is no better than its parts. A rerun did not reproduce the 46.4: the top tenth took 31.1, 30.7 and 25.9 against 9.8 random, and lines alone beat the product in two repos. Commit and ticket units share 18 to 20 of the top 20. Raw churn lists fill with generated files. The delivery stability findings with AI use are explained by larger changes.
