rules.note: Change coupling across a boundary is arch.measures.3.

rules.rule: A merge-candidate report lists modules with one importer that change with it, near-duplicate modules, ports with one implementation and private functions with one call site; it is report only.
rules.detail: A root or command module imports everything by construction, so it does not count as the one importer. Near-duplicates are found by token clones (renaming every exported name beats a name match for free). Interfaces with one implementation are listed when no second is named. No floor is set: a single call site is often right and floors misfire. A new merge candidate blocks until the change merges it or says why not. It is read beside code.size.2.
rules.why: Every size rule pushes towards splitting and nothing reported the opposite. Across six repos 93 packages had one importer, 33 changed with it, 31 of those on a command root, 2 left to read; a clone finder found about 9 clone pairs in one repo in 0.9 s.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion merge-report: one-importer packages excluding command roots, co-change over tickets, token clones from dupl or jscpd, private single-call functions, printed at land. Plant: a copied package fires; the same copy with every exported name changed also fires through the clone finder. Control: a package with two importers is not listed

v1 class our-cli. report only: knip (modules with one importer), private functions with one call site via the TypeScript walk of code.size.2, and jscpd for near-duplicate modules. Plant: a fixture with one single-importer module and one single-call-site helper lists both. Control: a module with two importers is not listed

open: The trial sample was located and not read in full; 0.5 and 3 are guesses; no gate is justified by the web evidence.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; D for the web

rules.rule: Types are listed by method count, with no limit, so a god object that is under every file-size line is visible.
rules.detail: A small analyser counts methods per type, leaving out fakes. Grouping methods by the fields they use does not do this: it flags fakes and data records, a mutex used in every method hides it, and it missed a 49-method server. A type whose method count rises above its baseline blocks until answered.
rules.why: The types with the most methods were 49 (a server), 35 (a config) and 33 (a call type). Field cohesion tried flagged 49 hits across six repos, of which 1 to 2 of 12 in one repo were plausibly true.

checks.note: v1 class our-plugin. a go/analysis analyzer or go/types script prints methods per type (non-fake, no limit); a rise above the baseline blocks until answered. Plant: a type whose method count rises above its baseline blocks; the dropped cohesion form was planted with a God type and a Whole type. Control: a type with an unchanged method count passes

open: Would become a firm rule only with a method-count ceiling and data on the cheap cure (embedding a struct moves methods without reducing them).
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; no fault in our record

rules.rule: Only the expected callers can reach a daemon, and being local is never an identity: peer credentials or the gate's identity are checked on every request, never a header alone; each route and each state-changing command declares who may call it; every route and command passes one admission check; and a route or command with no entry fails.
rules.detail: Socket permissions or loopback bound who can reach the daemon; they decide nothing about who the caller is. A loopback or container-bridge address is anybody. A command run on the machine builds the same identity value a route builds (a local principal from the peer credentials of its own process) and passes the same admission check, with no bypass for being on the machine. A request no source vouches for is refused (service.authz.8).
rules.why: Practice; a bridge address is anybody, and a local bypass is the door every later surface walks through. Written as a Go test in the kit or the store test helper; no separate program.

unless.reason: It serves nothing.

checks.note: table test comparing the route and command tables with a caller list that refuses wildcards; peer-credential test from another user; a test that a command reaches the core only through the admission check; the gate door package exists. Plant: a route or a state-changing command added with no entry fails, and a request from a loopback address with no identity that is admitted fails. Control: every route and command listed and admitted through the one check passes

open: A test from another user or address is proposed; no plant was recorded in the catalogue.

rules.rule: A route the machine cannot serve is absent from the route index and answers 404 with one fixed reason to every caller, never 403; a route declares its methods and any other method answers 405 with Allow; and a GET writes no state beyond one declared cache.
rules.detail: The route index and the 404s come from one table, so a capability the machine lacks is reported the same way to a caller who may and one who may not use it. Each refused method has a negative test. A GET may fill the one cache it declares; anything else it writes (a note, a counter, a last-seen time) is a defect, and only an operation that changes things records what a look observed. Errors follow service.errors.4: a non-2xx status with the JSON error body.
rules.why: These are the places a reader has to guess, and a reader that guesses breaks. 404, not 403, keeps a capability list from leaking what a caller may not see; a GET that writes makes a look change what it looked at.

checks.note: a table test that builds the index and the absent-route answers from one table; a generated negative test per route for every method not listed; a test that snapshots the store before and after every GET route and allows only the declared cache to differ. Plant: a missing capability that answers 403, a route that accepts an unlisted method, and a GET that writes a note each fail. Control: a 404 with the fixed reason, a 405 with Allow, and a GET that leaves the store unchanged pass

rules.note: service.contract.9 holds the GET rule for a service; this is the daemon twin.

rules.rule: Every local HTTP server, in any language, listens on loopback by default, answers only expected Host names, checks Origin against an allow list, needs a custom header for a request that changes a cookie, sets strict cookie attributes, and refuses to listen wider without TLS and a login.
rules.detail: A local server is any HTTP server that runs on a person's machine: a daemon, a CLI's serve command or a development tool, written in Go, TypeScript or a language added later. Strict cookie attributes are HttpOnly, Secure where TLS is on, SameSite=Strict and a Path. A wider listen address is refused at start unless TLS and an identity source are configured. Each language ships the same shared test; a new language adds its binding, the rule does not change.
rules.why: Held in one program already; a browser DNS-rebinding run was not done. A local server is attacked the same way whatever language it is written in.

checks.note: the same shared request table run against a TypeScript local server (Host, Origin, cookie header, listen address). Plant: a TypeScript local server bound to 0.0.0.0 with no TLS, or answering Host evil.example, fails. Control: a loopback server that refuses unexpected Host and Origin passes

shared test that sends a request with Host: evil.example to the page handler and expects refusal, lifted from the program that has it. Plant: a handler without a Host check returns 200 and fails. Control: a handler that refuses unexpected hosts passes

open: A browser rebinding run was not done.

rules.rule: A state-changing request to a local server is accepted only from the server's own origin, not merely the same site, and a change a browser sends from anywhere else is refused.
rules.detail: Same-site is not enough: every host under one private-network domain is one site on the Public Suffix List, so another device's page on that network would pass a same-site check. The check compares the full origin (scheme, host and port) with the server's own, and a request with Sec-Fetch-Site other than same-origin, or an Origin not its own, is refused. Applies to a local server in any language.
rules.why: Three programs have a cross-site refusal; a same-site rule leaves a measured hole on a private network where every device shares one site.

checks.note: the standard library's cross-origin protection wrapped around the handler (present in Go 1.27.3, run go doc) plus an Origin equality check, tested with a POST carrying Sec-Fetch-Site same-site from a sibling host. Plant: a same-site POST from a sibling host that is accepted fails, and a cross-site POST that is accepted fails. Control: a same-origin POST passes
the same request table run against a TypeScript local server. Plant: a same-site POST from a sibling host that is accepted fails. Control: a same-origin POST passes

rules.rule: A peer's identity is believed only from the gate's own connection, on every request, and a spoofed identity header is ignored; the identity value is built only in the door packages, and the core reads no request header or URL.
rules.detail: A door is any way in: a route, a command, a watcher, a card. Each door builds the one identity value (who, what they may do, which door, the subject) and hands it to the core; the core decides from that value alone. An analyser over the core packages refuses any use of the request type, its headers or its URL.
rules.why: Held in the shared door package. A core that reads a header can be steered by any caller who can set one, and one identity value is what keeps every later door under the same check.

checks.note: door package tests that read identity only from the gate connection on every request. Plant: a request with a spoofed identity header that sets identity fails. Control: identity from the gate connection passes

an AST test over the core packages refusing any reference to the request's header or URL, and any construction of the identity value outside the door packages. Plant: a planted header read in a core package fails. Control: a core that takes only the identity value passes

rules.rule: Every http.Server sets ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout and IdleTimeout, every http.Client has a Timeout or a context deadline, request bodies pass through a size cap, and all of them are constructed by the shared web package; outbound hosts come from configuration, never from a request.
rules.detail: A fetch that follows a user-supplied address resolves and checks it first (server-side request forgery). forbidigo with type analysis bans the default client, the bare get and post calls and the bare listen call outside the shared web package; the security scanner's G112 and G114 are on (both verified firing on 5 Nov). The scanner did not flag a client with no timeout or a server with only a header timeout, so the other timeouts and the body cap are asserted by a test on the shared constructors.
rules.why: A client with no timeout hangs a CLI too, so this applies to any program that builds an HTTP server or client. A construction analyzer was considered and not chosen: forbidigo on the type name also hits parameter and return types (verified false positive).

unless.reason: A program that builds no HTTP server or client has none to time out.

checks.note: forbidigo on the default client and bare HTTP calls outside the shared web package, gosec G112 and G114, and a test on the web package's constructors forbidigo runs with analyze-types: true; the constructors live in the shared web module, and the body cap is http.MaxBytesReader. Plant: http.Get and ListenAndServe outside the web package fail, and a server with no ReadHeaderTimeout fails. Control: the web package's constructor passes

rules.review_question: Does any outbound host here come from a request, and is it resolved and checked first?
open: Half rule (calls banned, constructors tested); outbound-host request forgery stays review.

rules.rule: A daemon that serves a page gets its security headers in one place, tested, and an embedded page uses html/template or the framework's escaping, never text/template for markup.
rules.why: Practice; a daemon test reads the headers and a depguard ban covers the template package. It binds only a daemon that serves a page; no target does today, and a daemon that answers an API only declares so (daemon.lifecycle.3).

unless.reason: A daemon with no page has no page to serve.

checks.note: depguard ban of text/template in web packages, plus a daemon header test. Plant: a text/template import in a web package fails, and a response missing the policy header fails. Control: html/template and the full header set pass

rules.rule: A daemon that holds another program's key exposes only a named list of fixed requests, each with its address and request fixed in code, never a pass-through proxy.
rules.detail: A caller names a question from the list; it never supplies a path, host, method or header that reaches the other program. A new question is a new entry in code, reviewed. Values a caller may pass are typed and checked against the entry's own allow list.
rules.why: A proxy that forwards a key forwards it to anything a caller can name, which turns a read key into whatever the other program's API allows.

checks.note: a test over the keyed client asserting every outbound request comes from the fixed table, and an analyser refusing a request URL or path built from a caller's input in that package. Plant: a handler that forwards a caller's path to the other program with the key fails. Control: a named question with a fixed address passes

rules.rule: Proposed, promoted when the design that introduces a privileged helper is approved: a privileged helper runs only a closed list of verbs with fixed absolute command lines, checks each value against a list it builds itself, uses no shell and an empty environment, arms each mutating verb, and has a planted hostile-caller test.
rules.detail: The helper is its own binary with its own import closure. Each verb is an entry with a fixed absolute command line in a system-protected folder; a caller passes only values, and the helper checks each against a list it reads itself from the system, never one the caller sends. A mutating verb runs only when armed by the owner. Promotion: when the operator approves the privileged-helper part of the design named in evidence (its part 2), status becomes active, strength Hard, and the check is built; until then the rule binds nothing and is not reported as a gap.
rules.why: A privileged helper is the one place a bug becomes root. The shape is ruled, but the design it encodes is still proposed, and a rule ahead of its own design is what decision 64 warns against.

checks.note: a hostile-caller test that sends unknown verbs, extra arguments, shell metacharacters, a value outside the helper's own list and a set environment, and asserts each is refused with nothing run. Plant: a helper that runs a caller-supplied argument or inherits the caller's environment fails. Control: a listed verb with a listed value, armed, passes

open: Proposed (decision 47): promoted when the operator approves part 2 of the access design.
The registration-by-privilege twin is cli.commands.27, promoted when that design merges.

rules.rule: A setting that decides whom a daemon believes has no default and is never detected, and a missing or unknown value opens no listener, believes nobody, and is named by doctor.
rules.detail: The trust mode (which identity source a listener believes) is written by the owner. The daemon never infers it from the platform, the network or a running process. Start with the value missing or unknown logs the reason, opens no listener, and doctor prints the key and the allowed values.
rules.why: A misconfigured daemon must refuse rather than believe everybody, and a detected mode changes when the machine changes, without anyone deciding.

checks.note: a start test with the trust setting missing, and one with an unknown value, asserting no listener opens and doctor names the key. Plant: a daemon that falls back to a default trust mode when the key is missing fails. Control: a daemon that opens no listener and names the key passes

rules.rule: Data a program manages that cannot be fetched again has a scheduled backup through a tool behind an interface (copy, list, restore, check), a record of the last good copy, and a check that restores a sample and compares it.
rules.detail: The program lists which of its data can be fetched again (an image, a package, a cache) and which cannot; the second list is backed up. The interface has one adapter per backup tool, and a tool added later is one adapter. The record names the copy, its time and its check result, and status reports its age. The check restores a sample into a fresh folder (cli.commands.28) and compares it byte for byte; a failed check is a bad event. The schedule rides a run the manager already makes where it can (daemon.lifecycle.5).
rules.why: A backup nobody has restored is a hope, not a backup; the record of the last good copy is what tells a person how much they would lose today.

unless.reason: Data that can be fetched again needs no backup.

checks.note: a test against a fake backup tool asserting the scheduled run copies each listed path, writes the last-good record, and that the check restores a sample and fails on a planted difference. Plant: a check that reports good without restoring fails, and a corrupted sample that passes the check fails. Control: a check that restores and compares passes

rules.note: store.recovery.1 holds the restore drill for every store; this rule adds the schedule, the interface and the record.

rules.rule: A deployed stack the program writes names its image by tag and its update check compares the running digest with the registry; every port it opens binds loopback and is published only through the private network's serve, never publicly; and a change to shared network or identity policy that reaches other devices is printed for the owner to apply, never applied by the program.
rules.detail: The tag is the image's moving tag; the update check reads the registry's digest for it (within the daily budget of daemon.outbound.2) and reports what would change. Exact pins stay the rule for code dependencies (supply.install.4); a stack's image is not a code dependency. A port bound to 0.0.0.0 or a public address, or published through a public relay, is refused when the stack is written. Shared policy is anything another device or person reads: the private network's access list, its DNS, an identity provider's groups. The program prints the exact lines and where they go.
rules.why: A home server that pins images never updates, which is worse than a tag plus a digest check that says what changed. Loopback plus the private network's serve makes a written stack safe by construction, and printing shared policy keeps a program from reaching past its own machine.

unless.reason: A program that writes no deployed stack has no image, port or shared policy to place.

checks.note: a golden test over the stack writer asserting image references are name:tag, every published port binds 127.0.0.1 or ::1, and no public relay setting is written; a test that the shared-policy command prints and calls no write API of the network or identity provider. Plant: a stack with a port bound to 0.0.0.0 fails, and a writer that calls the network's policy API fails. Control: a loopback-bound stack and a printed policy diff pass

rules.note: supply.install.4 is rewritten under the same card to scope exact pins to code dependencies.

rules.rule: A daemon serves one health document (ready flag, program version, commit, start time) of the same shape from one shared handler; liveness never calls a dependency and readiness does.
rules.detail: A deployed program alerts a person on failing health. Staged rollout is not required. The version fields repeat the CLI's --version (cli.exit.3).
rules.why: Practice and own measure; the shared handler is what makes the shape the same.

checks.note: start test fetching the health document from the shared handler; a handler made to fail must go red; liveness stays green when a dependency breaks, written as a Go test in the kit or the store test helper. Plant: a liveness handler that checks the dependency fails. Control: a handler with the shared shape passes

rules.rule: A daemon signals readiness by its service manager's own mechanism, only after it can serve; a daemon that can hang also sends the watchdog ping while it runs, or its notes say why not; and a test proves the signal follows the listen.
rules.detail: Under systemd a resident daemon is Type=notify and sends READY=1 after it listens; a socket-activated daemon (daemon.lifecycle.5) takes its listener from the manager, which holds the socket before the daemon starts, and still sends READY=1 once it can answer the request that woke it. Under launchd, which gives no readiness call, the daemon writes a version file in its run folder once it listens, and the install check reads that file and asks the socket for an answer. A daemon that leaves on idle stops sending the watchdog ping only as it exits. A manager added later names its mechanism in the test table; the rule does not change.
rules.why: Practice (systemd man page). Without a signal the manager or the install check treats a daemon that has not yet listened as up, and starts dependants or keeps a broken upgrade.

checks.note: start test with one row per manager: under a fake notify socket READY=1 arrives after the listener is up and not before; under launchd the version file appears after the socket answers and not before. Plant: READY sent before listen fails, and a version file written before listen fails. Control: the signal after listen passes

rules.note: Rewritten with daemon.lifecycle.5 (idle by default) as the R-15 amendment to D-T53 asks.

rules.rule: An observation of another machine or device changes nothing on it: the kinds of probe are a closed list in one function, a test refuses a planted new kind, and a probe that disturbs its target is dropped.
rules.detail: A probe that wakes a disk, wakes a sleeping machine, opens a session (an SSH or TCP connection to a service port) or asks a power state that spins a device up is a disturbance. The closed list is the only place a probe kind is added, and adding one is a reviewed change with its reason written beside it.
rules.why: A monitor that wakes what it watches is lying about idle and breaks idle by default (daemon.lifecycle.5) silently.

checks.note: a test over the probe package asserting that every network or device call goes through the one probe function and that its kinds equal the closed list. Plant: a planted TCP connect probe outside the list fails. Control: the listed probes pass

rules.rule: A program that replaces a running one keeps the previous binary and puts it back by itself when the new one does not answer healthy within a stated window; the revert is tested with a candidate built to fail.
rules.why: Own measure: of eight programs, one has a working guard, three do it manually and four have none.

unless.reason: It has no binary to replace.

checks.note: start test installing a candidate that exits at start and asserting the previous binary runs again; shared upgrade helper. Plant: a failing candidate with no revert makes the test fail. Control: a healthy candidate stays installed

rules.note: The install-by-rename rule is cli.commands.5; the revert of an install is F-22's, held here.

rules.rule: A running old daemon is not mistaken for the new one when the command starts; the command compares the daemon's reported version.
rules.why: A command that talks to a stale daemon draws results from the wrong version.

checks.note: Go test starting an old stub daemon and running the command; the health document's version is compared and the old one is not treated as the new. Plant: a command that discards the version field fails. Control: a command that compares the version passes

open: The web side's version-pairing rule is daemon.lifecycle.3.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: R
rules.note: The web catalogue lists it for the TypeScript side with a Go twin; the Go row is held here.

rules.rule: A daemon that serves a page pairs page and server versions: the contract carries a version, the page reads it on the first answer and again on every reconnect, and a mismatch stops or reloads the page with a sentence, never draws wrong.
rules.detail: An upgrade with a page open stops or reloads. One pairing helper is shared; one program writes a schema field and never reads it. A daemon declares whether it serves a page; a daemon that answers an API only declares so, serves no HTML, and its readers learn the API number at setup instead (daemon.lifecycle.7).
rules.why: Unproven in two programs (a pairing constant and a number helper); the test is not built. No target serves a page today and each makes a page a separate program, but the rule is right for the day one does.

unless.reason: A daemon that declares it answers an API only has no page to pair; its readers are held by daemon.lifecycle.7.

checks.note: browser test against a stub daemon serving contract version N+1: the page must stop with the mismatch sentence; a second test restarts the stub with a new version while the page is open and the page must reload or stop. Plant: a stub with the wrong version and no sentence fails; a page that keeps drawing after a version change fails. Control: a page that stops with the sentence passes

rules.note: Merges the first-answer pairing rule with the reconnect rule, as one browser test holds both.

rules.rule: A daemon that embeds a page is not silent when the page is missing: a build without the page serves a clear 404 and does not compile when the embedded folder is empty.
rules.why: A blank 200 for a missing page is invisible; held in part by the doctor command. It binds only a daemon that embeds a page; no target does today.

unless.reason: A daemon with no page has nothing to embed.

checks.note: build without the page; a test asserts a clear 404 body; the embed directive fails to compile on an empty directory. Plant: serving a missing page that returns a blank 200 fails. Control: a clear 404 passes

rules.rule: A daemon is asleep by default: where its service manager can start it on its socket it is started that way and exits after a stated idle time, a daemon that stays resident states why in a recorded decision with its measured idle cost, and no timer of its own runs while nothing needs it.
rules.detail: Under systemd a .socket unit starts the service; under launchd the Sockets key does. A Go daemon takes the socket either manager passes with go-socket's listen.Activated, by the name the unit gives it (a launchd Sockets key), and a process the manager did not start is told so (listen.ErrNotActivated) rather than handed nothing. The idle time is a named constant, and the exit after it is a clean exit (daemon.units.3 does not restart it). Where the manager cannot hand a socket over to this program, the daemon stays resident but sleeps in accept between requests, and the decision says so. A timer of the daemon's own (a watch, a refresh) starts with the work that needs it and stops when that work ends. Applies to every daemon whatever it serves; a new manager adds its socket setting to the test table.
rules.why: Idle power is measured on a home server and on a laptop battery; a process that keeps itself awake costs watts every hour of every day. It also keeps a daemon's behaviour explainable: nothing happens unless something asked.

checks.note: unit-render test asserting a socket unit or the launchd Sockets key and a named idle-exit constant, or a recorded decision named in the unit's notes; a start test that sends one request, waits past the idle time and asserts a clean exit with no timer left running. Plant: a resident unit with no socket and no recorded decision fails, and a daemon still running past its idle time fails. Control: a socket-started daemon that exits cleanly after its idle time passes

rules.rule: Every start reconciles what an earlier run left (locks, units, ids, sockets, temporary files) and reclaims what nothing owns, and a test plants an orphan of each kind and proves it is reclaimed.
rules.detail: Reconciling is read, compare, then reclaim: a lock whose holder is gone is released, a unit or id no record names is removed, and each reclaim is logged with what was found. Remove and wipe commands reclaim the same kinds. A new kind of persisted state adds its orphan to the test table, so the rule stays true as state kinds grow.
rules.why: A daemon that cannot start cleanly after a crash is fixed by hand at the worst moment, and nothing may be left running unwatched.

checks.note: a start test that plants one orphan per state kind in the table and asserts each is reclaimed after start. Plant: a stale lock left by a killed process that blocks the next start fails. Control: a start that reclaims every planted orphan passes

rules.note: go.concurrency.5 clears in-memory state when its cause ends; this rule covers persisted leftovers.

rules.rule: A reader of a provider that answers an API only learns the provider's API number at setup and in doctor, and on a mismatch draws nothing of the provider's, names which side to update, and doctor reports it with the deploy line.
rules.detail: The number is the provider's one contract number (service.contract.2). A reader keeps the number it was built against, compares it with the provider's at setup and on every doctor run, and on a difference shows the sentence and the commands that bring the older side up, never a partial answer.
rules.why: A reader that draws a provider's answer of another shape draws wrong numbers with confidence; checking once at setup and in doctor costs nothing at run time.

checks.note: a reader test against a stub provider reporting number N+1, asserting setup and doctor stop with the which-side sentence and that no provider data is drawn. Plant: a reader that draws the provider's answer under a mismatched number fails. Control: a reader that stops and names the side to update passes

rules.rule: A daemon's logs have a level and a time; hold no secret, sign-in code, token, prompt, conversation, device or address; mark a field reported by an untrusted peer as reported; and go where the service manager reads them or to a capped, rotated file in the daemon's run folder that a caller can neither grow without bound nor forge. The log line is designed, not built.
rules.detail: A capped file has a stated size and rotation (for example 1 MiB) and refusals are rate-limited per peer, so a caller cannot fill the disk through the log. A value from a peer is written as a field, never spliced into the message, and control sequences are stripped. The list of things never logged is a list in the logging package that a canary test walks; a new kind of sensitive value is added to the list, not to each call.
rules.why: Practice; a secret in a log outlives the process that wrote it, and a program that runs agents handles prompts and conversations that are as private as a secret. A log a caller can grow or forge is an attack on the disk or the record.

checks.note: sloglint in golangci-lint (attr-only, no-global, context options; to verify) plus a run-the-binary test that parses logs for level and time and a canary secret that must not appear. Plant: a log of a canary token, prompt or address fails, and a file log that grows past its cap fails. Control: a log line with level, time and no canary passes

open: Secret-free needs the canary test; the sloglint option set is to verify.
rules.note: The version-and-run-id rule for every log line is go.logging.2.

rules.rule: Journal lines carry a priority prefix under JOURNAL_STREAM, and none without it.
rules.why: Evidence T; the test is planned (fix A9).

checks.note: terminal test that sets JOURNAL_STREAM and asserts each line carries the systemd priority prefix; without it no prefix The prefix is <N>, the systemd priority; the test runs through uitest. Plant: a line without a prefix under the variable fails. Control: a prefixed line passes

rules.rule: An audit record is an append-only file the program owns, the service manager's journal may hold a copy but is never the record, and a daemon answers a person in plain words, writing the underlying tool's own words only to its log.
rules.detail: The audit file lives in the program's state folder, is opened for append only, and survives a journal rotation. A tool's raw error (a service manager's message, a library's text) goes to the log with the command that produced it; the answer to the person says what happened and what to do in the program's own words.
rules.why: An audit record that rotates away with the journal is not an audit, and a raw tool message shown to a person is noise at best and a leak of internals at worst.

checks.note: a test that the audit writer opens its file append-only in the state folder and that a journal-only audit fails; a test that drives a failing tool and asserts the person's answer holds none of the tool's text while the log does. Plant: an audit written only to the journal fails, and an answer that carries a service manager's raw message fails. Control: an append-only audit file and an answer in the program's own words pass

rules.rule: A daemon's outward events are one closed list with a versioned payload, pushed through channels behind an interface, and documented per event in an example file that the gate holds equal to what the daemon sends.
rules.detail: Each event names its subject, its data and the version of its payload. The channel interface has one adapter per kind (a push service, a webhook, a kind added later); the event list does not change when a channel is added. The example file lists every event with a sample payload, and a test renders every event through the real encoder and compares it with the file in both directions, so an event sent but not documented, or documented but never sent, fails.
rules.why: A notification channel is a contract nobody tests unless the list is closed and held to its document; a silent drift is found by a person who missed an alert.

unless.reason: A daemon that sends no notification has no event list.

checks.note: a test that encodes every event in the closed list and compares the set and each payload with the example file, both ways. Plant: an event added in code and missing from the example file fails, and a field renamed in code fails. Control: a list equal to the example file passes

rules.rule: A notification is sent only on a change; when no earlier state is readable the first run sets a silent baseline; sends are limited per subject and event; quiet hours hold back all but a bad event; and notifying rides an existing run, never a new timer.
rules.detail: A fresh install or a lost state file sends nothing on its first pass and records what it saw. The rate limit is a stated count per subject, event and day (for example one). Quiet hours are the owner's setting; an event marked bad passes through them. The check that may notify runs inside a run the daemon already makes (a request, a scheduled job that exists for its own reason), so notifying adds no wake-up (daemon.lifecycle.5).
rules.why: Noise is what gets a channel muted in its second month, and a timer added only to notify costs idle power every hour for an alert that seldom comes.

unless.reason: A daemon that sends no notification has nothing to rate.

checks.note: a table test: an unchanged state sends nothing, a fresh install sends nothing, a second send within the limit is dropped, a quiet-hour good event is held and a bad one passes; and the timer analyser of daemon.resilience.6 finds no timer in the notify package. Plant: a fresh install that sends a notification for every subject fails, and a notify package with its own ticker fails. Control: a change after a baseline sends one notification passes

rules.rule: A client carrying a credential follows no redirect and reports one as an error naming the callee; a request to an owner-configured address puts its token in a header, never the address, signs the body with a timestamp, resolves the name once and dials the address it checked, needs https outside loopback and private networks, and sends nothing a read permission would not show.
rules.detail: The shared client sets a redirect policy that returns an error when the request carries a credential. A webhook or similar call uses an Authorization header, an HMAC over the timestamp and the body, a stated timeout (for example 10 seconds), and a dialer that connects to the resolved address it validated, so a DNS answer cannot change between the check and the dial. Plain http is allowed only to loopback, private or private-network addresses. The body is built from what the read permission for that subject would return, never from internal state.
rules.why: Each closes a real leak: a key sent on to a redirect target, a token in an address that lands in a log, a DNS rebind between check and dial, and a payload that tells a channel more than its reader may know.

unless.reason: A program that builds no HTTP client calls nothing out.

checks.note: tests on the shared client constructor: a credentialed request to a stub that redirects must fail naming the callee; a webhook to a stub asserts the header token, the signature over timestamp and body, a single resolve and a dial to the checked address; an http address outside private ranges is refused. Plant: a client that follows a redirect with an Authorization header fails, and a token in the query string fails. Control: the shared client refusing the redirect and signing the body passes

rules.note: daemon.access.5 and service.outbound.2 hold timeouts; this rule adds where a credential may travel.

rules.rule: A record or answer about an outbound channel never holds its address or token, its failure text is the program's own words, length-capped and cleaned, and a call to an outside service whose allowance is shared has a daily budget in code and uses the cheapest request that answers.
rules.detail: A channel is shown by name and kind only. A failure from the far side is reduced to a short sentence of the program's own with control characters stripped, and the raw text goes to the log without the address or token. A shared allowance is one the caller does not own alone (an anonymous rate limit, a public registry's quota); the budget is a constant per service and day, counted in the program's state, and a call past it is skipped with a sentence. The cheapest request is the one that reads the least (a HEAD, a digest, a conditional request).
rules.why: A channel address often is its credential, so any record that holds it leaks it. A shared public allowance spent carelessly is taken from everyone who shares it.

checks.note: a canary test that configures a channel with a canary address and token, drives a failure and reads every record, answer and log line for the canary; a test that the budget table has an entry for every shared-allowance client and that the call past the budget is skipped. Plant: a channel status answer carrying the webhook address fails, and a registry client with no daily budget fails. Control: an answer naming the channel only, and a budgeted client, pass

rules.rule: A daemon bounds its work: a request body cap, a cap on concurrent requests and bounded queues.
rules.why: Practice; unbounded work turns a burst into an outage. Part of the supervision row, whose restart half is daemon.units.3.

checks.note: test that sends more than the cap and sees a refusal. Plant: a handler with no cap accepts the oversized request and fails. Control: the capped handler refuses it

rules.rule: A panic in a goroutine ends the process, so every goroutine recovers at its edge or the supervisor restarts it, and the restart has a stated limit.
rules.why: Practice. Goroutine ownership itself is go.concurrency.2.

checks.note: start test with a panic in a goroutine, asserting recovery at the edge or a supervised restart within the limit The start test is a panic-in-goroutine test. Plant: a goroutine that panics and takes the process down with no restart fails. Control: a goroutine that recovers passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Failed work parks with a reason and a redrive path (a dead letter), and a redrive filters for what can still resolve.
rules.why: Practice; parked work with no reason or no way back is lost work.
rules.review_question: Where does this failed work park, with what reason, and how is it redriven?
open: Dead-letter redrive is review; no check is named.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A retried path is safe twice: one helper calls any daemon route or job handler twice and compares state; a repeated idempotency key replays the stored outcome and the same key with a different request conflicts.
rules.detail: The list of writing routes is taken from the contract, not from the author. The same double-call helper serves the command rule (cli.commands.6) and is required for daemon routes by an analyser.
rules.why: Practice only; it would become a rule with a duplicate-effect fault in one of our daemons. The command-side twin is cli.commands.2.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. shared twice-call helper plus a list of writing routes from the contract; a test fails when a writing route lacks a twice-test. Plant: an append-on-every-call handler fails. Control: an idempotent handler passes

open: Proposed plant for a repeated idempotency key; no duplicate-effect fault in a daemon of ours so far.

rules.rule: Retry discipline: one constructor carries the policy; it retries only idempotent calls, at one layer, with backoff, jitter and a budget, and hand-rolled retry loops are banned.
rules.detail: A syntax rule flags a sleep or timer inside a loop around a call with an error check outside the retry constructor; retry libraries are banned by depguard; a behaviour budget test checks the retry ratio, because recursion or a ticker passes the form.
rules.why: Practice only; only the retry-library ban is cheap. It would become a rule with a retry fault in the run log.

unless.reason: A program that retries nothing has no policy to carry.

checks.note: ast-grep ban of a sleep inside a loop around a call, and depguard ban of retry libraries. Plant: a hand-rolled retry loop fails. Control: a call through the retry constructor passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A daemon reads the machine only on a request or during a run it already pays for; a watcher waits on its source's own event stream and never polls; one short cache shares a round of reads between concurrent readers; and a timer, poll or resident sampler for a value nobody is reading needs a measured idle cost and a recorded reason.
rules.detail: The cache lives for a stated short time (for example 15 seconds) and serves readers that arrive while a read is in flight or fresh; it is never refreshed on a timer. A value only known while watched is left out after a restart, not carried forward. An exception names its measured cost (daemon.resilience.7) and its reason in a recorded decision.
rules.why: A poll costs power every hour whether anyone looks or not, and it makes behaviour depend on a clock no one set. Reading on request keeps idle cost at zero and every read explainable.

checks.note: a syntax rule refusing time.NewTicker, time.Tick and a sleep inside a loop outside the packages listed with a recorded decision; a test that runs the daemon idle with no requests and asserts no probe or read is made. Plant: a ticker that samples the machine every minute with no recorded decision fails. Control: a read on request through the shared short cache passes

rules.rule: A recurring run or a daemon read states a processor and memory budget, measured on the real machine before it ships and again when it grows.
rules.detail: The budget is a number in the code or the decision beside it, with the method of the measure (for example the tree's CPU time through proc.Usage, run interleaved with and without the work, other work paused) and the date and machine it was taken on. A change that adds work to the run, a new probe or a shorter interval is measured again before it merges.
rules.why: A measured budget turns a preference for quiet into a check; an unmeasured run grows by small additions until the machine never sleeps.

checks.note: v1 class record. a release check that every recurring run and probe in the run table has a budget entry with a measured value, a method, a machine and a date no older than its last change. Plant: a new recurring run with no budget entry fails. Control: a run with a measured budget dated after its last change passes

rules.rule: Service-manager files (plist, unit) are well formed, and each comes from a template.
rules.why: Practice; a malformed plist is silently ignored by the manager.

checks.note: plutil -lint on the rendered plist (macOS), the unit-render test of daemon.units.2, systemd-analyze verify on a Linux host. Plant: a malformed plist fails. Control: the rendered plist passes

open: The plutil plant was run in an earlier trial; the Linux verify step needs a Linux host.

rules.rule: A daemon runs with the least identity that can reach what it serves, from one template per service manager, with a sandbox wherever the manager offers one, and its notes state the trust line.
rules.detail: Least identity is chosen per platform, not assumed: a separate system account where the manager can give one (systemd DynamicUser= or User=), and on a single-user machine the owner's own account (a launchd LaunchAgent), never root, when a separate account would need more privilege to reach the owner's data than the owner already has. A daemon never runs as root to serve owner-level requests. Each supported manager has its own template; a manager added later adds a template and a golden, and the rule does not change. The notes name who may reach the daemon, what that caller gains, and which manager settings hold the line. The rendered templates are byte-compared to a golden; systemd-analyze verify and systemd-analyze security with a threshold run on Linux (the threshold makes the command exit non-zero above an exposure level, per a systemd commit; not run, no Linux box here); plutil -lint runs on macOS, and the plist names no UserName of root.
rules.why: Practice; a daemon with more identity than it needs turns any bug into a compromise of that identity. On a laptop a separate account is more exposure, not less, so the principle is least identity with the trust line written down.

checks.note: render each manager's template and byte-compare to a golden; systemd-analyze security --threshold N on Linux; plutil -lint on macOS and a test that the plist sets no root identity; a test that the notes carry a trust-line section. Plant: a systemd template dropping a sandbox directive fails, and a plist run as root fails. Control: the full template for each manager passes

open: Security threshold behaviour is from source, not run.

rules.rule: The unit template restarts the daemon on failure only, with a backoff and a stated limit set in each manager's own terms; an idle exit is a clean exit and is never restarted; a one-shot job is never placed where the manager reruns it at load or login; and the health document counts restarts.
rules.detail: Under systemd: Restart=on-failure with RestartSec and StartLimitBurst plus StartLimitIntervalSec, never Restart=always, so a daemon that leaves after its idle time (daemon.lifecycle.5) stays down until its socket wakes it. Under launchd: KeepAlive with SuccessfulExit false and a ThrottleInterval, never a bare KeepAlive true for a job that exits on idle. A one-shot job (an update, a migration) has neither RunAtLoad nor KeepAlive and is not written to a folder the manager loads at login (under launchd, not in ~/Library/LaunchAgents); it is written in the program's state folder, started from there and removed when it ends, and doctor names one that is left. A manager added later states its own restart, backoff, limit and one-shot settings in the test table.
rules.why: A daemon that dies and stays dead is an outage no one sees; the limit stops a crash loop. A restart on a clean idle exit keeps a process awake that should sleep, and a one-shot job left where the manager loads it reruns at every login.

checks.note: unit-render test with one row per manager asserting restart on failure only, a backoff and a limit (systemd Restart=on-failure, RestartSec, StartLimitBurst; launchd KeepAlive SuccessfulExit false, ThrottleInterval), that a one-shot job's plist or unit has no load-time or keep-alive key and is written outside the login-loaded folder, and that the health document carries a restart count. Plant: a unit with Restart=always, a plist with KeepAlive true on an idle-exit daemon, and a one-shot plist in the LaunchAgents folder each fail. Control: restart on failure with a backoff and a limit, and a one-shot job in the state folder, pass

rules.note: Split from the daemon bounds-and-supervision row; the other parts are daemon.resilience.1 to 3. Rewritten with daemon.lifecycle.5 (idle by default) as the R-15 amendment to D-T53 asks.

rules.rule: Each state file has one writer; a privileged process writes only files it alone owns, in a folder no less privileged account can write; and a daemon that runs as a person passes only requests that give a process of that person nothing it did not already have.
rules.detail: A test lists every state file with its one writer and its folder, and fails on a file with two writers or a privileged writer in a folder another account can write. A route or verb that would widen what a caller of the person's daemon can do (a passed write, a passed POST, a run of a command the caller could not run itself) is refused until a design rules it, and the route table marks each route as read or as ruled by a named design.
rules.why: A root writer in a folder a person owns can be tricked by a link into writing anywhere, and a person's daemon that passes more than the person has is a privilege raise for anyone who reaches it.

checks.note: a table test of state files, writers and folder owners against the code's write paths, and a route-table test that refuses a writing route with no named design. Plant: a second writer of one state file fails, and a privileged write into a person-owned folder fails; a passed POST route with no design fails. Control: one writer per file in its own folder, and read-only passed routes, pass

rules.note: store.seams.4 records writers per seam; this rule binds the privilege of each writer.

rules.rule: Every doc carries its type, status and version or as-of date, in typed front matter or in one fixed header line or status paragraph, read by one schema, and indexes are generated from it, never written by hand.
rules.detail: A repo declares one container for these fields: typed front matter, a fixed header line (Version, Status and Ages-with), or a bold status paragraph that opens the doc. Whatever the container, one shared parser reads it into the same fields and validates them against one JSON Schema; a doc with no type or status fails, and a doc in a container other than the declared one fails. The sidebar or index (a table of notes included) is generated from the folders and these fields, or checked against them by a test, never kept by hand. Every doc has a named owner, in the fields or in one owners file.
rules.why: No pinned repo had front matter; without a type, a status and an owner nobody can tell a current record from an old one or who keeps it true. The invariants are the rule; the container is the repo's choice, so a repo that already writes a header line or a status paragraph is held to the same fields without a rewrite.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. one shared docs check (companion docs) reads the declared container (front matter, header line or status paragraph) into one record and validates it against one JSON Schema with ajv; the index is regenerated and diffed. Plant: a doc with no type fails; a doc in an undeclared container fails; a hand-edited index row fails. Control: a complete doc in the declared container passes

open: Note, 8 Nov 2026: the indexes this rule names and a repository still writes by hand (the decisions index and the decisions section of the architecture document, the agent instruction file’s table of documents, the list of rules not yet met) are this rule not yet applied, and the shared-files guide lists them. Authored files also carry no digest chain (docs.freshness.8).
A remark front-matter plugin was rejected: last published in 2023.
Applies to UI repositories only once their catalogue carries the row.
rules.note: Merges the Go row, the UI documentation row and the reference's typed-doc and owner rules.

rules.rule: The docs/ folder holds typed documents that are true now and marked records, and working material such as epics, handovers and run notes lives outside it.
rules.detail: Marked records are of three kinds, each typed so the docs check knows it is a record. A superseded decision note stays, marked at its top with its successor, keeping its old sections and its rejected alternatives with their reasons. A history log (what landed, when) is append-only and marked as history; an edit to an earlier entry fails. Unadopted proposals live in one marked folder with an index and bind nothing until a decision adopts them; nothing outside that folder cites a proposal as a rule. Nothing in docs/ is deleted to retire it.
rules.why: Notes mixed into the docs folder read as current fact and go stale unseen. A record that is marked is not that risk: deleting it loses the reasons behind the current design, and marking it keeps them without letting them pass for current fact.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the docs check fails a file under the docs folder that has no valid type, a superseded note with no successor link at its top, an edit to an earlier entry of a history log, and a citation of a proposal from outside its folder as binding. Plant: a handover note placed under the docs folder fails; a history log with a changed earlier line fails; a superseded note with no successor line fails. Control: the same note under the work folder passes; a marked superseded note passes

rules.rule: A non-generated doc carries an as-of date and reads as a record of that day, a date-only change is reported, and a superseded section carries a dated note naming the note that replaced it, which links back.
rules.detail: A section that a later note replaces keeps its text; a dated line at its top names the replacing note, and the replacing note links back to the section. A generated doc carries no as-of date (docs.freshness.7).
rules.why: A date bumped with no content change makes an old claim look fresh, and a section replaced without a note reads as current.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a diff check in the docs check (a date-only change) fails an as-of change with no other content change in the same file, and a section supersession note whose target does not link back fails. Plant: a doc whose only change is its date fails; a superseded-section note naming a note with no back link fails. Control: a date moved with its content passes

open: Proposed; the plant was not run.

rules.rule: A doc states a current fact only where a check holds it, and says what is built and what is only designed.
rules.detail: Generated reference is regenerated and diffed in the gate, numbers come from a script, paths are links that the link check follows, and every other doc is a dated record of the day it was written. A doc never says to build to a design that is frozen or to a thing that is not built.
rules.why: A product doc still said "Build to it today" for a frozen tree.

checks.note: the gate regenerates each generated reference doc and fails on a diff. Plant: a generated reference doc edited by hand fails. Control: a freshly generated doc passes

rules.review_question: Does this doc say what is built and what is only designed?
open: The built-against-designed clause is review; only the generated-reference part has a check.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: A (one product doc still said "Build to it today" for a frozen tree)

rules.rule: A decision is never edited in place: it is superseded by number, the superseding record names the old one, the old one is marked, and the links point both ways.
rules.detail: A decision has a number that is never reused. A repo declares its container: one file per decision, numbered decisions inside design notes, or entries in one append-only log amended by dated sub-entries. In every container a reversal is a new decision that names the one it replaces, the old one gains a superseded mark that names its successor, its text stays, and every cited decision number resolves.
rules.why: A decision that supersedes another without the back link leaves two live answers, and an edit in place loses what was decided and why. The invariants are the rule; the container is the repo's choice.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the docs check reads the declared container, fails a decision whose text changed after it landed (other than its superseded mark), a supersession without the back mark, a reused number and a cited number that does not resolve. Plant: a decision superseding another without the back link fails; an edit to a landed decision's text fails. Control: a new decision with links in both directions passes

rules.rule: A stub, a placeholder return or a not-implemented body in shipped source is reported.
rules.detail: A syntax scan counts not-implemented throws, TODO returns and stub bodies. It is a report, not a gate.
rules.why: A shipped stub looks like a feature.

checks.note: ESLint no-restricted-syntax (Biome form is a GritQL plugin) on throw new Error("not implemented") and TODO returns, as a report. Plant: a fixture stub is counted. Control: a real body is not counted

open: The false-positive rate is unknown.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: A

rules.rule: A generated doc says so in its first lines with the command that makes it, the gate regenerates and diffs it, and the help text and the doc for the same subject come from one source.
rules.detail: The source is the program's command registry (one declaration per command with its summary, the version it arrived in, what a second run does and who may run it); help, help --json, the README's command table, the MCP tool list, agent skill text and the generated guide are rendered from it. A generated file opens with a line that says it is generated, by which command, and not to edit it. The gate runs the command and fails on any difference. Prose about a command that is not generated links to the generated part instead of restating it. There is one registry and help prints it; MCP tools and the skill text are generated from it. Help is written once, the README's command table is generated from it, and a test fails when they differ. A guide generated from lessons beside the code says not to edit it here.
rules.why: A command described once and rendered everywhere cannot drift: the agent's skill, the tool list and the README are the program's own words, not a second copy of them.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a shared generate-and-diff step in gragas that runs each generated doc's named command and fails on a difference or on a generated file with no generator line. Plant: a hand edit to the generated command table fails; a generated file with no generator line fails. Control: a freshly generated doc passes

open: Planned (R-15 sequencing): binds once the shared generator or test exists in gragas.
rules.note: The command-registry rule itself is in the CLI part; this is its docs half.

rules.rule: No hand-written file carries a digest of the current state: a digest lives in the generated output, and a change to the state adds a note with a reason.
rules.detail: A chain whose newest line must equal the digest of the current state is wrong for every change in flight after any other lands, and the fix is a hand edit in a file nobody else should edit. The digest moves into the generated listing's header; the reason moves into a note per change, a new file with the date and at least a few words of why. The check is that when the listing's digest differs from the base's, the change adds a note. What is lost is the chain's proof that every past listing was recorded; the notes and the history give the same answer with one more command. Ratchets whose point is a hand edit that can only lower a count are not chains and stay.
rules.why: Own measure: a file of this kind changed in 10 commits in three days, and every one appended a line to a chain, so any two changes in flight conflicted and the second one's digest was wrong after the rebase.

sources.says: A change is one small file in a folder; the release step joins them.

checks.note: the listing's check fails an authored file that holds a changes chain key and fails a changed listing with no new note. Plant: a chain line appended by hand fails. Control: a note file added with the regenerated listing passes

open: Proposed until the listing check reads notes. That is step 8 of gragas#477 (surface notes replace the digest chain); it has no tool key to bind to until then.

rules.rule: Each program owns a glossary of its terms, held to its code by a check, and a product term is defined once and linked wherever it appears.
rules.detail: The glossary lists each term with its definition, its aliases (prior names and outside words it translates) and the names that were retired, with what was retired when. Every schema, event or public name the program publishes is a term; every term names one of those or a retired name; every retired name in the lint configuration is in the glossary. Every page and help text links the first use of a term on it to its glossary entry, and the same thing carries the same name everywhere. A map of which program owns which concept sits beside the glossaries. An editor that shows a term's definition on hover is an aid for people only; agents read the glossary file.
rules.why: Fault evidence in our own repos: word faults 7, 3 and 2 in three repos, and the old organisation name found 181 times in one repo by a spell tool. Names that drift between pages and services make a reader and an agent guess which thing is meant.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a glossary data file lists each term, its page and its banned alternates; (a companion glossary check) fails on the built pages when the first use of a term on a page does not link to its glossary anchor, and the retired-word check (cspell flagWords) fails the alternate names. Plant: a page that uses an alternate name fails; a page that mentions a term without the link fails. Control: a page that uses the term with its link passes

rules.review_question: Is this a new name for a thing the glossary already names, and is every published schema or event a term?
open: Half holds: names and links are checks; whether a new name is the same thing as an old one is review.
Planned only: no link check exists yet.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: A (word faults 7, 3 and 2 in three repos)
rules.note: Held for words in code by docs.glossary.2. Glossary-to-code consistency (every published schema or event is a term) is a check the part still has to design.

rules.rule: A retired word fails where it is typed, in code, comments and docs, and the failure names the right word.
rules.detail: The retired-words list maps each retired word to its right word, and the failure message carries that right word. It covers identifiers, comments, strings and markdown, and a word retired in every sense fails in docs and comments as well as code. A retired identifier is not the same as a retired word: a name kept as a code name (a wire value or a compound the registry still requires) stays allowed. The list lives in one shared place and is synced into each repo, and each repo's own linter holds the names it retired so a retired name fails in the service that retired it. A write-time hook runs the scan on the edited file.
rules.why: A retired name that keeps appearing spreads back into new code. A spell tool found 181 hits of the old organisation name in one repo alone, and only one repo had a gate (five retired words).

checks.note: typos (crate-ci/typos) over identifiers, comments and docs with a retired-words file mapping each word to its right word under extend-words; fallback cspell flagWords with word->replacement entries, and ignoreRegExpList for retired identifiers kept as code names. Plant: a retired word in a comment, in an identifier and in a markdown file each fails and names the right word. Control: a file using the right word passes

ESLint no-restricted-syntax with an Identifier or Literal selector holding the retired names as a regex and the right word in the message, no plugin (Biome form is a GritQL plugin on the same names). Plant: an identifier or string literal using a retired word fails with the right word in the message. Control: the right word passes
forbidigo or ast-grep with the right word in the message. Plant: an identifier using a retired word fails with the right word in the message. Control: the right word passes

open: A retired word that is also a normal word needs a context rule that the typos tool cannot give: list it as exact-case only.
cspell splits camelCase and so sees single words only: names belong to the identifier scan.
Whether the shared list's home is the standards repository is proposed, not settled.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: own measure (a spell tool found 181 hits of the old organisation name in one repo, which has a retired-words check)
rules.note: Merges the retired-word rule from the spell-check row with the per-program retired-identifier rules.

rules.rule: Each word set that two programs share has one definition, and a machine-readable code is kept apart from its sentence in a closed, documented set.
rules.detail: For exit codes the check is the one in the code part: a documented table compared with the constants. Other shared word sets live in one data file consumed by every language through the generator, with a schema that separates the machine code from the sentence a person reads.
rules.why: Two programs that each spell out a code or status word drift apart, and a code that is also a sentence cannot be changed without breaking readers.

rules.rule: Printed text, the README and the how-to guides carry no code identifier, no word from a listed set of internal jargon, and no internal doc path, register, issue, rule or decision id, which belong in the register, the design notes and commits.
rules.detail: Printed text is every string the program shows a person: help, hints, errors, prompts and status rows. A code identifier is a package, type or function name as it appears in the code. The jargon list is one data file per repo, next to the glossary. An id is any pattern the citation resolver knows (rule, decision, ticket, register row) and any path into the docs or design folders. Design notes, the register, agent files and commits may use all of these. A word a person needs that is also an identifier is defined in the glossary and spelled the way a person says it.
rules.why: A person reading help or a guide cannot follow an internal name or id anywhere, so it is noise that also leaks how the code is built; the id belongs where the people who can follow it read.

rules.rule: Docs have no broken file link or anchor, checked offline in the gate, and external links are checked by a separate command that runs as a non-blocking step of the release recipe, never as a gate step and never on a schedule.
rules.detail: Relative links and heading anchors are checked offline, with fragments included (without --include-fragments the anchor breaks are not seen). External links are checked by their own command over the network, with a cache; the release recipe runs it and prints its result in the release record, and a dead link opens a finding but does not stop the release. The gate never reaches the network for links. A docs-site build that fails on broken links is the same rule when a site exists; no docs site is run today. Docs and agent instruction files are checked alike. Docs also have no markdown error and pass spelling.
rules.why: One broken file link in one repo and 36 fragment failures in one file of another, on 5,800 links of which 4,200 are remote. A site that is down for an hour is not the repo's fault, so it must not stop a push, but a dead source must still be seen before a release goes out.

rules.rule: A backticked path in a comment or doc resolves or the comment says it is a dead path and why, a dependency version named in prose equals the lockfile's, and a sentence claiming CI or a workflow runs a command is checked against the workflow files.
rules.detail: The resolver reads comments and docs. A version is a package name followed by a version in prose; it is compared with the lockfile (go.sum, the package lock) and fails on a mismatch. A CI claim is a sentence that names a workflow, CI or a hosted runner and a command; the command must appear in a workflow file with the trigger the sentence names, so a doc that says CI runs the gate on push fails when no workflow does.
rules.why: A comment that points at a path that is gone sends a reader and an agent to nothing; a version or a CI claim in prose is a second copy of a fact whose home is the lockfile or the workflow, and it goes stale first.

rules.rule: A README keeps the shape of its kind: a directory README answers what is here, how to run it and where the rules are and points to AGENTS.md, a package README states what it is, what it exports, what it may import and how it is tested, and a CLI's product README has a fixed order of parts.
rules.detail: The kind follows from where the README sits: the repo root holds the product README, a package root a package README, any other folder a directory README. The product order is: a claim, what it is, install, getting started, the commands table (generated from help), longer parts, limits, where things live, documentation and contributing. A new kind adds its shape here and to the check, never a README with no kind. The package README's import line agrees with the declared import table.
rules.why: A README with a known shape is read in one pass by a stranger and can be partly generated; a README that does not point to the rules sends an agent and a person to guess.

rules.rule: No em dash in any tracked file, no semicolon in text a program prints, and headings are in sentence case; docs may use the semicolon.
rules.detail: The em dash scan reads every tracked text file, code and data included; a repo's own rule format uses another separator. The semicolon scan reads the strings a program prints (messages, help, errors, status rows), not docs and not code syntax. The heading scan reads markdown, HTML and .astro files. Words kept in data files are exported as text for the scan to read. In source strings a lint rule rejects string literals that contain an em dash, and a printed-string literal that contains a semicolon. ESLint form: `no-restricted-syntax` on such literals. Biome form: a GritQL plugin on the same literals.
rules.why: Punctuation style is checkable and drifts without a check; evidence D. An em dash is the mark that most often survives from generated text, and a semicolon in a terminal line splits one fact into two half-sentences.

checks.note: a plain scan for the em dash over every tracked text file. Plant: a line with an em dash in a doc and in a data file fail; a doc with a semicolon passes. Control: a clean sentence passes

rules.rule: Written output puts the point first and is honest about what it knows, text the program prints carries no joke, aside or personality and a status row is a fact, not a sentence, and a check refuses a filler-word list and the not-X-but-Y form in docs and printed text.
rules.detail: There are two registers. Docs may be warm and may joke. Text the program prints (help, errors, status rows, prompts) is plain fact: no joke, aside, exclamation or first person, and a status row is a value with its label. A repo keeps one list of refused filler words and phrases in its style config, and the check also refuses the not-X-but-Y construction. Point-first order and honesty stay with the reader.
rules.why: Printed text is read in a hurry and parsed by scripts, so personality there is noise; the filler patterns are the ones a model reaches for and a reader stops trusting. Tone, honesty and order cannot be checked by a pattern, so a reader or a model lens judges them.

rules.rule: A measured figure in a doc carries its date, the machine and whose measurement it is, a claim about outside behaviour cites a source and what it says, and a doc that generalises from one machine says so.
rules.detail: No figure claims more precision than its source: a source in whole units gives no decimal, an estimate is marked as one (≈), and a remainder the doc cannot explain is its own row, never spread over the rest. A doc says what it can and cannot promise. Generated figures carry the same three facts from the generator.
rules.why: A number without its date and machine reads as a property of the product when it is one reading on one day, and a figure with more decimals than its source is a claim nobody measured.
rules.review_question: Does each figure in this doc say when, on what machine and by whom it was measured, and does it claim more precision than its source?

rules.rule: Storage keys are built only by the shared key builder; no code assembles a key string by hand.
rules.detail: Partition and sort keys, index keys and key prefixes come from functions in the store's key-building layer. A string that looks like a key (an entity prefix joined with an id) anywhere else fails.
rules.why: Hand-built keys drift between writers and readers, and a typo returns nothing instead of failing.

checks.note: ESLint no-restricted-syntax on template literals and string concatenation that build a key prefix outside the key-builder module. Plant: a handler that writes `USER#${id}` itself fails. Control: the same key from the key builder passes
forbidigo on key-prefix string literals outside the store package. Plant: a key prefix literal in a handler fails. Control: the key builder's own literal passes

rules.rule: Each table has a checked-in list of its access patterns, and every query function maps to a line on it.
rules.detail: Each line names the question and the key or index that answers it in one request. A query function in the key-building layer that matches no line fails; a line with no query function is reported.
rules.why: A DynamoDB model is designed from its access patterns and cannot be made generic later: a new pattern needs a new index or a data migration. Without the list, the next pattern is found in production as a scan or a filter that reads the whole partition.

checks.note: a test iterates the key builder's query functions and fails when one is not named on the access-pattern list. Plant: a query function on an unlisted index fails; a list line naming a function that does not exist fails. Control: every query function listed passes

rules.review_question: Which access pattern is not on the list, and how would it be added?
open: Agents add a global secondary index to make a new query work, which locks in an unplanned pattern; the review question is the guard until the test exists.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice (argued from the modelling guidance, no fault in our record)

rules.rule: Each table's design note states the highest write rate one partition-key value will see and what happens beyond it, and a read that must see its own write goes to the base table, not a secondary index.
rules.why: Hot partitions throttle even when the table's total capacity is enough, and secondary indexes update asynchronously, serving only eventually consistent reads.
rules.review_question: What is the highest write rate any single value of this partition key will see, and what happens on a read after a write through an index?
open: Measure: the service's throttle counts per table, read at release.
No plant yet: a seeded table keyed on the current date, with every write on one value, must be flagged.
Look up current per-partition throughput figures before quoting any.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice (argued from the service builders' own account)
rules.note: Agents pick a key from the entity's natural fields, such as a date or a tenant, which concentrates writes.

rules.rule: A change to what a table holds is additive where it can be, and otherwise a migration with a written plan whose backfill is resumable and safe to run twice.
rules.detail: Additive means readers default a missing attribute and writers add it as items are touched. A change that rewrites every item, or a new index that needs a backfill, is an extract-transform-load job with a written plan: a parallel scan, batched writes, resumable, idempotent.
rules.why: A new access pattern on existing data usually needs a full rewrite, and a one-off script run once and never retested leaves the table half migrated when it fails.

checks.note: the backfill runs twice in a test against a local table, and the second run changes nothing. Plant: a backfill that appends instead of setting fails the run-twice test. Control: an idempotent backfill passes

rules.review_question: What do old and new readers see while the backfill is half done?
rules.note: Agents write the one-off script and run it once; the run-twice test is the guard.

rules.rule: A Scan runs only in a migration or an export named on a short allow list, and a filter expression is never how a query gets its result.
rules.detail: If removing a filter expression would change the answer a user sees, the key design is wrong and the access-pattern list needs a new line. The scanned-to-returned item ratio is measured per action.
rules.why: A filter is applied after the items are read, so every removed item is still paid for and the response size limit is hit before the filter runs: a filter cannot save a bad model.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing ScanCommand and FilterExpression outside allow-listed migration and export paths. Plant: a Scan in a handler's action file fails. Control: the same call in an allow-listed migration passes
forbidigo on the DynamoDB Scan call outside allow-listed paths. Plant: a Scan call in a handler fails. Control: a Scan in an allow-listed migration passes

rules.review_question: Does any query rely on a filter expression for its result, and is the access-pattern list missing a line?
