rules.rule: Aggregate writes go only through the shared write toolkit's versioned write functions; deletes are allowed only in allow-listed short-lived actions; audit tables are append-only.
rules.detail: Every service that uses DynamoDB writes aggregates through the toolkit, which owns the version check and the conditional write. A delete outside the allow list fails. An audit table, such as a record of sign-in events, accepts inserts only. The toolkit has a conformance suite that every release runs.
rules.why: One write path is the only place where conditions, versions and retries can be proved once and trusted everywhere.

checks.note: ESLint no-restricted-imports and no-restricted-syntax on PutCommand, UpdateCommand and DeleteCommand outside the toolkit and the delete allow list. Plant: a raw update in a service action fails; a delete outside the allow list fails. Control: a write through the toolkit passes
the toolkit conformance suite, run at every toolkit release. Plant: a toolkit write that drops its version check fails the suite. Control: the released toolkit passes

rules.rule: Every insert-if-absent and every read-modify-write uses a condition expression in the same call; uniqueness beyond the primary key is kept by a guard item written in the same transaction; a retried transactional write carries a client token.
rules.detail: Check-then-write is the case this rule exists for, written in one conditional call instead of a read followed by a write.
rules.why: Uniqueness and association checks written as read-then-write are broken by races. A transactional write with a client token is idempotent for a window, so a retry does not write twice.

checks.note: the toolkit conformance suite runs two concurrent creates with the same unique value and expects one success and one typed conflict, and retries a transaction with the same token and expects one write. Plant: a toolkit write that skips its condition lets both creates through and fails the test. Control: the conditional write passes

rules.rule: Where an item carries a time-to-live attribute, every read that must not see an expired item checks the attribute itself.
rules.detail: The table's deletion of expired items is cleanup, never the moment of expiry.
rules.why: Expired items are deleted only eventually, typically within about two days, so a session or processing-key table that trusts deletion honours an expired token for that long.

checks.note: a toolkit read-helper test inserts an item whose expiry is past and still present, and asserts the helper does not return it. Plant: a read helper that does not compare the attribute fails. Control: the helper that compares it passes

rules.rule: Every gate run goes through one shared gate command that runs every check at each tier, from the hooks and from the land job.
rules.detail: The same command serves every tier (on write, commit, stop, push, land, full or after release), chosen by a flag, and it is the same in every repo: one gate script, shared, with no second entry point that runs checks. A Go repo's single `check` target and a TypeScript repo's single gate script are both this command. The hook's list is a declared subset of the land job's list: the land job calls the push tier and then the full tier, and the full tier holds what the push leaves out (the tests, the vulnerability scan, the conformance check), so every member of either runs before main.
rules.why: Separate entry points drift: a check is added to one and not the other. A hook that runs a fast subset of its own reports green for what the land job would refuse, so the subset is declared in the land job's list, and the land job runs every member of it and of the full tier on the merged tree before main: nothing the land job would refuse reaches main.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. The gate command's own test walks the rule registry and fails when a registered check is not reachable from the command at its home tier, or when a hook or land job calls anything but the command. Plant: A check registered with a home tier but missing from the command fails; a hook that runs a private list of checks fails. Control: Every hook and the land job calling only the one command passes.

One shared `check` make target from a shared Makefile fragment that the hooks also call. Plant: A check target defined in the Makefile but not reachable from `check` fails. Control: All check targets reachable from `check` passes.

open: Today one TypeScript repo's pre-push hook runs only the fast gate subset, so the one-command rule is not yet true there.
rules.note: Same rule as the shared gate script, the one gate command per tier and the gate orchestration kind (see tools). The scope-planning half of the TypeScript source is gates.command.4.

rules.rule: An agent-time check finishes within 2 seconds on the edited file or runs at the agent's stop; the finding appears where the author is.
rules.detail: After each edit the changed file is formatted and linted by a warm, untyped, time-capped step: a long-lived lint server (one per worktree, started by the setup step and restarted when its status check fails) plus the formatter, with a hook timeout of about 15 s. If the server is unavailable it falls back to the untyped lint config rather than skipping, and it never runs the type checker. For Go, gofmt and goimports on one file take 0.02 s and need no server, so the 2 second check is the home. The hook wrapper times each check and fails the registry test when one exceeds 2 s on one file.
rules.why: A finding shown after the author has moved on costs a round trip; a slow edit-time check is turned off. One sample each under load: gofmt on one file 0.02 s, go vet on one package 1.76 s, golangci-lint 1.38 s.

checks.note: The hook script wraps each on-write check in a timer and exits non-zero over 2 s on one file; the check registry test fails on an on-write check with no timer. Plant: A check that sleeps 3 seconds fails the timer. Control: gofmt on one file passes.

Post-edit hook running the pinned warm lint server with `--fix` and the formatter on the edited file, falling back to the untyped hook lint config; no type check; 15 s hook timeout. Plant: A file with a fixable lint error is fixed on write; with the server stopped the untyped fallback still runs. Control: A clean file is left unchanged.

open: No agent-time hook is committed in any Go repo today.
The 2 second figure rests on single samples under load.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The stop tier runs the fast checks, blocks on red naming the failing step, and never claims green for what it skipped.
rules.detail: The agent-stop hook runs the stop tier. A skip is named in the verdict and printed, and the cheap tier runs on stop. The skipped list is the one gates.plants.8 requires.
rules.why: A stop hook that reports green for a skipped step teaches the agent to stop early.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. The stop-tier hook exits non-zero on a red step, naming the step, and prints the skipped steps. Plant: A stop run with one failing step blocks and names it; a run that skips a step prints it. Control: A fully green stop run passes and lists nothing skipped.

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: C

rules.rule: The template gate script arms the hooks first, then runs every member and accumulates the results, never stopping at the first red, and prints the cheapest failure first in its summary.
rules.detail: One gate script is the template for every repo. It arms the hooks, then runs every member: the structural check of the managed root files, the supply-chain config check, lint, the type check, the tests and the scans. Each member's findings print under its name. A summary line counts green, findings and could not run per member, ordered so the cheapest, most informative failure is shown first. The exit is 1 if any member found something, 2 if any could not run and none found, 0 otherwise. A member's failure never hides another member's result.
rules.why: One script per repo drifts. A gate that stops at the first red shows one failure per push, so a change with three faults takes three pushes; accumulating shows all of them at once, and the summary still puts the cheap failure in front.

checks.note: The shared package's proof test generates a repo from the template, plants a failure in two members and asserts both are reported, the summary order and the exit code. Plant: A template that stops after the first failing member fails the test. Control: The shipped template passes.

rules.rule: A gate script that sets `pipefail` does not pipe into `grep -q`, `head` or `read`; capture the output first, or count.
rules.detail: With pipefail, a producer that dies of SIGPIPE when the reader exits early flips the pipeline status. Gate pipelines carry `pipefail` (the shared `check-gate-commands` check: workflow run steps declare a shell with it, or set it), and a pipeline whose consumer is `grep -q`, `head` or `read` is a finding. Shellcheck does not catch this. The structural rule is a `gatescan` rule.
rules.why: Latent: no shell file sets pipefail yet (0 of 36), 73 sites pipe into grep -q or head in shell files and 6 in Makefiles, so the first repo to add pipefail would flip statuses. The planted gate_bad.sh printed ok with the forbidden word present and shellcheck exited 0.
rules.note: Retired with gragas#1654. A gate member is a program command, not a shell script, and a hook body is one exec of the runner (gates.hooks.9), so no gate pipes shell output into grep, head or read.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. A structural shell-parser rule (ast-grep on shell) flags a pipeline under pipefail whose consumer is `grep -q`, `head` or `read`; a workflow check requires `pipefail` on gate run steps. Plant: A gate_bad.sh that prints ok with the forbidden word present is flagged; a run step without pipefail fails. Control: Capture-then-grep passes.

open: The best-practice review rated this only a possible rule, since no script sets pipefail today; it binds when a gate script adopts pipefail. The tier shown is the tier of the check once built.

rules.rule: Gate tiers are not chained with `&&`; each tier runs and reports on its own.
rules.detail: Chaining tiers with `&&` lets an early failure hide the later tiers' results and lets a skipped tier read as green.
rules.why: A chained script reports only the first red, and a short-circuited tier never prints that it was skipped.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. A structural scan of gate scripts and Makefiles for tier steps joined by `&&`. Plant: A script that runs two tiers joined by `&&` is flagged. Control: Tiers run as separate steps pass.

open: Source states this in the same sentence as the pipe rule and gives no measured case for the `&&` half.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure

rules.rule: A Taskfile declares each task once, beside itself, and a generator registers its generate and check tasks in the tier lists from its own block; no shared line names every task.
rules.detail: A single line that lists every task is rewritten by every change that adds one, and the two tasks that run every generator are edited by every change that adds a generator. Each task carries its own declaration, and each generator adds its tasks to the tier lists (push, land, release) from its own block. A test over the Taskfile fails a task that is declared twice or listed in no tier, and a generator with a generate task and no check task.
rules.why: Own measure: in three days a build file changed in 24 commits, and 18 of them rewrote the phony line or the two generator recipes.

checks.note: a test over the Taskfile lists its tasks, the tiers that name them and the registered generate and check tasks. Plant: a task declared twice fails; a generator with no check task fails. Control: each task declared once beside itself passes

open: Proposed until both halves are checked. The phony half landed with its test in PR 472 (gragas#470 item 1); the per-generator registration is step 5 of gragas#477. It has no tool key to bind to.

rules.rule: A program that declares supported platforms runs its tests on each of them, not only builds for them, on our own machines; the hosted machines run only at a release; a test that needs one platform says so through the platform table, never through a runtime check in the test.
rules.detail: The platforms a program supports are data on the program. Every test runs on our own machines, one leg for each platform, and the hosted machines run only at a release. A leg that has run on a platform is the proof for that platform only. A native run on a system the Mac cannot reach is owed to the next lent window: the change that needs it is queued, and the lent machine posts a comment whose first line is the system, the commit and pass or fail. A test that needs one platform is listed against it in the platform table, so the other legs do not run it; a test that asks the operating system at run time whether to skip itself is a finding. supply.release.7 holds the compile at push for every shipped platform and tests.isolation.11 holds that a verdict names the machine it ran on; this rule holds that the gate itself runs on each one.
rules.why: A build that compiles for a platform proves nothing of what runs there; the fleet's own gate ran on one platform while the program declared two.
rules.note: Retired with gragas#1654, superseded by the one-system vision: where a product holds no code of one operating system (the os-code check finds no tagged file, the host layer and the exemptions included) its gate runs vet, lint and dead-code for each system of the project's list, by GOOS, on the one machine (code.deadcode.1, supply.release.7); what differs by system is the platform libraries' own proof. A native run owed to a lent window stays a loan by label, not a leg of every program's gate; a member's own needs are gates.command.30.
rules.review_question: Which platforms does this program declare, and has the gate run on each of them, not only built for them?
open: Planned check: a test over the platform table and the gate's legs that lists each declared platform with no leg, and each test that reads the operating system to skip itself. Plant: a declared platform with no leg fails. Control: every declared platform has its leg passes. No tool key to bind to: it is the work of gragas#409 to gragas#411. The rule was adopted (C8), so it is active and read in review until a check binds it; a member's own platform claim is gates.command.30.

rules.rule: The gate has tiers by moment: commit runs the check-only members in seconds, push runs the whole gate within its budget, review asks whether an independent reader accepts it in one round or two, landing proves the candidate once, release adds only what proves a release, and on demand holds the deep runs, which block nothing.
rules.detail: Six moments, each with one question and one budget. Commit holds only members that read and never rewrite (gates.hooks.3). Push holds every member a pushed tree must pass, and its budget is a measured number (tests.measures.9, tests.measures.2, tests.measures.10). Review is the one moment with no members: its budget is rounds, one and two at most, and its rules are agents.review.1 to .7. Landing proves the merged candidate once (gates.land.12, gates.land.16), and a pass bound to a tree is not run again for the same tree (tests.selection.7). Release is push plus the members that prove only a release: the crash-injection run and the reproducible-build dry run, with the cross-platform compile already at push. On demand holds the long fuzz run and the heavy race run (tests.generated.6, tests.runners.6); an on-demand run is asked for and reports, and no tier waits for it (gates.command.26). On demand is not a tier a member moves to: it holds only the runs listed for it, and adding one is the owner's ruling. A member names its tier in data (gates.command.3), and a member that cannot meet the budget of its own moves only to a later blocking tier (push to release), never to a timer, never to on demand and never out of the gate. There is no moment below push: the builder's hand-in is the whole push tier (gates.command.31). Each moment has an owner, and a stack adds members to these moments and never a moment of its own.
rules.why: The release tier took 27 minutes 47 seconds, most of it fuzz and heavy race runs that found two bugs in 260 commits; cut back to the push tier plus crash injection and the dry run it is about 1 to 1.5 minutes.
rules.review_question: Which moment does this member belong to, and is it cheaper at an earlier tier or does it prove only a release?
open: Planned check: the member table's tier column holds only members of the tiers above, and the on-demand set is exactly the on-demand runs (the long fuzz run and the heavy race run), so no other member sits there. The members change in gate/members.yaml, a protected path, and is the work of gragas#638's follow-up tickets.

Planned check: the commit moment of gragas#698 is held by tests, which no check row names until a preset tool key runs them. TestTheRepositorysTiersRunTheirRegisteredMembers holds the commit tier to format, generated-files, secrets-staged and supply-shape; TestThePushStillRunsWhatTheCommitLeavesOut holds the push tier to every commit member again, and the commit's prelude to leaving out only the fetch; TestTheStagedScanRefusesASecretTheCommitAdds and TestTheSupplyHoldsItsShape hold each commit member to its plant and its control. The protected-staged member went with the landing check (gragas#912).

rules.rule: The members of a tier run at the same time by default; a member waits only for the member it declares it needs, and that order is kept and shown, never hidden.
rules.detail: A member that reads what another writes declares `after` that member in the member table, and the runner keeps the edge when it runs the members in a pool. The report names each member, how long it ran and, for a member held back, the member it waited for. The pool never stops or cancels the other members at a red, so a tier still runs everything and lists every failure (gates.command.12, never stops at the first red). Results are collected and printed as the serial runner prints them (cheapest first, failures cheapest first), and the stamp and the budget are unchanged. A member that passes only because another one ran first, with no `after` declared, is a finding the first time a run orders them the other way.
rules.why: The pre-push tier ran fourteen members one after another and kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy; a hidden ordering (one test needing a file another member writes) is what a parallel runner would break first.
rules.review_question: Does this member read something another member writes, and does it declare that member?
open: Planned check: a plant that orders two members the wrong way and sees the one without its `after` fail. The runner and the member table change in gate code and gate/members.yaml, protected paths, and are the work of gragas#638's follow-up tickets.

rules.rule: Tools are installed only when a pin changes, and checked once per run: the check is the guard and the install is the fix.
rules.detail: A run checks every tool against its pin first, and installs only when that check fails or when a pin file (the tool list, the lock files, the explorer lock) changed since the last green check, which a sum beside the tools folder records. The gate keeps its own check so it stays self-sufficient, and the build file's check target does not run a second one before it. The one check left is the whole pin check: every program's sha256 against the tool list, the refusal of a name the list does not pin, and the network-block proof with its version read-back, where the system gives a block; where it gives none (sandbox.ErrNoBlock) the check is refused by name and never passes unblocked. The sum decides only whether to install, never whether to check; it is unsealed, so it is a cache and not a verdict. A tool off its pin fails the check and nothing else runs.
rules.why: Every push installed the tools again and checked all eleven twice, 5 to 13 seconds of a tier whose budget is a minute, and the second check changed nothing.
rules.review_question: Does this run install tools whose pins did not change, or check them more than once?
open: Planned check: the run prints the number of tool checks and installs, and a run with an unchanged pin file reports no install. The build file and the tool command change in gragas#638's follow-up tickets.

rules.rule: A repo enforces its rules with no helper tool installed: the gate and the hook run in a clean clone with that tool absent from PATH.
rules.detail: The gate and the hooks use only standard tools and the repo's Taskfile tier (the push tier for the hook). The check runs the gate in a clean clone with PATH stripped of our own helper CLIs, for example with a minimal environment. A repo does not depend on a command that a fresh checkout lacks.
rules.why: A gate that needs a helper nobody installed is skipped silently on a fresh machine or in a clean clone. Five of seven Go repos have a tracked pre-push hook, two have none (V-88).

checks.note: Run the gate in a clean clone with a minimal PATH (`env -i PATH=<minimal> make check`), using the shared hook and Makefile fragment; a recipe in the shared fragment using standard tools only. Plant: A Makefile line that calls the helper CLI fails the clean-clone run. Control: The shared fragment alone passes.

rules.rule: The gate reports how many CPUs it kept busy on average beside its wall time, and a tier that keeps a small share of them busy is a finding.
rules.detail: The report states the busy share and the CPU count it was judged against. A tier whose members could run together but whose busy share stays low is a finding that names the serial member or package that holds the rest back. The share is read with the host's load beside it (tests.measures.1), because a busy host lowers the share a run can take, and the finding is judged on a quiet run (tests.measures.9).
rules.why: The gate's own report said it kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy while the tier broke its budget; the number was printed and nothing acted on it.
rules.review_question: How many CPUs did this tier keep busy, and what holds the rest idle?
open: Planned check: a tier report with a busy share under a stated floor fails on a quiet host. The share is printed today and no floor is set; the floor comes from the measured result of gragas#638's follow-up tickets.

rules.rule: After the documented setup, every member passes on a fresh clone, with no file an earlier run left behind and no ordering between members that is not declared.
rules.detail: The proof is a run of the tier in a clone made from the remote, after the setup the README names and nothing else. A member that needs an ignored file says which member writes it (gates.command.18). A member that needs a module graph, a tool or a platform step that only the setup of an earlier run primed is a finding. The release dry run is the usual place it shows.
rules.why: A second machine hit two reds on its first run: the release dry run failed until a cross-platform module graph was primed, and a docs test failed until an ignored file a different member writes existed.
rules.review_question: Would every member of this tier pass in a clone made from the remote after only the documented setup?
open: Planned check: the hourly release run on a clone from the remote, which is the fresh-clone proof for every member at once. The run and its schedule belong to the fleet, not to the rule data.

rules.rule: A lint step never fails or waits because another lint runs on the same host: it runs with `--allow-parallel-runners` on the one shared cache.
rules.detail: golangci-lint refuses to start while another copy runs as the same user, and the gate runs it with `--allow-parallel-runners`, which takes no lock, so two copies on one host both run. The cache is the same folder as before: the tool's cache code is safe for several processes on one machine to share, and it will not corrupt the cache, so no cache per run is needed and none is made. `--allow-serial-runners` is not used: it waits on a host-wide lock with no deadline, so every repository on the host queues behind one lint, and the wait counts against the tier's budget as a red that says nothing of the code. The rule does not rely on a job queue that runs one gate at a time, because a queue that allows several runs does not prevent the clash, and a second repository on the same host is outside any queue. It lands with the parallel members (gates.command.18), which make the clash likelier, and never after them.
rules.why: Runs of three repositories failed with "parallel golangci-lint is running", a red that said nothing of the code; the shared cache is safe for it, so no run needs to wait.

sources.says: It is safe for multiple processes on a single machine to use the same cache directory in a local file system simultaneously. They will coordinate using operating system file locks and may duplicate effort but will not corrupt the cache.
--allow-parallel-runners: Allow multiple parallel golangci-lint instances running. If false (default) - golangci-lint acquires file lock on start.
It lands with P1, not after.

rules.review_question: If two copies of this lint step start together on one host, do both run, on the one shared cache?
open: Held in gragas by internal/lintrunners_test.go: no tracked Go or Makefile source names the serial flag, and a Makefile lint line carries the parallel one; a plant of each goes red.

Planned check: a plant that starts two lint copies together and sees both pass, with the control of a lint run with neither flag failing the second. The lint member lives in gate/members.yaml, a protected path, and is the work of the runner tickets.

rules.rule: A repo's own Taskfile lists every check as a member of one of three tasks named pre-commit, pre-push and release, each member a line of `cmds:` with its own `timeout:`, and `gragas check` verifies that contract; a repo differs from another only in which commands fill each tier, and any other difference is a recorded exemption with an expiry.
rules.detail: There is no shared runner and no members file: each repo runs go-task from its own Taskfile, pinned in a tool modfile, and `gragas check` reads the Taskfile and holds it to this shape. A member is a `cmd:` with a `timeout:`; the `timeout:` is read on the member, because go-task ignores one on the task and ignores any key it does not know, so a misspelt `timout:` passes in silence and the check must refuse it itself. A member that times out is killed and the run is red (go-task exit 208), but a child it started in the background can outlive it, so a member starts none. `cmds:` run in order and the run stops at the first red member; a member that may be red without stopping the run says so with `ignore_error: true`, and that line is read as an exemption with its reason. `deps:` run in parallel, and a tier uses them only for members that do not share a folder, a file or a port. A tier is verdict-true only when nothing in its environment changes the verdict, and the tier pins or clears what can: `TASK_DRY` (runs nothing and exits 0); `GOFLAGS` when it holds any flag that selects or skips tests or changes what is built (`-run`, `-skip`, `-count`, `-mod`, `-tags`: `-run=TestPass` turned a red tier green, and so did `-run=NoSuchTest`), which the tier clears or sets itself; and `TASK_CORE_UTILS`, which can switch a member from the real utilities to Go's bundled ones (a GNU flag can stop working), so the tier sets it and a member does not depend on a GNU flag. `TASK_CONCURRENCY` only serialises `deps:` and changes no colour. A repo with nothing to run says so in its Taskfile, so an empty tier and a missing tier are not the same thing. gates.command.1 holds that one command runs every check; this rule holds that the list the command reads has one shape everywhere. Evidence: the spike in gragas#926, Linux (comment 6883855603) and Windows (comment 6883909209); the macOS half is owed.
rules.why: Six projects of one fleet ran six gate shapes, and 39 repositories of another ran 39: most stopped at the first red, two kept a stamp keyed to a 24-hour age, and 36 of 38 checked nothing at commit.

rules.review_question: Is every check of this project a member of the pre-commit, pre-push or release task of its own Taskfile, with a timeout on the member, and does `gragas check` hold the Taskfile to that?
open: Planned check: `gragas check` reads the Taskfile for the three tier names, each member's `cmds:` and `timeout:`, and a key it does not know. Plant: a check run outside the tiers, a member with no timeout and a misspelt key each fail. Control: a Taskfile whose members all carry a timeout passes. No tool key is bound yet; the check is the work of gragas-new-3 (gragas#929).

rules.rule: A browser, a container image and a tool that is not a module are tools: pinned by version or digest, installed per project when the pin changes, and a gate never prunes a cache it shares with another project.
rules.detail: gates.command.19 holds that a tool is installed when its pin changes and checked once per run. This rule says what counts as a tool. A browser the tests drive is pinned and installed by the project; a container image is pinned by digest and pulled before the lock, never inside a start call; a tool that is not a module of the project's language is pinned by checksum (supply.provenance.7). A cache shared between projects on one host is never pruned by one project's gate, because the next project's run pays the install again.
rules.why: One project's gate pruned browsers from the shared cache on every run, and another reinstalled its packages every push for 6 to 8 seconds; in a third fleet installs of 106 to 180 seconds sat in no budget and a stale install after a lockfile change gave 170 false lint errors.
rules.review_question: Which browsers, images and non-module tools does this gate use, where is each pinned, and does any step prune a shared cache?
open: Planned check: the tool pins file lists each browser and image with its version or digest, and a scan of the gate scripts for a prune or clean of a shared cache path. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A lint or test tool gets its worker count and its cache in every tier, derived from the pool's capacity, and a tool's settings never depend on which slot or host the run lands in.
rules.detail: The worker count comes from the capacity the job tool sets on the child process (gates.command.27, tests.runners.2), and the cache folder is the same in every tier, so a warm run is warm whether it runs at push, at land or at release. Two checks on one host never refuse each other (gates.command.22). A setting that differs by slot kind gives the same tool two speeds and a budget that cannot be set.
rules.why: One lint command took 394 seconds cold in one slot kind, about 128 seconds in the other, and 8.8 seconds warm with four threads; the same command, three speeds, and a push that was 65 percent that one member.
rules.review_question: Does this tool's worker count come from the pool, is its cache the same in every tier, and would it run the same in another slot?
open: Planned check: the members file names the worker variable and the cache path for each lint and test member, and a literal worker count in a gate command fails. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A run off the cycle, scheduled or on demand, exists only if someone watches it: it is named in the members file, its result is logged where the hub reads it, and a red opens an issue the same day.
rules.detail: The on-demand tier holds the deep runs (gates.command.17): the long fuzz run, the heavy race run, a cross-browser run, a tier that needs cloud credentials. Each is a row of the members file with the tier on demand, so the list is one list. A run is asked for by the owner or asked of the owner, and the hub's daily race run on the main branch is one such run. A run that nobody reads is not a check, and a red that waits for the next run to be noticed is a red main that nobody knows about. tests.runners.7 holds the race case; this rule holds every run off the cycle.
rules.why: One project's daily race run stopped silently and its main branch failed the race detector with nobody knowing; another fleet ran integration, characterisation and mutation checks by hand with no request path, no log and no issue on red.
rules.review_question: Is this run a row of the members file, where does its result go, and who opens the issue when it is red?
open: Planned check: every on-demand member has a log location and the log holds a run within its stated period. Plant: an on-demand member with no log location fails. Control: one with a log and a recent run passes. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: The pool's capacity is the host's cores divided by its slots, set on the child process by the job tool and never written into a recipe; a member's weight is a promise and a cap, and a member heavier than the capacity runs when the pool is empty.
rules.detail: tests.runners.2 holds the worker count of a test or browser runner. This rule holds the pool that runs the members (gates.command.18). A member declares its weight, the pool admits members while their weights sum to the capacity, and a member that uses more than its weight is a finding. Nothing in a recipe or a script hard-codes the number: the job tool knows how many slots the host runs and sets the capacity once.
rules.why: One web project went red with every test passing when uncapped test workers ran beside other gates: worker timeouts rose 1, 6, 12 over three runs; capped, 9,428 of 9,428 passed. Three slots on 15 cores gave a load of 26 with no gain in total work.
rules.review_question: Where does this pool read its capacity, does each member declare a weight, and is any number hard-coded in a recipe?
open: Planned check: the runner refuses a members file with a member and no weight, and a scan of the recipes for a literal parallelism number. No tool key is bound yet; the shared runner is the work of gragas#642.

rules.rule: A check never writes the tree it reads: a generator check works in a copy and compares, a formatter checks and never rewrites, and where a member must write, every member that reads its output declares that it runs after it.
rules.detail: Members run at the same time (gates.command.18), so a member that rewrites a file under another member is a race. The generated-files check regenerates into a temporary folder and diffs. The format check lists the files that differ and exits non-zero. A member that writes an artefact others read, such as a build, is named in the readers' after edge, and that ordering is shown in the report. A hook that formats and restages is the opposite of a check.
rules.why: One project's generate check rewrote the live tree, so the tests beside it failed 6 of 6 in a parallel trial; two commit hooks of another fleet ran the formatter in write mode and restaged.
rules.review_question: Does this member write anything under the tree, and if it must, does every member that reads the result declare it runs after?
open: Planned check: the runner runs each check-only member on a read-only copy of the tree and fails one that writes. Plant: a format member in write mode fails. Control: the same member in check mode passes. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: On a shared host a heavy run takes a slot and a light command runs bare; the slots admit heavy runs by class, landings ahead of re-gates and experiments, and one heavy job in flight per agent.
rules.detail: A heavy run is a tier, a test suite, a build or anything that uses the pool's capacity. A light command is a type check of one file, a push, a lint of one file, a listing. Holding a slot for a light command makes the agents behind it wait for nothing. The job tool holds the slot classes; this rule says only that there are classes, that a landing comes first, and that an agent has one heavy job at a time.
rules.why: In one fleet a type check, a lint prune, a git push and one unit-test file held heavy slots; experiments held 360 slot-minutes in two days; and agents waited at least 2,846 minutes for heavy slots over two days.
rules.review_question: Is this command heavy or light, does it take a slot only if heavy, and is a landing ahead of it in the queue?

rules.rule: Every rule names one home tier and its time budget in the rule data; a check that cannot meet its tier's budget moves to a later tier, never to a timer.
rules.detail: The tiers are on write, before commit or at the agent's stop, before push, at land, and after release. The rule data carries a tier column and a budget per rule, validated by schema (the tier column is schema-checked), and the gate runner reads the tier from the data to decide when a check runs. A test checks that each tier's measured wall time is inside its budget from the gate summary. A rule with no tier fails the schema.
rules.why: Tiers written as prose tables drift from what runs. A check that is too slow for its tier and is run "at most every so often" by a timer is not a gate any more.

rules.rule: Every member declares what it needs (the network, a browser, a service) and not the system it runs on; one whose need this host lacks is reported as skipped with the cause by the tier check, is listed every run and never passes quietly, and a skip is red at land and at release unless a dated exemption names the machine the gate cannot reach.

A member whose need this host lacks, such as the network on a host that has none, is not run, and the tier check reports it as skipped with the reason, every time (go-task's own `platforms:` filter skips a member in silence, so the report is the check's, never go-task's). At push a skip is allowed, because the builder's machine may lack a browser or a runtime. At land and at release a skip is red, because those moments prove the whole project, unless a dated exemption names the machine that would run it; the one exemption today names Windows. No Job Object and no network-block prefix is part of the rule: how a host runs a member is the host's own affair. A vulnerability check that needs the network reports not checked when offline, never a pass. tests.admission.5 holds the test side; this rule holds the member.

rules.rule: Each moment of the cycle has an owner: the builder runs commit and push on their own machine, the hub lands and releases, an on-demand run is asked for, and nobody runs a later moment's tier as their hand-in.
rules.detail: The builder's hand-in is the push tier, run by the pre-push hook on the builder's machine. The hub runs the landing proof on the merged candidate and the release tier on a fresh clone of the tag. A builder who runs the release tier, or a full post-land run, before every push runs a moment that is not theirs and pays its cost per change. rules.rule: Where a repo turns test selection on, what a tier runs is chosen by a planner from declared scope rules for that tier, from what changed; a full uncached run always satisfies the gate, and a repo whose full gate fits its push budget runs the full gate.
rules.detail: Selection is optional. The default is the whole gate on every push, with tests uncached (a cached pass is a claim about a run that did not happen). A repo turns selection on only when its full gate does not fit the push budget of gates.hooks.4. Then the scope rules are one declared file per repo (path classes mapped to checks and tests), a selector picks the packages, domains or journeys from the changed paths and the dependency graph, the runner reads tier and budget, and the plan is built by the selector from the path-class table. The tiers, scopes and targets are a written table. Whatever selection is on, a full uncached run is always accepted as passing the gate.
rules.why: Three target repos run the whole gate on every push, and a selector is a second program that can be wrong. Where the full gate does not fit, a hand-picked subset lets an author choose what proves their own change, so the subset comes from declared rules.

rules.rule: The planner fails closed to a full run on a global-class path, an unplaced path, a dirty tree, an unresolvable range or a failed graph build, and says why.
rules.detail: A change that cannot be placed runs every check and journey. Global-class paths include package manifests and lockfiles, compiler and lint and build and test configuration, shared style files, generated type declarations, infrastructure and environment files, the test kernel, API specs, generated code, the domain map and the gate scripts themselves, and also `go.mod`, `go.sum` and build files for Go. Also full: an unknown path, a file with no owner or two owners, an unresolvable range, a dirty tree at the land tiers, a failed graph build. An empty or missing input fails. A change to the selector selects everything. Message catalogues that have their own validator are not global-class, and the planner does not widen to the full suite for them.

rules.rule: The pre-push hook is installed and runs the whole gate on the pushed tree within its measured time budget, and a range it cannot resolve fails closed.
rules.detail: The pre-push hook runs the one gate command (make check or its equivalent) on what is being pushed: every member, including the root-file structural check (the managed files equal their template), the tests uncached, the scans and the cross-OS builds. It is the gate, not a sample of it: no hosted job on push repeats or replaces it. Its wall time is measured against the budget of gates.hooks.4; a member too slow for that budget moves to the release workflow, never out of every gate. When the pushed range cannot be resolved the hook fails; it never falls back to "nothing to check". The hook runner reads one committed file for both pre-commit and pre-push.
rules.why: With no push CI a push that skips the gate moves the failure straight to main. A hook that runs a subset leaves the rest of the gate with no tier at all.

rules.rule: The pre-push hook runs the whole gate, its wall time is measured and reported against a budget, and a check too slow for it moves to the release workflow, never to a push or pull-request workflow or a hosted land job.
rules.detail: The budget is a number in the repo's gate config with its reason (the targets run their whole gate in about a minute). The pre-push wrapper measures the hook's wall time on every run and reports it with the budget, and the gate fails when the measured time stays over the budget for the recorded number of runs. The fix for an over-budget hook is to make a member faster or to move that member to the release workflow on the tag (the crash-injection run and the dry build are the usual cases), where it still blocks the release; fuzz and the heavy race run are on demand and block nothing (tests.generated.6, tests.runners.6). A member never moves to a workflow triggered by push or pull request, or to a hosted land job, and never out of every gate. The pre-commit hook stays check-only and cheap (gates.hooks.3).
rules.why: Heavy hooks invited `--no-verify` at a reference team, so the time is measured, not guessed. With no push CI the only place a slow check can go and still bind is the release.

rules.rule: A builder's pre-push hook may run the commit tier plus build, vet, lint and the selected tests, with the whole push tier run on another machine when the push lands and on the train candidate.
rules.detail: The whole tier still runs on every pushed head and on the candidate before main moves, so nothing reaches the default branch unseen; a branch on the remote may be red for a few minutes. A pull request with a red whole run is sent back. The whole-tier proof at landing is run by the landing step itself, never read from another machine's report, as nothing at landing reads a stamp. Adopting this rule replaces the wording of gates.hooks.1 and gates.hooks.4 ("runs the whole gate"), which are retired or reworded in the same change.
rules.why: After the concurrency and parallelism rules a push is about 50 seconds and the hook is no longer the bottleneck of the day; a lighter hook would cut the builder's wait to about 15 seconds at the price of a red branch for a few minutes.

rules.rule: The pre-push hook runs the push tier and does nothing else, the logic lives in the runner, a push from a hosted workflow never runs the local hook, and a known hole in the bypass deny is a finding.
rules.detail: gates.hooks.1 and .4 hold that the hook runs the whole gate within its budget, and gates.hooks.5 that the bypass flags are refused. This rule holds the shape of the hook: one line that calls the runner with the tier's name. A loop, a substitution or a check written in the hook itself is logic the runner should hold, and it is not measured, not stamped and not shared. A tag push made by a hosted workflow does not run the local hook again, because the tag's tree is the tree the release tier proves. Where a project has no paid hosted check, the hook is the only check, and a hole in the deny (a spelling of the bypass the deny does not match) is a finding to close, not a note. The hook body is a single exec of the runner (`exec task pre-push`), so it has no shell of its own to differ by system.
rules.why: One hook with a quadratic shell substitution cost 374 seconds of a 391 second push and 210 seconds of every commit; four publishes ran the gates twice, 403 seconds, because the tag push re-fired the hook; and a deny written after a bypass came 9 hours 15 minutes later with a hole in it.

rules.rule: Main moves only by a reviewed change whose merged tree the checks passed: the lander runs them on the merged tree, then squash-merges; where a repo has no lander, the owner fast-forwards main to the exact tree the pre-push hook passed, or has the gate run again on the merged tree first.
rules.detail: The change is reviewed (the author's own included), and the owner merges it or says to. Where a repo runs the lander, the lander checks out origin/main plus the squash in a scratch clone, runs the repo's own checks there (its Taskfile's pre-push tier, or make check in gragas), and only then squash-merges. Where it does not, the pre-push hook has run the full gate on the pushed tree (gates.hooks.1), and the owner either fast-forwards main to that exact commit, so the tree that moves main is the tree that ran, or, when main has moved since or the merge is a squash, has the gate run again on the merged tree before main moves: a squash onto a main that moved is a tree that never ran. There is no stamp, no stored verdict and no hash record: a pass is the run just made on the tree about to move main, never a claim carried from another tree, another machine or the author's word. In both forms nothing else moves main: no direct push to main and no merge of a tree the checks did not pass.
rules.why: A merge path that skips the check is the path that gets used. With no hosted land job the binding between the tree that was merged and the run that passed it is that the run is made on that tree, just before the merge; a pass on one tree must never be claimed for another.

rules.rule: A stamp is a claim keyed to the exact tree, its settings and its tools, and it only lets a rerun on the same key be skipped; it is never keyed to a commit or an age, landing and release never take it as proof, and a member that reads a moving source pins that source by digest in the key.

A vulnerability database or a remote list the member reads is part of the key as a digest, or the stamp is stale the moment the source moves. rules.rule: A green report says how many tests, files or stories each member ran and the delta against the merge base; a member that ran nothing is red, a count that fell against the merge base fails landing, and an instrument counts as a guard only once it has been seen to fail.
rules.detail: gates.plants.8 holds that a check prints its input count and that zero inputs is not a pass unless declared. This rule holds the counts per member and the comparison. The count is read from the tool's own output, never from a list of files. The delta is against a count made on the merge base in the same run, not against a stored report, so a test script removed from a manifest, a target changed to do nothing, or a story set that stopped playing shows as a fall. A member that ran nothing is red whatever the tool's exit code: a Go package with no tests makes gotestsum print `EMPTY <package>` and `DONE 0 tests` and exit 0, so the tier reads that output and a member that found no test exits 1. A setting of the environment that selects or skips tests (`GOFLAGS` with `-run` or `-skip`) can hide a red test: when it leaves no test the zero count makes the member red, but when it leaves one (the Windows run's `-run=TestPass` gave `DONE 1 tests`, exit 0) only the fall of the count against the merge base shows it, and that holds only if the base ran without the flag: clearing the flag is the guard (gates.command.23), the count its backstop. A new instrument (a mutation run, a lint rule, a contrast check) is planted red once (gates.plants.1) before its green counts. Evidence: gragas#926, Linux (comment 6883855603) and Windows (comment 6883909209).
rules.why: One fleet published two versions of a design system with no test script, 4 days 20 hours with 20 spec files unrun and a green gate; a green with 18 story plays unrun passed review; 13 of 14 mutation runs tested nothing; eleven instruments were green that had never been able to go red.

rules.rule: A gate's wall time excludes the time it waited for a slot; queue wait and slot hold print on their own lines, and a timed step records the load and whether it held a slot.

A step timed outside a slot at a high load says so, because its number is inflated by an amount nobody can state.

rules.rule: A banned import or code pattern is a lint error whose message names what to use instead, and the ban lists ship empty and are filled by later rules naming the owning package.

The import and syntax ban lists exist but ship empty; each later rule fills its part naming the owning package in the message, so a ban doubles as a capability registry: each concern has one importable owner and the alternatives are banned by name.
rules.why: A ban without a message is satisfied by guessing the nearest bypass.

rules.rule: A repo's own gate imports nothing from the code it judges, and reaches it only through a declared internal export or the built binary.
rules.detail: A gate that needs facts from the code reads them through an export declared for gates (an internal entry the package lists for that use) or by running the built program and reading its machine output. Importing the package it judges is a finding: a fault in the subject then breaks or bends the gate, and the gate passes whatever the subject's own code says. The import rule names the gate folder and the internal exports it may reach.

rules.rule: Every check has a planted violation that turns it red, a clean control and a refusal case, and the gate runs that plant at least once per tier.
rules.detail: A check that cannot fail is not a check. A rule with no plant is a finding, and a new rule ships with its plant and a failing-test message that names the fix. Plants lead adoption in every repo (decision 38). Every registered check carries a planted-violation fixture, a clean control and a refusal case, and the gate fails when a registered check lacks one (a registry walk). For analyzers the fixture form is the analysis test package with `// want` comments; for forbidigo, ast-grep and conftest-style rules the fixture is a tiny module run through the real tool. Plants run first in the gate. The plants must exist before the check is turned on, and the plant of an old check is never deleted in the change that weakens it (that is a gate weakening, see protection).
rules.why: No Go repo plants one for each of its gates; one repo's drift check failed 13 of 35 entries and was not in its make check. One web repo's 82 plants never ran in `make check` because the layer check ran without its self-test flag. Another has 85 plants on main (135 on a branch). A self-test run is held in one repo (73 plants).

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. A selftest command: the runner executes every plant fixture per rule and per tier, plant plus clean control, and a registered rule with no plant directory fails. Plant: Register a check with no fixture; delete one plant fixture and the runner fails. Control: A check with the full triple (plant, control, refusal) passes.

rules.rule: A rule that can fail in two directions is proved by a pair run, and cannot be at gate level without all the plants.
rules.detail: The pair run: the too-much case planted, the too-little case planted by a different instrument, a just-right case of the same size, the cheap cure applied to each failure, and a third result for not applicable. A row marked two-sided is refused promotion to gate with only the too-much plant. The plants need a reader who is not the row's author. Applies to rules that are balances (size, duplication, coverage, test count).

rules.rule: A gate fails closed on a missing tool, missing input, empty input or a pending marker unless the check declares that 0 inputs is valid, has no flag that softens a finding or an exit, and only members of the gate line count as evidence.
rules.detail: A zero is not an absence until a known positive proves the instrument. The runner wraps every check: an input count of 0 fails unless the check declares `zero_ok`, in which case it returns the third result (gates.plants.8). The type check runs in every gate and fails closed when its inputs, such as generated infrastructure types, are missing (for example `tsc --noEmit` after `sst install`, with the `.sst/` directory absent being red). Tools already fail on an empty glob (ESLint exits 2; a test runner with a file filter matching nothing exits 1); the runner closes the gap for custom checks and name filters. The self-test runs each check on an empty input and requires a refusal. A gate has no non-fatal mode: there is no strict, warn-only or soft flag, a finding is always exit 1, and exit 2 means could not run. A convenience hook (a phase guard, a reminder) may fail open, but it is not a gate member and is never cited as evidence that a rule holds; only members of the gate line are evidence.
rules.why: A pending check exited 0 at a reference team; a secrets test skips when its scanner is missing; scanners that read nothing read green; a spec that cannot fail ran against nothing. A softening flag is the switch somebody turns on the day the gate is red.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. rules.rule: Weakening a gate needs a non-author: a different session with a stored verdict tied to the content that names the weakening in words, checked at land.
rules.detail: Every agent pushes as one identity, so a trailer proves nothing: "non-author" means a different session with a stored verdict, content-hashed, which names the weakening in words. A named person signs only a short list: gate config, protected paths and new dependencies (decision 31). The change records its reason. Weakening means raising a ceiling, removing a check, turning error to warn or off, narrowing where a rule applies, or deleting a plant. A change to a sensitive path (infrastructure and permissions, migrations, gate config, shared packages, the applies-to data) or a new dependency needs sign-off by someone other than the author. The trailer form (a `Gate-Change:` line naming a reviewer and a reason, checked by a `commit-msg` hook job) remains the record of the reason and the first, cheap check; the stored verdict is the one the land check relies on. The known way round is starting a second session to rubber-stamp, so the verdict must name the weakening in words and the list stays short enough for a person to sample.
rules.why: No Gate-Change trailer exists in any of seven Go repos (0, verified), and nothing stores such a verdict. A sign-off passed as a land argument stops a missing and a self sign-off but not a land-runner who names someone falsely. This row rests on decision 31 (4 November).
