rules.rule: When a candidate conflicts only in files a generator owns, landing regenerates them and continues; a conflict in any hand-written file goes back to the builder.
rules.detail: A file is generator-owned when a generator in the repository's own tools writes it and gen --check holds it, and the landing step reads that list from the base revision, never from the candidate. When every conflicting path is on it, landing takes the base side, runs the generators, commits the result as the landing step's own commit, and runs the checks again; nothing is merged as text. One hand-written path among the conflicts returns the whole candidate to its builder, with the paths named. The regenerated files are never reviewed by hand, because the generator and its check are what a reviewer approved. The list of generated paths is read from the base revision's generators, built from the base, so a candidate cannot add a path to the list that judges it. A regenerate never changes a hand-written file: if running the generators would alter any path they do not own, the landing fails and the candidate returns to its builder. The regenerated tree is a new tree and gets the full proof: nothing is served from either side's stamp, and the generated-file check and the tier run on the result. A generated path that is also protected keeps needing a verdict on the regenerated bytes; landing never writes a verdict, and if the base holds none for those bytes the landing fails with the need and the digest.
rules.why: The fleet's run log of 8 Nov 2026 (trains 2 and 2b) shows each landing sending the waiting candidates back through a rebase, a full check run and sometimes a new verdict. A conflict in a generated file is the part of that cost with no judgement in it: the fix is the command that wrote the file, and a builder adds nothing by running it.

sources.says: Committed generated documents are held by a script that regenerates and compares.
Committed generated files are held by a script that fails when they are out of date.
A merge driver is defined in the clone's own configuration, never in the repository, and the union merge leaves added lines in an order the user must verify.

checks.note: a landing test with a fixture repository: two candidates that add a package each conflict in the generated join; landing regenerates it and passes. Plant: a candidate that conflicts in a generated file and also in a hand-written file is landed without being sent back, or its generated file is merged as text, and the test fails. Control: the same pair with only the generated file in conflict lands, and the one with a hand-written conflict returns to its builder

open: Proposed until the landing step regenerates. The work is in the lander's merged-tree check (task landing; scripts/land went with gragas#912): it has to read the generator list from the base, regenerate, and a fixture has to hold it. It comes from a ruling and has no step in gragas#444, whose nine steps hold no landing-regenerates step. It is filed as gragas#464; this rule is the engine side of it.

rules.rule: A blocking check has a measured false-positive rate under 10 percent; a check above the bar drops a level.
rules.detail: For every check that blocks, keep a count of hits, suppressed hits, findings later overturned, and the agent time spent satisfying a failure, from the delivery record, and report them per check. A check that is mostly suppressed is changed or dropped. A check above the bar drops a level (blocking to ratcheted to review) by a recorded decision; the reporter itself never demotes a check, because that would be a gate weakening. The 10 percent bar is a practice figure and a guess on UI gates. A failing test is never rerun to green.
rules.why: A check that wastes agent rounds taxes every ticket, and time spent satisfying a wrong finding is invisible unless recorded. One lint rule has 40 of 40 hits suppressed; one repo has 26 init functions each suppressed with a reason (V-55). No UI gate has an override count today.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. The runner counts hits, suppressions and overridden hits per rule from the delivery record and prints the false-positive share; a check above the bar blocks its next change until the answer (the decision to rework, demote or keep) is recorded. Plant: A fixture log with known counts yields the known share, and a check over the bar blocks until answered. Control: A check under the bar passes.

rules.review_question: Which blocking check is above the false-positive bar, and what was decided about it?
open: Strength is a judgement: the Go row's enforcement note proposes Hard (suppressions per check may only fall; a check above the bar blocks until reworked) and the web row proposes Answered. Answered is used until the ratchet on per-check suppressions exists.
The review-only part (does the first screen name the failing check) is gates.quality.2.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice (Tricorder); own measure
rules.note: Merges the Go and web false-positive rows and the measure of suppressed and overturned findings.

rules.rule: A failing rule's message names its home and the fix; a failing test's first screen names the check, the expected and actual values and the one line to rerun it, and the rest goes to a file.
rules.detail: The rule table requires home and fix fields in every rule message; for our own lint plugin rules a plugin lint enforces the message format and docs URL. The first screen of a failing test is a review question. No line limit is set because none is measured.
rules.why: A message that does not say what to do is satisfied by guessing. Argued, not measured; no measured number is cited.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. Rule-table schema requires `home` and `fix` fields in every rule message; for custom lint rules the eslint-plugin-eslint-plugin rules report-message-format and require-meta-docs-url. Plant: A rule message without a fix line fails the schema. Control: A message naming home and fix passes.

rules.review_question: Does the first screen of this gate's failure output name the failing check and the line to rerun it?
open: Half: message form is mechanical; the quality of the first screen is review.
rules.note: Merges the web message rule, the new-rule-ships-with-a-message half and the first-screen sentence of the false-positive row.

rules.rule: Every gate on main is green, so that a red result means something.
rules.detail: A failing test is never rerun to green, a blocking check has a measured false-positive rate (gates.quality.1), and the release backstop (a full run at the tag) catches what selection missed.
rules.why: A main that is sometimes red teaches everyone to retry, and a retry hides a real fault.
rules.review_question: Is any gate on main red or retried, and why is it not fixed or removed?

rules.rule: A new check runs on one real repo before it is required anywhere, and the trial is recorded.
rules.detail: Shared checks run over existing repos at pinned commits with a control run, so a result cannot pass by accident, and a dry adoption report is written per tool, before any check is required. The trial needs a known positive. The registry refuses a required check with no trial record; that a trial was real and was read is judgement.
rules.why: A check that has never run on real code misfires on first contact and gets switched off.

checks.note: v1 class record. The registry refuses a required check with no `trialled_on` field and run record. Plant: A required check with no trial record is refused. Control: A required check with a trial record passes.

rules.review_question: On which real repo was this check trialled, and who read the result?
open: Recorded as a possible weak rule by the enforcement review; it binds when promoted.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure
rules.note: Merges the single-sentence rule with the trial scripts rule.

rules.rule: A gate is one you can explain in a sentence.
rules.detail: A required one-line `why` field on each rule row with a length cap gives presence only; a model lens checks that the sentence matches the check.
rules.why: A gate nobody can explain gets weakened or removed without understanding.
rules.review_question: Does the one-line reason on this rule match what its check actually does?
open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: D

rules.rule: Debt is a shrink-only list: a new rule starts with today's violations frozen, and a gate fails when a cell gets worse.
rules.detail: Below the milestone a gate fails only when a cell gets worse; the change that needs a higher baseline cannot raise it, because the check compares the working figure with the figure at the merge base. Lowering is free. Each metric is a committed file per entry. A list may not grow without a person typing the growth switch (`--write --grow`) and a named second reader (second-reader), the stored verdict of gates.protection.1. A bulk suppression file alone is not a ratchet: it records existing violations, fails new ones and can only shrink, but it needs the registry of gates.ratchets.4 beside it.
rules.why: Held in one Go repo (ratchet files, plant none recorded) and in two web repos (numeric baselines with the grow switch). A new rule that cannot start frozen is never adopted.

bad.code:
# the counted lines: 12 at the merge base, 13 in the work tree
debt: 13

good.code:
# the counted lines: 12 at the merge base, 12 in the work tree
debt: 12

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. Ratchet helper (lifted from the repo that holds it): a metric file per entry; the check fails when the working-tree figure exceeds the figure at the merge base (`git show <base>:file`); raising needs the stored verdict. Plant: Raise a baseline number in a branch; it fails against the base. Raise it with the growth switch but no verdict; refused. Control: Lowering the number passes.

The debt key of the gragas preset, which gragas check computes: the lines of the work tree that count as debt against the merge base's. Plant: one more counted line than at the base is a finding. Control: the same count or fewer passes (internal/core/audit/repo_test.go)

ESLint bulk suppressions (built-in suppressions file); an unused suppression fails by default and the pass-on-unpruned flag is never used in a gate. Plant: A new violation not in the suppressions file fails; fixing an entry without pruning it fails. Control: The pruned file passes.

open: Plant was never recorded in the repo that holds the Go ratchet; run it once when the helper is lifted.
The alternative, a repo-local script, is caught by the shared-gates rule that ratchet files go through the helper path.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: own measure; A (baselines in two web repos)
rules.note: Merges the Go debt rule, the web shrink-only list rule, the baseline-only-shrinks rule and the bulk suppression tool entry.

rules.rule: A module move is its own change before the change that uses it: a codemod moves the files and rewrites specifiers, mocks, citations and every baseline key in one commit, and one owner makes all moves.
rules.detail: The codemod moves files and rewrites import specifiers, mock strings, comment citations and every registered baseline's path keys in the same commit, with zero logic change and an entry in the blame-ignore list. One mover owns every move change at a time. A move commit may rewrite baseline keys, never their count.
rules.why: Concurrent moves conflict, and a move mixed with logic cannot be reviewed.
rules.review_question: Is this move a separate change, by the one mover, with every baseline key rewritten and no logic edit?
open: Single-owner part is a process judgement with no check yet; the check mechanics are in gates.ratchets.3 and gates.ratchets.9.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: D
rules.note: v1 review check (review is not a v2 check class): Review of move changes against the single-owner list; the key rewrite is held by gates.ratchets.3.

rules.rule: A fingerprint covers the fact the item answers, never the bytes of the file that holds it; an answer about an import is keyed to the import set.
rules.detail: The item of a reviewed answer is what was asked: that package P imports I, that a function has a given length class. The fingerprint is a digest of that fact (the sorted import list of P's non-test files, the function's class), so an unrelated edit to the same file renews nothing and a change to the fact fails the gate until a reason is recorded. Two answers about one file no longer renew together. Where the fact is the file itself, as with a size class, the file digest is right. The answer's schema names the kind of fingerprint, and a file fingerprint on an answer about an import is refused. File-level review of a wiring file is a protected-path question, not a fingerprint.
rules.why: Own measure: 13 fingerprint renewals in three days, as many as additions, because two answers share one wiring file and every edit to it renewed both.

checks.note: the measure step recomputes the import-set fingerprint and fails an answer whose fact changed with no new reason, and refuses a file fingerprint on an import answer. Plant: an unrelated edit to the importing file renews nothing, while adding an import fails the answer. Control: an answer with the reason recorded passes

open: Proposed until the measure step fingerprints the import set. That is step 7 of gragas#477 (answers as a folder of entries); the measure code is a judge path, so the change needs a security review. It has no tool key to bind to until then.

rules.rule: A baseline is a numeric ceiling per file that only falls, and raising it needs a stored second-party verdict.
rules.detail: A single count hides one file growing while another shrinks (the existing file baseline in the Go repo is the `file-baseline`), so the ceiling is per file. A baseline entry that no longer applies also fails.
rules.why: The first size ratchet at a reference team recorded one violation for a file that grew from 400 to 3,000 lines. The Go baseline files are 39, 40, 79 and 828 lines (V-24).

checks.note: Ratchet helper with a numeric ceiling per file for size; a baseline entry that no longer applies fails. Plant: Append lines to a baselined file past its number; it fails. Control: Shrinking the file passes.

open: Plant never recorded in the repo that has the file baseline; run once when the helper is lifted.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A baseline survives a rebase, a rename and a deletion without resetting, and a baseline entry for a missing file fails.
rules.detail: On a missing path the ratchet helper looks up the rename in the diff against the base: if the path was renamed the entry must move with its number not raised; if deleted the entry must be removed in the same change; otherwise fail. A structural move (renaming or moving a module, package or route) rewrites the keys of every baseline and suppression list it touches and never their counts: the sum of each baseline before and after is equal and no key names a missing path. Stale suppression keys already fail in the ESLint bulk suppression file and in dependency-cruiser's known-violation list (dependency-cruiser behaves the same) -- ESLint bulk suppression file and in known-list tools.
rules.why: Without this, a rename resets the baseline to zero and hides the debt. Not measured in Go; the web half rests on a stale entry failing (exit 2) until pruned.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. Ratchet helper checks renames with `git diff -M --name-status` against the base and compares the per-baseline sums before and after a move. Plant: Rename a baselined file without moving the entry; fails. Double a count during a move; fails. Control: Rename with the entry moved and the count unchanged passes.

A baseline key naming a path that no longer exists fails (bulk-suppression and known-list tools exit non-zero on a stale entry). Plant: Renaming a file without rewriting its suppression key fails; rewriting the key passes. Control: Unrenamed file passes.

open: Half holds on the web side: the sum-equality script (about 15 lines) is unbuilt, so doubling a count during a move is not seen.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice; D

rules.rule: Every baseline is a count made against the merge base, with an owner, a ticket and the stage by which it is zero; growth against the merge base, or any non-zero count at the stage, fails.
rules.detail: There is no stored list of baselines. The count is made on the merge base and on the head in the same run, so a count that grew fails however the change got there, and a baseline that nobody wrote down cannot be forgotten. The owner, the ticket and the zero-by stage sit in the config that owns the baseline, as a dated TODO which a lint rule turns into an error on the day. The zero check reads the current milestone and fails on anything non-zero at or past the stage; the last stage's gate fails while any count is above zero. One parent issue with sub-issues per rule drives the legacy debt to zero.
rules.why: A ratchet that never reaches zero is a permanent exemption; whether our baselines have shrunk was never measured. A reference team's countdowns to zero paid off.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. A count made on the merge base and on the head, plus a zero check reading the milestone; a baseline with no owner or stage is a finding. Plant: A count that grew against the merge base fails; a last stage with count 1 fails. Control: A count within its stage that did not grow passes.

open: The expiry horizon is capped by data, and that cap is a guess (see gates.exemptions.4).
The counts against the merge base are the work of gragas-new-2 (gragas#928); no tool key makes them yet.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; D (a reference zero-check runs)
rules.note: Merges the owner and zero-by rules from both sides, the registry rule and the ESLint suppressions plus expiring-comment tool entry.

rules.rule: A baseline at zero is deleted and its rule becomes a plain error; an empty registered baseline file that still exists fails.
rules.detail: At zero, the baseline file goes and the rule is absolute; a non-empty baseline at or past its stage fails. The check fails on the empty file so the deletion is not forgotten.
rules.why: An empty baseline left in place lets the rule quietly regrow.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. The zero check fails when a registered baseline file exists with a count of zero. Plant: A zero baseline file left in place fails. Control: The file deleted and the rule error passes.

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: D

rules.rule: No new file on a legacy path; the legacy count only shrinks and the baseline is deleted at zero.
rules.detail: Anything outside the declared layout is legacy, and the count of legacy files only falls. On the Go side, files outside the standard layout are counted and the count only falls. On the web side, files in no declared layer are a shrink-only list that is deleted at zero.
rules.why: A legacy area that can take new files never empties.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. Ratchet helper counts files outside the declared layout and applies the shrink-only rule. Plant: A new file added outside the declared layout fails. Control: A new file inside a declared layer passes.

open: The declared layout is project-specific; the rule is generic and the layout comes from each project's rule data.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Each shared package has a file-count ratchet that only shrinks, and growth needs an explicit gate-change record.
rules.detail: A package over its size has a written reason and the count of large files only falls; raising a shared package's ceiling is a gate change (gates.protection.1).
rules.why: A shared package that grows without a count becomes the place everything lands.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. The ratchet helper applied per shared package; growth requires the stored verdict. Plant: Adding a file to a ratcheted shared package fails without a verdict. Control: Removing one passes.

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Related to the per-file ceiling (gates.ratchets.2), which counts lines; this counts files per package.

rules.rule: A review-class item carries a fingerprint; when it changes, the gate fails until a reason that resolves to a ticket or decision is recorded.
rules.detail: A generated port-surface file per package, diffed in the gate like the export list of a shared package. It covers exported and unexported interfaces and the parameter structs they take; a function parameter on a port goes on the fingerprint too. A `Do(op string, args ...any)` shape would freeze the surface, so it is banned. The value is a committed diff a reviewer sees, not the reason: most landings already name a ticket, so a resolving reason costs nothing. Whether the second case (a consumer broken unseen) is real stays review.
rules.why: A port surface changed on 25 of one repo's 472 landings, 11 of another's 82 and 37 of 964 in a third; real changes by construction, so 0 false fires. Struct-only changes this form cannot see: 18, 11 and 1.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. Check command `companion check port-surface`: generated port-surface file per package diffed in the gate; the reason must resolve to a ticket or decision id. apidiff covers only the exported API (to try). Plant: A new method with no reason fails; a field added to a parameter struct (owed, passes today). Control: The same diff with a reason naming a ticket passes; an unchanged port passes.

rules.review_question: Did this port change break a consumer that the diff did not show?
open: Note, 8 Nov 2026: the item is the fact answered. For an answer about an import the item is the import, so its fingerprint covers the importing package’s import set and an unrelated edit to the file renews nothing (gates.ratchets.11). This is this rule read on the item it names, not loosened.
No fault in our record; it would become a hard rule if a landed port change breaks a consumer unseen. The plant for a parameter-struct field is owed.

rules.rule: A commit that moves or renames files changes no behaviour and carries no logic edit.
rules.detail: A similarity check on renames at commit: for a commit marked as a move, every entry in the rename diff at 100 percent similarity must be a pure rename; a mixed commit fails. Moves are declared, because an unmarked move that changes behaviour passes. The known way round is moving, then editing, in two commits, which is the wanted result. A move commit is added to the blame-ignore list (`.git-blame-ignore-revs`). The thing moved is a separate change from the work that uses it.
rules.why: Mixed moves hide the real change from a reader (principles report P-02 section 5.14). Argued, no fault of ours.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. `git diff -M100% --name-status` on a commit whose subject starts `move:`: every entry must be R100; a mixed commit fails. About 30 lines over git. Plant: A commit marked `move:` that renames a file and edits one line fails. Control: A pure rename passes.

rules.review_question: Does this commit move files and also change behaviour?
open: Detection works only for declared moves; undeclared moves pass, and the cheap cure is not to declare. It would become a hard rule if moves were detected without a declaration (rename detection on every commit with edit-size limits), which needs a build the evidence does not justify.
rules.note: Merges the Go move rule, the web move rule and the handbook rule that a move commit changes no behaviour.

rules.rule: A gate or repo reader of YAML refuses a duplicate key.
rules.detail: The keys of a YAML mapping are unique (YAML 1.2.2, section 3.2.1.1). A reader of the gate registry, the repo checks or the dev tool's own files that takes the last of two equal keys lets a second definition override the first without a word, so the strict reader is the one every such reader calls and the permissive one is banned in those folders.
rules.why: A duplicate key in a gate list drops the first entry silently and the gate passes with a check missing (gragas#1733, class 4).

checks.note: golangci-lint forbidigo bans ordered.ParseYAML in internal/dev/gate, internal/repo and cmd/gragas-dev and names ParseStrict. Plant: a file in internal/dev/gate that calls ordered.ParseYAML is reported (internal/parse_strict_test.go). Control: the same call in another folder, and ParseStrict in the gate, pass.

bad.code:
// a gate list read so that a key written twice keeps the last one
rows, err := ordered.ParseYAML(data)

good.code:
// the strict reader refuses a key written twice
rows, err := ordered.ParseStrict(data)

rules.rule: A standard is active only while it links the check that enforces it; a rule with no check is marked as an instruction and does not bind anyone.
rules.detail: The rule data is validated by a JSON Schema that requires either a `check` or `instruction` on every row, and the registry repo's gate (make check and the pre-push hook) fails otherwise. A rule stays unbound until its check exists, so the grid cannot lie; a changelog ledger lists rules not yet on (for example todo and skip bans, an unknown-cast comment rule, deep relative imports, and ticketed suppressions in tests).
rules.why: The reference team learned this the hard way; the ledger idea comes from the same team. No fault in our own record; the schema uses a standard validator, no program built.

checks.note: Rule data validated by a JSON Schema (a standard validator) requiring `check` or `instruction` on every row. Plant: A rule row with neither fails. Control: A row with a check, or marked instruction, passes.

open: The schema validator is not chosen (check-jsonschema or ajv).
rules.note: Merges the standard-links-its-check rule, the Go no-check-is-an-instruction rule and the ledger of unbound rules.

rules.rule: The first project on a rule pack runs a pilot list of framework-specific checks, signed by a named person, before others adopt it.
rules.detail: Every pack row runs on the first project with a plant before a second project on that framework starts; until then the pack is admitted by pilot. For React, the pilot list covers: a gated loader sends nothing without permission, a loader-created entry is not persisted when it must not be, search serialisation round-trips, the production build loads under the declared script policy, and the router test helper renders in the story tool and the unit runner. The list is signed by a named person; a stored signed file could be presence-checked, but who signs is the point.
rules.why: A rule pack that was never run on real code has unproven plants.
rules.review_question: Has the first project on this pack run every pack row with a plant, and who signed the list?
open: Binds with the first React project; the list then becomes a file that land reads.
rules.note: Merges the pilot rule and the pack-admission route.

rules.rule: Growing the rule set is one change that adds the rule, its check, its plant and its grid cell together.
rules.detail: The boundary preset ships an empty extension list that later rules append to; a new shared rule lands with its check and its plant in one change. A gate check in the registry repo: a change adding a rule row must also add the check id, plant and grid cell (diff scan).
rules.why: A donor lesson: rows were added without their checks.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. Land refuses a new rule row with no check, plant or grid cell (diff scan in the registry repo's gate). Plant: A rule row added with no plant is refused. Control: A row added with its check, plant and cell passes.

open: Would become a hard rule when a rule enters without its plant; Hard from the enforcement record.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure; reference lesson

rules.rule: A status board is derived from the gate registry, not typed, and a page is generated from the rule data.
rules.detail: The board is generated from the registry and committed, with a generate-then-check drift gate. Generated pages show the rules, the debt and the progress. A hand edit of the board fails.
rules.why: Hand-typed status at a reference team said 3 enforced where the computed count was 0. Our own criteria column of checks is hand-typed, which is the same fault.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. Status board generated from the rule registry and committed, with a generate-check drift gate. Plant: Edit the board by hand and the check fails; a registry rule with no fixture shows as unproven. Control: A regenerated board passes.

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: A (reference)
rules.note: Merges the status-board rule, the page-generator tool and the generated-views kind.

rules.rule: The rule-by-repo grid is computed from resolved configs; a rule set to warn is not counted as enforced, and a tool whose config cannot be read shows "unreadable", never "no".
rules.detail: The grid generator reads the resolved config (for golangci-lint, `golangci-lint linters --json`, to try) and counts error severity only. The gate fails if the committed grid differs from a regenerated one (generate-then-check).
rules.why: The reference team's computed grid said 0 enforced where hand-typed status said 3.

checks.note: v1 class record. A grid generator reading resolved configs; a gate test fails a hand-typed cell. Plant: A rule at warn counted as enforced fails; a hand edit of the grid fails. Control: A regenerated grid passes.

rules.review_question: Is any grid cell hand-typed or counted from a rule at warn?
open: Donor fault only (no fault in our record); becomes a hard rule if our hand-kept status is found wrong.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure

rules.rule: Every rule row states its status, the check that enforces it, its zero-by, and the failure it prevents, and has a fixture.
rules.detail: The rule table requires status, enforced-by and zero-by fields on every row, and a failure-prevented sentence and a fixture on every rule.
rules.why: A rule row without these cannot be told from a wish.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. Rule-table schema requires status, enforced_by, zero_by, failure and fixture. Plant: A row missing any field fails the schema. Control: A complete row passes.

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: A (reference)

rules.rule: Findings from a platform review are pinned as tests, so each accepted ruling is held by a check that names it, or says it is an instruction.
rules.detail: Examples of review tests: config shape, exact licence match, last value wins, no package runner, the skip list agrees with the byte-equal list, no rule below error. An accepted decision links the check that holds it or says instruction.
rules.why: A ruling with no check is forgotten by the next change.

checks.note: Tests in the shared package named after each review finding that pin the ruling. Plant: Reverting a ruled setting fails the test that names it. Control: The ruled configuration passes.

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Rule ids are unique, every claim in a rule resolves to a file or command that exists, and every cited rule id and ticket exists.
rules.detail: A rule-link checker (`companion check rule-links`) walks the rule data: unique ids, every backticked file, command or id resolves, every rule id or ticket cited (each rule row states its zero-by) in code, docs, cards and change descriptions exists (rules in the rulebook, tickets in the index). A URL link checker is a candidate for external links. A ticket names only things that exist.
rules.why: 52 "claim false" lines in the first review; the guides test in one repo is the model.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. A rule-links check command: unique rule ids, resolvable backticked claims, cited ids exist (the guide-names-real-tests test is the model). Plant: A duplicate id fails; a claim naming a missing file fails; a cited rule id that does not exist fails. Control: A registry with unique ids and resolving claims passes.

open: On the web side no check yet verifies that a cited rule or ticket id exists.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: own bugs (52 lines)
rules.note: Merges the Go unique-id rule, the web citation rule and the rulebook-committed rule.

rules.rule: Every rule is assigned to exactly one owner or card, and a generated roster fails when a rule is unassigned or doubled.
rules.detail: A generator over the rule data and the cards: every rule id assigned once; unassigned or doubled fails. Where the source asks for a named owner who reads changes to sensitive paths, a CODEOWNERS file is not available (one GitHub identity), so a named non-author reviewer by trailer carries it.
rules.why: A donor lesson: a generated roster failing on unassigned or doubled rules. No fault of ours counted.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. A roster generator over the rule data and cards. Plant: A rule with no card, and a rule on two cards, both fail. Control: One owner each passes.

rules.rule: At each stage exit, list the rules whose check has not fired in a stated window and the rules with no owner, and keep each with a reason or remove it; the exemption list and extension table are reviewed too.
rules.detail: A silent rule may be working, so a firing count alone never removes one; the window is a guess and the output is a report that opens a review. Fire counts per rule come from gate logs. A row that no concern used in two stages is questioned, and a recurring workaround becomes a row.
rules.why: Rows only accumulate; the window is a guess (principles report P-02 section 7.3).

rules.rule: A shared check moves by rung (review, ratcheted, zero, enforced); its rung is a field on the rule and a move is announced.
rules.detail: The rung field is in the rule table. Rung adoption for a repo with debt (the adoption order is in the handbook): off, then suppress all in a no-logic change, then error for new files, then the registry stage, then zero. A firing count alone never removes a rule.
rules.why: A shared check that changes level silently surprises every repo that takes it.

rules.rule: Base rules apply to every project; a kind or a framework brings a rule pack of its own, a pack adds rows and never edits a base row, and an exemption is per kind with a one-line reason, as data.

rules.rule: Gates are generic and shared by version: one lint stack, with config rendered from one shared source into each repo and checked byte for byte; a project adds only its own rules.
rules.detail: The gate files in each project equal the version-locked template output, and only parameters are project-owned. For Go: golangci-lint has no `extends` or `include`, so the shared config (base plus packs) is copied into each repo by a sync command and a check re-renders in memory and compares bytes, listing every stale path. Sibling repos run the same shared gates and presets published once, with the runtime floor aligned, and a parity check fails when a resolved config drifts from the preset version (one Go version across the estate).
rules.why: 5 distinct lint configs among 6 repos (V-25).

Go lint config has no merge, so a repo may add only named fields in a separate local file that the check reads by meaning. A loosened setting fails; the strictness flags (strict compiler flags) stay on.
rules.why: A repo that can add keys to its overlay can turn the base off.

rules.rule: A migration is swept within a deadline, then the old way is blocked.
rules.detail: The sync check compares each consumer's lock with the newest allowed shared version; a consumer older than the migration deadline in the migration record fails its own gate. It applies to code migrations and to contracts read by programs another owner deploys; it does not apply to a config key spelling, and a program whose readers all change in the same release keeps no old way to sweep.
rules.why: Three adoption issues were open since 27 October with no end date.

rules.rule: A check that exists is in the gate, or it is deleted, and the gate list is derived from the gate files themselves, never typed into a second list.
rules.detail: Every make target named as a check is reachable from the `check` target. Where a repo keeps its gates as files, each gate file declares its own metadata (name, rules held, budget, exit voice), and the gate command builds its member list by reading those files; a list typed by hand in a Makefile, a config or a doc is a second home that drifts and is a finding. A bespoke check script moves into the standard lint or import-rule tool and is then deleted: import rules go to the dependency-boundary linter or a repo test, one lint stack carries the rest, and a check that is not in the gate is deleted. Data validators of configuration files are not domain scripts and stay.
rules.why: A drift check that is not in the gate fails 13 of 35 entries unseen (V-27). The scan is a `gatescan` rule. A gate list typed apart from the gate files loses the gate that was added last.

checks.note: A gate scan: every Makefile target named as a check is reachable from `check`; a recipe in the shared Makefile fragment, standard tools only. Where gates are files, a test that the member list the gate command runs equals the set of gate files. Plant: A check target not reachable from `check` fails; a new gate file missing from a typed member list fails. Control: All targets reachable passes; a list derived from the files passes.

rules.rule: A check replaced by a standard tool keeps a rule-by-rule parity table, and the replacement fires all the old check's plants before the old check is removed.
rules.detail: The table maps each old rule to a lint rule, a spec, or "dropped" with a reason; the remaining hits are then fixed or exempted with a ticket and an expiry. The replacement change runs the old plant corpus against the new config in the same change (a parity run); a plant that stops firing fails the swap. Deleting the awkward plant first is a gate weakening (gates.protection.1). Applies to home-made regex style scripts and any home-made check.
rules.why: A replacement silently narrows coverage, and only plants prove parity.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. The replacement change runs the old tool's plant corpus against the new config (`--parity old-plants-dir`). Plant: A replacement that misses one old plant fails the swap. Control: A replacement that fires every old plant passes.

rules.note: Merges the parity-table rows of both sides and the "check that exists is in the gate" replacement half.

rules.rule: No tracked path is a symbolic link.
rules.detail: A tracked entry of mode 120000 fails the check, naming the path. A link reads as a file on one system and as a text file holding a path on another, so the checkout differs by system.
rules.why: A repository that must check out the same on every system cannot hold an entry whose meaning depends on the system that wrote it.

checks.note: The link key of the gragas preset, which gragas check computes. gragas check reads the tracked list from git. Plant: a tracked symlink fails, naming its path. Control: a tree of regular files passes.

rules.rule: No two tracked paths differ only by case.
rules.detail: Two tracked paths that are equal once case is folded fail the check, naming both. On a case-folding file system the second overwrites the first.
rules.why: A checkout on a case-folding system keeps one of the two files and loses the other without a message.

checks.note: The fold key of the gragas preset, which gragas check computes. gragas check folds the case of each tracked path and fails a pair. Plant: two paths that differ by case fail, naming both. Control: distinct paths pass.

rules.rule: An interrupt (Ctrl-C), and SIGTERM where the system sends one, stop the program cleanly through signal.NotifyContext.
rules.detail: The program ends on os.Interrupt, and on syscall.SIGTERM where the system sends one, through signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM); Go maps Windows' Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Break, close and logoff onto those two. A matrix test starts the built binary or daemon (testenv.Binary.Start), interrupts it (Running.Interrupt) and asserts exit within 5 seconds with the done or interrupted code and that a temp file or socket it owns is removed. The old signal notify call is banned in favour of NotifyContext outside the one serve helper.
rules.why: Own measure: used in 5 of 6 repos. A daemon that ignores the interrupt is killed by the service manager and loses its state.

rules.rule: A package that starts a goroutine is tested with the race detector and a leak check; the race run is in the release gate and runs locally after any change that starts or changes a goroutine; and it may sit outside the pre-push gate only when it is over that gate's measured budget.
rules.detail: The race run is a make target (make race) in the shared Makefile fragment. It runs in the release workflow, on a tag or by manual dispatch, and never on a push or a pull request. When a change adds or edits a go statement, the pre-push hook runs the race target for the touched packages. While the whole race run fits the pre-push budget it stays in make check. A recipe lists the packages with a go statement and greps for the leak check in their tests. Which leak check is open: the leak library's test-main verifier or the runtime's goroutine-leak profile.
rules.why: Practice. No repo uses the leak library; only one runs the race detector by default. The profile found one planted leak in verification. No push CI: the gate runs locally, and a check too slow for the hook moves to the release workflow, not to a hosted job.

checks.note: race flag in the release gate and the race make target; a pre-push hook step that runs it for packages whose go statements changed; companion check goroutine-tests (go/packages finds production packages with go statements and requires goleak.VerifyTestMain or the goroutineleak profile in that package's tests); a recipe form uses go list -f. Plant: a package with a goroutine and no leak check fails; a push that changes a go statement without the race step fails the hook; a release workflow without the race run fails the workflow check. Control: a package with the test-main verifier passes

rules.rule: Code is sequential by default: a goroutine is added only where a measured gain is cited at the go statement, an adapter adds no goroutine, poll or timer, and a slow read is cached on demand with a stated hold and bound.
rules.detail: The citation is a comment on the line above the go statement naming the measurement (what, how much, where it is recorded). An adapter is a plain call: a go statement, time.Ticker, time.NewTimer, time.AfterFunc or a loop around time.Sleep in a host or adapter package is a finding. A cached read states how long it holds and how many entries it keeps, and nothing reads while nobody asks.
rules.why: Concurrency is the largest source of bugs that show only years in, and a measured reason at the call is the cheapest guard. Keeping adapters free of polls is what keeps a program idle when nobody asks.

checks.note: ast-grep rule for a go statement with no measurement comment above it, and forbidigo on go statements, tickers, timers and AfterFunc in adapter packages (path rule over the host folder). Plant: a go statement with no comment above it fires; time.NewTicker in internal/host/linux fires. Control: a go statement with a measured-gain comment in the core passes

rules.rule: At commit, gofmt and go mod tidy run as diffs that list what differs and never rewrite the tree.
rules.detail: The format member runs gofmt with the list flag and fails on any file named; the tidy member runs go mod tidy with the diff flag and fails on any output. Neither writes, so both run beside the other members (gates.command.28) and inside the commit hook's seconds (gates.command.17). The fix is the same command in write mode, run by the person, not by the hook.
rules.why: A commit hook that rewrites files and restages them is the opposite of a check, and two hooks of one fleet did exactly that; a tidy that writes in the hook races the members beside it.

sources.says: If a file's formatting is different from gofmt's, print its name to standard output.
The -diff flag causes go mod tidy not to modify go.mod or go.sum but instead print the necessary changes as a unified diff.

rules.review_question: Do the format and tidy members of this commit tier list differences and exit non-zero, or do they write?
open: The tidy member runs (make tidy, tests in cmd/gragas-dev/tidy_test.go), but no check row names it: a check that binds no preset tool key counts in checks-unresolved, checks-without-fix and, on this instruction, advisory-with-checks, and each baseline may only fall. tools/ is held to go.mod and go.sum in full, because the installer puts tools/go.sum back as committed after it primes the module cache (gragas#767). The format half has no check either.

rules.rule: The push lint runs vet and the shared lint preset with the parallel-test linters on, and a test that runs alone carries a serial comment that names the process state it needs.
rules.detail: tests.runners.4 holds that a test is parallel by default and a serial one says why. This line names the tools that hold it in Go: the linter that reports a test without a parallel call, and the one that reports a parallel call in the wrong place. The stated reason is a comment of the form `// serial:` with the state the test needs, and the linter's own disable comment is not the reason. A test that only needs a variable for a child process sets it on the child's environment and stays parallel.
rules.why: Four of five projects in one fleet had zero parallel tests, and one project's 152 serial tests took 136 seconds on about one CPU; the linter finds the missing call before the tier report does.

sources.says: Detects missing usage of t.Parallel() method in your Go test. ... Tparallel detects inappropriate usage of t.Parallel() method in your Go test codes.

rules.review_question: Are the two parallel-test linters on in this project's lint preset, and does each serial test carry a serial comment naming its state?

rules.rule: The stamp key holds the Go build settings that change a verdict, the flags variable, the cgo switch, the experiment variable and the toolchain, and a run inside a workspace file gets no key.
rules.detail: gates.land.15 holds that a stamp is keyed to the exact tree, its settings and its tools. For Go the settings are GOFLAGS, CGO_ENABLED, GOEXPERIMENT and the toolchain version, read from the go tool, not from the shell. A workspace file changes which module code a build sees without changing the tree, so a run under one is not keyed: it runs, and nothing is stamped or served.
rules.why: A stamp that ignores a build setting serves a green for a build nobody ran; a workspace can point a build at a sibling checkout the tree does not hold.
rules.note: Retired with gragas#907. There is no stamp and no key for it to hold the Go build settings: the tiers run every time, so the settings are read from the environment of the run itself.

sources.says: A space-separated list of -flag=value settings to apply to go commands by default
If GOWORK is set to off, the command will be in a single-module context.

rules.review_question: Which build settings are in this stamp's key, are they read from the go tool, and what does the runner do under a workspace file?
open: Planned check: the runner's report lists the key's fields and a test changes each setting and sees a new key. No tool key is bound yet; the shared runner is the work of gragas#642.

rules.rule: The tools step fetches the whole module graph, so a fresh clone builds, and cross-compiles once for one other system as a smoke, with the network blocked.
rules.detail: gates.command.21 holds that a fresh clone passes after the documented setup, and supply.install.2 that the build runs with the network blocked after the install. A cross-compile for another system pulls modules the first never needed; the tools step downloads them once and the one cross-compile smoke runs offline. It is a smoke that no code of one system crept into the product, not a build per shipped system. One run that primed the cache is not setup.

Held by the golangci preset (default: standard turns it on): most of what it reports is an err overwritten before it is read, which is an error swallowed
