rules.rule: An error is wrapped with %w and context saying what was being done, and compared with errors.Is or errors.As.
rules.why: Practice; a wrapped error compared with == silently stops matching.

checks.note: golangci-lint errorlint (errorf %w, comparison, type assertion on wrapped errors); wrapcheck stays off because it contradicts do not annotate when it adds nothing. Plant: fmt.Errorf("read: %v", err) fails, and err == io.EOF on a wrapped error fails. Control: %w and errors.Is pass

rules.review_question: Does this wrapped error say what was being done, not only that it failed?
open: Half: the %w and comparison half is the rule; the context half is review. The plant exists from an earlier linter trial.

rules.rule: Panic is for programmer errors only and never crosses a package's API, and an unchecked type assertion is banned.
rules.detail: A panic outside main and tests sits on a one-file-per-entry allow list that only shrinks. A type assertion without the ok check is an unchecked error return. Whether a panic crosses a package API is review.
rules.why: Own measure: panics outside main in our repos: 6 (20 in all), 8, 3, 2, 5 and 0.

checks.note: golangci-lint forbidigo with type analysis on the builtin panic outside main and tests with a shrink-only allow list; errcheck check-type-assertions for the unchecked assertion (forcetypeassert was skipped as a duplicate) forbidigo runs with analyze-types: true. Plant: panic("boom") fails, and x := v.(string) fails. Control: a panic in a path excluded by the exclusion rules passes
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on errcheck names this rule.

rules.review_question: Can this panic reach a caller of the package's API?
open: Run with golangci-lint 2.14.0. Whether a panic crosses a package API is review.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure

rules.rule: Only main calls os.Exit or a fatal log; a command returns its ending as a value (an exit status, or a typed result or error mapped to one in one place); and every refusal is testable in process.
rules.detail: An exit call or a fatal log call outside main is a finding; the linter's per-rule cap is off so repeats are not hidden. Test files are excluded by path (a test main may call exit). A command function is func Verb(...) int or returns a typed ending or error; either way exactly one function maps endings and errors to the exit codes of cli.exit.1, by word or type, never by message. A test calls each command in process and reads its ending.
rules.why: Own measure: 0 exits outside the main package everywhere today; a library that exits cannot be tested or reused. The part that protects is the lint: no exit outside main, so every path is testable in process. Both Go target programs return an ending because a refusal is a value they print on three surfaces, and forcing an error type in between adds a layer with no reader.

unless.reason: It has no main package.

checks.note: golangci-lint revive deep-exit plus forbidigo as a second net, with max-issues-per-linter and max-same-issues set to zero so repeats are not hidden; an ast-grep count of functions that map to exit codes, which must be one. Plant: os.Exit(3) and log.Fatalf in a non-main package each fail; a second switch from error to exit code in a command package fails the count. Control: main calling os.Exit with the code from the one mapping function passes
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on forbidigo names this rule.

open: Test main calling exit is legal in old Go, so test files are path-excluded.

rules.rule: Error strings follow one style (lowercase, no trailing punctuation), and any exception is written down once.
rules.why: Practice. The ruling on style is open: the linter rule is disabled in three configs today, and a repo that keeps sentence-style errors lists the exception once in rule data.

checks.note: golangci-lint staticcheck ST1005 enabled once the style is ruled, with a written exception list in rule data. Plant: errors.New("Cannot open file.") fails. Control: errors.New("cannot open file") passes

open: Blocked on the style ruling (conflict C-15); the mechanism is ready once settled.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Nil flows (a map lookup or a nil pointer followed by a field read) are checked, advisory, with a count that only falls.
rules.why: Practice. Findings today: 206 in one repo and 106 in another; 75 tracker issues of the tool mention false positives.

checks.note: nilaway with the module included, run at tier 3; findings ratcheted per package against a baseline file that only falls; the tool pinned by pseudo-version in a tools module Invocation: nilaway -include-pkgs=<module> ./... Plant: a map lookup then field read and a nil pointer then field read give two findings. Control: the guarded forms give none

open: Advisory plus a ratchet: the count cannot rise, nothing else fails. It fails the rule definition only if the ratchet is skipped.
The tool has no tagged release (pushed Oct 2026, source says).
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Each error is handled once, logged or returned and not both; a new sentinel or typed error exists only when a caller branches on it.
rules.why: Practice; no fault in our record. Run on two repos: 0 real hits, so adoption debt is zero where tried.

checks.note: errlogreturn as a standalone analyzer or a plugin: reports a function where one error reaches a logger and a return on the same path; conservative, so log and return on different branches pass. Plant: slog.Error then return fmt.Errorf in one branch reports both lines. Control: a function that only returns passes, and a boundary function that logs then returns an exit code passes

rules.review_question: Does a caller branch on this sentinel or typed error, and is the error both logged and returned here?
open: Half: the log-and-return half is the rule; sentinel-only-when-branched is review.
The tool is days-old in practice (first release Oct 2026): pin the version and keep the plant as its selftest. Four other repos not run.

rules.rule: An error crossing a process or wire boundary travels as a word from a closed list plus detail and is typed again on the other side, and callers compare with errors.Is or errors.As, never the message.
rules.detail: The wire form is a word and a detail field; the receiving side maps the word back to the sentinel or typed error of the closed list, and an unknown word becomes one typed unknown error carrying it. A comparison of err.Error() or a strings.Contains on an error message is a finding.
rules.why: Typing an error again after a flattening joint keeps callers off message strings that change; it is the Go side of the one refusal value of cli.errors.2.

checks.note: ast-grep rules for err.Error() compared with == or passed to strings.Contains, HasPrefix or EqualFold, plus a round-trip test per boundary encoding every word and decoding it back to errors.Is equality. Plant: if err.Error() == "busy" fails; a word added to the list with no decode case fails the round-trip test. Control: errors.Is(err, ErrBusy) after a wire round trip passes

rules.rule: A Go program starts from one layout template: programs live under cmd/<name>/ and everything else under internal/, with no pkg/ folder; adapters live under one host folder, one package per platform or per external tool, and the core lives outside it; and every package sits in a layer named in the import table.
rules.detail: The template is rule data (the layer and import table), so a new program starts from it one to one: cmd/<name>/ (wires and registers implementations, nothing else), internal/core/ (the domain), internal/core/api/ (routes and their JSON result types), port packages (interfaces only, each with its fake), slot packages with their registries, internal/host/<platform or tool>/ (adapters, such as host/linux, host/launchd), internal/door/ (listeners), internal/config/, internal/cli/<group>/ and internal/cli/ui/ (the only terminal code), and leaf packages. A layout test walks the module tree and lists packages: it fails on any directory named pkg, on a main package outside cmd/<name>/, on a non-test package at the module root or outside cmd/ and internal/, on an adapter outside the host folder, and on a package with no layer in the table. A library repo is declared kind lib in rule data and is exempt, since a library has exported packages at its root. The popular project-layout repository (golang-standards/project-layout) is not a standard.
rules.why: Practice; all six of our Go repos follow cmd and internal. A shared layout makes a port, an adapter or a command findable across programs by an agent that has read one of them, and the two Go target programs already agree on the names.

unless.reason: A library has exported packages at its root and no cmd folder.

checks.note: layout test in the shared gate pack (go test over the module tree with a directory walk and the package list), the layer table and kind lib read from rule data. Plant: a pkg/util directory with one file fails; a main.go at the module root fails; an adapter package internal/launchd outside the host folder fails; a package missing from the layer table fails. Control: cmd/foo/main.go plus internal/core and internal/host/linux, each in the table, passes

open: Rendered from the same layer table as the import rules of the architecture part; arch.structure.6 points at the template per kind of program.

rules.rule: No init functions outside the main package, or their count only falls.
rules.why: Own measure: init functions in our repos today: 26 in one, 1 in another, 0 in the rest. The linter is enabled in six of six configs.

sources.says: Checks that no init functions are present in Go code.
The one surveyed command line program that registers commands from init functions through blank imports, which makes the command set depend on import side effects.

checks.note: golangci-lint gochecknoinits in the shared config; the count only falls through a new-code-only setting or an existing-debt baseline; a justified init carries a nolint with a reason New-code-only is golangci issues.new-from-merge-base. Plant: func init() in an internal package fails. Control: no init passes

rules.note: Promoted in E4 (gragas#1740) under a ruling there: enforced-without-examples rises by the count until baseline.json goes at the switch (gragas#1743), and no examples block is written.

rules.rule: No replace directive in go.mod and no go.work file in a committed tree.
rules.why: A local replace builds on one machine only and hides the real dependency; a workspace file changes resolution for everyone who checks out.

sources.says: replace directives only apply in the main module's go.mod file and are ignored in other modules.

checks.note: golangci-lint gomoddirectives with an empty replace allow list (verified 5 Nov that a replace line is reported as a local replacement not allowed), plus a one-line tracked-file check for go.work in the gate scan. Plant: a replace line fails, and a committed go.work fails. Control: neither passes

rules.rule: Shipped binaries are built with cgo disabled.
rules.why: A cgo binary links the host's C library and breaks the static, copy-anywhere build. Own measure: set in 5 of the 7 programs today (verified); the library repo and one scraper set none.

unless.reason: A library ships no binary.

checks.note: grep of build recipes for CGO_ENABLED=0, and go version -m on the built binary. Plant: a build with cgo enabled fails. Control: a build recipe with it disabled passes

open: Proposed as a gate; no plant recorded in the catalogue.
rules.note: The dependency-side counterpart is a supply-chain rule held by the supply part.

rules.rule: A daemon logs through log/slog or a handler of it, output for a person goes to stderr, and no fatal log call appears outside main.
rules.detail: A handler of slog includes a library that implements slog.Handler (for example a terminal-styled handler at a terminal and JSON without one); the program logs through the slog API either way. The standard log package is denied in the daemon kind; the logger is passed in and messages are static with key-value attributes, so a printf-built message is a finding. A fatal log call outside main is held by go.errors.4. A CLI is exempt until the shared logger leaf exists. What a daemon log holds and where it goes is daemon.logging.1; the audit record is daemon.logging.3.
rules.why: Own measure: only one of our repos uses slog (3 files); another has a log.Fatal. One logging API with a choice of handler keeps styled terminal output and machine logs from being two code paths.

unless.reason: The shared logger leaf that wraps the handler does not exist yet; go.logging.2 holds for both kinds once it is built.

checks.note: golangci-lint sloglint (no-global all, static-msg, kv-only) plus depguard deny of the standard log package in the daemon kind. Plant: import "log" and log.Printf in a daemon package fail, and slog.Info with a message built with a printf fails. Control: a logger passed in with a static message, through any slog.Handler, passes

open: Output for a person to stderr is held by the CLI part's matrix test.

rules.rule: Every log line from a daemon or a long CLI run carries the program version and a run id from one handler, so a CLI call and the daemon it spoke to can be joined.
rules.detail: One shared logger constructor adds the version and the run id. A matrix test runs the binary or daemon with logging on, parses every stderr or log line as JSON and asserts both fields; the default logger is banned so lines cannot bypass the handler.
rules.why: Practice. A run id exists in 10 files of one repo and 2 of another; a request id nowhere; 21 files write to stderr directly.

unless.reason: It has no log output of its own.

checks.note: shared logger constructor adding version and run id from one slog handler; matrix test parses every log line as JSON and asserts both fields; sloglint no-global all The constructor is ui.NewLogger, which wraps the shared slog handler. Plant: a log line through the default logger with no run id fails the parse assertion. Control: a logger from the constructor passes

open: Depends on the shared logger leaf existing; the rule falls to best practice if that handler is not built.
The marginal assertion on the matrix helper is cheap, its cost being carried by the CLI part's terminal rules.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Interfaces are small, and a function accepts interfaces and returns concrete types.
rules.why: Practice. One repo declares 98 interfaces; their sizes were not measured; the linter flagged a 40-method port in another.

checks.note: golangci-lint interfacebloat with a ceiling of 10 methods; iface covers part of return-concrete (ireturn was skipped for false positives). Plant: an interface with 12 methods is reported at a ceiling of 10. Control: a small interface passes

rules.review_question: Does this function accept the smallest interface it needs and return a concrete type?
open: Half: the size half is the rule; accept-interfaces-return-concrete is review. The ceiling of 10 is a choice.
The control for the plant was not run.

rules.rule: A concept gets a named type, the zero value is useful, and generics come only after the same code was written several times.
rules.why: Practice; judgement. Nothing decides that a concept needs a type.
rules.review_question: Is this primitive-typed parameter a concept that needs its own type, and is the zero value of this new type useful?
open: A count of type-parameter declarations is a hint only (report); no check on named types or zero values.
Blocked: no tool decides a concept needs a type.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: No checks for states that cannot happen, and no wrapper or function that only forwards a call; pass-throughs are counted per package and read as a list, with no limit.
rules.detail: A types-aware analyser counts free functions that forward to a function of the same shape, and wrappers whose every method has the same signature as the call it forwards, with no type conversion. Dispatchers and adapters that convert types are exempt; an adapter that imports what the core may not is a seam and exempt; a fake alone does not earn the exemption.
rules.why: Practice; no fault among the 60 sampled. Free forwarders today: 48, 12, 11, 18, 2 and 2 across six repos; 39 of the first 48 forward inside our own module, in clusters left by moves, 9 are false hits.

checks.note: v1 class our-plugin. types analyser that counts forwarding free functions and wrappers and prints the list per package; a golangci module plugin with a trivial-forwarder rule is a host-free alternative to try first. Plant: a forwarding type fires; a type with one extra method fires only partly. Control: an adapter that converts types passes

rules.review_question: Does this wrapper do anything the call it forwards does not, and is this check for a state that cannot happen?
open: A new pass-through blocks until answered. Measure: no limit and no fail line, since a ratchet is beaten for free by one extra statement and a layer rule can demand the alias.
Whole-type wrappers: 1 hit in six repos plus one exempt.
The alternative plugin (BSD-3, v0.2.0, Sep 2026) was not run here; try it on the clones before building.

rules.rule: The resource and context linters are on: bodyclose, noctx, and in a repo that imports the SQL package sqlclosecheck and rowserrcheck.
rules.why: A leaked response body is a daemon-lifetime bug. Practice; priced in the linter trial.

unless.reason: A program that does not import the SQL package needs neither of the two database linters; a rule-data field marks it.

checks.note: golangci-lint bodyclose and noctx always; sqlclosecheck and rowserrcheck where the SQL package is imported. Plant: an http.Get whose Body is never closed fails, and db.Query with rows.Err unchecked fails. Control: closed and checked passes
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on noctx names this rule.
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on contextcheck names this rule: a function that receives a context passes it on and does not start a fresh one.

open: Plants must run once; the record sits beside the data part's rule.
rules.note: Moved here from the Postgres part, since the linter set is Go's.

rules.rule: Go tests use the standard testing package only, every test helper calls t.Helper, a table case is named by its claim, and a test checks one behaviour.
rules.detail: An assertion or mock library import in a test file is a finding (tests.doubles.2 bans mock libraries for every language). A function in a test file that takes a testing.TB, *testing.T or *testing.B and is not itself a test calls t.Helper first. A table case name says what holds (refuses a retired key), not an index or input. One behaviour per test is review.
rules.why: A helper without t.Helper reports the failure at the helper's line, not the caller's, and a case named by its claim is the failure message a person reads first. The standard package keeps tests readable by anyone who knows Go.

checks.note: golangci-lint thelper (t.Helper first in helpers) and depguard denying assertion and mock modules in test files; an ast-grep rule for table case names that are empty or numeric. Plant: a helper taking *testing.T with no t.Helper call fails; import of an assertion library in a test fails; a case named "case 1" fails. Control: a helper calling t.Helper first and a case named by its claim pass
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on depguard names this rule.

rules.review_question: Does this test check one behaviour, and does its name say what it claims?
open: The language-free half (non-empty loops, a negative test per guard, a cost line) is tests.admission.2.

rules.rule: A package's tests build with every sibling package outside its declared imports unresolvable, and a suite that still passes with its subject package's non-test source removed fails as vacuous.
rules.detail: The Go form of the sibling-hiding resolver: a gate step lists each package's test import closure (go list -deps -test) and fails when it holds an internal package not allowed for that package's layer in the import table, so a test cannot reach a sibling the package itself may not. The subject-deleted run uses go test -overlay to replace every non-test file of the package with an empty file of the same package name; a suite that compiles and passes is vacuous. A module's tests make another module's data only through that module's exported API or their own fixtures.
rules.why: A suite that passes with its subject deleted is the cheapest mutation test there is, and siblings unresolvable is what makes a package extractable in fact, not only by the import table.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion check test-closure (go list -deps -test against the layer table) and a subject-deleted run with go test -overlay per package. Plant: a test in internal/core importing internal/host/fs fails the closure check; a test that asserts only on its own fixture passes with the package emptied and fails the vacuous run. Control: a test whose closure stays inside the layer's allowed imports and fails with the subject removed passes

open: The language-free rule and the TypeScript resolver are tests.isolation.13 and the ts part.
An overlay that empties a package can break the compile of its tests rather than pass them; only a compile and a pass counts as vacuous. Not run yet.

rules.rule: Each function bundle has a size budget, and a built handler bundle over its byte limit fails the check.
rules.detail: A size-limit tool bundles each handler entry with the build bundler and compares it with the limit in the package manifest (a list of path and limit). In Go, binary size is recorded as a metric, not a gate.
rules.why: A large bundle slows cold start and approaches the platform package limit without anyone choosing it.

checks.note: size-limit with its bundler plugin, one entry per handler with a byte limit in the package manifest. Plant: a handler bundle over its limit fails. Control: a bundle under the limit passes

open: No limit value is chosen; it should be set from measured bundle sizes of existing handlers.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure

rules.rule: Function permissions are granted only through managed policy ARNs on the role, never through a standalone policy attachment.
rules.detail: In Go, a unit runs with its own identity and sandbox from one template, and CI tokens are scoped.
rules.why: A standalone attachment lies outside the role definition, so the role cannot be read as the full list of what a function may do.

checks.note: ast-grep rule over the infrastructure code failing a standalone role policy attachment or inline policy on a function role. Plant: a function role built with an attachment resource fails. Control: managed policy arns on the role pass

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every function has a pinned role name from one table and receives the shared baseline grants.
rules.detail: A function with no entry in the role-name table fails, so a new function cannot be deployed with a generated role name. In Go, a daemon unit has its own identity and sandbox from one template.
rules.why: A generated role name changes on replacement and breaks everything that names it, and a function without the baseline misses logging and tracing grants.

checks.note: ast-grep rule over the infrastructure code failing a function whose logical name is absent from the role-name table or whose role omits the baseline policy. Plant: a function added with no role-name entry fails. Control: a function in the table with the baseline passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A middleware or plumbing library is imported only by the one package that owns that concern.
rules.detail: For the handler wrapper (ordered before, after and error steps) the owner is the shared runtime package; no other package imports the middleware engine. The same holds for each concern with an owner, enforced by import rules; a direct dependency outside the list fails. In Go there is one importable owner per concern.
rules.why: A library imported in many packages has many configurations, and a fix or an upgrade must be found in all of them.

checks.note: import-restriction rule (ESLint no-restricted-imports or an ast-grep rule) allowing the middleware engine only in the shared runtime package, and a dependency-allow-list check on package manifests. Plant: a service package importing the middleware engine directly fails. Control: the runtime package importing it passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: The service rule one-shared-bootstrap states the same for every entry; this is the Lambda binding naming the handler middleware engine.

rules.rule: At commit every JSON file of the theme parses, comments allowed where the platform allows them, and every schema block in a section parses.
rules.detail: A theme's settings, templates and locales are JSON, and each section carries a schema block the platform reads. A file that does not parse is a page that does not render, found at publish otherwise. The check read 395 files in 0.06 seconds on the measuring host. It reads and never writes (gates.command.28).
rules.why: A broken JSON file or schema block reaches the live theme if nothing parses it first.
rules.review_question: Does this commit tier parse every JSON file and every schema block of the theme?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the parse member at commit with its file count in the report. No tool key is bound yet; the stack has no tool record in this rulebook.

rules.rule: Every locale file has every key of the default locale; a new gap fails, and the gaps that exist today sit in a reviewed baseline with an owner that only shrinks.
rules.detail: gates.ratchets.1 holds that debt is a shrink-only list frozen at adoption. The parity check compares each locale's keys with the default's, and the baseline holds the missing keys per file at adoption, so the member is green on the day it lands and red on the first new gap. The baseline's length prints in the report.
rules.why: Eleven locale files of one fleet's theme miss 3 to 9 of 315 keys today; a check with no baseline would stay red and be ignored.
rules.review_question: Does every locale of this theme carry every key of the default, and how long is the parity baseline today against last release?
open: Planned check: the parity member reads the baseline and fails on a key missing that the baseline does not list. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: At push every render, include, section and asset reference resolves to a file, and every block tag is closed.
rules.detail: A reference to a snippet that does not exist and an unclosed conditional each render as an error on the live page. The check walks the templates, resolves each reference against the theme's folders and counts the tag pairs; a prototype did both in 0.06 seconds. It is a push member because it reads the whole theme, and it reads and never writes.
rules.why: A missing snippet and an unclosed conditional were both found by a prototype of this check in one fleet's theme, and nothing else would have found them before the page rendered.
rules.review_question: Does this push tier resolve every reference of the theme to a file and check that every block tag is closed?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the reference member at push with its reference count in the report. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: The platform's theme linter runs at push with the repository's own config, as a member beside the reference check.
rules.detail: The linter knows the platform's objects, filters and deprecations, which the reference check does not; the reference check runs in milliseconds, which the linter may not. Both are members, so a failure names one. The linter's cost was not measured on the host that studied the stack, so its moment is push until a measurement says otherwise (gates.command.3).
rules.why: A theme with no linter in its gate ships the deprecations and the misused filters the platform's own tool would have named.
rules.review_question: Is the theme linter a member of this push tier with the repository's config, and what did it cost in the last run?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the linter member with its cost once measured. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: At push the layout files are scanned for secrets, with an allowlist that holds a third-party widget's public embed id and nothing that is a credential.
rules.detail: supply.secrets.1 holds the secrets scan; a theme's layout files are where a script tag with a key would sit. A public embed id of a widget looks like a secret to a scanner and is not one; it goes on the allowlist with its owner (gates.ratchets.1), and the list prints its length.
rules.why: A trial secrets scan found hits that were not credentials in three repositories of one fleet, and a theme's layout carries exactly the kind of public id that a scanner flags.

sources.says: You can ignore specific findings by creating a .gitleaksignore file at the root of your repo.

rules.review_question: Does this push tier scan the layout files for secrets, and does every allowlist entry name a public id with an owner?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the scan member and the allowlist is a registered baseline. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A release pushes the theme to an unpublished theme and renders the home, a product and a cart page as a preview before anything is published; a change is never deployed straight to the live theme, and the gate holds that rule, not a script alone.
rules.detail: The store's command line pushes to a theme by id. The release member pushes to an unpublished one, then a render member fetches the three pages from the preview and fails on an error or an empty page. The live theme changes only by publishing the previewed one. A repository script that does this is the convention; the release tier is the rule, so a push that names the live theme fails the member. The cost was not measured on the host that studied the stack.
rules.why: A theme deployed straight to the live store is live before anyone has seen a page of it.
rules.review_question: Which theme id does this release push to, which pages does the preview render, and can any member reach the live theme?
open: Planned check: the release member's command names a theme id that is not the live one, held by a test over the members file. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: At commit every link between pages and to an asset resolves offline, and for a docs repository every Markdown link too; the first run freezes a reviewed baseline of the broken links that exist, and it only shrinks.
rules.detail: docs.links.1 holds that docs have no broken file link, checked offline in the gate. This line places the check at commit for pages, where it took 0.16 seconds for 1,747 inputs, and gives it a baseline (gates.ratchets.1) for a repository that already breaks it, so the member is green on the day it lands and red on the first new broken link. External links are a release step, never a gate member (docs.links.1). The secrets scan of the staged diff runs at commit as for every project (supply.secrets.1).
rules.why: One fleet's design pages had 1,752 broken references on the first run, 1,733 of them from one file; a check with no baseline would stay red and be ignored.

sources.says: Only check local files and block network requests

rules.review_question: Does this commit tier check every link offline, and how long is the baseline today against the first run?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the link member at commit and the baseline is a registered baseline. No tool key is bound yet; the docs part's link checker is the candidate.

rules.rule: At commit the ledger or index that lists the pages matches the pages on disk: every page is listed and every listing is a page.
rules.detail: A repository of pages keeps a list of them, as an index page or a data file. The check compares the list with the files both ways in 0.16 seconds. docs.freshness.1 holds that an index is generated and never written by hand; where the ledger is generated this check is the generated-files diff, and where it is written this check is what keeps it true.
rules.why: A page not in the ledger is a page nobody finds, and a ledger row with no page is a broken link on the index.

rules.rule: At push every page has a rendered golden at one width a person reads, updated only by a person reading the diff, a narrow-width property that the page does not overflow sideways, and the accessibility engine over it.
rules.detail: tests.journeys.8 holds one golden width and properties at the narrower ones for any screen; this line is its form for a page. The golden is the rendered page at the width a person reads; the property at a phone width is no horizontal overflow; and the engine runs over each page as web.accessibility.1 has it for an application. Neither was measured on the host that studied the stack, which had no browser run.

rules.rule: The maximum number of database connections the services can open at once is computed from the concurrency the infrastructure allows, checked to be under the cluster limit, and the session timeouts are read back.
rules.detail: The budget is function concurrency times pool size, summed over services that share a cluster, written as data. The connection config sets a statement timeout and an idle-in-transaction timeout, and a test reads them back with SHOW on a fresh pooled connection. A measure sits beside it: connection count and the age of the oldest open transaction, read by hand at each release. Whether a managed pooler is used was not checked.
rules.why: The first big surprise of a growing service is the remaining-connection-slots failure; a runtime that scales to many instances makes the sum large and spiky. Agents raise a pool size to cure a timeout and move the queue (inference).

rules.rule: Transactions are opened only through the one shared transaction helper, which retries the serialisation and deadlock codes a bounded number of times and surfaces a typed failure after that.
rules.detail: The codes are 40001 and 40P01. A transaction makes no call outside the database. For a program in Go the same is one helper that retries serialisation failures, found by a scan for a transaction opened outside it.
rules.why: A stronger isolation level obliges the application to retry, and a helper without the retry loses the write or fails the user. A forced serialisation failure on a real container is the only ordinary test that sees it.

checks.note: a toolkit test forces a serialisation failure on a real container and expects a retry and then a typed error; a raw transaction call outside the helper fails ESLint no-restricted-syntax. Plant: a helper without the retry fails the forced-failure test; a transaction opened outside the helper fails. Control: the helper with a bounded retry passes

rules.rule: A transaction that reads a set and writes on its strength states, as arguments to the helper, which invariant it protects and the isolation level it runs at, and the anomaly the level prevents.
rules.detail: The default level, Read Committed, is right for a single-row read-modify-write and wrong for reading a set and then inserting on the strength of it. The review asks: which invariant does this transaction protect, which anomaly would it suffer at this level, and what does the code do on a serialisation failure.
rules.why: An agent copies the default level and cannot see the race, since no ordinary test produces it. The choice of level is made against a named anomaly, and the engine version matters (postgres.engine.1).

checks.note: a write-skew pair (two concurrent transactions each reading a sum and then inserting) run at the helper's chosen level must end with the invariant held or a retried failure. Plant: a write-skew pair run at the default level breaks the invariant and fails. Control: the same pair at the chosen level holds or retries

rules.rule: Tests run on the engine version production runs; an in-process build of the engine over the real migrations counts as that engine when its major version matches production; a test of roles or connections runs a server build; a version below a stated floor or on a known-bad list fails; and a contract suite pins the behaviour the data layer relies on.
rules.detail: An in-process build (for example PGlite) runs store tests and gates fast over the real migrations; it does not model roles, grants, connections or the superuser, so a test of those runs on a server build of the same major. The in-process major is read and compared like the container's. The container's server version equals the version declared in infrastructure and is compared with a floor file kept as data. The contract suite covers concurrent writers on one row, retry on conflict, ordering, time-zone handling and 64-bit integer width, and runs once per named engine. A container tag is never a floating one. Editing the known-bad list is a protected path.
rules.why: An engine version is part of the contract, and a bug fixed in a later version is a fault carried until the move. A neighbouring engine's write-ahead-log bug stood for years, and a company using it saw corruption in its backup snapshots. Agents bump an image tag to make a build pass (inference).

checks.note: the container's or the in-process build's SHOW server_version compared with the version in the deployment definition and with a floor file, a tag on tests that need roles or connections that refuses the in-process engine, and a contract suite run once per named engine. Control: a matching version passes

rules.rule: A migration that adds an index names the query it serves and the write path that pays for it, and unused indexes are listed from the engine's own statistics at release.

A two-column index is useless to a query on only its second column, and an index on every column makes every write maintain all of them. A failed concurrent build leaves an invalid index that still costs writes.
rules.why: A small development database hides an index that no query uses; agents add an index per query just in case (inference).

rules.rule: Migrations are numbered in order and append-only: a landed migration is never edited, each carries a checksum the runner checks, and the schema after replaying every migration equals the schema file and the DDL the data model generates.
rules.detail: The model is the one source (postgres.queries.1): the replayed schema is compared with the DDL generated from it, and a difference fails; the model is never regenerated from the replayed schema. A change to the schema is a new migration. The runner refuses to start when a landed migration's checksum differs from the one recorded when it ran.
rules.why: A gap or a reorder changes what replay produces, a schema file that drifts from replay misleads the types and the review, and an edited landed migration means two databases that ran different text under one number.

checks.note: a test that migration numbers are consecutive, that each landed migration's checksum equals the recorded one, and that the schema after replaying every migration on a container equals the committed schema file and the DDL the model generates. rules.rule: Migrations stay compatible with the running version, in the order expand, migrate, then contract.

rules.rule: A migration that starts an expand-and-contract change records the date by which the old column or table is removed and names the readers alive during the deploy; the gate fails a leftover past its date.
rules.detail: The date sits in the migration header as contract-by in the same register as other exemptions. The question for the readers is which ones will be alive during this deploy. The header line reads contract-by with a date, for example contract-by: <date>.
rules.why: If the contract phase never runs you end up worse off, with two versions supported for good; agents add the new column and forget the old (inference). The transition is needed only when several clients are coupled to the schema.

rules.rule: Migration text has a class header and notes for renames, splits, merges and removals, no down scripts, no risky extensions, and states the delete behaviour of every reference; and a program that applies migrations at start backs up first, and restores the backup and refuses to start when a migration fails.
rules.detail: No CREATE EXTENSION, dblink or foreign data wrapper; every REFERENCES states ON DELETE. With no down script the way back from a failed migration is the backup taken just before it; the program names the backup in its log and exits non-zero after restoring.
rules.why: A down script gives false comfort for a step that cannot be reversed, and an unstated delete behaviour is a decision nobody made. A migration that fails halfway at start leaves a store no version can read unless the copy from just before is put back.

checks.note: a migration-text lint for the class header, the notes, the ban on down scripts and risky extensions, and ON DELETE on every REFERENCES. Plant: a migration that creates an extension, or a REFERENCES with no ON DELETE, fails. Control: a conforming migration passes

rules.rule: Query types are generated from the program's one data model, which is the single source of every shape; the live schema is checked against the model, never the model against the live schema; and SQL is built with a typed query builder so every table and column is checked at compile time.
rules.detail: The model is declared once, in one schema library, and generates the table types, the DDL, the JSON Schema and the API and tool contracts; no second schema library owns a shape. The gate regenerates every derived file from the model and fails on a diff, and compares the schema after replaying every migration with the DDL the model generates (postgres.migrations.1). Types are never generated from the live database. A new derived shape (a new contract kind) is one more generator from the same model.
rules.why: A query written as a string fails at run time on a renamed column; types from the model fail the build instead. One model that generates every other shape is the strongest guard against a type, a table and a contract drifting apart over years, and a source chosen once cannot be argued about per change.

rules.rule: Naming, check constraints, mandatory columns, primary keys, references and audit columns hold in the live schema; a reference to one of several kinds is a foreign key per kind in an exclusive arc, never a kind and an id in text; and a rule enforced in SQL is tested in SQL against the replayed migrations, never re-implemented in code to be tested.

A status column has a check. An exclusive arc is one nullable foreign-key column per kind and a check that exactly one is set. A law the database enforces (a check, a trigger, a constraint) has a SQL test (pgTAP or plain SQL run by the test runner) on a database built from the migrations; a copy of the law in application code to test it is a second implementation and is refused in review.
rules.why: A convention held only in migration text drifts from what the database actually holds. A kind-and-id text reference is one the database cannot check, and a law tested only through a copy in code proves the copy.

rules.rule: A table that records facts is append-only: a trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE for every role, the superuser included, and a test drives it.
rules.detail: The trigger raises on UPDATE and DELETE (and TRUNCATE where the engine allows a trigger on it); a grant alone is not enough because the superuser bypasses grants. A correction is a new row that refers to the one it corrects. The table is marked append-only in the model, so a new fact table gets the trigger from the same declaration.
rules.why: A recorded fact that can be changed is not a record, and a trigger outlasts every application that writes to the table.

rules.rule: A library that owns tables keeps them in its own schema, migrated by the library at a pinned version, and only the program's own schema is held to the DDL its model generates.
rules.detail: An auth library, a job queue or the migrator's ledger each get a Postgres schema of their own. The program never writes their tables by hand, and its migrations never touch them. Upgrading a library moves its pin and runs its own migrations.
rules.why: A library schema lets a library be upgraded without touching the product's tables, and keeps the model-equals-DDL check (postgres.migrations.1) from failing on tables the model does not own.

rules.rule: At commit the formatter runs in check mode and the linter runs without fixing; neither rewrites a file.
rules.detail: The formatter's check mode lists the files that differ and exits non-zero; the linter reports and does not fix. Both read and never write (gates.command.28), so they run beside the other commit members inside the commit hook's seconds. The fix is the same tool in write mode, run by the person. Their cost was not measured on the host that studied the stack.
rules.why: A hook that rewrites files is the opposite of a check, and a formatter in write mode races the members beside it.

rules.rule: The requirements are pinned with exact versions, or a lock file carries hashes; a minimum-version pin gives a fresh venv whatever is newest.
rules.detail: supply.install.1 holds that one package manager installs from the lockfile only and that the lockfile is the pin. For a project with a plain requirements file the pin is an exact version per line; where hashes are carried the installer refuses anything it cannot match. A line that says at least a version is not a pin.
rules.why: A requirements file with minimum-version pins gives every fresh venv a different tree, and a check that passed on one cannot be said to pass on the next.

rules.rule: The venv is built from the pins and rebuilt only when the pins change; a run checks it once and installs nothing when the check passes.
rules.detail: gates.command.19 holds that a tool is installed when its pin changes and checked once per run. The venv is this stack's install; the check compares the installed set with the pins, and the install runs when they differ or the pins file changed. The measured cost was 1.08 seconds plus 0.86 seconds warm.
rules.why: An install on every push is paid on every push, and an install that never checks the pin lets a stale venv pass for the pinned one.

rules.rule: At push every source file is byte-compiled, so a syntax error in a file nothing imports is found.
rules.detail: An import smoke (py.cycle.5) proves only the files the imports reach. The byte-compile walks the tree and compiles each file, in about 0.05 seconds, and a file with a syntax error fails it whether or not anything imports it. It is a member of its own, quiet on success.
rules.why: A file nothing imports can carry a syntax error for months and fail the day something imports it.

rules.rule: At push an import smoke imports every package in a fresh interpreter.
rules.detail: The smoke proves the packages import with the venv as pinned, in about 0.03 seconds. The interpreter is the one the venv pins, so its version is already in the stamp key through the pin (gates.land.15); the host's own build string is no part of the key.
rules.why: One fleet's desktop tool was red on import on the host that studied it, and a stamp that ignores the interpreter would have served the green of another host.

rules.rule: At push the tests run with workers from the pool and a type checker runs as its own member.
rules.detail: tests.runners.2 holds that the worker count comes from the pool's capacity and is never hard-coded; the test tool's automatic worker count is the tool's own reading of the host and is capped by the pool's number (gates.command.27). The type checker is a member of its own, so a type failure names it. Neither was measured on the host that studied the stack.
rules.why: A serial test run holds one CPU while the pool has more, and a type check inside the test command hides which one failed.

rules.rule: At push the program runs headless on a checked-in input and its output is compared with a checked-in expected file, read by a person.
rules.detail: A replay golden is the one test that runs the whole program. tests.generated.5 holds how a golden a person reads is approved; this line places one in the push tier for a program that has a headless mode. A replay that proves only that the program did not crash is a start, and the expected file grows as the output does.
rules.why: One fleet's desktop tool had no test that ran it; a replay was the cheapest proof that it starts and produces its output.

rules.detail: supply.scans.7 holds the vulnerability scan in the full gate the land job runs before main, and supply.secrets.1 the secrets scan at commit; this line names the inputs for the stack: the requirements file for the first, the staged diff for the second, with the allowlist a shrink-only baseline that has an owner (gates.ratchets.1). rules.rule: Every route declares who may call it and with which permission; a permission follows one grammar of three parts (owner.subject.action) written in the casing the program declares, with owner names reserved; a machine declares only permissions for subjects it has, so a grant naming an undeclared permission is refused; and a route with no entry fails.
rules.detail: The declaration names the auth mode and the permission. Each part of a permission is in the program's declared casing (service.contract.10); the rulebook names no default. The subject part may come from config (a named folder, a named device), and only subjects present on this machine are declared, so no grant can name an absent path. An owner name is reserved to the program that owns it. A new subject kind is one more entry in the declaration; the grammar does not change. In Go, each daemon route declares its allowed callers.
rules.why: A route with no declaration is open by omission; the gap is invisible until someone calls it. One grammar is what makes permissions readable by a stranger in year five, and a grant for a subject the machine lacks is a grant that waits for a path to appear.

rules.rule: A token a program issues is stored only as a hash and shown once, and a secret that must be kept as a row is encrypted under a key that comes from the environment, never from the same store.
rules.detail: The plain token is returned once at issue and never again; lookup is by hash. A secret the program must use later (a connector's key) is encrypted before it is written, and the key is read from the environment or a key file named by path, so a copy of the store alone reveals nothing. A new kind of secret takes the same path.
rules.why: A token readable from a database dump is a live credential in every backup; hashing and encryption close that leak in every program that holds one.

rules.rule: A list read returns only the items the caller may read, an empty list when there are none; a single item the caller may not read answers as not found; and a writing route whose answer reveals state also requires the read permission for that state, with a refusal that reveals nothing.
rules.detail: A list is never refused with 403 for holding items the caller may not see; it is cut. An item the caller may not read is not said to exist. An action needs the read permission as well as the act permission; act without read gets the bare refusal with no detail.
rules.why: A 403 on one item tells the caller it exists, and an action answer that carries state leaks what the read permission would have hidden.

Identity headers from a proxy are believed only on the socket that proxy reaches. A duplicated identity header answers 400. Each tool reads the gate itself, so each decision has one home.
rules.why: A forwarded permission is a decision with two homes, and a header believed on any listener can be set by anyone who reaches another one.

rules.rule: Acts reserved to a person are an explicit list granted to no agent or system actor, pinned by a test, and every change to who may do what appends who, when, the command, the reason and the lines changed to a history only the privileged writer can write.
rules.detail: The person-only list names permissions in the program's grammar (service.authz.1). A grant of a listed permission to an agent or system actor is refused at write time and at load. The permissions file is written whole by one command under a lock with a revision; the history is append-only and owned by the privileged account (root on a machine, the identity owner in a service). A new act joins the list by one entry.
rules.why: In an estate where agents hold tokens, the person-only list is the rule that matters most, and a permission change no one can trace cannot be reviewed.
