rules.rule: Field visibility is applied only through one shared owner module.
rules.detail: One shared package performs permission checks, scope enforcement and field filtering, as plain functions and as middleware. In Go, redaction and secret handling of output goes through one owner and a secret is never printed.
rules.why: Field filtering written per route is forgotten per route; a field leaks from the route that missed it.

checks.note: import and ast-grep rules limiting the field filter and scope enforcement to the shared authorisation package. Plant: a handler that deletes fields by hand to filter output fails. Control: the shared filter call passes
import rule giving one package the redaction function, and a test that a secret is never printed. Plant: a secret value printed fails. Control: a redacted value passes

rules.rule: Permission mappings point only at live (active) definitions.
rules.detail: In Go, every reference in a rule or doc resolves and a vocabulary is declared once.
rules.why: A mapping to a retired permission grants nothing or, worse, something else.

checks.note: a registry test resolving every permission mapping to a definition with status active. Plant: a mapping to a retired permission fails. Control: a mapping to an active one passes

rules.rule: A service keeps no accounts, passwords or login page of its own and is never an OpenID Connect client; no code verifies credentials by hand or calls the identity service on every request; and token signing exists only at the identity owner.
rules.detail: Identity comes from the gate in front of the service (service.authz.15). A user table with a password column, a login route, a session-cookie issuer or an OpenID Connect client library outside the identity owner is banned. Token verification code (key sets, signature checks) and symmetric-key signing are banned outside the identity owner. In Go, no home-made credential checks outside the one owner, and the security linter runs.
rules.why: A service with its own login is a second identity system to patch forever. Hand-rolled verification is where algorithm and expiry mistakes come from, and a per-request call to the identity service makes it a point of failure for all traffic.

checks.note: ast-grep rules failing token verification or HS-family signing calls and identity-service HTTP calls outside the identity owner package. Plant: a handler that decodes a token by hand fails. Control: verification through the shared bootstrap passes
gosec enabled and forbidigo on credential check primitives outside the one owner package. Plant: a hand-written token check outside the owner fails. Control: the owner package passes

a dependency ban on OpenID Connect client and password-hashing libraries, and a route lint refusing a login route, outside the identity owner. Plant: a service that adds a login route and a password hash fails. Control: a service that reads identity from the gate passes

rules.rule: The access catalogue passes one shared conformance test, and a request no source vouches for is refused on every route, reads and static files included, with no guest answer; a service without a catalogue refuses everything.
rules.detail: Deny by default covers reads as well as writes: a GET, a list, a health detail beyond liveness, and a served folder are refused without an identity. The refusal is 403 with no hint of what exists. Only routes the catalogue marks public, each with a written reason and never a writing route, answer without an identity. In Go, a shared check fails closed when a required declaration is missing.
rules.why: A missing catalogue that is read as nothing to check turns every route into an open one, and an open read is how a system leaks what it would refuse to change.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. shared conformance test run in every service and daemon, sending a request with no identity to every route and static path in the catalogue and asserting a refusal unless the route is marked public with a reason. Plant: a read route or a static file served to a request with no identity fails, and a catalogue-less service that serves any route fails. Control: a service with a conforming catalogue passes

rules.rule: Only the identity owner touches the identity provider.
rules.detail: In Go, only one package touches an external identity or credential store.
rules.why: Every service that talks to the identity provider can change its users and credentials.

checks.note: import-restriction rule allowing the identity provider SDK in the identity owner package only. Plant: a service importing the identity provider SDK fails. Control: the owner package passes
depguard rule limiting the credential store package to the one owner. Plant: a second package opening the credential store fails. Control: the owner passes

rules.rule: Every service entry point is built by one shared bootstrap, and the plumbing libraries it wraps are imported only inside it.
rules.detail: The bootstrap runs a fixed sequence for every entry: contract validation, authentication context, logging with a correlation id, secrets, and the error envelope, in that order. A service writes only its own business code. The shared bootstrap is the one place a plumbing library (request middleware, logger, validator) is imported; a direct import anywhere else fails. The same shape holds in Go: each program is assembled by one shared run helper and its plumbing packages are imported only there.
rules.why: Many entries each wiring their own plumbing gave as many pipelines as services, each missing a different step. One owner means a step is fixed once for all.

checks.note: ast-grep or import-restriction rule failing an import of any request-middleware, logger or validator library outside the shared bootstrap package. Plant: a handler file that imports the middleware library directly fails. Control: the same import inside the bootstrap package passes

depguard or import-rule table naming the shared run helper as the only importer of the plumbing packages. Plant: a program package importing the plumbing package directly fails. Control: the run helper importing it passes

open: The reference estate lists the plumbing libraries by name; the allow-list of banned imports is to be built per product from its own bootstrap.

rules.rule: No service keeps a local copy of a shared plumbing step or handler factory, and the count of copies only falls.
rules.detail: A step copied into a second repository moves to the shared module, and the number of copies is counted and may not rise. This covers handler factories and each plumbing step written again by hand (validation, auth context, logging, error mapping).
rules.why: Copies drift. The reference estate counted dozens of hand-copied plumbing steps beside a shared package that was meant to replace them.

checks.note: ast-grep rules for the known shapes of each plumbing step and handler factory outside the shared package, with a shrink-only count in the ratchet. Plant: a new local handler factory fails. Control: a service that imports the shared factory passes

a ratchet counting copies of shared steps outside the shared module, failing when the count rises. Plant: a copied step added to a program fails the count. Control: a program using the shared module passes

open: The starting count of copies is to be measured per product.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: own measure

rules.rule: No service writes its own data-layer plumbing: error tables, certificate bundles, integer parsers, outboxes or key builders.
rules.detail: Store opening, error mapping, number parsing and key building each have one owner in the shared data toolkit. A service that needs one imports it.
rules.why: Each service writing its own database error table or integer parser repeats the same bugs in a different place.

checks.note: ast-grep rules for hand-written error-code tables, integer parsers, certificate bundle loading and key builders outside the shared data toolkit. Plant: a local SQLSTATE table in a service fails. Control: the shared toolkit call passes

import and forbidigo rules limiting store opening, error mapping and key building to the one owning package. Plant: a second package opening a store connection fails. Control: the owner package passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Related to no-local-plumbing-copy: that rule counts copies of request steps; this one covers the data layer.

rules.rule: Every route unit has the same closed set of files: handler, contract and schema.
rules.detail: A route folder holds exactly the handler, its contract declaration and its schema, so a new route has a fixed shape and a generator can find all three. In Go, programs sit under one commands folder with the rest under an internal folder, so a new command has a fixed home.
rules.why: A route missing its contract or schema is invisible to the generated API description and the access catalogue.

checks.note: a repo test walking route folders and failing on a folder missing the handler, contract or schema file, or holding an unlisted file. Plant: a route folder without a schema file fails. Control: a complete folder passes
a repo test over the commands folder layout and the layer table. Plant: a command outside the commands folder fails. Control: a command in its home passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A route contract may use only a closed set of keys (path, query, body, headers); any other key fails.
rules.detail: The closed set is checked by the contract builder and by a lint, so a misnamed key (for example params) cannot silently drop validation. In Go, command and config declarations refuse unknown keys and the command tree is compared with a stored file.
rules.why: An unknown key in a contract is ignored by the validator, so the input it was meant to constrain goes unchecked.

checks.note: contract builder typed to the closed key set, plus an ast-grep rule failing any other key. Plant: a route contract with a params key fails. Control: a contract with path, query, body and headers passes

strict decoding of command and config declarations with unknown fields refused, and the command tree compared with a stored file. Plant: a declaration with an unknown key fails to load. Control: a declaration with known keys loads

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Request steps run in a pinned order, so a request without authentication never reaches the handler.
rules.detail: The bootstrap fixes the order of steps (origin check, authentication, authorisation, validation, handler, error mapping) and no step can be reordered or skipped by a service. In Go, a daemon checks the caller on every request before any handler, and its steps are bounded.
rules.why: An authentication step placed after validation or business code lets an unauthenticated request touch the handler.

checks.note: a shared bootstrap test sending an unauthenticated request through every registered route and asserting the handler is never called, and a test asserting the step order list. Plant: a route whose handler runs without a verified identity fails. Control: every route refusing before the handler passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The exposure mode of the entry origin check is an explicit code argument from the deployment tier, never ambient configuration.
rules.detail: A public entry passes enforce; an internal entry passes the disabled mode explicitly. No environment variable selects the mode. In Go, a daemon states its reach (socket, loopback, tailnet) as a code argument, and the peer check is never a header alone.
rules.why: A mode read from the environment can be switched off by a configuration slip, opening a public entry without anyone changing code.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a bootstrap call whose origin-check mode argument is not a literal. Plant: a bootstrap call passing the mode from an environment read fails. Control: a call passing the literal mode passes
a rule failing a server constructor whose reach argument is not a constant. Plant: a reach read from a flag or environment fails. Control: a constant reach passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The environment is read only in the config module, with a short exempt path list that only a reviewed rule change may extend.
rules.detail: In Go, os.Getenv is banned outside the config package, which reads with os.LookupEnv; the terminal variables sit in the shared UI package.
rules.why: Environment reads scattered through code mean no one can list what a service needs to run, and a missing variable fails at first use.

checks.note: ESLint no-restricted-properties on process.env, or an ast-grep rule, with a short exempt path list in the rule config. Plant: a process.env read in a handler fails. Control: a read in the config module passes
forbidigo on os.Getenv outside the config package. Plant: os.Getenv in a handler package fails. Control: the config package passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The environment is parsed once, by a schema in the config module, and the rest of the code reads the typed result.
rules.detail: In Go, every config key and variable has a reader, a default and a doc row, read in one package.
rules.why: Parsing at each use repeats the defaults and coercions, and a bad value fails late.

checks.note: a test that the config module exports one schema parse and a rule failing a second parse call. Plant: a second parse of the environment fails. Control: one parse at start passes
a test that every config key has a reader, a default and a doc row. Plant: a key with no doc row fails. Control: a documented key passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The infrastructure environment map of a service validates under the same schema the service parses at start.
rules.why: A variable named in the infrastructure but not in the schema (or the reverse) is found by a failed deploy or a failed start, not by a check.

checks.note: a test that loads the infrastructure environment map and parses it with the service config schema. Plant: an infrastructure variable missing from the schema fails; a required schema key missing from the map fails. Control: a map that parses passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Consumers deduplicate atomically and tolerate redelivery.
rules.detail: The processing key is written in the same transaction as the mutation. In Go, a command is safe to run twice and a torn last line is ended before append.
rules.why: Delivery is at least once: a consumer that cannot take the same message twice does its work twice.

checks.note: the shared consumer wrapper writes the processing key in the mutation transaction, proven by the shared twice-helper delivering each message twice. Plant: a consumer that sends a call on each delivery fails the twice test. Control: a consumer using the wrapper passes
a test running each command twice and a torn-line append test. Plant: a command that duplicates its effect on a second run fails. Control: an idempotent command passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: The same shared twice-helper is the check of replay-and-conflict in the contract concern.

rules.rule: The lifetime of a processing key (the record that stops a consumer doing the work twice) is at least the longest time a message can return: dead-letter retention, a redrive, a replay from an archive.
rules.detail: The key lifetime is a named constant and a test asserts it is at least the longest configured redelivery path. The key table is the consumer processing-key table. Where the store expires keys, expiry must not be the authority on whether a key still counts, because the store deletes an item only some time after its stamp (the book says up to about two days; verify against current documentation).
rules.why: If the key expires first, the second delivery is a first delivery again. Perfect deduplication needs an unbounded lookup, so in practice it is a bounded window kept with expiry, sized to the application sensitivity to duplicates.

checks.note: a test that reads the key lifetime constant and the dead-letter retention and redrive window in the same infrastructure and fails when the lifetime is shorter. Plant: a key lifetime shorter than the dead-letter retention fails. Control: a lifetime at least as long passes

rules.review_question: How long can this message come back, and how long is its key kept?
open: The expiry delay of the store is quoted from a book and not verified.
With agents: they pick a lifetime that looks tidy (inference).

rules.rule: Every subscription has a dead-letter path with redrive.
rules.detail: In Go, queues are bounded, but there is no park-and-redrive of failed work yet.
rules.why: A message that fails for good with nowhere to go either blocks the queue or is lost.

checks.note: an infrastructure scan failing a subscription or queue consumer with no dead-letter queue and redrive policy. Plant: a subscription with no dead-letter target fails. Control: one with a queue and a redrive policy passes

open: In a daemon the park-and-redrive of failed work is a gap with no row yet.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Work that fails for good goes to a dead-letter queue with a reason, and a redrive filters by what can still resolve (the target still exists, the state has not moved on) and does not blindly replay.
rules.why: A dead-letter queue is a snapshot with no expiry: a message that failed for good days ago acts on state that has since changed, and a blind redrive replays that stale intent. Silent retry forever is the default an agent writes.
rules.review_question: Where does this work go when it fails for good, and what stops a redrive acting on a stale state?
open: No plant: a seeded redrive tool that replays a message for a deleted resource must be flagged.
rules.note: Extends subscription-has-dead-letter-redrive and the permanent-versus-transient rule, which say nothing about a stale message at redrive.

rules.rule: Non-request entry points release their resources (connection pools, handles) in finally.
rules.detail: In Go, every goroutine has an owner that stops it and signals stop cleanly, and typed errors exist only where a caller branches.
rules.why: An entry that leaks a pool on the failure path exhausts connections when the runtime reuses the process.

checks.note: ast-grep rule requiring the non-request wrapper to call closePools() in a finally block. Plant: a wrapper that closes pools only on the success path fails. Control: a close inside finally passes
goleak in tests and a rule that each goroutine started has a stop owner. Plant: a goroutine without a stop path fails. Control: an owned goroutine passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A non-request entry point acknowledges a permanent refusal and throws a transient failure to the dead-letter path.
rules.why: Retrying a message that can never succeed wastes the queue; acknowledging one that would have succeeded loses it.

checks.note: a wrapper test that a validation refusal returns without throwing and a downstream timeout throws. Plant: a wrapper that throws on a permanent refusal fails. Control: a wrapper that acknowledges it passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: In Go, a failed read names its cause through a code table and a transient one is retried with back-off.

rules.rule: A queue-triggered consumer reports failure per item, so one bad message does not return the whole batch, and its batch size times its worst item time stays inside the function timeout.
rules.detail: The worst-case item time is a stated figure and a guess until measured. Where the platform offers to halve the batch on failure, that does not replace the per-item report.
rules.why: A throw from a handler holding a batch can fail every item, and the others are redelivered: harmless with deduplication but wasteful, and it hides which message is bad. A batch the function cannot finish in time fails as a whole and will fail again unless the time or the batch size changes.

sources.where: ch. 9 (batch event-processing parameters; commit offsets only after processing has completed)

checks.note: wrapper test: a batch with one poison message returns only that item as failed; a test asserting batch size times a stated worst-case item time is under the function timeout. Plant: a wrapper that throws on the first bad item fails. Control: a wrapper reporting the one failed item passes

open: Per-item failure reporting for queue-triggered functions is a platform feature known and not verified here.
With agents: holds (inference).
rules.note: Extends permanent-ack-transient-throw. Related to the function timeout rules in the Lambda part.

rules.rule: A consumer parses an event with a reader that ignores unknown fields; a file written by a person (a config, a catalogue) refuses unknown keys.
rules.detail: The test is who wrote it: a typo at a keyboard must be seen, and a newer peer must not break an older one. A strict object type in a schema library rejects an extra field, which is a quiet way for an additive producer change to break an old consumer.
rules.why: Strictness at a person keyboard catches typos; strictness at a peer breaks independent release.

checks.note: a consumer test feeding each registered schema plus one extra field that must pass, and a config test feeding an unknown key that must fail. Plant: a consumer whose parser is strict fails on the extra field; a config that ignores an unknown key fails its test. Control: a tolerant event reader and a strict config reader pass

open: With agents: an agent may mark a peer message as config; the way round is visible in the choice of parser (inference).
rules.note: Beside the rule that an unknown query key from a client is a 400, which is correct for a client request.

rules.rule: The catalogue entry of each event family states a policy for late and out-of-order events as a business decision, and each consumer states what a replay does to its side effects (an email resent, a marketplace call repeated).
rules.why: A strategy for late events is a business choice (drop, wait, or accept for a grace period): some events must be handled wherever they land and others may be discarded. A replay is something every consumer must expect, because events can be reread from a past point.

sources.where: ch. 6 (out-of-order and late-arriving events; handling late events)

checks.note: catalogue schema test requiring a lateness policy field and a replay note per family. Plant: a catalogue entry with no policy field fails the catalogue test. Control: an entry with both passes

rules.review_question: What happens to an event that arrives a week late? What does a replay resend?
open: The archive and replay behaviour of the bus was not verified.
An agent cannot infer a business policy, so the question goes to a person (inference).
rules.note: Extends consumers-deduplicate-atomically, which says nothing about an event that arrives a week late or after its successor.

rules.rule: The API contract is regenerated from code and diffed in the gate against the committed copy and against the contract at the merge base with the main branch, so editing or deleting the committed file does not pass a break.
rules.detail: The contract document is never hand-edited: the gate regenerates it from the route schemas and fails on any difference from the committed file; the file is written with LF line ends and compared byte for byte, so a checkout that changes line ends is a difference too. The same gate regenerates the contract at the merge base and applies the compatibility check of service.contract.2 between the two, so a change that edits the code and the committed file together is still compared with what main had. A missing committed file fails. In Go, the command tree and public surface are generated to a file and compared the same way.
rules.why: A contract written by hand drifts from the code it describes, and a generated client built from it then lies. A gate that the same change can edit is not a gate; the merge base is the copy the change cannot touch.

checks.note: gate step that regenerates the contract from the route schemas and fails on a diff with the committed file. Plant: a route added without regenerating the contract fails. Control: a regenerated, committed contract passes

gate step that regenerates the contract at the merge base with main and compares it with this change's contract under the program's compatibility mode. Plant: a change that removes a field and edits the committed file to match fails; a deleted committed file fails. Control: an additive change with a regenerated file passes
generated command tree and public surface file compared with the committed copy and with the merge base. Plant: a command added without regenerating the file fails. Control: a regenerated file passes

rules.rule: A program declares one casing for its JSON fields, query parameters and machine values, with no implied default, and a lint on the generated contract holds every name to it; parameters are typed and defaulted in the contract, GET carries no body, an absent field is omitted, times are RFC 3339 and durations are the strings a person types.
rules.detail: The casing is one declared value per program (for example lowerCamelCase or lower_snake_case), read by the lint; a program with no declaration fails, and the rulebook names no default. Machine values are enum members, error codes (service.errors.2), status values (store.schemas.3), event fields (service.events.4) and permission parts (service.authz.1). A field the platform has no such thing as is omitted; null is used only for a value that could not be read, with its reason. A casing added later is one more value the lint accepts; the rule does not change.
rules.why: What a reader needs is consistency within one program's contract; an estate-wide casing would break working contracts for no reader's benefit, and an implied default lets a program skip the decision.

checks.note: Spectral rules in the shared ruleset reading the program's declared casing: field, query parameter and enum value casing, schema type and default present, no requestBody on get, date-time format on time fields; a missing declaration fails the lint. Plant: a name in a second casing, a GET with a request body, or a program with no declared casing fails. Control: a typed parameter in the declared casing with a default passes

rules.note: In Go, settings resolve in one order with defaults and a flag has one meaning.

rules.rule: There is one contract document per exposure tier, each with its own access mode.
rules.detail: The internal document sets one internal access mode on every operation and the public document sets none, so a route cannot sit in the wrong tier by accident. In Go there is one command tree file per program and each daemon reach is stated.
rules.why: One document for both tiers makes the access mode a per-route guess.

checks.note: a contract test asserting every operation of the internal document carries the internal access mode and every operation of the public document none. Plant: an internal operation in the public document fails. Control: a correctly placed operation passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every operation has a one-sentence summary.
rules.why: The summary is what generated documentation and client method comments show; none means the operation is described by its path alone.

checks.note: Spectral rule operation-summary in the shared ruleset. Plant: an operation with no summary fails. Control: an operation with a one-sentence summary passes

revive exported rule and a help-line test requiring a doc comment on every exported name and a true help line on every command. Plant: an exported name without a comment fails. Control: a commented name passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Public names (routes, operation identifiers, property keys) avoid the words the product has retired.
rules.detail: The check reads the retired-word list and runs over the contract paths, operation identifiers and property keys. In Go, flag, command and JSON field names are held to the same list.
rules.why: A retired word in a public name outlives every rename in docs and code, because callers cannot change it.

checks.note: a Spectral pattern rule with a notMatch override over paths, operationIds and property keys, taking the repository retired-word list. Plant: a path containing a retired word fails. Control: a path with the current word passes
the identifier scan over flag, command and JSON tag names against the retired-word list. Plant: a JSON tag with a retired word fails. Control: a current tag passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A consumer imports the producer type of an API or event, or translates it at its own edge; it never copies another service names or enums.
rules.detail: A copied enum drifts silently when the producer adds a value. In Go, one domain reaches another only through an interface the caller declares, so names are translated at that edge.
rules.why: A copy of another service names looks like a type but is a second source of truth.

checks.note: import-boundary rule plus a type-equality test between the consumer edge type and the generated producer type. Plant: a locally declared enum duplicating a producer enum fails the equality test. Control: an import of the producer type passes
a layer table rule allowing a cross-domain call only through a caller-declared interface. Plant: a package importing another domain concrete type fails. Control: the interface at the edge passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Events are held by the event-payload rule; this is the general form for API types too.

rules.rule: A consumer of another of your programs pins the provider's published examples at a named commit, runs its real parsers over every one, checks its pin against the provider's main branch before a release, and an empty example set on a live consumer fails.
rules.detail: The provider publishes one example answer per path or event, generated from its own tests. The consumer copies them at a commit it names, and its tests run the same parser the program runs on each example, so a field the consumer reads that is renamed, removed or retyped fails in the consumer's own build. Before a release the consumer compares its pin with the provider's main and fails when they differ without a new pin. The provider can then retire what no one reads, and a change in what someone does read, which a plain diff reports as harmless, is caught. A field list alone is weaker than parsing the examples and does not satisfy the rule.
rules.why: A generated client depends on the whole response schema, so the provider cannot tell which fields anyone reads and with no window before cutover can retire nothing. Consumer-driven contracts let the provider learn what its consumers use; the article limits the idea to one enterprise or a closed community, which is the case here. Such a test runs on the other party rhythm of change and should raise a task more often than it breaks a build.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. a consumer test that runs the real parsers over every pinned example, and a release step that compares the pin with the provider's main. Plant: a provider example with a renamed field the consumer parses fails; a pin behind the provider's main at release fails; a live consumer with no examples fails. Control: a provider adding a field passes

open: Where the check runs is unsettled.
Holds more strongly with agents: both sides are written in separate repositories and an agent cannot see another repository expectations unless a file puts them in view (inference).
v1 reference, not yet a source: Fowler, consumer-driven contract testing note
rules.note: Extends no-breaking-change (provider side, answers did anything change) and the generated-client rule.

rules.rule: Delete, cancel, close, release and ensure-style commands return success when the goal state already holds, and the operation description says so; a stale revision stays a conflict and a thing that never existed stays not found.
rules.detail: The line drawn: define away operation semantics, never input errors. The form is callee-only, stated on the operation and not decided at the caller, so it cannot become a swallow in the caller. A measure goes beside it: a count of handlers that catch a duplicate or a not-found and continue; that count signals swallowing dressed as ensure.
rules.why: Without the rule each handler decides whether already-done is an error, and agents decide differently. Argued from the technique of defining errors out of existence, which works where no caller needs the information and fails on untrusted input; no case from the reference estate.
rules.review_question: Does any caller need to know the goal state was already reached, and is the rule stated on the operation?
open: No plant: a seeded handler that swallows a real not-found as success must be flagged by the reviewer.
rules.note: Extends the replay and not-found-versus-conflict rules: those say how to tell conflict from missing, not that an already-done command is a success.

rules.rule: Where a command effects in another service complete after the response, the operation description says so and says how a caller learns it is done: an event, a status resource, or never needed.
rules.why: A caller reads a 200 as done; a command that writes the database first and the event second is read-after-write for its own service only, so another service may still act on stale state. Argued from the treatment of requests within an event-driven flow.

sources.where: ch. 13 (handling requests within an event-driven workflow)

rules.review_question: Which effects of this command complete after the response, and where does the description say how a caller sees completion?
open: No plant: a seeded command that writes an outbox row and describes itself as complete must be flagged.
rules.note: Applies to command operations whose handlers write the outbox. Nearest: the command-route shape rule fixes the route form, not what a 2xx promises.

rules.rule: A provider names no consumer in its shipped code, examples or config and never reads a consumer's code or tests, and a repository test holds the list of reader names out.
rules.detail: A consumer is named only as a reader in the provider's docs. The provider keeps a list of the names of its known readers (programs, pages, tools) in its test data, and a whole-word test over shipped code, examples and config refuses any of them. A reader added later is one more name in the list.
rules.why: A provider that names its consumer has made the consumer part of its contract, and every reader after the first inherits a shape made for someone else. Rules already stop a consumer naming its provider loosely; nothing stopped the reverse.

checks.note: a repository test with the reader-name list, run whole-word over shipped code, examples and config. Plant: a config comment that names the page that reads the API fails. Control: shipped files that name no reader pass

rules.rule: An answer and a config carry meaning only (a name, number, sentence, state or permission), never layout or styling, no field is named for where a reader draws it, and a whole-word test over every field name refuses place words.
rules.detail: Presentation is an icon, a colour, a tile, a card order or a heading. The place-word list starts with short, tile, card, heading, tab and bar, and it also refuses the word kinds that name drawn text by suffix (figure_text, phrase, text) in the program's declared casing. The list lives in one file and grows by entry; a field named after a place on a page is renamed before merge.
rules.why: A field named tile is a contract with one page's layout, and the page will change; meaning-only answers are what let a second reader (a CLI, an agent) use the same answer.

checks.note: a whole-word test over every JSON field name in the generated contract and every config key, against the place-word list. Plant: a field named card_title fails. Control: a field named title passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: target: two design records of one program (no presentation in answers or config, no icon, colour, tile, card order or heading; a field named after a place on a page is renamed before merge; a whole-word test over json tags, with B2's suffix kinds)

rules.rule: A program declares whether its readers are owned or independent, and its contract changes by that mode. With owned readers a break is allowed only when it raises the one contract number in the same change and every known reader changes with it, nothing is kept for an old reader, and a missing field is an error, never defaulted. With independent readers no change breaks the last released contract, a removal or change of meaning is deprecated for one minor release before removal, and below 1.0 such a change is at least a minor release with an entry that says what to rename.
rules.detail: The mode is one declared value per program, with no default: a program with no declaration fails the gate. Owned readers are readers the same owner deploys in step (its own CLI, page or sibling program); independent readers are any the owner cannot change (a published library, a public API). With owned readers the contract carries one integer raised in the change that removes a path or field, retypes a field or changes a permission; an addition does not raise it; the gate fails when the shape loses or changes anything and the number did not move. There is no deprecation window, no field marked going and no old-and-new fallback. With independent readers the gate compares the contract with the last release and fails on a change that breaks a caller (a removed field, a new required parameter, a changed type) unless the item was marked deprecated in a release at least one minor earlier. In Go, a removed flag or field or a changed exit code fails and an undeclared API break refuses the release.
rules.why: A silent break reaches callers that were never told. Owners of every reader found that a compatibility layer is where their bugs lived; a publisher to readers it will never see must give them notice. One rule with a declared mode stays true for both and keeps the check mechanical.

checks.note: gate step that reads the declared reader mode (none fails), then with owned readers fails a shape that loses or changes anything unless the contract number rose in the same change, and with independent readers fails a removal not deprecated in an earlier minor release. Plant: owned readers, a removed field with the number unchanged, fails; independent readers, a removed field never deprecated, fails; a program with no declared mode fails. Control: owned readers, a removed field with the number raised, passes; an additive change passes in either mode

oasdiff run against the last release of the contract (independent readers) or the merge base (owned readers), its breaking-change list fed to the mode step above. Plant: removing a response field is reported as a break. Control: adding an optional field passes
apidiff or gorelease refusing an undeclared break at the tag, plus the command tree diff. Plant: removing an exported field without a declared break fails. Control: an additive change passes

open: Both diff tools are chosen but not yet run on a planted break.
cli.output.4 is rewritten under the same card for the CLI's own surface.

rules.rule: A numeric field names its unit in its key; where a reader would format it the answer also carries the formatted text from the one formatter; and a sentence in an answer travels with the numbers it was built from, with a test that fails when the two disagree.
rules.detail: The unit is a suffix in the program's declared casing (for example memory_mb, cpu_pct, uptime_s, power_watts), and a bare numeric key with no unit fails unless it is a count or an id. The formatted text sits beside the raw number (memory_mb and memory). The server computes order, totals, peaks and their times, sentences and downsampling; a number a reader still has to work out is a defect in the answer (web.structure.4 holds the page side).
rules.why: A unit in the field name is the cheapest way never to ship a number in the wrong unit, and a sentence tested against its inputs stays honest after a formula changes.

checks.note: a lint over the generated contract refusing a numeric field with no unit suffix outside the count and id list, and a test per sentence field that parses the numbers out of the sentence and compares them with the fields beside it. Plant: a numeric field named memory with no unit fails, and a sentence that says 3 beside a field of 4 fails. Control: memory_mb with memory beside it, and a sentence that matches its fields, pass

rules.rule: The contract is linted for path casing, operation identifiers, security on every operation, declared error responses and paging.
rules.detail: The shared lint ruleset also holds two house rules: each operation identifier is camelCase so generated client names stay stable, and every 4xx and 5xx response declares a body schema. Operation names in the contract follow one table. The ruleset applies to a daemon that publishes an HTTP description; a command-line program contract is its command tree.
rules.why: Names and error shapes that vary across operations make generated clients unstable and error handling per call.

checks.note: Spectral over the generated contract with the shared ruleset and the two house rules. Plant: an operation with a snake_case identifier or an error response with no body schema fails. Control: a conforming operation passes

rules.rule: The contract lint set extends the recommended rules, every recommended rule that defaults below error is promoted to error, and a test regenerates that list so a tool upgrade that adds a warning turns the suite red.
rules.why: A rule left at warn is read by nobody; a new warning arriving with an upgrade must not slip in unseen.

checks.note: a test reading the resolved ruleset from the installed lint packages and comparing the list of non-error recommended rules with the committed list. Plant: upgrading the lint package so a new warning appears fails the test. Control: an upgrade that adds no warning passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Held with the same ruleset as contract-lint; this is the upgrade guard on it. In Go, the resolved set is read and compared after a tool upgrade.

rules.rule: A request is validated once at the boundary against the route contract, and the handler receives only typed, validated input.
rules.detail: One validator checks every request, and the response, against the route contract. In Go, input is parsed once at the edge, unknown keys are refused, outside paths are confined and exit codes are tested; daemon JSON output is held by a golden and a schema test.
rules.why: Validation repeated or skipped inside handlers leaves paths that accept what the contract says they must not.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a handler that re-parses the raw body or reads an unvalidated request field. Plant: a handler reading the raw body fails. Control: a handler using the validated input passes
a golden and a schema test on daemon JSON, with strict decoding at the edge. Plant: an unknown key accepted at the edge fails. Control: a refused unknown key passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: No operation returns a status code its contract does not declare.
rules.why: A caller written from the contract cannot handle an outcome it was never told about.

checks.note: the response validator failing any status code absent from the operation contract, exercised by the contract conformance test. Plant: a handler that returns a 418 not in its contract fails. Control: a declared status passes

rules.rule: Every mutating request carries a version precondition (the revision it was based on) and an idempotency key.
rules.detail: A write based on stale state is refused as a conflict. The key lets a retry be told from a new request. In Go, a write command is safe to run twice, but there is no stale-write precondition on shared state yet.
rules.why: Without a precondition a late retry overwrites newer state; without a key a retry doubles the effect.

checks.note: contract lint failing a mutating operation without a revision precondition and an idempotency key parameter. Plant: a POST with neither fails the lint. Control: a mutation declaring both passes

open: In Go the precondition on shared state and the stored-outcome replay for daemon requests are gaps with no row yet.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A repeated idempotency key replays the stored outcome; the same key with a different request conflicts (409). One shared helper proves it by calling every writing operation and every event consumer twice.
rules.detail: The helper walks the operationId of every operation with a write method, taking the route list from the contract and the consumer list from the subscription definitions, never from the author. It runs each operation and consumer twice against the real store with the same input and asserts the state equals one run, counting calls to test doubles at unmanaged edges (mail, a marketplace, a publish). The same key with a changed body must return the conflict. The cost decides the tier: tier 2 if the container fixture is fast enough, otherwise tier 4; it has not been timed.
rules.why: The middleware that implements idempotency can be satisfied by a package nobody applied. In the reference estate both toolkits had the middleware and one service did not use it. Exactly-once delivery does not exist, only at-least-once with idempotent handling.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. shared helper walking write operations and subscribed handlers, calling each twice and comparing store state, with key-reuse conflict assertions. Plant: a handler that appends a row or sends a call on every invocation fails the twice test; a key reused with a changed body returning success fails. Control: a handler that is idempotent passes

shared Go test helper calling every contract route twice and hashing the state folder; a retried write with the same key replays the stored outcome. Plant: a handler that appends a log line on each call fails; a key reused with a changed body must return conflict. Control: an idempotent handler passes

open: In Go there is no stored-outcome replay for daemon requests yet: the rule is held for a repeat run that changes nothing or says so.
Whether the twice test runs in tier 2 or tier 4 is not timed.
Built because every rule binds from adoption; if the operator would rather not build for evidence D this part becomes a best practice.

rules.rule: No GET request changes state.
rules.detail: The shared twice-helper also calls every GET and checks the state is unchanged; a GET handler that appends a log line, writes a row or sends a call fails.
rules.why: Caches, prefetchers and retries call GET freely; a GET with effects turns each of them into a write.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. the shared twice-helper hashing state before and after every GET route from the contract. Plant: a GET handler that appends a row on each call fails. Control: a read-only GET passes

rules.rule: The suite starts one shared container per package in its global setup, and each test gets its own database cloned from a migrated template, never a container per file or a migration per test.
rules.detail: tests.isolation.3 holds that heavy fixtures start once and are reached through a helper; this line gives the shape for a service. The global setup starts the engine once, runs the migrations once into a template, and each test clones the template into a database of its own. A container per file costs seconds per file; a clone costs milliseconds. A bind timeout that never changes whatever the load means the knob is not connected to the pool.
rules.why: Four files cost 19 seconds per container per file against 7 seconds shared, and a template clone took 68 to 136 milliseconds against 210 to 322 to migrate; a container per file inside a fixed 10 second bind budget failed three tiers on the timeout.

sources.says: Testcontainers is a library that supports tests, providing lightweight, throwaway instances of common databases

rules.review_question: How many containers does this package start per run, where does the migration run, and how does each test get its database?
open: Planned check: the container count in the test member's report, one per package. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A container image the tests use is pinned by digest and pulled in the tools step, before the lock and never inside the container's start call.
rules.detail: gates.command.24 holds that an image is a tool. A pull inside the start call runs under the test's bind timeout and under the heavy-test lock, so a slow pull looks like a slow container and holds the slot for the download. The tools step pulls by digest when the pin changes (gates.command.19), and the start call finds the image present.
rules.why: A pull inside the start call in one fleet made a constant bind timeout fire on the network, and nobody could tell the pull from the start.

sources.says: When pulling an image by digest, you specify exactly which version of an image to pull.

rules.review_question: Where is this image's digest pinned, which step pulls it, and does any start call pull?
open: Planned check: the tools pins file lists each image with its digest and the tools step pulls it. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: The integration tier is a member of the push or the release tier, never a command outside every hook, and a skipped database test prints as a skip and is counted, never a quiet pass.
rules.detail: gates.command.17 holds that a check belongs to the earliest moment where it fits the budget, and gates.command.30 that a member which cannot run here prints SKIPPED. The integration tier that needs the container runs at push where it fits and at release where it does not; it is a row of the members file either way. A test that skips because the database is absent is a skip in the report, and red at land (tests.admission.5).
rules.why: The integration tiers of eleven services in one fleet, 68 and 229 seconds in two of them, ran outside every hook and nothing proved them; two packages' own gates skipped 24 and 15 database tests quietly.
rules.review_question: Which tier of this service holds the integration tests, and how many database tests did the last run skip?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the integration member in push or release, and the report's skip count for it. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: At release a cross-service end-to-end tier proves what no unit suite can: it measures the state the services hold, never the response alone, and marks the data it writes with a run marker.
rules.detail: A response that says accepted proves the request was read; the order, the row or the event it should have produced is the thing to read back. Each run writes its marker into the data it makes, so the tier finds its own rows and leaves the rest alone, and a teardown removes them (tests.journeys.6). The tier is a release member with a net field (gates.command.30).
rules.why: One real order was lost in one fleet with every unit suite green, because nothing read the state after the response.
rules.review_question: What state does this cross-service tier read back after each request, and how does it find the rows it wrote?
open: Planned check: the tier's report lists the state reads per journey and the marker. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: The deploy is a release member run by the hub after the tier, and a package that publishes has a publish workflow that runs the push tier first.
rules.detail: supply.release.1 holds that a release runs the full gate first and that only the release workflow on the tag publishes. This line places the deploy and the publish in the members file: the deploy is a release member with an after edge to the tier, run by the hub (gates.command.31), and a publish is the same shape. A package that publishes with no workflow publishes from a working checkout nobody proved.
rules.why: Six packages of one fleet publish with no workflow, and one service has no deploy on record.
rules.review_question: Is this service's deploy a release member with an after edge to the tier, who runs it, and does the publish workflow run the push tier first?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the deploy member at release with its after edge, and the publish workflow's first job is the push tier. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: No empty catch and no catch that returns a default.
rules.detail: In Go, every error is handled or returned and nothing is swallowed.
rules.why: A swallowed error turns a failure into missing data that surfaces far from its cause.

checks.note: ESLint no-empty and an ast-grep rule failing a catch block that returns a literal or a default value. Plant: an empty catch fails; a catch returning an empty list fails. Control: a catch that rethrows or maps the error passes
errcheck and a rule failing a discarded error. Plant: an ignored error return fails. Control: a handled error passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Beyond goal-already-holds-is-success in the contract concern, whose count of catch-and-continue handlers signals swallowing dressed as ensure.

rules.rule: An error code is a value from the program's own closed typed list, written in the casing the program declares (service.contract.10), and a code is never reused for a new meaning.
rules.detail: The rulebook names no default casing: the code list is linted against the program's one declared casing, and a program with no declaration fails. In Go, exit codes are one tested table and typed errors are a closed set.
rules.why: A code that changes meaning breaks every caller that branches on it, and a code in a second casing is a second vocabulary for one reader to learn.

checks.note: a typed code list and a test failing any thrown code not in the list, plus a diff of the committed list against the last release that fails on a changed meaning. Plant: a thrown string not in the list fails. Control: a listed code passes
exit codes held in one tested table and a test over the typed error set. Plant: an exit code outside the table fails. Control: a table code passes

the casing lint of service.contract.10 run over the error-code enum in the generated contract. Plant: an error code in a casing other than the declared one fails. Control: codes in the declared casing pass

rules.rule: An error message is a developer diagnostic and is never shown to users; users see a text chosen from the code.
rules.why: A raw message leaks internals and changes with every refactor.

checks.note: contract tests asserting the user-facing text is mapped from the code and the message field is absent from the public error body. Plant: a public error body that carries the exception message fails. Control: a body with only code and request id passes

rules.note: In the front end a machine code is separate from its sentence in a closed documented set.

rules.rule: Each contract lists its error codes as one enum, referenced by every error response; an error is always a non-2xx status with the JSON error body, including errors raised before the handler runs or by a proxy in front of it; and a 2xx never carries an error.
rules.detail: Errors raised before the handler include a filtered request and a gateway 401 or 403; a proxy in front of the program is configured to answer with the same JSON body, never an empty 502 or an HTML page. A 200 with an error field, an error flag or an error sentence inside is a defect. In Go, the exit-code table and the command tree list every code and are compared.
rules.why: A code the contract does not list cannot be handled by a generated client, and platform codes are the ones nobody remembers. A reader that has to look inside a 200 for an error is a reader that guesses, and one that guesses breaks.

checks.note: Spectral rule failing an error response whose body does not reference the shared error-code enum, and a test that the enum covers the platform codes. Plant: an error response with a free-text code fails. Control: a response referencing the enum passes

a contract test that drives each error path, a request refused before the handler and a request through the proxy to a stopped program, and asserts a non-2xx status with the JSON error body; a lint refusing an error field in any 2xx schema. Plant: a 200 answer with an error field fails, and a proxy that answers an empty 502 fails. Control: a 4xx or 5xx with the JSON error body passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice; target: a design record of one program (every error is a non-2xx status with a JSON error body, a 200 with an error inside or a proxy's empty 502 is a defect)

rules.rule: Every error carries a request id a user can quote, from the handler and from the gateway.
rules.detail: In Go, every log line carries a run id and errors name the next step.
rules.why: A user reporting an error with no id leaves support to search by time and guess.

checks.note: an end-to-end test requesting a failing route and a gateway-refused route, asserting the error body and header carry a request id that appears in the logs. Plant: a gateway refusal with no request id fails. Control: an error with an id found in the logs passes

open: In Go, the error shown to a person carrying a quotable run or request id is a gap with no row yet.

rules.rule: Every event payload is defined once, by the service that emits it, in a shared package with its schema committed beside it; consumers import the type or map it into their own words at their edge.
rules.detail: The package holds the schema for every event and the committed schema file is generated from it. A service defines the name and fields of its own events only; a consumer never declares a second copy. In Go, journal and message shapes are versioned in the shared module and its surface is listed, and a shape that crosses a boundary has one source.
rules.why: Two definitions of one event drift, and the break shows up in a consumer in production.

checks.note: a test failing an event schema declared outside the shared events package, and a diff of the committed schema file against the regenerated one. Plant: an event schema declared inside a service fails; a committed schema file that differs from the generated one fails. Control: an event imported from the shared package passes
a surface listing test over the shared message package and a duplicate-shape scan. Plant: a second declaration of a boundary shape fails. Control: one shared shape passes

rules.rule: Event names (the detail-type of the event) follow one pattern: domain, entity, action and version, lowercase and dot-separated.
rules.why: A name that varies in shape cannot be matched by a rule or a subscription filter and hides the version.

checks.note: a catalogue test matching every registered event name against the pattern, and that an active family has a catalogue entry naming an owner. Plant: a name with capitals or without a version fails. Control: a conforming name passes
a test that journal and event names are one closed set in one pattern. Plant: a name outside the set fails. Control: a conforming name passes

rules.rule: A service publishes only the event families it owns.
rules.detail: In Go, each piece of shared state has one writer and one owner.
rules.why: Two publishers of one family make the schema owner ambiguous and break the consumers who trust it.

checks.note: a catalogue-driven scan failing a publish call whose event family names another owner. Plant: a service publishing a family owned by another fails. Control: publishing its own family passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every event payload extends a base envelope with schema version, event id and actor, and its fields use the casing the program declares (service.contract.10).
rules.detail: The rulebook names no default casing; the key-casing lint reads the program's declaration and a program with none fails. In Go, versioned files and JSON carry a version inside and journal lines are one write.
rules.why: Without a common envelope a consumer cannot deduplicate by id, route by version or attribute the actor.

checks.note: a type test that every registered payload schema extends the envelope schema, and a lint on key casing against the declared casing. Plant: a payload without an event id fails. Control: a payload extending the envelope passes
a test that every versioned file and message carries a version field. Plant: a message without a version fails. Control: a versioned message passes

rules.rule: An event is validated against its schema before it is published.
rules.detail: In Go, an effect is not run until its record is written and input is parsed at the edge.
rules.why: An invalid event on the bus breaks every consumer; a failure at the source is cheaper.

checks.note: the funnel publish function parses the payload with the registered schema and a unit test that an invalid payload throws. Plant: publishing a payload missing a required field fails. Control: a valid payload publishes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A new event family states its prospective consumers and which of them needs each field before its schema is fixed, and carries one fact: no type field that selects between meanings, and no event whose only job is to tell another team to do something.
rules.detail: The event carries the full result of that action, not a copy of the whole entity, so consumers need not call back. The residual risk is a discriminator inside the payload and an event used as a command.

With agents: they copy the whole entity into the event because it is the shortest path (inference).

rules.detail: A report of families with no subscriber (orphans) is a measure beside it. The catalogue schema requires the fields and a scan of subscriptions in the infrastructure checks them against the visibility field.

checks.note: catalogue schema test requiring the four fields, plus a scan of subscriptions in the infrastructure against the visibility field. Plant: a subscription to an internal family from another domain fails; an entry with no data class fails. Control: a public family subscription passes

rules.rule: A breaking payload change gets a new version of the event name (the detail-type), and schemas are diffed against the last release.
rules.detail: In Go, a versioned file says what it does with older and newer versions, and a breaking change fails the release.
rules.why: Consumers deployed against the old shape break silently when a field they read is removed or changes meaning.

checks.note: the schema diff step against the last release failing a change to a live family without a new version name. Plant: removing a required field from a live family fails. Control: an additive optional field passes

a test that a versioned file declares its handling of older and newer and a breaking change fails the release check. Plant: a breaking change without a version bump fails. Control: an additive change passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Event compatibility follows the program's declared reader mode (service.contract.2). With independent readers each event family states its compatibility mode, full by default, a loosening is a recorded exit, and consumer tests are fed fixtures from every released version of the family schema. With owned readers a breaking event change raises the family's version and moves every known consumer in the same change.
rules.detail: Independent readers: the schema-diff step reads a compatibility field from the catalogue and tests the matching directions (old consumers read new events and new consumers read old events); a consumer test iterates the committed schema history. The backward direction matters for replay, for a redriven message in a dead-letter queue, and for a consumer deployed before its producer. Plain JSON has no built-in rules for full compatibility, so the check has to live in the diff tool. Owned readers: the gate fails a breaking change whose version did not rise or whose known consumers were not changed in the same change, and no fixture of a retired version is kept.
rules.why: Loosening later is easy and tightening is hard, so a publisher to readers it cannot change starts at full. An owner of every reader moves them together, and keeping old shapes for readers that no longer exist is where bugs live.

sources.where: ch. 15 (testing schema evolution and compatibility; creating mock events using schemas)

checks.note: schema diff reading the reader mode and, for independent readers, the family's compatibility field and the matching directions, plus a consumer test iterating the committed schema history; for owned readers, a check that a breaking change raised the version and touched every listed consumer. Plant: independent readers: removing a required field from a live family fails, and adding a required field without a default fails the backward direction; owned readers: a breaking change with the version unchanged fails. Control: an additive optional field passes both directions; an owned-reader break with the version raised and every consumer moved passes

open: Tier 2 or 3 depending on where the history fixtures live.
With agents: holds, because agents change producers and consumers at a high rate (inference).
rules.note: Extends breaking-change-new-version, which says breaking without a direction.

rules.rule: With independent readers a breaking change creates a new family, the old one is marked deprecated in the catalogue with a sunset date, the producer writes both during the migration, and the gate fails an old family past its date. With owned readers dual writing and sunset windows are an exception that needs a recorded reason, and a retired path or name is removed in the change that replaces it, with a test asserting it is gone.
rules.detail: Independent readers: a catalogue field status and sunset exist; a subscription to a deprecated family needs a recorded exit; the gate fails a deprecated family past its sunset. The sunset length is a guess and not a measurement. Owned readers: there is no old-and-new fallback, no field marked going and no grow-only promise; the replacing change deletes the old name, and a test asserts the old path, field or family no longer exists.
rules.why: Without a date the migration never finishes and near-duplicate families run on, and new services subscribe to the old one. Where the owner deploys every reader, a second stream is a compatibility layer with no reader to serve.

sources.where: ch. 16 (breaking schema changes; eventual migration via two event streams)

checks.note: catalogue gate reading the reader mode: for independent readers it fails a deprecated family past its sunset and a new subscription to a deprecated family without a recorded exit; for owned readers it fails a dual write with no recorded reason and a replaced name with no gone-test. Plant: independent readers: a live family with a field removed and no new family fails, a deprecated family past its sunset fails, a new service subscribing to a deprecated family fails; owned readers: an old name kept beside its replacement fails. Control: an independent-reader family within its sunset passes; an owned-reader replacement that deletes the old name with a test passes
