rules.rule: A liveness check does not call a dependency and a readiness check does; a start test breaks a dependency and asserts liveness stays green while readiness changes.
rules.detail: The test is two-sided: it fails a liveness that checks the dependency and a readiness that does not. It applies only where a health or readiness route exists (a gateway check, a deploy check, a journey pre-check), because a function runtime has no liveness probe of its own. Whether the reference services expose such a route, and whether a load balancer reads it, was not checked.
rules.why: A readiness probe that checks a shared dependency can fail on every instance at once, so a small slowdown removes the whole service. The tension is a thorough check against the harm of a false positive across a fleet. The known way round is a shallow readiness that checks nothing, which the second plant catches.

checks.note: a start test with a broken dependency: liveness stays green, readiness turns. Plant: a liveness handler that checks the dependency fails the test; a readiness handler that ignores it fails too. Control: a liveness that ignores the dependency and a readiness that reports it passes

open: Whether the services expose a health route at all was not checked; this is inference.
rules.note: Beyond born-with-same-alarms, which says what alarms each service has and not what a health route may check.

rules.rule: Every service is born with the same alarms on errors, throttles and latency, from one shared component.
rules.detail: The shared alarm component is held by the infrastructure part. In Go, a daemon serves one health document, signals readiness and logs with version and run id, and its work is bounded and supervised. There is no alerting on a failing health document for a deployed program yet.
rules.why: Alarms added by hand per service are missing in the service that fails.

checks.note: an infrastructure scan failing a service stack that does not use the shared alarm component. Plant: a service stack without the shared alarms fails. Control: a stack using the component passes

open: In Go, alerting on failing health for a deployed program is a gap with no row yet.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: The component itself is the rule of the SST part (alarms); this rule is the service obligation to use it. They would be held by one check.

rules.rule: A service that owns job runs records each run in one shared job-run schema, through one shared recorder, and exposes them through one shared operations contract.
rules.detail: The shared operations contract serves the runs at /ops/job-runs, and every run validates against the shared job-runs schema.
rules.why: Each service inventing its own run log leaves no single answer to what ran last night and what failed.

unless.reason: a service that owns no job runs has nothing to record

checks.note: a contract test that the service's job runs validate against the shared job-run schema and are listed by the shared operations endpoint. Plant: a job that writes its own ad hoc run record fails the schema test. Control: a run written by the shared recorder passes

rules.note: Placed in DynamoDB by the first pass; it is a service rule whatever the store.

rules.rule: There is no raw console output; logs are structured JSON, bare (no extra wrapper), and carry a correlation id and an event number on every line; and the set of top-level log field names is a committed contract compared with a real emitted line in the gate.
rules.detail: The field-name contract is a committed list of the top-level keys a line may carry. The gate runs the program, captures a real line and fails when a key is added, removed or renamed without the list changing in the same change. In Go, a daemon logs with slog, every line carries a version and run id, level and time, and there is no log.Fatal outside main.
rules.why: Unstructured lines cannot be searched or joined across services, and a line without a correlation id cannot be placed in a request. A log field renamed by accident breaks every dashboard and metric filter silently.

checks.note: ESLint no-console and an ast-grep rule failing a log call outside the shared logger. Plant: console.log in a service file fails. Control: a call through the shared logger passes
forbidigo on log.Print and fmt.Print and log.Fatal outside main, and a test that the slog handler adds version and run id. Plant: a fmt.Println in a daemon fails. Control: a slog call passes

a snapshot test that captures a real emitted line and compares its top-level keys with the committed field list. Plant: a renamed top-level field with the list unchanged fails. Control: a line whose keys equal the list passes

rules.rule: The logger redacts secret keys and never logs request or response bodies, and redaction is proved by planting a value in each redacted field and reading the real emitted line.
rules.detail: The redacted keys are one configured list (for example authorization, token, secret, key, password, cookie). The proof drives the real logger and output, not a mock, with a canary value in every listed key, and fails when the canary appears. A key added to the list is proved by the same test. In Go, a secret is never printed and no secret reaches the log.
rules.why: Logs are copied to more places than the data they come from, and a secret or a body in them outlives every other control.

checks.note: a logger test that plants a canary in every redacted key, reads the real emitted line and asserts redaction, and an ast-grep rule failing a log call that passes a body object. Plant: a log line holding a token value fails. Control: a redacted key passes
a test that no secret value is printed by the slog handler. Plant: a logged secret fails. Control: a redacted value passes

rules.rule: A request the service rejects (validation failure, refused permission) is logged at warn, not error.
rules.why: A client mistake logged at error floods the alarms meant for service faults.

checks.note: a bootstrap test rejecting a request and asserting the log level is warn. Plant: a rejection logged at error fails. Control: a warn line passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: No logger is constructed outside the runtime package; one owner creates the logger.
rules.detail: In Go, one slog handler with version and run id, level and time.
rules.why: A second logger gives a second format and misses the redaction.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a pino( call or a new Logger construction outside the runtime package. Plant: a pino or logger construction in a service fails. Control: the runtime package constructing the logger passes
depguard rule allowing slog handler construction in the one logging package only. Plant: a second handler construction fails. Control: the owner passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Each log metric filter matches a log line the code really emits.
rules.detail: In Go, every claim in a rule resolves to a file or command that exists.
rules.why: A filter written against a line that is never emitted counts nothing, and the alarm on it never fires.

checks.note: a test extracting each metric filter pattern from the infrastructure code and asserting a log call in source emits a matching line. Plant: a filter whose pattern matches no emitted line fails. Control: a filter matching an emitted line passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A new service integration enters only through the provider published contract and a generated client, with no hand-written client and no permission string copied from local code.
rules.detail: One change adds the contract sync, the generated client, the owning domain services list, the regenerated permission registry and the generated test handlers. Every service client is generated from a published contract, or is listed as missing with a ticket; each operation of a permissioned contract carries its permission. In Go, a provider paths, headers and fields live in one adapter and a shape that crosses a language boundary has one source.
rules.why: A hand-written client is a second reading of the callee contract, and it goes stale without anything failing.

checks.note: a gate step that every client package is the output of the generator from a published contract or has a ticketed missing-entry, and that no client file is hand-edited. Plant: a hand-written client module fails; a client whose contract is not published and not listed fails. Control: a generated client passes
a test that each provider has one adapter and a boundary shape has one generated source. Plant: a second hand-written adapter fails. Control: one adapter passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every outbound call has a timeout, and the timeout is non-optional on the shared client.
rules.detail: In Go, every HTTP client has a timeout or a context and the shared surface is listed; clients carry timeouts.
rules.why: A call without a timeout holds a worker for as long as the callee stays silent, and the failure spreads upstream.

checks.note: the shared client constructor typed with a required timeout and an ast-grep rule failing a fetch or client construction without one. Plant: a client constructed with no timeout fails. Control: a client with a timeout passes
forbidigo on http.Get and a default client, plus a lint requiring a timeout or context on every client. Plant: a default http client fails. Control: a client with a timeout passes

rules.rule: Request signing lives in one client package.
rules.detail: In Go, identifiers are made in one function and the primitives are banned outside the owner.
rules.why: Signing code in many places is verified in none; one owner can be proved once.

checks.note: import restriction on the signing library to the client package. Plant: a service that imports the signing library fails. Control: the client package passes
depguard and forbidigo on signing primitives outside the one owner package. Plant: a signing primitive used outside the owner fails. Control: the owner passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: No callee host or gateway identifier appears as a literal in source (`src`); it comes from configuration or a derived name.
rules.why: A literal host pins a stage and cannot be moved; it also hides which services a program depends on.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a URL or gateway identifier string literal in source files outside the config module. Plant: a source file with a callee host literal fails. Control: a host read from the config module passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: In Go, one function builds identifiers and URL writing is confined to one owner. Beyond the SSRF rule, which concerns a host that arrives in a request.

rules.rule: The shared client forwards the trace id and the caller token on every call.
rules.detail: In Go, a run id joins a command-line call to the daemon it spoke to.
rules.why: Without the trace id a request cannot be followed across services; without the caller token the callee cannot authorise the original user.

checks.note: a client test calling a stub callee and asserting the trace header and caller token arrive. Plant: a client that drops the trace id fails. Control: a client forwarding both passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The shared client throws on an unresolvable callee, a signing failure and a non-2xx response; it never returns a default.
rules.detail: In Go, errors are returned and never swallowed.
rules.why: A client that turns a failure into an empty result passes the fault downstream, where it looks like missing data.

checks.note: client tests against a stub returning 500, an unknown host and a signing error, asserting a thrown error each time. Plant: a client returning undefined on a 500 fails. Control: a thrown error passes

rules.rule: Retry lives in the one shared client constructor: idempotent calls only, at one layer, with exponential backoff and jitter, a bounded number of attempts and a retry budget (retries as a fraction of requests). A hand-rolled retry loop is not allowed.
rules.detail: The behaviour test runs the client against a handler that always fails and asserts the attempts stay under the budget; it checks behaviour as well as form because the known way round a loop ban is recursion or a timer. The attempt count (three) and the budget (about 10 percent of requests) are examples from the SRE book, not numbers measured on these services. A measure goes beside it: the retry ratio. In the reference stack the layers that can each retry are the cloud SDK, the shared client, the queue redelivery and the function async retry; whether all four are active on a given path was not checked.
rules.why: Three retries at each of five layers multiplies to a 243-fold load on the bottom layer. Retry traffic can keep a system overloaded after its cause is gone (metastable failure). Reasoning from incident analysis, not a measurement of the reference estate.

sources.where: timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a loop with a catch and a setTimeout or sleep outside the shared constructor. Plant: a hand-rolled retry loop fails the scan. Control: the shared constructor retry passes

behaviour test running the client against an always-failing handler and asserting attempts under the budget and no retry of a non-idempotent call. Plant: a client without a budget fails; a retried non-idempotent call fails. Control: a budgeted client passes

open: The attempt count and the 10 percent budget are examples, not measured.
Which of the four retry layers are active on a path was not checked.
rules.note: Extends every-call-has-timeout and clients-generated-from-callee-contract, which say nothing of what the retry policy must be. A Go binding is reserved: the shared client keeps back-off for later.

rules.rule: An outbound call host comes from configuration; where a feature stores a customer-supplied address (a callback, an image URL), the code resolves it and checks it against an allowlist before it fetches.
rules.why: A server that fetches an address an attacker chose reaches things the attacker cannot (server-side request forgery). Argued; whether any service takes an address from a request was not traced.
rules.review_question: Can any part of this outbound address come from a request?
open: Review until a plant exists: a seeded handler that fetches body.url must be flagged.
An agent passes a URL straight through (inference).
rules.note: Beyond no-callee-host-literal: that keeps hosts out of source and says nothing of a host that arrives in a request.

rules.rule: A consumer whose work includes a call to an outside API is rate-limited: it has a concurrency ceiling set below that API published limit, and a replay or redrive of its queue is throttled by the same ceiling.
rules.detail: A consumer marked as calling an outside API must set a maximum concurrency, and the value must come from a named constant with the third party limit beside it.
rules.why: A replay or backlog runs at the speed of the consumers, so an outside API can be hit at many times its normal rate after a redrive. Argued; no case from the reference estate.

sources.where: ch. 13 (third-party API replay surge) and ch. 7

checks.note: infrastructure scan failing a queue consumer marked as calling an outside API when it sets no MaximumConcurrency or the value is not a named constant with the limit beside it. Plant: a marketplace-calling consumer with no concurrency cap fails the scan. Control: a consumer capped below the documented limit passes

rules.review_question: What does a replay of this queue do to the API it calls?
open: With agents: holds (inference).
rules.note: Extends subscription-has-dead-letter-redrive and the concurrency-cap rules in the AWS part, whose guard already reads the queue maximum concurrency but ties it to no limit.

rules.rule: Only one funnel module imports the event bus client; every service publishes through it.
rules.detail: In Go, every outward effect goes through one wrapper that records it.
rules.why: A bus client imported in many places gives many publish paths, each with its own failure handling and none that can be replayed.

checks.note: import-restriction rule allowing the bus client package in the funnel module only. Plant: a handler importing the bus client directly fails. Control: the funnel module importing it passes
depguard rule allowing the bus client package in the one effect wrapper only. Plant: a program package importing the bus client fails. Control: the wrapper passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: There is exactly one outbox implementation, in the shared toolkit.
rules.detail: In Go, one shared implementation of write-ahead intent and atomic state replace, with no copies.
rules.why: Each service writing its own outbox repeats the transaction, retry and replay logic and gets different gaps.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing an insert into the outbox table outside the shared toolkit. Plant: an insert into the outbox table from a service fails. Control: the toolkit write call passes
import rule and duplicate-implementation scan limiting write-ahead intent code to the shared package. Plant: a second implementation of an intent journal fails. Control: the shared package passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The outbox is written only by the toolkit call that takes the open transaction, so the event and the change commit or roll back together.
rules.why: An event written after the commit can be lost when the process dies between the two writes; an event written before it can announce a change that rolled back.

checks.note: toolkit test that the outbox write function requires a transaction argument, and a scan failing any outbox write outside it. Plant: an outbox write outside a transaction fails. Control: a write inside the toolkit transaction call passes
a test that the intent is written before the effect and the journal is append-only with atomic replace. Plant: an effect run before its record is written fails. Control: intent then effect passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The relay publishes an outbox row idempotently and supports replay, and in production it always creates the sweep that picks up rows the live path missed.
rules.why: A relay that publishes twice on a retry, or cannot be told to publish again, turns every outage into manual work.

checks.note: relay test publishing the same row twice and asserting one delivery key, a replay of a range of rows, and the production sweep being created. Plant: a relay that publishes a duplicate on retry fails. Control: a replay of a past range passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A failed outbox row is never deleted.
rules.why: A deleted failed row is an event that happened and can never be published or investigated.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a delete on the outbox table, and a toolkit test that a failed row is retained. Plant: a delete of a failed row fails. Control: marking a row failed and keeping it passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The outbox row is the event as the public contract defines it, not a copy of the internal row, and the toolkit call that writes it validates the event against its registered schema inside the transaction, so a bad event rolls the change back.
rules.detail: The relay check at publish time stays as a second line. For a store whose stream forwards item images, the outbox is an explicit item written in the same transaction and shaped as the contract, and the stream forwards only those items; a plain stream of item images publishes the internal shape.
rules.why: Serialising after the write leaves a pile of unpublishable events that people must salvage and can reorder what was published; serialising before the write fails the business operation instead. That is the trade, and why it needs a decision and not a default. Exposing the internal model is an anti-pattern: consumers should see only public contracts.

sources.where: ch. 4 (liberating data using outbox tables; isolating internal data models; ensuring schema compatibility)

checks.note: toolkit test that hands the writer an event failing its schema and asserts the transaction rolled back and no outbox row exists; a second test asserts the outbox payload equals the contract and holds no internal column names. Plant: an invalid event must not persist the business change; an outbox row copied from the table own columns fails. Control: a contract-shaped event passes
a scan for outbox payloads built from a table row object. Plant: an outbox write whose payload is a table row fails. Control: a payload built from the contract type passes

open: Argued, not measured; no case from the reference estate.
With agents: an agent writes the internal struct straight into the row because it is the shortest path (inference).
rules.note: Extends validate-before-publish (validation at publish time, after the commit) and outbox-written-in-open-transaction.

rules.rule: The event bus name is derived from the stage, never declared by hand.
rules.detail: In Go, every path and identifier of persistent state is made by one function from the program name.
rules.why: A hand-declared bus name drifts between stages and lets a stage publish onto another stage bus.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a string literal in a bus name position and requiring the derivation helper. Plant: a literal bus name fails. Control: the derived name passes
forbidigo and an identifier-builder rule requiring state paths to come from the one naming function. Plant: a hand-built state path fails. Control: the naming function passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The derived bus exists before a service publishes to it.
rules.detail: In Go, a daemon signals readiness before it serves and a missing dependency is not silent.
rules.why: Publishing to a bus that has not been created fails silently or at first use in production.

checks.note: an infrastructure scan asserting every bus a service publishes to is declared by a stack that deploys earlier or in the same stack. Plant: a service that publishes to an undeclared bus fails. Control: a service with its bus declared passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Per-entry failures of a batch publish are read and retried.
rules.detail: A batch call can succeed as a whole and still report failed entries. In Go, every error is handled or returned and a multi-step change says rollback, resume or none.
rules.why: A batch publish that returns success while some entries failed loses those events with no error.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a bus batch call whose result failed-entry count is not read. Plant: a batch publish ignoring the failed entry count fails. Control: a call that retries failed entries passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: One shared component gives every service the same alarms on errors, throttles and latency.
rules.detail: In Go, a daemon serves one health document and is bounded and supervised.
rules.why: Alarms written per service are missing where the failure is.

checks.note: an infrastructure rule failing a service stack that does not instantiate the shared alarm component, and a unit test that the component creates the three alarm types. Plant: a stack without the component fails. Control: a stack using it passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: The service obligation to use it is the service rule born-with-same-alarms; one check holds both.

rules.rule: Infrastructure is declared only through the shared constructs, not raw cloud resources or overrides.
rules.detail: A raw function resource (sst.aws.Function), a raw table (aws.dynamodb.Table), raw gateway resources (aws.apigateway.*), a bundler override, function layers, local components and a bare network configuration (vpcConfig) each fail; the shared construct sets them. In Go, unit files come from a template and are checked, not hand-written.
rules.why: A raw resource skips everything the shared construct sets (grants, logging, retention, naming), and the gap appears in the one service that used it.

checks.note: ast-grep rules failing sst.aws.Function, aws.dynamodb.Table and aws.apigateway.* constructors, the bundler override key, layers, local component imports and the bare network configuration in the infrastructure code. Plant: a raw function construct fails. Control: the shared function construct passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The program name is written in exactly one place in the infrastructure code.
rules.detail: In Go, every path and identifier of persistent state is made from the program name in one function.
rules.why: A name repeated in many places is renamed in some.

checks.note: ast-grep rule failing a string literal equal to the program name outside the one service definition file. Plant: the program name as a literal in a second file fails. Control: a reference to the service definition passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The log format, log groups and the stage name are set only by one shared component or file.
rules.detail: No logFormat: JSON option set per function, no raw LogGroup, and the stage variable ($app.stage) read only in the one stages file (stages.ts). In Go, one logging handler with version and run id, and the environment read only in config.
rules.why: A log format or stage read set in many places drifts: the metric filters and alarms then miss some functions.

checks.note: ast-grep rules failing a logFormat option, a LogGroup and a read of $app.stage outside the shared component and the stages file. Plant: a function setting its own log format fails; a stage read in a handler file fails. Control: the shared component and stages file pass

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Infrastructure code never imports application source.
rules.detail: In Go, the entry and storage layers follow a layer table, and deploy code under its own folder imports no program package.
rules.why: Infrastructure code that pulls in application modules runs them at deploy time and ties a deploy to application internals.

checks.note: an import-boundary rule on the infrastructure folders forbidding imports from the application source folders. Plant: an infrastructure file importing a handler module fails. Control: one importing the shared constructs passes
depguard or a layer-table test: deploy code imports no program package. Plant: a deploy package importing a program package fails. Control: deploy code with its own helpers passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: The infrastructure tool and its shared components package are exact-pinned to one version across the repository, and no local-path link (file: or link: protocols) reaches the main branch.
rules.detail: One version of the tool is in use. A local-path dependency is for experiments and fails at land. The same holds for the build tool in Go: tools pinned once and no replace directive or workspace file in a committed tree. A no-local-link rule is also supply hygiene.
rules.why: A range or a local link makes the deployed infrastructure depend on something the repository does not hold.

checks.note: a check over package manifests failing a version range on the tool and its components package, a second version in the lockfile, and any dependency with a local-path protocol. Plant: a manifest with a caret range on the tool fails; a link: dependency fails. Control: an exact version passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Related to the supply-chain pin rules; kept here because the pin is for the infrastructure tool.

rules.rule: Services deploy only through one deploy guard, and the land check fails on the deletion or replacement of a state-bearing resource.
rules.detail: The guard reads the plan and refuses a plan that deletes or replaces a database, bucket, queue or identity resource without a recorded exit. In Go, an upgrade is by rename, the previous binary is kept, and it is put back by itself when the new one does not answer healthy.
rules.why: A replacement of a stateful resource is a deletion with a new name; the plan shows it, and only a guard stops it.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. the shared deploy guard run in the land step on the plan output, failing on delete or replace of state-bearing resources. Plant: a plan that replaces a table fails. Control: a plan that only updates a function passes

open: A deploy path that bypasses the guard (a direct deploy command) is not yet caught.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Imported identity, IAM and DNS resources carry retain-on-delete, so removing the stack does not remove them.
rules.detail: The infrastructure rule set also requires grants only through managed policies and a pinned role name for every function (the Lambda part holds those two) as one set of rules over the infrastructure code. In Go, a binary never rewrites shared state and removal must not take user data.
rules.why: A resource the stack only imported belongs to others; deleting the stack must not delete it.

checks.note: ast-grep rule over the infrastructure code failing an imported identity, IAM or DNS resource without retain-on-delete. Plant: an imported user pool without retention fails. Control: an imported pool with retention passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Beyond the AWS rule state-bearing-resources-retained, which covers state the stack owns.

rules.rule: A lock is a kernel advisory lock, non-blocking by default, with a deadline on any blocking wait; the order of two locks is written and tested; it is taken only through the platform's lock package, and any failure other than held stops the run.
rules.detail: forbidigo (type-aware) bans Flock and FcntlFlock calls outside the lock package, with a plain-text check for the raw system-call number and the four planted files kept as the fixture pair; a depguard row bans the third-party flock module, with an owner-lock rule that exempts the lock package's own path. A test checks that the claim fails when the lock folder is unwritable. The atomic-write package's own two calls are exempt.
rules.why: Fourteen production files call flock directly. In two programs the claim function treats every error except held as success. A trial planted four lock forms and the pattern flagged 2 of 4.

unless.reason: Only the owner carries the lock implementation.

checks.note: forbidigo (analyze-types) on Flock and FcntlFlock outside the lock package, a plain-text SYS_FLOCK check, depguard on the third-party flock module, and a claim test. Plant: unix.Flock, an alias of it and unix.FcntlFlock fire; a raw syscall of the flock number fires the plain-text check. Control: the lock package passes

open: The pattern misses one of five planted forms (a POSIX record lock, FcntlFlock with F_SETLK, and the raw syscall pass), so the plain-text check stays.
The shared claim helper in the platform environment is proposed; the rendered depguard config needs an owner-lock rule.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: own measure (read; the claim shape verified)

rules.rule: A lock that guards correctness across hosts hands out a monotonically increasing fencing token, and the store checks it on the write.
rules.detail: It applies where a lease or lock stands between two hosts and a double execution would corrupt data and not merely waste work. The write that follows is rejected by the store if the token is older than one it has seen. Most answers are a conditional write on a revision (store.consistency.3), which makes the question cost nothing.
rules.why: A lease can expire during a pause while the holder goes on writing; the same shape appears when an invocation is frozen and thawed or an at-least-once delivery runs the same work twice (inference, not measured; no case from the estate).
rules.review_question: Can a paused holder of this lock still write after its lease ends, and what refuses it?
open: No plant exists; a seeded change that takes an advisory lock or a lease row and writes without a conditional check must be flagged.
v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice (a published argument separating locks for efficiency from locks for correctness)
rules.note: Agents reach for a lease and stop there (inference).

rules.rule: A mutation carries a version precondition; compare-and-set puts the version in the condition, and a conflict is a typed outcome distinct from not found.
rules.detail: Both read as zero rows affected unless told apart. The test asserts the stale write's values are absent, so a retry that re-reads and overwrites fails. The request carries the revision in its body. Not-found and conflict are different typed outcomes (not-found for a missing row, a conflict for a stale one).
rules.why: An update without the version in its condition overwrites a newer write silently.

unless.reason: There is nothing to mutate.

checks.note: a store test with two writers (one stale) and a missing row, asserting the stale write's values are absent. Plant: an update without the version in the condition fails the two-writer test; a stale write and a missing row must give different typed errors. Control: the conditional update passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: practice (not measured)
rules.note: The kernel-lock rule does not cover this; the engine-specific forms are in the Postgres and DynamoDB parts.

rules.rule: The intent is written before the effect and a record that cannot be written stops the effect; no message is published inside a database transaction (transactional outbox).
rules.detail: The run record is opened after the lock is taken, so a refused second run writes no record. The outbox writes the row in the transaction and publishes after commit; whether a message can go out for a change that then rolls back is a review question.

rules.rule: Backup uses the engine's own interface, and for every store that cannot be rebuilt a restore drill restores a backup or a point in time to a new path or instance, runs an integrity check and compares counts with the source; a file copy of a live store is not a backup.
rules.detail: Counts are compared against a minimum from the fixture, so a drill over an empty store fails. The drill is started by hand or by a release, never by a timer. For a managed relational store the restore goes to a new cluster; for an embedded store a test backs up a populated store, restores it and checks. Anything you cannot re-derive from other data counts as not rebuildable. The embedded-store integrity query is the engine call integrity_check.
rules.why: A copy taken during writes may not be a backup. A neighbouring system found its corruption because its pipeline snapshotted and checked its backups. No row covered backup or restore before this one, and an unrebuildable store is a plain file (store.seams.6), so the embedded checks bind no store today.

unless.reason: A rebuild replaces a restore.

rules.rule: A versioned file carries its version inside it and the reader says what it does with an older and a newer one; schema changes are forward-only numbered steps, each in one transaction with the version bump.
rules.detail: A newer file is left untouched and reported. A step marked rebuild runs only in one runner on a dedicated connection, in this order: foreign keys off before BEGIN, BEGIN IMMEDIATE, create new, copy, drop old, rename new, a foreign-key check that must be empty or roll back, version bump, COMMIT, foreign keys on and read back. Shipped steps may not be edited (a diff against the last tag). Tests use one fixture per released version plus a next fixture. The foreign-key check is the engine call foreign_key_check. The shipped-steps-unchanged half is the recipe git diff <last tag> -- <steps dir>, run against the directory of steps.
rules.why: One program renames a newer hours file aside, so a downgrade moves real data away. No repository tests a file written by build N against N-1 and N+1. Latent today: one program's migrations are column additions only, one has no foreign-key setting and one has no ALTER TABLE.

rules.rule: Each named real engine has a contract suite pinning concurrent writers, retry on conflict, order, time and integer width, and an engine version floor.

rules.rule: A store port is agnostic at the level of intent, not of engine: the consumer declares it, narrow, with domain verbs, domain values and typed failures, and states its guarantee; an atomic act is one named method.
rules.detail: The adapter uses every strength of the engine inside the method. Rule data names the store ports, and on those a type check bans the generic verbs Get, Put, Exec, Query and Do, SQL string parameters, untyped maps and the database package's types, and finds Begin, Tx, Commit and Rollback in method names. Off a store port those verbs mean nothing (6 of 8 hits in a trial were process or guest verbs). A type-based scan of core exported signatures resolves the underlying type, and a type parameter is not an untyped value. A report lists core functions that take a port and also branch. Error-text matching is a report only: it had no true hit in 10 and is beaten for free by copying the text into a variable. The review asks: name one capability of this engine the port forbids the core to use; name the second engine and where it is written down; are these domain verbs or storage verbs; what does the port say about failure. Example of a banned port method: Exec(sql: string, ...args). Typed failures are named values such as not-found and version-mismatch.
rules.why: A generic query method keeps the driver out of the core but carries the engine's shape. The evidence strains the ruling: seams earn their keep through testability far more than through swapping engines. SQL detection is weak because a struct field holding SQL passes.

rules.rule: A store is opened in one place that sets its modes and error mapping, and a test reads them back.
rules.detail: For an embedded file store the modes are write-ahead log, a bounded busy timeout, foreign keys on as the connection default, immediate write transactions and one writer connection. Turning foreign keys off is banned outside the one rebuild runner, DSN strings included. A busy failure is typed (store.seams.2) and a store with a manual checkpoint says why. A store that cannot be rebuilt sets the full-sync pragmas unconditionally and the read-back asserts them. What a caller does on busy is a review question. Opening a store outside the store package is counted and is zero. The pragmas for full sync are fullfsync and checkpoint_fullfsync. The literal scan matches foreign_keys=OFF and the DSN forms foreign_keys(OFF) and foreign_keys(ON), by regex foreign_keys\s*(=|\()\s*(0|off), firing on OFF and silent on ON.
rules.why: One Go program lacked the immediate transaction mode and error classification. Through the pure-Go driver both full-sync pragmas read 0, unlike the command-line client, and no repository set them; the clause binds no store yet because an unrebuildable store is a plain file (store.seams.6).

rules.rule: Every file a program writes, state or config, is replaced whole only by the atomic write: written to a temporary file in the same folder, flushed, renamed into place and its folder flushed, with the original mode and owner kept and a link written where it points; a bare write, rename or create onto such a path, and a new hand-written temp-then-rename, are violations.
rules.detail: The rule covers a person's config that a command edits as much as the program's own state: the atomic write keeps the mode and owner of the file it replaces and, when the path is a symbolic link, writes the file the link points to and leaves the link. A new kind of file a program writes goes through the same helper; the rule does not list kinds. Banned outside the owner package: os.WriteFile, os.Rename, os.Create, os.CreateTemp, os.Link, (*os.Root).Rename and unix.Renameat, with a per-file shrink-only allow list for legitimate non-state uses (counts today per repository: WriteFile 1 to 23, Rename 1 to 14, Link 0 to 9). Atomic-write libraries that do not flush the folder are not imported. An ast-grep shape rule of the same intent stays as advice, with its five known bypasses kept as fixtures. The root-confined variant stays in the Linux-only programs. Verified under golangci-lint with forbidigo: the selector is flagged where it is taken, so f := os.Rename and r.Rename on an os.Root both fire.
rules.why: Thirteen bodies replace a whole file and twelve of them are outside the owner; 52 non-test WriteFile sites exist and 14 replace a state file in place. A helper that makes the temp file elsewhere is caught only because CreateTemp is banned too. A config rewritten by a bare write loses its mode, its owner or the link a person made, and a crash halfway leaves half a file.

checks.note: forbidigo (analyze-types) banning the write primitives outside the atomic-write package with a per-file shrink-only allow list. rules.rule: A path from outside (a flag, a config value, an environment variable or a request) is confined before use, and an archive or folder from outside is unpacked under traversal, link and size limits, with each refused entry named.

rules.rule: A dependency version younger than the release-age window of 7 days is refused unless the module is our own release, and the check at land reads publish dates from the lockfile.
rules.detail: The window is 7 days (replacing the earlier 14 days). Our own modules are exempt: a module under the organisation's own module path, at a release tag (vX.Y.Z, never a pseudo-version or a pre-release), with no replace and a publish time that can be read, does not wait. A land check reads publish dates from go.sum and the lockfile, because an install that follows a lockfile installs a young package that is already locked. The rule states what it defends against: a bad release that is noticed quickly, not a long campaign. A maintainer change is shown in the bump. The young-version case is planted and run before the rule counts as a gate. The package manager setting is the minimum-release-age setting (min-release-age for npm). Publish times come from the proxy .info record for Go. An install that follows the lockfile, such as npm ci, installs a young locked package. The lockfile read for web is the package manager lock (pnpm-lock.yaml). The npm setting min-release-age is one line: install only versions older than N days.
rules.why: In the xz backdoor, version 5.6.0 was 33 days old and 5.6.1 was 19 days old at discovery, so a two-week window would have admitted both. The other supply rules (provenance, licence, scans, install scripts) do the work the window cannot. In the web estate an install that followed the lock passed a young locked entry, and one repository set the window to one day.
rules.note: Retired (22 Nov 2026): no release-age window is held, in gragas or in a project it ships to. The id is frozen and is not reused.

rules.rule: A release-age cooldown is set for the package manager at add time, numeric, and equal to the release-age window of seven days, read as the package manager reads it (the last value wins).
rules.detail: The estate value is 7 days (10080 minutes), the release-age window of supply.age.1, the same in every project and equal to the template and to the window the tools are held to: one number, neither under it nor over it (replacing the earlier 14 days, 20160 minutes). The check reads the resolved setting, handles comments and quotes, and compares with the template. The setting lives in the workspace file (pnpm-workspace.yaml).
rules.why: A setting that is absent, non-numeric or overridden by a later line looks present and does nothing.
rules.note: Retired (22 Nov 2026): no release-age window is held, so no cooldown setting is read back. The id is frozen and is not reused.

rules.rule: A security skip of the age window names an advisory id that resolves, and a waiver names every package it lets through, with a reason, an owner and the date all are clear.
rules.detail: A skip with no advisory id is refused; a skip naming a real advisory in a vulnerability database passes. A waiver for a new vendor release lists each transitive package under the window and the date by which all of them are old enough. A waiver for a new vendor major lists its transitives under the window (for example @inlang/sdk, @inlang/plugin-message-format, kysely, @napi-rs/wasm-runtime) with the date all are clear; an update-bot cooldown of seven days is the reference window. The reference waiver covered @inlang/paraglide-js 3.0.0 published that week and everything it pulls in.
rules.why: A fast lane for security fixes is also an attacker's route, because the second xz release arrived looking like a fix; a skip an agent can claim must therefore resolve to a real advisory.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the age check resolves each skip's advisory id in a vulnerability database and parses each waiver as an exception record listing every package and the clearing date. Plant: a skip with no advisory id fails; a waiver with no clearing date fails. Control: a skip naming a real advisory passes

rules.rule: The integrity and provenance signatures of every locked package are verified, and a version with weaker publishing evidence than an earlier one is refused.
rules.detail: Go modules are checked against go.sum and the checksum database. For packages, a trust policy that forbids a downgrade of publishing evidence is read back, and where the package manager has no signature-audit command the intent is a provenance check on the lockfile diff.
rules.why: A release that loses the provenance attestation its predecessors had is the signature of a stolen publishing token.

rules.rule: A vendor family updates as one group: exact pins, a stated minimum age, a provenance check on the lockfile diff, one family bump per change, and a 0.x release only through a labelled pilot with a removal path.
rules.detail: A bump that touches one member of a family must touch all members in one change. Each member is past the age line, and a waiver of the age rule names each package it lets through and the date all are clear. Go families, such as a terminal-UI set or a database-driver pair, move together the same way. Example family: @inlang/paraglide-js and @inlang/plugin-message-format are pinned exactly; the vendor sub-packages are neither pinned nor overridden, and there is no overrides block.
rules.why: A family bumped member by member leaves versions that do not fit each other, and a bump mixed with others hides which change broke.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion lock-diff reads a families data file: a bump touching a family must touch all members in one change, with exact pins, each past the age line, a trust check on the lock diff and one family bump per change. rules.rule: A dependency bump is its own change: one direct bump per commit, no source file touched, after its cooldown, with the trial counts in the change.
rules.detail: The commit check compares the manifest and lockfile with the base: more than one direct dependency changed in one commit fails, a manifest or lockfile change together with non-manifest files fails, and the commit message carries a Trial line with the counts. For Go the scan is on go.mod with non-module files; indirect lines are left out because a module graph brings them in. A vendor family counts as one bump. There is no bump bot; the owner lane opens bumps. The diff scan for web reads package.json and the lockfile together with non-manifest files.
rules.why: A bump mixed with source edits hides the change a reader should see, and a bump can ride inside a large refactor unseen. The known way round is hiding the bump in a refactor, which the same scan catches.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion lock-diff compares the manifest and lockfile with the base; more than one direct change in a commit fails, and the message must carry a Trial line. Plant: two direct bumps in one commit fail; a commit with a bump and a source edit fails. Control: one bump with a Trial line passes

rules.rule: Consumer lag behind the shared module and lockstep pairs are reported with the release as the unit, lag is not gated by a fixed window, each consumer moves its require when it is ready, and a breaking module change fixes every caller the owner keeps in the same change.
rules.detail: One module version in every program. The report compares the shared module's version in each program's go.mod with the latest tag and its date, and shows each consumer's distance from the latest shared module and the pairs that release together, with the release as the unit. Nothing fails on lag: a consumer moves its require when it is ready. A change to the shared module that breaks its surface fixes, in the same change or the same coordinated release, every caller in the repositories the owner keeps, so no kept consumer is left on a broken path. The lag is reported in minors per module, the root module and each separately versioned module on their own, and a waiver whose trigger is "until the shared module bumps" is listed beside the lag, so the release report reads "one module lags three minors; three waivers wait on it". The tag-date read needs network access to a private module.
rules.why: A consumer that lags keeps running code the owner has already replaced, so the lag is shown. A fixed window forces every consumer to the newest version on the owner's schedule, which arch.measures.6 itself names as a cause of coupling; fixing callers in the breaking change is what keeps a lagging consumer safe to move later. A pair that must always release together signals a misplaced boundary.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion report currency lists each consumer's go.mod require of the shared module against the latest tag and its date, and the lockstep pairs; a release check of the shared module fails a breaking surface change (supply.release.2) whose change does not update the callers in the kept repositories. Plant: a breaking change to the shared module with an unfixed caller in a kept repository fails. Control: a consumer two tags behind is reported and passes

How a check in the shared module's repository finds callers in other kept repositories without hosted CI is to be built.

rules.rule: Related shared modules are tagged together, and a separately owned package has its own versioning.
rules.detail: A shared root module and its sub-module are tagged together; the design-tokens package is not in that tag and defaults to its own semver (decision 28). A release check that the tags match runs in the owner repository only. The deprecate-first form is the //go:fix inline directive.
rules.why: The sub-module tags came about 64 minutes and two commits after the root tag, so the pair was not atomic.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a release script check that the root and sub-module tags match, in the owner repository only. Plant: a mismatched tag fails. Control: matching tags pass

rules.rule: A shared release plans who pays for each bump: consumers pay in lockstep, an upgrade comes with a codemod or a list of what changes, and a new shared rule lands as a minor with each repository recording its debt first.
rules.detail: A breaking tag without a changelog section that lists what consumers change is refused. A cross-repository sweep tool opens a pull request in each repository for a codemod. Debt may not grow on a bump. The changelog tool kept is git-cliff (decision 17).
rules.why: A release that does not say what consumers must change shifts the cost silently. The changelog of an earlier shared release is the shape of such a list.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. release step refuses a breaking tag without a changelog section listing what consumers change; consumer lag report from tag dates and lock requirements. rules.rule: A shared package's version range spans minors on purpose, since a caret on a 0.x version pins one minor and could never resolve the next release.
rules.why: A caret range on 0.x means the next minor is a different compatible set, so the range never reaches it.

rules.rule: A library's release clock runs from the last fix merged to its consumers' main branch, the bump in each consumer has an owner, and the hand-off is logged like a review round.
rules.detail: supply.bumps.2 holds that consumer lag is reported with the release as the unit. This rule holds that the release is not done at publish. The release names the consumer's bump and who makes it, and the hand-off is a row where the hub counts rounds (gates.measures.5). A program's release clock runs from the last fix merged to published; a library's runs on to the consumers' main.
rules.why: One fleet's design-system releases reached its main web application in 2 hours 45 minutes, 5 hours 30 minutes, and once not in 5 days, because nothing linked a publish to its consumer.
rules.review_question: Who bumps each consumer of this release, where is the hand-off logged, and when did the last release reach the consumers' main?
open: Planned check: the release record names each consumer and the commit on its main that took the bump, and a release with a consumer still on the old version after a stated window is listed. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A dependency is maintained: no module is archived and none has gone without a release or a push for 24 months in Go, and a web dependency has a release within 12 months or a written finished note.
rules.detail: An unmaintained or abandoned dependency is removed. A banned one that is already present stays on a shrink-only list. Go checks archived and last-pushed state per direct module through the host API (the network is needed, so at land or after release). The web check reads the newest release date of each direct dependency from the registry, and a finished note is an exception record. Transitive age is a report only. Examples removed in the reference: @uiw/react-json-view (alpha), @dnd-kit, zpl-renderer, and other rotting packages.
rules.why: A library nobody maintains carries unfixed vulnerabilities. One archived Go module was found in the baseline and nothing else.

rules.rule: No prerelease, 0.x, alpha or release-candidate major enters production except through a labelled pilot with a removal path.
rules.detail: For Go, v0.x is normal and the shared modules are below 1.0, so only a prerelease tag or a pseudo-version on a direct requirement needs a pilot entry in the allow file; indirect lines are left out because the module graph brings them in. For the web, a 0.x browser dependency needs a pilot record. The 0.x transitives of an accepted pilot are accepted through that pilot. Example: the 0.x transitives of @inlang/paraglide-js are accepted through one named pilot.
rules.why: A prerelease or an unreleased commit changes without notice and carries the same risk as a bump mixed with other edits.

rules.rule: One package manager, pinned, installs from the lockfile only; the lockfile is the pin, it is verified, and a version conflict is never hidden.
rules.detail: For Go: go.sum is committed, go mod verify passes, builds use -mod=readonly, and no gate or release script uses -mod=mod or go get. For JavaScript: install with the frozen-lockfile form only, one package manager for the whole estate, and a peer mismatch fails the install instead of being silenced (a legacy-peer switch is removed). Go has no peer ranges, so that half does not transfer. The strict install form is --frozen-lockfile; peer mismatches are not hidden (legacy-peer-deps is removed). The gate scanner (gatescan) bans -mod=mod and go get in gate and release scripts.
rules.why: An install that resolves again can differ by day. In the web estate a package manager that honours the cooldown refused a young locked entry while another passed it, so the choice of manager is part of the defence.

checks.note: go mod verify, GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly, and a scan that bans -mod=mod and go get in gate and release scripts. Plant: a gate or release script that runs go get, or a tampered module cache, fails. Control: a clean tree passes

rules.rule: Each check tool has one pinned version and runs from the pinned install, passing its exit code through; no tool is run through a package runner that could fetch a same-named stranger.
rules.detail: A test fails if the runner's name appears in a shipped file. No go run of a package at a version at gate time, and no go get or -mod=mod in gate or release scripts. The licence checker is one of the tools run from the pinned install (license-checker with the others such as depcruise, spectral, cspell and markdownlint).
rules.why: A check that fetches its own tool at run time can be replaced by whatever has that name, and a changed version gives a changed verdict.

checks.note: a test that fails if a package runner name appears in a shipped file, and a wrapper that runs each named tool from the package's own pinned install. Plant: a shipped script that calls the runner fails the test. Control: a script that calls the pinned install passes

rules.rule: The module tidy command leaves no diff, and the language version is one the estate supports.
rules.why: A stale unused require is a dependency nobody chose, and an unsupported language version silently skips fixes.

rules.rule: After the dependencies are installed, the build, the type-check and the tests run with the network blocked, and generated output comes from committed inputs.
rules.detail: No CDN or latest-tag URL in a build config; no download at build time; a code generator's output fails the build when it did not compile. A build step that declares a fetch as its own input, such as a content build that reads a remote source, is exempt, because that fetch is the build's input. A Go build runs behind go-proc's network block (sandbox.Run) with GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly and GOPROXY=off; a JS build runs under a sandbox runtime with an empty domain allowlist. Where the system gives no block (Windows today: sandbox.ErrNoBlock) the run is refused by name and never made unblocked. Install itself needs the network and runs before. The install step is npm ci or its frozen equivalent; the build and type-check run after it with no network. A message-format plugin loads from disk through node_modules, not from a URL. The sandbox is @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime; a scan of gate and release scripts by gatescan bans -mod=mod and go get.
rules.why: A build that reaches the network can differ by day and is an exfiltration route. How a block is made differs by system, so the rule names the behaviour and the refusal, never one means.

checks.note: build and type-check run under a sandbox runtime with an empty allowed-domain list, and are refused by name where the system gives no block. Plant: a node fetch of the registry under the sandbox with no allowed domains fails; a build step that fetches at build time fails. Control: the offline build step passes

go-proc's network block with GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly and GOPROXY=off; where it gives none (sandbox.ErrNoBlock) the step is refused by name, never run unblocked. Plant: a build step that fetches at build time fails. Control: a build that reads only the module cache passes

No gate proved a build with the network off before this rule.

rules.rule: The manifest pins the package manager by name with an error on mismatch and a minimum version, so an old tool that would ignore a setting silently refuses to install.
rules.detail: The settings check reads the package manager pin as part of the check-npmrc command of the reference.
rules.why: A package manager older than the settings file ignores the settings, so the cooldown and install-script guards vanish without a message.

checks.note: a settings check that reads the manifest field and requires the manager name and a minimum version. Plant: a manifest with no manager pin fails. Control: a manifest pinning the manager and its minimum version passes

rules.rule: Direct code dependencies use exact versions, ranges are allowed only for peers, and the exact-pin rule covers code dependencies, not the images a program writes into a stack it deploys.
rules.detail: Every direct dependency in a manifest or module file names one exact version; a peer dependency may name a range. The rule is about code the build resolves. A stack file that a program writes for its owner (a compose file, a service unit) may follow an image's release tag and update by comparing the running digest with the registry; how such stacks are written is held by the daemon and deploy rules, not here. An image the release itself builds is pinned by digest (supply.release.9). The second opinion rule is prefer-absolute-version-dependencies (and the dev form).
rules.why: A range on a direct dependency means two installs of one commit can differ. In the web baseline none of 32 direct dependencies was a range. Extending exact pins to the images a program deploys for its owner would forbid the update path that design chose on purpose.

checks.note: syncpack semver groups with an exact range, a separate group for peers that allows ranges; npm-package-json-lint prefer-absolute-version rules as a second opinion. Plant: a caret range in dependencies and a tilde range in devDependencies each fail. Control: exact pins pass

rules.rule: A shared package whose peer range lags a major tool is replaced or overridden on record.
rules.why: A peer range that excludes the installed major forces a silenced install, which hides every other peer conflict.

checks.note: strict peer dependencies so an unmet peer fails the install; every peer rule or override entry carries an exception record naming reason, owner and expiry. Plant: a shared package whose peer range excludes the installed tool major fails the install. Control: the same install with a recorded override passes

rules.rule: No package runs an install script unless it is named on a reasoned allowlist.
rules.detail: Either of two settings blocks scripts, and the last value wins as the package manager reads it. The few packages that need a script are rebuilt by an explicit step after an install with scripts off. Go modules run nothing at fetch, and the one native build step is removed by building without cgo, so the rule has no Go check. The npm form is ignore-scripts, with the allowlisted few rebuilt explicitly.
rules.why: An install script runs arbitrary code on every machine that installs, which is the usual route of a package takeover.

checks.note: strict dependency-build setting true with the named build list, read back from the resolved config, last value wins. Plant: the setting off fails the read-back; a package with a script that is not named fails. Control: the setting on with a named package passes

rules.rule: Every install-script allowlist entry names the package, an owner and a reason of at least ten characters; the file must parse, and an absent file is fine.
rules.why: An allowlist without owner and reason becomes a list nobody can review or expire.

rules.rule: No phantom imports: the lock has exactly the declared direct dependencies, a binary run by name is a declared dependency, in a workspace the root manifest holds no dependency a package imports, and each package declares exactly the siblings its import rules allow, checked both ways.
rules.detail: A bare package-runner call resolves an unlisted tool to whatever has that name, so every binary used must be a declared dependency. A non-flat install layout keeps an undeclared import from resolving. The install is the frozen-lockfile form so a mismatch fails. In a workspace, a dependency in the root manifest resolves from every file, so the root holds only workspace tooling that no package imports. Each package's manifest declares exactly the packages its units may import under the layer table (arch.layers.12): a declared sibling it may not import fails, and an allowed import it does not declare fails.
rules.why: A package that resolves only because something else installed it breaks the day that other package changes, and a bare runner call can fetch a stranger. A root dependency hides the same phantom import inside a workspace.

checks.note: knip with unlisted, unresolved and binaries issue types set to error, a non-flat node_modules layout, and a frozen install that fails when the lock and manifest disagree; a workspace check that the root manifest's dependencies are imported by no package and that each package's declared siblings equal the siblings its import rules allow. Plant: an import of a package that is not in the manifest fails; a binary run by name that is not declared fails; a root dependency imported by a package fails. Control: a declared import passes

open: knip needs its framework plugin active or it reports files used only from template files as unused. Not re-run.

rules.rule: The toolchain is at one version in every project, with the same presets, the toolchain a gate ran on is the one the lockfile names, each dependency has one version across a workspace's packages, and siblings are linked as workspace dependencies.
rules.detail: A preflight on every gate host compares the runtime version with its pinned file, the package manager with the manifest field, and the frozen install offline, and lists missing tools; a non-zero result stops the gate. A runtime-major file is rendered from the template answer so one major holds across declarations. One preflight serves Go and web. The preflight frozen install is install --frozen-lockfile --offline. In a workspace each third-party dependency resolves to one version across all packages, and a package depends on a sibling only through a workspace link, never a published version of it.
rules.why: A gate that ran on a different toolchain than the lockfile names proves nothing about the shipped build. One tool version per estate removes a class of drift.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion preflight on every gate host (runtime against the pinned file, manager against the manifest, frozen install dry check). Plant: a host with the wrong runtime major fails. Control: a matching host passes

sherif 1.13.0 over the workspace manifests (one version per dependency, workspace links for siblings). Plant: two packages declaring different versions of one dependency fail; a sibling declared by a published version fails. Control: one version per dependency and workspace links pass

one pinned version per tool in the tools module, run by the gate and never fetched at run time, with the preflight naming missing ones. Plant: a gate host with a missing or wrong tool version fails the preflight. Control: a matching host passes

rules.rule: Each concern has exactly one importable owner chosen in a data file, the alternatives are banned by name, and the failure message says what to import instead.
rules.detail: The owner is a module, a standard-library package or a shared package. The concern table is the rulebook's list of libraries: one owner per concern with the alternatives named, and every verdict in it is a candidate until ruled. The table is data validated by a schema that requires an owner and the alternatives. A direct dependency that is not in the table fails, and a banned name in source or in a manifest fails. Existing uses of a banned library are a list that only shrinks and never gains an entry. Until the data file exists, the rule for a project is an instruction, and the check reports not applicable with the count of entries (zero) rather than passing. The first entries of a web project's table follow its framework part. Example plant: left-pad as an unlisted name and lodash as a banned one. The allow-file is the shrink-only list of existing uses. Existing uses are suppressed into a suppressions file (eslint-suppressions.json, written with --suppress-rule) that never gains an entry. The build-time cap flag is --max-issues, set to 0. Examples of banned alternatives in a web table: react-hook-form (the form pick is TanStack Form, a settled pick), react-hotkeys-hook, react-i18next and react-intl; the full lists belong to the framework parts.
rules.why: Without one owner per concern, each author picks a library and the build carries several for the same job. In the Go estate no repository had a ban list, and one would have failed the terminal-colour ban on day one; all 32 direct dependencies of the web estate hit no ban, so the cost of binding is low.

checks.note: depguard rows generated from the ban table, with the issue cap set to zero so the first run is not truncated. Plant: an import of a banned library fails with a message naming the owner. Control: an import of the owner passes
Held by the golangci preset, whose comment on gomodguard_v2 names this rule: a module the register bans is refused in go.mod, with the owner named as the one to use

syncpack lint with a config generated from the packages data file (one version group per allowed package, one banned group per banned name, a final banned catch-all so any unlisted direct dependency fails) plus ESLint no-restricted-imports generated from the same file for names in source. Plant: a banned name and an unlisted name in a scratch manifest each fail. Control: only listed packages with exact pins pass
JSON Schema check of the concern table requiring an owner and alternatives on every entry. Plant: a table entry without an owner fails. Control: a complete entry passes

v1 reference, not yet a source: Go language rulebook sources GL-1 and GL-5 (own reports)
