rules.rule: A test-only module is absent from the non-test build.
rules.why: A module linked only for tests that reaches the shipped build enlarges what ships.

checks.note: go list -deps without tests compared with the allow file; reports not applicable with the count while there are zero test-only modules. Plant: a test-only module in the production dependency list fails. Control: a clean list passes

open: Not applicable today: zero test-only modules.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Each shipped binary has a declared closure of the internal packages and external modules it may link, checked per binary by a test with a shrink-only allow list, and the count of linked modules only falls.
rules.detail: For each binary the repository declares which internal packages and which external modules it may link, citing the concern each external module serves. A test lists each binary's real dependency closure (go list -deps for the binary's main package) and fails on any internal package or module outside that binary's list, so a helper or guest binary that links a host package fails even when the main binary may. The allow list only shrinks without a recorded exemption, and the count of linked modules per binary only falls. An empty allow file is refused with a distinct exit code, not read as a pass. The test runs in the local gate.
rules.why: A module can be linked without anyone having chosen it. In the Go estate, direct requires ranged from 7 to 15 per repository and linked modules from 38 to 47, and no repository had an allow file. A count per repository hides a small binary that has grown the large one's dependencies, which is where a trust line breaks.

checks.note: a per-binary closure test comparing go list -deps of each main package with that binary's allow list in rule data, with the count cap and the empty-file refusal; golangci-lint gomodguard_v2 with the allowed-modules list generated from the union of the lists for the direct half. Plant: a guest binary that imports a host package fails; an import of a module that is off every list fails. Control: each binary linking only its listed packages passes

open: The direct half is off the shelf; the transitive cap is our own script and was planted 72 of 72 in a trial.
v1 reference, not yet a source: Go estate dependency reports GL-2 and GL-3 (own reports)

rules.rule: A new third-party module meets a bar: a permissive licence, a release or push in the last 12 months, more than one committer or a named organisation, and a module graph small enough to read.
rules.detail: The change that adds the module carries a row in the concern table, one sentence on what the standard library lacks, and the weight of the dependency. The facts are measured by script; the sentence is read by a reviewer.
rules.why: A dependency chosen without facts is accepted on a name; the bar turns the choice into measurable items.

checks.note: a facts script over the module proxy and the repository host API, plus a module-graph script, failing on bar items. Plant: a module with no licence fails. Control: a permissively licensed, active module passes

open: The standard-library sentence is a review item; the facts script is a recipe to write, not a program to build.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
v1 reference, not yet a source: Go estate dependency report GL-5 (own report)

rules.rule: A commit that adds a dependency to any manifest section is justified in its pull request and signed off by someone other than its author; a version bump of an existing dependency does not count.
rules.detail: Every manifest section counts: runtime, development, optional and peer dependencies. The signature is held by a stored verdict from a different identity on changes to the protected path list. The justification text is read by a reviewer.
rules.why: Adding a dependency is the largest single change of supply-chain surface; one author should not make it alone.
rules.review_question: Does the pull request say why this dependency is needed, what it replaces, and does it carry a sign-off from someone other than its author?
open: The independent signature depends on a stored non-author verdict, which today cannot be told apart because every agent pushes as one identity.
rules.note: v1 review check (review is not a v2 check class): protected-path rule requiring a stored non-author verdict on manifest changes; a model reads the justification in the pull request

rules.rule: The standard library comes before a new dependency or a home-made helper, before a part is written the change names the maintained tools surveyed and why none fits, and a part a maintained tool already does well is not rebuilt.
rules.detail: Order of preference: the standard library, then a maintained tool or library that does the job, then our own code. A change that adds a new part (a module, a command, a parser, a protocol client) names the maintained tools it looked at and the reason each was not used; "none surveyed" fails the review. Where a maintained program does the job, the program uses it through an adapter (arch.ports.6) and reads its machine output (arch.ports.20) rather than reimplementing it.
rules.why: A dependency or a helper for something the standard library already does is weight with no gain, and a part rebuilt where a maintained tool exists is code we now maintain alone.
rules.review_question: Does the standard library or a maintained tool already do what this new dependency, helper or part does, and which tools were surveyed?
open: Whether the standard library or a tool would do is semantic and not checkable by tool. A partial aid is a linter that flags helpers replaced by the standard library.
v1 reference, not yet a source: Go standard library first (own report GL-5)
rules.note: v1 review check (review is not a v2 check class): a model checks whether the standard library covers the new module, beside the allow-file row that new modules already need, and a required survey field in the change template (presence only) for a new part

rules.rule: A new library is a row of the register of libraries, which names the job, what it replaces and the alternatives it bans, and it passes the supply-chain gate and logs the replaced use as debt with a date by which it is gone.
rules.detail: The register is rulebook/lang/go/libraries.yaml. One concern keeps one library: the row names its job, the library to call, where an import of it is allowed, the modules and hand-written code it replaces, and the ban for the alternatives (depguard imports, forbidigo patterns). A row that is chosen and bans something becomes a row of the Go preset; a row that needs a spike, or is conditional, does not. The places still using the replaced code are listed in the debt record with a zero-by date. The replaced use may be a hand-written copy object or vocabulary.
rules.why: A library added beside the old one doubles the code for a concern and leaves the old one to rot.
rules.review_question: Does the change that adds this library say what it replaces, ban the alternatives and record the replaced use as debt?
open: The table row and the supply-chain gate are mechanical; whether the replaced use is named is judged.
rules.note: v1 review check (review is not a v2 check class): the concern-table check (supply.intake.1) fails a library without a table row; a model reads the change for the replaced use and the debt entry

rules.rule: A dependency that does what the platform already does is on the ban list.
rules.detail: Advice-only plugins that report native replacements: @e18e/eslint-plugin and eslint-plugin-depend.
rules.why: A package that repeats a built-in feature adds code, update work and attack surface for nothing.

checks.note: ban entries (name, reason, platform export that replaces it) in the packages data file become banned syncpack groups. Plant: a banned platform-duplicating dependency fails. Control: a manifest without one passes

open: An advisory plugin that reports dependencies with a native replacement exists; it was not run and is advice, not the gate.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every banned or watched library has a named re-entry trigger, and the ban list covers the library family, not only the member in use.
rules.detail: A trigger is a version, a stated need or a measured threshold.
rules.why: A ban with no way back is either ignored or never revisited; a ban of one family member leaves the others open.

checks.note: the packages data file validated by JSON Schema (ajv) requiring a re-entry field on every ban entry. Plant: a ban entry without a re-entry trigger fails. Control: an entry with one passes

open: Half of this holds: the schema half is enforced; whether the family is complete is judged by a person. Proposed to split it.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A dependency's API is one that models write correctly without prompting.
rules.why: A library whose API models misuse costs repeated rework in agent-written code.
rules.review_question: Write a sample against this dependency's API with a model and score whether it is correct without prompting.
open: No measure exists for agent fit; it would change if a repository logged how often agents misuse a dependency API.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every installed package carries a licence on one shared allowlist, weak copyleft (MPL-2.0) passes only when the package is used unmodified, and strong copyleft, unlicensed or unknown licences fail.
rules.detail: Allowed examples are MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC and 0BSD. MPL-2.0 is allowed for a package used as published: a patch, a vendored edited copy or a fork of an MPL-2.0 package fails until its changed files are published under the same licence and the exception is recorded. AGPL, GPL, SSPL, UNLICENSED and an unknown licence fail. What ships to the browser is held to a stricter list than the rest. Our own modules are skipped by path or scope. The policy ships once: allowed SPDX ids, the weak-copyleft list with its unmodified condition, an own-scope skip, dated exceptions and clarifications. The check runs in the gate command the pre-push hook runs. Go uses its own licence tool with the allowed list and with our modules ignored (without that, they report no licence found). Go form: go-licenses check ./... --allowed_licenses=<list> --ignore=<our modules>. Web alternative: license-checker-rseidelsohn with --onlyAllow.
rules.why: A strong copyleft licence in a shipped dependency can force the product's source open, and an unlicensed one gives no right to use it. Weak copyleft binds only the files of the package itself, so it is safe while those files are not changed.

checks.note: go-licenses check with --allowed_licenses and --ignore for our modules, in the gate command the pre-push hook runs. Plant: a dependency with a disallowed licence gives exit 1 and a not-allowed message. Control: the allowed list with our modules ignored exits 0

pnpm licenses list over the lockfile against an allowlist in the packages data file with a stricter list for production dependencies, and a check that no MPL-2.0 package is patched (patchedDependencies) or vendored; license-checker with --onlyAllow is the alternative. Plant: a scratch dependency with GPL-3.0 fails; an MPL-2.0 package listed in patchedDependencies fails. Control: MIT passes; an unmodified MPL-2.0 package passes

open: Neither web tool was run; an existing check script in a web repository was read only. The Go tool was verified.

rules.rule: The licence judgement is exact SPDX satisfaction of the allowlist; an empty tree, a declared but uninstalled dependency, a missing licence or non-SPDX text all fail.
rules.why: A licence check that passes on nothing found passes on a broken install.

checks.note: a test of the licence command with an empty tree, an uninstalled dependency, a missing licence and a non-SPDX string. Plant: an empty tree fails. Control: a tree of allowed licences passes

rules.rule: A dated licence exception covers one named package and one licence, only as a development dependency, and fails once expired.
rules.why: A broad or undated exception becomes the way round the policy. A licence exception never covers shipped code.

checks.note: the licence command rejects an exception naming more than one package or licence, a production dependency, or a past expiry date. Plant: an expired exception fails; an exception for a production dependency fails. Control: a current exception for a development dependency passes
a licence exception names the module, the reason and an expiry. Plant: an exception without an expiry fails. Control: a dated exception passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A licence guessed from a file needs a clarification entry naming the same package and file; the own scope is skipped by name.
rules.why: A licence read from a file's text is a guess, and a clarification records who decided it.

checks.note: the licence command requires a clarification entry for a guessed licence and skips the own scope by name. Plant: a guessed licence with no clarification fails. Control: a clarified entry passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Every shared module a program requires has a licence file, and its visibility is known to the check.
rules.detail: All packages are private for now (decision 1), so the check treats every shared module as private and requires the licence file anyway. Revisit before the first repository goes public.
rules.why: Three released versions of the shared module had no licence file and the module is private, which the licence scan flagged.

checks.note: repository view and a licence-file check on each shared module in go.mod, a recipe in the shared makefile fragment. Plant: a module without a licence file fails. Control: a module with one passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: own measure; three released versions of the shared modules had none

rules.rule: LICENSE and NOTICE sit at the repository root, and every artifact that bundles third-party code ships a generated notices file equal to what it bundles, compared in the gate.
rules.detail: The root holds the project's own LICENSE and a NOTICE naming the project and its copyright. Each artifact that bundles third-party code (a binary, a bundle, an image, a packed package) carries a third-party notices file generated from the exact set of packages it bundles, with each package's licence text and any NOTICE it ships. The gate regenerates the notices for each artifact and fails when the committed or packed file differs. Apache-2.0 and MPL-2.0 notices travel with the code that carries them.
rules.why: Most permissive licences are conditional on keeping their notice; an artifact that bundles code without it breaks the licence that allowed the bundle. A hand-kept notices file drifts from what the artifact holds.

checks.note: a gate member that checks LICENSE and NOTICE at the root and regenerates each artifact's notices file from its bundled package list (go-licenses save or report for Go, the package manager's licence listing for web) and compares it with the shipped file. Plant: a new bundled dependency without a regenerated notices file fails; a missing NOTICE at root fails. Control: a notices file equal to the regenerated one passes

gragas check reads the repository's goreleaser config and reports an archive whose files do not carry LICENSE and NOTICE. A repo with no goreleaser config gets no finding. Plant: an archive listing no NOTICE is reported. Control: an archive listing both passes

rules.rule: A vendored token file equals the source at its named version, by hash, in the path agents take.
rules.why: One program's header said version 9 while the source tokens said 1, so a copy had drifted from what it named.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. companion tokens verify reads the version and sha256 in a lock file and compares them with the vendored file and the registry version. Plant: editing a vendored token file by one byte fails; a lock naming version 9 for a package at version 1 fails. Control: restoring the file passes

open: When tokens are consumed as a package dependency, the package manager's lock integrity covers it and this rule reduces to the lockfile check.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: A: a vendored header said version 9 against a source at version 1

rules.rule: A part copied between sites records where it came from, with a header naming the source repository, version, path and a hash.
rules.detail: The header form is copied-from: <repo>@<version> <path> plus a hash.
rules.why: A copy with no origin cannot be updated or checked against its source.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. files placed by companion sync carry a copied-from header with a hash; the sync check fails when a header is missing or the hash differs from the source at that version. Plant: a synced file with its header removed fails; a drifted body fails. Control: an intact synced file passes

open: Half holds, for synced copies only. A hand copy dropped in with no header is not seen unless the cross-repository clone scan finds it (a known gap).

rules.rule: Generated files name the version of the tool that made them.
rules.detail: Generated files start with the standard "Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT." line and a version token. Regeneration is go generate.
rules.why: A generated file with no banner is edited by hand and its tool version is lost.

checks.note: a banner check that generated files start with the standard line and a version token. Plant: a generated file missing the banner fails. Control: a file with both passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice
rules.note: Split from a bundled source row that also held two other rules, kept as supply.provenance.5 and supply.provenance.6.

rules.rule: If a repository has generators, regenerating leaves no diff; with zero inputs the check reports not applicable with the count.
rules.detail: The rule is in the gate list from the start. Its input count is the number of go:generate lines, zero today, and it declares zero a valid state: it returns not applicable with zero inputs and the count (decision 26) until the first generator appears. The generator lines counted are //go:generate lines.
rules.why: A stale generated file passes review because nobody regenerates it. No Go repository used go:generate in the seven checked, which the count shows, with the build-constraint lines as the positive.

checks.note: go generate ./... followed by git diff --exit-code; not applicable with count 0 while no go:generate line exists. Plant: a stale generated file fails. Control: freshly generated files pass

open: The two repositories without Go files have a zero that says nothing.

rules.rule: There is one token file for design tokens, and every copy of it is a recorded vendored copy.
rules.why: Two token files drift apart; the bundled source row asked for one.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a single tokens source in the repository, with the sync and verify checks of supply.provenance.1 for every copy. Plant: a second token file that is not a recorded copy fails. Control: one source and its recorded copies pass

open: The source row reads only "one token file" inside a bundled row; this wording is an interpretation.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: Build and gate recipes are Taskfile tasks that run the program's own commands, with standard tools only.
rules.why: A recipe written as shell for one system silently differs on another; a task that runs a program command has no shell of its own to differ, so the rule asks for no claim of which systems it works on.

checks.note: a task in the Taskfile using standard tools only and no shell line of its own. Plant: a task that runs a shell pipeline fails. Control: a task that runs one program command passes

open: Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice

rules.rule: A program fetched into an image, a tool cache or a build is pinned by version and verified before use by a signature or a checksum from its publisher's https origin, its version is read back, and a verification that cannot run stops the step.
rules.detail: Every fetch names an exact version. Before the fetched program is used, it is checked against the publisher's signature where the publisher signs, and otherwise against a checksum fetched from the same https origin as the program (never a checksum kept beside the download URL on a mirror). The program is then run to print its version, which must equal the pinned one. A missing signature tool, an unreachable checksum or a version mismatch stops the step with could not run; the step never continues unverified. Locked packages are held by supply.age.4; this rule covers what a package manager does not fetch.
rules.why: A program fetched outside the lockfile has no integrity check unless the step does one, and a step that skips a check it cannot run installs whatever the network handed it.

checks.note: a test over image build files and fetch scripts that every download is followed by a signature or checksum verification against the publisher's https origin and a version read-back, with no fallback branch that skips the check. Plant: a download step with no checksum check fails; a checksum fetched over plain http fails; a verify step guarded by || true fails. Control: a pinned download verified against the publisher's checksum and read back passes

rules.rule: A release is built from a clean annotated tag on main by one recipe that runs the full gate first and never pushes, an install is made only from such a build and reads the installed version back, and where something is published only the release workflow on the tag publishes it, with publish refused unless CI is set.
rules.detail: The release recipe (make release or its equivalent) refuses anything but a clean checkout of main, runs the full gate unless a local stamp shows that this exact tree passed it (gates.land.1), writes or checks the changelog entry (supply.release.5), tags with an annotated tag and builds. It never pushes; the person pushes the tag. An install or deploy refuses a checkout or build that is not exactly a clean release tag, and after installing reads the running program's version and commit back and compares them with the tag. Where something is published (a package, an image, a release page), only the release workflow triggered by the tag publishes it, with the publish job needing every test and build job (supply.release.6); a command refuses to publish when the CI environment variable is not set, and the first publish of a package is from the workflow too. There is no CI on every push and no run is scheduled: each release prints the age of the last whole run, and no weekly or other scheduled run is added (decision 66, which replaces decision 34). The recipe also runs non-blocking steps that need the network, such as the external link check (docs.links.1): each prints its findings and never stops the release.
rules.why: A shared package can otherwise publish from a laptop with whatever the laptop holds, and an install from an untagged tree is a version nobody can name. The invariant three target repos share is one recipe from a clean tagged main after the full gate; CI is the only place that holds the publish token.

checks.note: the release recipe refuses a dirty tree, a branch other than main or a lightweight tag, and contains no git push (a scan of the recipe); the install step compares the installed version with the tag; a require-ci command refuses a publish unless CI is set. Plant: a release from a dirty tree is refused; a publish with the CI variable unset is refused; an install from an untagged build is refused. Control: a release from a clean annotated tag on main, published by the tag-triggered workflow, passes

open: Neither the workflow linter nor the security audit checks the trigger set; the policy tool reads YAML 1.1, so the on key arrives as the string true and the policy reads that key.
The workflow-trigger half is held by supply.workflows.1.

rules.rule: The release tier runs from a fresh clone of the tag, never from a working checkout; the release dry run is a release member with its cost listed; and a member that needs the tag says so and runs last.
rules.detail: supply.release.1 holds that a release is built from a clean annotated tag by one recipe that runs the full gate first. This rule holds the members: the push tier plus the release members, all at once (gates.command.17), on a clone made from the tag so no file of a working checkout reaches the build. The dry run of the release tool is a member with its cost, so a broken release config is found before the release and not at it. A member that needs the tag to exist (the changelog check, the publish) declares it and runs after the others.
rules.why: One project found its broken release config only at release, because the dry run was not a member; a release from a working checkout carries whatever that checkout holds.
rules.review_question: Does this release run on a fresh clone of the tag, is the dry run a member with its cost, and which members need the tag?
open: Planned check: the members file holds the dry-run member at release with a cost, and the release recipe clones the tag before it runs. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A hosted release workflow maps its jobs to the members file and ends with the runner's report, installs once and never per job, and a reproducible build builds each artifact twice from two clean copies and compares byte for byte, one reproducibility proof for each artifact.
rules.detail: supply.workflows.5 holds that a workflow which runs gate members runs the one gate command. This rule holds the release workflow's shape: each job is a member or a group of members of the release tier, the last job prints the runner's report with its counts (gates.measures.6), and the install runs once into a cache the jobs share. supply.release.3 holds the same bytes from any directory; this rule runs that proof for each artifact, two clean copies each, the artifacts in parallel (gates.command.18).
rules.why: Hosted release workflows of one fleet installed per job and had no success on record in seven repositories; a release that builds once cannot say its bytes are reproducible.
rules.review_question: Which member does each job of this release workflow run, how many times does it install, and is each artifact built twice and compared?
open: Planned check: the workflow linter's job list is compared with the members file. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A release is refused on an API break that is not declared, checked before the tag is pushed.
rules.why: A break the author did not declare turns every consumer's next bump into a surprise. The tag step is the last moment the check can run, because the tool refuses once the tag exists. A real break was found in the shared module.

checks.note: gorelease at the tag step before the tag is pushed, and apidiff for the report. Plant: removal of an exported function fails. Control: a compatible change passes

open: v1 evidence, not yet a source: own measure; apidiff found a real break in an exported listener

rules.rule: A release is the same bytes from any directory: the build strips paths, and a script builds twice from two paths and compares.
rules.detail: It runs on the candidate at land when release files change, and again on the shipped artifact after publish as a report. The check is go build with -trimpath; a snapshot build (goreleaser build --snapshot) is made twice from two directories and compared with cmp.
rules.why: A build that embeds its path cannot be reproduced; two hashes from two paths prove it, and the flag that strips paths removes the difference.

checks.note: the release tool builds with the trim-path flag and a snapshot build is made twice from two directories and the binaries compared. Plant: a build without the flag gives two hashes. Control: a build with the flag gives one

open: A library ships no binary to build, so whether it is exempt is open.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: practice; the flag appeared in no repository

rules.rule: Release artifacts carry a checksum; an SBOM or a signature is added when a third party verifies it, and not before.
rules.why: A checksum lets a consumer detect corruption or substitution; heavier attestations cost work with no reader until a verifier exists.

checks.note: the release tool's checksum block, and a release check that the checksum file lists every artifact. Plant: a release without a checksum file, or a checksum file missing an artifact, fails. Control: a complete file passes

open: Half rule, since the checksum is checked by a step but whether an SBOM or signature is due is a judgement no check can make because no check can say a consumer exists.
rules.note: Retired by decision 65 (D-T96): provenance and an SBOM are shipped wherever the publisher offers them, not when a third party asks. The checksum half moves to supply.release.9 unchanged.

rules.rule: Every release has a plain-words changelog entry that a person writes or rewrites, a tool proposes the version with a named override allowed, a program with an API names its API number in the entry, and the release recipe never pushes.
rules.detail: The entry is written per change (each change adds its item under Unreleased) or as a draft the release recipe makes from the commits for a person to rewrite before tagging; either way a person writes the words, in plain language with a bold lead and no file names, function names or internal ids. A tool proposes the next version from the history since the last tag (git-cliff in the Go repos, a change-notes tool in a web workspace; the tool is chosen per repo), and the recipe accepts a named override (VERSION=vX.Y.Z) for a person's choice. A program with a versioned API names the API number in each release's entry. The release check fails a tag whose entry is missing or still the untouched draft. The recipe scan is run by a gate scanner (gatescan) and bans git push in the recipe.
rules.why: A tag with no entry gives consumers nothing to read, and a generated entry made of commit subjects is written for the author, not the reader. A version a tool proposes is not mistyped, and an override keeps the person's choice. A recipe that pushes releases without the person's last look.

checks.note: a release check that the changelog entry for the tag exists and differs from the tool's untouched draft, that the version equals the tool's proposal or the named override, and a scan that bans git push in the release recipe. Plant: a tag without an entry fails; an entry identical to the generated draft fails; a recipe with git push fails. Control: a tag with a rewritten entry and a push-free recipe passes

gragas check reads the repository's goreleaser config and reports changelog.disable set beside release notes, since the entry a person wrote would then be dropped. Plant: both set is reported. Control: a config that does not disable the changelog passes

gragas check reads a repository's .changie.yaml, where it has one, and reports a change file not named <issue>-<kind>. The changelog tool is chosen per repo, so a repo with no .changie.yaml gets no finding. Plant: a misnamed change file is reported. Control: well-named files pass

bad.code:
# .goreleaser.yaml, run with --release-notes: the changelog is turned off beside it
changelog:
  disable: true

rules.rule: After the tag build and before publish, a release step unpacks the archive, runs version and one start test and compares its digest with the one the tests saw; the publish job needs every test and build job, the workflow has no conditional or continue-on-error, and the publishing job runs no project code.
rules.detail: In the release workflow the publish job lists every test and build job as a need and runs only when all passed: no if: and no continue-on-error anywhere in the workflow, held by a test that reads the file. The publish job has no checkout of the project and runs none of its code; it only promotes the artifacts the build made (for example by undrafting a complete draft release). The publish job needs every job, has no if: and no continue-on-error, and runs none of the module's code. For a web project the archive's page is served and one start test is run. A page embedded in a daemon is tested through the daemon's archive. For a deployed function the bundle is unpacked, its handler invoked from the bundle, and its hash compared with the one the tests saw and with the code hash of the deployed function. A library ships no binary, so the Go rule has an exemption.
rules.why: A bundle can differ from the source the tests ran against through bundler options or an optional dependency resolved at build time. A last-modified time shows the function was updated, not that its bytes are the ones that passed. In one web estate 4 of 72 faults showed only on a real server after release.

checks.note: a release step before publish in the shared recipe that unpacks, runs version and one start test, and compares the digest. Plant: an archive with a wrong binary stops the release. Control: the right archive passes

v1 class our-cli. a release step after the build that unpacks the archive, serves its page, runs one start test and compares the digest; fails before publish. Plant: an archive with a wrong file inside stops the release. Control: the right archive passes

a release step that unpacks the function bundle, invokes its handler and compares the hash with the test run's and with the deployed code hash. Plant: a bundle with the wrong handler inside stops the release. Control: the right bundle passes

a test that reads the release workflow: the publish job needs every other job, no if or continue-on-error key exists, and the publish job has no checkout step. Plant: a workflow with continue-on-error on the test job fails; a publish job with a checkout step fails. Control: a workflow whose publish needs every job and only promotes artifacts passes

open: Whether this step would have caught the four faults is not traced.
Whether the check runs at tier 3 or tier 4 for a function bundle is not fixed.

rules.rule: The program is compiled and vetted at push, on the one machine the gate runs on.
rules.detail: One gate step runs go vet ./... at push for each system of the project's list (arch.ports.4), by GOOS on the one machine the gate runs on, as one step. It catches a compile fault only. What differs by system is the platform libraries' own proof, which is run on each system by loan and is not a leg of a product's gate.
rules.why: A compile fault is invisible until a later tier if the push does not vet at all. (An earlier version of this rule asked for a vet per shipped GOOS, because one program built only on Linux failed in six packages on Linux-only calls; a product now holds no such calls.)

checks.note: v1 class compiler. go vet ./... for each system of the list, by GOOS, on one machine. Plant: a file that does not compile fails. Control: a package that compiles passes

rules.rule: Binary size is recorded as a metric, not a gate.
rules.why: Five standard-library imports grew a binary 4.5 percent, which a 5 percent budget passes, so a budget gate would not have caught the growth that matters; the number is the value.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the stripped build size recorded in the baseline, with the release failing if the metric is not written

rules.rule: A release carries a checksum file listing every artifact; an SBOM, provenance and a signature are added the day a repo is public, and a container image is built from a base pinned by digest and runs as a non-root user.
rules.detail: Every release has a checksum file listing every artifact. A repo that is not public ships no SBOM, no provenance statement and no signature, and no check asks for them; the day a repo is made public its release config adds them wherever the place a release is published supports them (a package registry's provenance statement, a build attestation, an SBOM, a signed and notarized desktop build). An image is built by the release recipe from a base image pinned by digest, runs as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem except its volumes, whether the repo is public or not. What the publisher offers is read from its documentation when the release is set up and recorded in the release config; a publisher that adds provenance later is picked up by the next review of that config. Ruling: (no SBOM or signing while private) and gragas#907's table (a checksum file now; an SBOM, provenance and a signature the day a repo is public).
rules.why: A checksum lets a consumer detect corruption or substitution. Provenance, an SBOM and a pinned non-root base cost minutes once and age well; waiting for a third party to ask is waiting to be asked why not.

Plant: a checksum file missing an artifact fails; a public repo's publish without provenance on a registry marked as offering it fails; an image base by tag fails. Control: a release with a complete checksum file passes, and a public repo's with provenance and SBOM too

rules.rule: A known-vulnerability scan of dependencies runs in the pre-push gate (in the release gate only when it does not fit the push budget), over the source for Go and over the lockfile for web, its result is read as text, and it fails on high severity.
rules.detail: The scan is a member of the one gate command, so the pre-push hook runs it on every push; a land tier, where a repo has one, runs it again. When the scan's network wait does not fit the hook budget of gates.hooks.4 it moves to the release workflow and still blocks the release. For Go the scan is reachability-aware and runs in source mode with the tool pinned in the shared makefile fragment. For web it is the package manager audit with --audit-level high (severity-filtered) over the lockfile, pnpm-lock.yaml, with a planted vulnerable version and a clean control; its ignore entries carry an expiry date and a reason.
rules.why: A dependency with a known vulnerability is the cheapest way in for an attacker. Before this rule the word vulnerability had no hit in the web catalogue, and audit appeared only as a tier-4 report. The Go scan was in six of seven repositories already. Under decision 65 there is no hosted land job, so a scan placed only at land had no tier that runs.

rules.rule: No secret is committed: one pinned secret scanner runs at commit and in the pre-push gate over the whole history, a land tier where one exists runs it again, and a finding is reported by rule, file and line without the value.
rules.detail: The scanner config is chosen explicitly and not picked up by accident. A staged-file scan runs at commit, and the gate command the pre-push hook runs scans every commit in the history and the working tree as it is. A land tier, where a repo has one, repeats the full scan; it is never the only full scan. The documentation example key is allowlisted by default and is not reported. The staged-file scan is gitleaks protect --staged (git --staged in current versions). The commit scan is one of the three standing gates shared across repos (the others are the armed hook and the pipefail check), run by the shared hook file over the staged changes.
rules.why: A committed secret stays in history forever and must be rotated. The scan also reaches the web bundle, which must carry no secret. Under decision 65 there is no hosted land job, so a full scan placed only at land never ran.

rules.rule: Forbidden names come from a list kept outside the repository with its words stored as hashes; every tracked file, branch name and pushed commit message is scanned against it, the check fails when the list cannot be read, and in a public repo every commit's author and committer email is a no-reply address.
rules.detail: The forbidden names are the private facts of the people and places a repo serves: employers, people, machines, networks, addresses, households and the software a deployment runs. The list lives outside the repository (a path set in the environment) and holds each word as a hash, so the guard does not spell what it guards. The scan reads every tracked file, the branch name and every commit message in the pushed range, matching whole words case-insensitively against the hashes. When the list path is unset or unreadable the check exits 2 (could not run), never 0. Examples, fixtures and docs use stand-in names from an explicit stand-in list and documentation address ranges. In a public repository the pre-push hook refuses a commit whose author or committer email is not the host's no-reply address.
rules.why: A private name in history cannot be removed without rewriting it, and a public repository publishes every word of it. In one target repository a work email reached 217 commits before the check existed. A list kept in the repo would itself publish the names.

rules.rule: No workflow triggers itself: workflows run only when started (manual dispatch or a call from another workflow), or on a tag push for a release, never on a schedule, a push to a branch or a pull request.
rules.detail: The gate runs locally: make check and the pre-push hook (gates.hooks.1) are the only gate on a push, and no workflow repeats it on push or pull request. A release workflow runs on a release tag push or by dispatch, has a dry-run option and one verify file per export, and the first publish of a package is only from the workflow. A check too slow for the hook runs in the release workflow (gates.hooks.4). The check is parse-based: it normalises the on key (a scalar, an inline list, a quoted key and a map all count) to a set of events and allows only dispatch, call and push with tags. A check in the ast-grep style passed three of five cheap restructurings and was rejected; the parse-based check passed six of six. The same check runs on Go and web repositories. A conftest policy is the alternative form. Cases the check covers: on: push: branches (the push.branches key) fails while push.tags passes. A run step with -count=N above 1 is denied. The audit named dangerous-triggers covers only pull_request_target, workflow_run and issue_comment, so it does not cover trigger sets.
rules.why: Hosted minutes on every push are refused: the tag is the release and the local gate is the gate. Neither the workflow linter nor the security audit checks the trigger set, so a push trigger went unseen.

rules.rule: Every new or changed test passes a machine-run admission ladder at land: it builds, passes in file order, passes under several shuffle seeds, fails against a break the tool chooses, stays inside its budget and passes a bounded repeat.
rules.detail: The land step selects new and changed test functions only. Seeds are separate runs, because a count flag with one shuffle seed reuses one order for every repeat. The break is a mutant in the changed lines chosen by the tool, not the author (comparisons, logic, constants, returns, removed statements); a change with no mutant site prints n/a, and the n/a share is reported as the third result, since n/a is otherwise a free pass. A browser journey takes a break written for its claim, not a mutant. The bounded repeat is the one exception to no test twice on a tree (tests.selection.7): one step of the one proof, able only to fail (decision 32). Its bound, the seeds and the kill count are not set; any number would be a guess. Surviving mutants on changed lines in core logic and shared parts are reported. A test that mirrors the code passes the ladder, so review keeps that question. The browser-journey break is hand-written for its claim. The time limit is the per-package budget of the shared preset.
rules.why: Measured elsewhere: a published study admitted generated tests only if they built, passed repeatedly and added coverage, and about three in four built, 57 percent passed reliably and 25 percent added coverage; a scorer was tampered with in 39 of 128 agent runs (older models). Own bugs: 4 of 15 test drives in one fleet pass could not turn a test red.

rules.rule: A test name is a claim in plain English, and a table test names every case.
rules.why: Names are how a failure is read; a naming claim cannot be machine judged, only the presence of a case name can.

rules.rule: A test with no assertion, or only tautological ones, is refused, a test that loops over cases, files or items asserts the loop ran at least once with a planted empty case, every guard has a test that sees it refuse, and each test carries one line on what breaks for a person when it fails.
rules.detail: A tautology is a literal condition (a log, a literal truth), a comparison of an expression with itself or an equality check of a value with itself, never any constant: a test comparing named constants across packages is a real drift test. The check follows helpers that take the test handle, contract packages and table function values to find an assertion. A single trivial assertion passes this row and the ladder's mutant break catches it (tests.admission.1). A loop over cases, files or items found at run time (a directory listing, a glob, a parsed list) asserts its count is above zero, and the suite holds a plant that feeds it an empty set and must fail. A guard is any code that refuses (a check, a validator, a permission test, a gate rule); each has a test that drives it to refuse and asserts the refusal. The cost line is one comment above the test, in the words of the person who loses when it fails, not a restatement of its name. No test is disabled, focused or commented out (tests.admission.5). How each language writes the shape (helpers, table names) lives in its language part.
rules.why: Agents are the likeliest authors of weak assertions, and an empty loop is the second way a suite goes vacuous: it asserts nothing and passes. A guard with no negative test is an opinion. The cost line says what the signature cannot: why the test exists. Trial on the Go side of the assertion check: 11 hits in 5,767 tests, 0 to 1 true; the false ones trace to contract suites, table values, helper processes and skip-only tests. Low yield, kept because it costs nothing.

rules.rule: A test's expected value is a literal, the spec, a recorded sample of the real server or a generator with a stated invariant, never the code under test.
rules.detail: An analyser flags an assertion whose expected value is computed by calling the function under test or a copy of its expression, and a change that edits code and its expected literal together is flagged first for the reader (nothing sees output pasted in as a literal). Only the trivial form is mechanical. Tests are independent of the code they check: daemon samples, not mocks the agent also wrote.
rules.why: A test written against its own implementation verifies nothing (Khorikov); an agent will paste the code's own output in as the literal. Full independence cannot be checked, the cheap detectable form can.

rules.rule: In the default tiers a skipped, focused, disabled or commented-out test fails the gate, and a test whose precondition is unmet reports not measured, never a pass; an opt-in tier skips with the exact command that runs it and fails when asked to run without what it needs.
rules.detail: Default tiers are the ones the gate runs on every push and release. There a skip call, a focus mark, a disabled test or a commented-out test fails; a test that cannot run because a precondition is missing (a tool, a permission, a platform) reports the precondition as not measured in the verdict, and an empty list of cases is not a pass (tests.selection.8). An opt-in tier (real machines, root, a privileged container) is declared in the gate config with the command that runs it; when it is not asked for, each of its tests skips with that exact command in the skip message, and when it is asked for and its precondition is missing it fails, never skips. The skip count of the default tiers is zero; an existing repo that starts above zero holds a shrink-only count until it reaches zero. In Go the count is taken over t.Skip calls in _test.go files.
rules.why: A skip in a default tier is a test that silently stopped existing. Skips per test in our repos, raw and including environment skips: 102 of 1,645, 74 of 1,731, 68 of 1,020, 38 of 1,301, 25 of 271, 13 of 465.

checks.note: forbidigo on the skip calls outside files of a declared opt-in tier, with a shrink-only count per repo down to zero; an opt-in skip must carry the tier's command; skip counts per package from the JSON test summary. Plant: a new skip in a default-tier test fails; an opt-in skip whose message lacks the command fails. Control: an opt-in test that skips with its command when not asked for passes

@vitest/eslint-plugin no-disabled-tests, no-focused-tests and no-commented-out-tests at error (Biome form: `noSkippedTests` and `noFocusedTests` at error), with a zero count of skipped tests in the verdict of the default tiers. Plant: a test.skip or test.only in a default-tier file fails. Control: a suite with no skip passes

an opt-in tier run without its precondition must exit non-zero, never zero with skips. Plant: the root-only tier run as a normal user fails. Control: the same tier not asked for skips with its command

rules.rule: A test edited in the same change as the code it judges is flagged to the reader with a reason line, not refused; a removed assertion, an added skip, a focused test and a loosened literal are listed first.
rules.detail: A real behaviour change also edits its tests, so the flag is for the reader. A changed oracle, golden or fixture on the protected list needs a non-author.
rules.why: Weakening a test is the cheapest way for an agent to get green; a diff scan makes it visible. The scan with the same list serves Go and TypeScript.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. diff scan of test file removals listing removed assertions, added skips and loosened comparison literals first in the change summary; a flagged change needs a reason line. (Biome form is noFocusedTests and noSkippedTests, with a GritQL plugin for expect-expect). Plant: a diff that removes an expect fires; a focused test fires. Control: an added test passes

rules.rule: Tests do not mock our own modules, and no mock library is a dependency.
rules.detail: Mock libraries (gomock, testify mock, mockery and the like) are banned in go.mod and imports. In TypeScript a module mock or global stub of a module in the repo is banned in test files by a restricted-import or restricted-syntax rule. A fake stands only as in tests.doubles.4, small and written by hand.
rules.why: Mocking our own code makes the test a copy of the implementation. Own measure: no mock library in any repo today.

rules.rule: A repo keeps a file in a protected path marking each dependency managed or unmanaged; a double of a managed one fails a scan, and a double of an unmanaged one uses literal recorded bytes and asserts no calls on queries.
rules.detail: Managed means a database or queue our own services own; unmanaged means a third-party API. A double stands only at an unmanaged edge, is small and hand-written, and carries literal recorded bytes. A call assertion on a query (as opposed to a command) is wrong; whether it is wrong is a review question. The file is a protected path, since marking a dependency unmanaged is the known way round. Recorded bytes are the second choice: where the unmanaged program offers a fake account or a local server, the test runs the real program against it (tests.doubles.5).
rules.why: Khorikov's line: mock only the edge you do not control, and do not assert on calls that are queries. The file turns a ban of named paths into a check per dependency.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. data file per repo plus a scan for a double of a dependency marked managed. Plant: a hand double of a dependency marked managed fails the scan. Control: a real-engine test passes

Plant: a module mock of a managed dependency fails. Control: a mock of an unmanaged one with literal recorded bytes passes

rules.rule: A fake of a store exists only to inject a failure the real engine cannot cheaply produce, a contract test against the real adapter pins that failure, a fake serves its seeded rows and throws on any call it was not seeded for, and no fake returns a constant.
rules.detail: A fake answers from the rows a test seeded into it; a call whose arguments match no seeded row throws with the call it got, so a test that forgot to seed fails loudly instead of passing on a default. A fake whose method returns the same value whatever it is asked is refused. One contract suite per fake runs the same cases against the fake and the real adapter, and the failure the fake injects is one of those cases.
rules.why: A fake that drifts from the engine hides the bug; a contract test per fake proves it against the real one. A fake that answers an unseeded call with a default makes a test pass for a reason the author never chose.

checks.note: one contract suite per fake runs the same cases against the fake and the real adapter, including an unseeded call that must throw on the fake. Plant: a fake that returns a result the real adapter cannot fails the contract suite; a fake that returns a default for an unseeded call fails. Control: a fake pinned by its contract suite that throws on an unseeded call passes

rules.review_question: Which failure does this store fake inject, which contract test pins it, and does it throw on a call it was not seeded for?
open: A scan that a fake has a contract test is proposed only; the review question holds it until then.

rules.rule: Where a test needs an external program's behaviour it runs the real program against a fake account or server, and only where no fake account exists does it use recorded bytes; tests and stories use fakes generated from the contract, and hand-written network stubs are banned outside the generated folder.
rules.detail: The order of preference is fixed. First, the real external program, run against a fake account, a fake model or a local server it can be pointed at. Second, only where the program offers no such account or server, a double with literal recorded bytes at the unmanaged edge (tests.doubles.3), pinned by a contract test where the engine allows one (tests.doubles.4). A hand-written stand-in for the program's behaviour is never used. Generated mock handlers come from the spec, and a lint ban stops hand-written network stubs and per-feature fake harnesses outside the generated folder. In Go the equivalent of a generated fake is a small hand-written fake proved against the real one by a contract test (tests.doubles.4).
rules.why: A hand-written stub encodes what the author thought the server said, and recorded bytes freeze what it said once; the real program on a fake account says what it says today. Reference practice, one fake source for the whole repo.

checks.note: ESLint no-restricted-imports and no-restricted-syntax on network stub libraries outside the generated mock folder (Biome form: `noRestrictedImports` with the same list and a GritQL plugin for the stub calls). Plant: a hand-written network stub in a spec fails. Control: the generated handler passes

rules.review_question: Does this test stand in for an external program that offers a fake account or server, and if so why is the real program not run?
open: The Go side has no generated fakes; its equivalent is tests.doubles.4.
Whether a fake account exists is review until the repo lists its external programs with their test accounts.

rules.rule: Fixtures are the server's own output or held to its type in both directions, every enum member and nullable field has a sample, each supported platform has its own generated example set held exactly, and a test fails when an answer changes.
rules.detail: Fixtures come from the server side: its tests write golden JSON from the real encoder (an update flag run only in the owning repo, `-update`), and a check (`companion fixtures --check`) regenerates in memory and diffs (forward direction). In reverse, every golden path must be exercised by the demo world; the check lists golden paths absent from it and fails on a rise (shrink-only). A schema walk over the generated schema confirms a sample for every enum member and nullable field. A program that supports more than one platform keeps one example set per platform, written by one command from that platform's adapter or fake and held exactly; the answer for a feature a platform lacks is one shared body, not a copy per platform.
rules.why: Fixtures generated from samples run the wrong direction: goldens are the handler's bytes and the schema is a second check. Generators' defaults broke "null, never 0". Own bugs: 11, 6 and 6 faults across three repos. A single example set hides what one platform answers differently.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. fixtures check that regenerates the golden JSON in memory and diffs it; reverse check that every golden path is exercised by the demo world, shrink-only; schema walk for a sample of every enum member and nullable field; per platform, the examples command regenerates that platform's set and diffs it. Plant: a hand-edited fixture that differs from the golden fails, a new golden path absent from the demo world raises the count and fails, and a hand edit to one platform's example set fails. Control: a fixture equal to the golden passes

open: 167 of 588 golden paths are absent from one repo's demo world today, so the shrink-only check needs a baseline.
The reverse direction is planned; the forward direction is held in two repos.

rules.rule: Fixtures, stories, docs, tests and shipped examples use made-up names only, for people, machines, managed software, networks and addresses, checked against an explicit stand-in list.
rules.detail: Every name of a person, machine, container, image, network, domain or account in those paths is on a committed stand-in list, and any other name in a name-shaped position fails. Addresses use the documentation ranges (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32, the example domains), never a real MAC or host. A second check compares every tracked file, commit message and branch name with a roster of real names kept outside the repository or as hashes, never in clear text; the check fails when the roster cannot be read, rather than passing on an empty list. In a public repository every author and committer email is a no-reply address, refused at pre-push.
rules.why: Real names recurred in fixtures twice (own bugs), and a real host, address or person in a public file cannot be taken back. A stand-in list catches the name nobody thought to put on a roster; the roster catches the known ones in places the stand-in list does not cover.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a stand-in scan of fixtures, stories, docs, tests and shipped examples that fails a name or address not on the committed stand-in list or outside the documentation ranges. Plant: a fixture naming a host not on the stand-in list fails; an example config with a non-documentation address or a real MAC fails. Control: a fixture using only listed stand-ins and documentation addresses passes

v1 class our-cli. companion scan of every tracked file, commit message and branch name against a roster of real names kept outside the repo or hashed, failing when the roster cannot be read; the alternative for the file half is the flagWords setting of the spell checker (cspell 10.4.0). Plant: a fixture containing a name on the roster fails; a commit message with one fails; a run with the roster missing fails. Control: made-up names pass

the pre-push hook refuses a commit whose author or committer email is not a no-reply address, in a repository marked public. Plant: a commit with a personal email in a public repository is refused at pre-push. Control: a no-reply email passes

rules.rule: A failing test is never rerun to green, and a red suite is never accepted as the new normal.
rules.detail: No count above one and no retry step or loop in a gate script or workflow, and zero retries read back from the runner configs. The scan excepts the admission step by name (tests.admission.1, decision 32). A count of one is required by tests.selection.6 and is allowed. A green test list with a non-zero exit is classified as an infrastructure fault before any rerun (tests.flakes.5). A red suite is never re-normalised: the suite is green or the cause is ticketed.
rules.why: Own bugs: one repo's rule. The donor reruns three times to prove a flake; this catalogue bans reruns and quarantines on first sight.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. gate scan that parses Makefiles, shell gate scripts and workflow YAML and fails on a count above one outside the admission step, on a rerun-fails option and on retry steps or loops around the test command The scan fails on go test -count=3 (any -count=N with N above 1) and on gotestsum --rerun-fails; -count=1 is required by tests.selection.6 and allowed; the scan is gatescan. Plant: a Makefile line with a count of three and a workflow retry step each fail. Control: a count of one passes
runner and browser-test configs read back with retries at zero, and a restricted-syntax rule on numeric retry options. Plant: a config with retries above zero fails. Control: retries zero passes

rules.rule: A result that is not reproduced is quarantined on first sight, ticketed and counted; the quarantined test has an expiry date, by which it is fixed or deleted, and the count and oldest age are reported per repo.
rules.detail: A quarantine with no clock is a way to delete a test without saying so. Quarantine is a shrink-only list that does not lock landing but blocks the next proof-debt credit until ticketed; the cap and the expiry follow the exemption rules of the gates part. A quarantine that is a separate suite is not covered by the skip rule. Applies to repos with a flaky-test list.
rules.why: Fowler names the graveyard: tests left in quarantine are not helping regression coverage, and his remedy is a limit on how many or how long. Neither the cap nor the expiry has a number: both are guesses until a real quarantine set exists.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. quarantine list as exception records with cap and expiry through the shared exception parser; a count and oldest-age line per repo. Plant: an entry past its date is reported. Control: an entry within its date passes

open: The row should split: the ban on reruns is a rule, the quarantine cap and expiry are guesses with no stopping check; the count and age line is report-only at first.
Reference conflict: the donor quarantines after three passing reruns at the same revision; this catalogue quarantines on first sight and bans reruns.
rules.note: Merges our rule, the handbook's quarantine rule and the donor's flake-quarantine rule; they differ only in when a test is quarantined.

rules.rule: Record, per test, how often it failed on a tree that later passed unchanged, and report the rate with the machine load at the time.
rules.why: In one study 78 percent of flaky tests were flaky when first written, so the first sighting is early. Load from parallel agents is a flake source people rarely count: our own swings of 22 and 40 percent in one measurement were load noise. An agent facing a red will rerun it, so the gate must write the record.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. per-test history from gate records keyed by tree and load, written by the gate. Plant: a fixture history with one flaky test must count it. Control: a stable history counts zero

rules.rule: A test asserts counted work, never elapsed wall time; where timing is the point, it judges only on an undisturbed machine or as a ratio, and fixed waits carry a reason.
rules.detail: A time budget is measured by a script at low load. A loaded box gives no verdict, which is a bounded third result (an all-inconclusive run still locks). A scan for the wall-clock reading used as an argument of an assertion, with the remaining uses in test files on a shrink-only count; a wait deadline is legitimate and carries a marker or allow-list entry. A fixed-waits list and a flake counter exist beside it. Wall-time budgets are measured by a script at low load, never asserted in a test.
rules.why: Own bugs: 7 of 60 sampled bugs; one project fixed three cases, and 9 load flakes in 12 days read as waits, not pixels.

checks.note: v1 class our-plugin. typed check in the test-hygiene plugin that a wall-clock reading is an argument of an assertion call in a test; remaining uses on a shrink-only count ast-grep could match the pattern but has no types, so the Go check is the typed analyzer of the testhygiene family. Plant: a test that fails when elapsed time passes two seconds fails the check Planted Go form: if time.Since(t0) > 2*time.Second { t.Fatal() } in a test fails. Control: a deadline passed to a wait helper passes

Plant: a wait-for-timeout call and a network-idle wait each fire. Control: a spec without them passes

The load probe and the bounded no-verdict result are runner work, not built; its bound is still an open ticket in the donor and an all-inconclusive run still locks.

rules.rule: No rerun closes a red: the hub may rerun a red proof once on a quiet slot as a diagnostic and logs both results, the first red opens the ticket whatever the rerun says, and a second red quarantines the test with an owner and an expiry.
rules.detail: tests.flakes.1 holds that a failing test is never rerun to green, and tests.flakes.2 holds the quarantine with its expiry. This rule holds the one rerun that is allowed and what it is for. The rerun is a measurement: run alone on a quiet slot, it tells whether load exposed the fault. Its green does not close anything. The ticket names the test, the load at the red and the two results. A second red of the same test, in any run, moves it to the quarantine list (gates.exemptions.4), with an owner and the date by which it is fixed or deleted. A quarantined race skips its test at push and nothing else: the member still runs, so no member leaves push over one test, and the skip line names the test, the ticket and the expiry. At release a race-kind row's test is not skipped, so the release proves the fix. The first implementation is the shared module's tier quarantine list.
rules.why: Reruns hide what load exposes: one project's journeys flaked at load 76 to 202 and only under load; 13 red journeys of another were 75 of 75 green alone, and each had a cause and a fix.
rules.review_question: Was this red rerun, where are both results logged, did the first red open a ticket, and is this the second red?
open: Planned check: the landing record holds at most one rerun per red with both results and a ticket id. Plant: a red followed by a green with no ticket fails. Control: a red with its ticket passes. No tool key is bound yet.

The presence check looks for a func Fuzz function and a testdata/fuzz folder in each listed parser package; whether a stateable invariant exists for pure logic is the review half (tests.generated.2).

rules.rule: Pure logic with a stateable invariant (a formatter, a parser, a pure domain function) has a property test that generates its inputs.

rules.rule: Each deployed API (a daemon's routes, a service's endpoints) is fuzzed against its own contract, and its responses are checked against the contract.
rules.detail: Requests are generated from the API spec and responses checked against it; the running service answers what its spec says. In our programs help and JSON are golden and the command tree is diffed with the last tag, but a daemon's answers are not yet checked against a description.
rules.why: A page or client consumes the contract; only the server can prove it holds. The web side does not own this check.

rules.rule: Output a person reads is held by a golden file, and the gate compares without writing; a golden a machine reads fails on any change, and one a person reads is approved by a person.
rules.detail: git diff --exit-code on golden files after the compare run; the golden helper never writes in gate mode.
rules.why: Own measure: one repo's goldens-check target; the shared golden helper is used by nobody outside the shared UI test package today.

rules.rule: Long fuzz runs happen on demand, for a new parser in the pull request that adds it, and never as a blocker of a push, a land or a release.
rules.detail: The seeds checked in under tests.generated.1 run as ordinary tests in every tier, in seconds. The long run, which mutates the seeds for minutes, runs when the owner asks for it, or when the hub asks the owner first, and a pull request that adds a parser asks for one run of it in its description. A long run that finds a crash adds the failing input to the seeds in the same change as the fix. Fuzz is not a release gate: a release does not wait for it and does not fail for the lack of it.
rules.why: A fuzz run of 14 minutes 38 seconds found two bugs in 260 commits, both while a parser was new; at the release it cost more than every other member together and found nothing.

sources.says: These entries are run by default with go test, whether fuzzing or not.

rules.review_question: Does this change add a parser, and if so, does its description ask for one long fuzz run?
open: The owner's word is the trigger, so there is no machine check of a request. Planned check: no tier of the member table runs a fuzz member. That is the members change of gragas#638's follow-up tickets.

rules.rule: A size or depth cap on a parser is proved by the smallest input that crosses it, never by a large input, and an allocation or alias proof shrinks to the smallest size that still proves the cap.
rules.detail: tests.generated.1 holds that a parser of untrusted input has a fuzz target with seeds. This rule holds how its caps are tested. A test that feeds a large input proves the cap at a cost of seconds and under the race detector of tens; the input one byte over the cap proves the same thing in milliseconds. A proof that an alias bomb or a deep nest is refused is shrunk the same way. The seeds run in every tier and the long fuzz run is on demand (tests.generated.6).
rules.why: One project's alias-bomb proof took 23 seconds under the race detector and about 1 second once shrunk to the smallest input that crosses the cap.

rules.rule: Every parser of input the program did not write has a fuzz target with its seeds checked in, or is on a named exemption list that gives its reason, and the seeds run in every tier.
rules.detail: The program parses input it did not write when it reads config, a rulebook, a tool's output or a file a person edits. Each such parser has a fuzz function and a checked-in seed folder (tests.generated.1). A parser that cannot have a target, such as one that only wraps a library's own fuzzed parser, is named on a list in the project, one line each with its reason, and the list only shrinks. The seeds run as ordinary tests in the push tier and every tier above it; the long fuzz run stays on demand (tests.generated.6); the caps of a parser are proved by tests.generated.7.
rules.why: Fuzz found 2 bugs in 260 commits of one project, both while a parser was new; a parser with no target and no named reason is one nobody decided to leave unfuzzed.

rules.rule: A test inherits nothing from the run that started it: its own home and temp folder, and no agent or git variables.
rules.detail: A repo test refuses to pass the parent environment to a child process unless the call is marked. Every test package calls one shared isolate function at start-up (a TestMain in Go). In a child's environment a nil value, the parent environment as a whole and an append to it are all findings; the environment comes from the isolate helper. The agent and git variables removed are every GIT_* variable and the agent-session variables; the analyzer is named testenv.
rules.why: A test that inherits the caller's home, git settings or agent variables passes on one machine and fails on another. Own bugs: 6 of 60 sampled bugs. One repo has the isolate helper; three others copy a client that passes the parent environment through.

rules.rule: Each module's suite runs with sibling modules unresolvable, a suite that still passes with its subject deleted fails, and a module's tests make other modules' data only through that module's public commands or its own fixtures.
rules.detail: A module is a unit of the declared import table (the architecture part's layers). Its suite is run with every module it may not import made unresolvable, so a test cannot reach a sibling the code could not; how that is done is the language part's resolver form (ts.modules.5 for TypeScript; the Go form is held in the Go part). A separate drive deletes the module's own source and runs its suite: a suite that still passes loads nothing of its subject and is vacuous. A test that needs another module's rows creates them through that module's public commands or fixtures that module ships, never by writing its tables directly.
rules.why: A test that imports across modules passes for a module nobody could extract, a suite that never loads its subject proves nothing, and a test that writes another module's rows encodes that module's schema in a place its owner cannot see.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. a subject-deleted drive that removes each module's source in a scratch tree, runs its suite and fails when it passes; a scan that fails a test writing to a table owned by another module in the schema's owner map. Plant: a suite whose tests import only a helper and never the subject passes with the subject deleted and fails the drive; a test inserting into another module's table fails the scan. Control: a suite that fails with its subject deleted, and a test that seeds through the other module's command, pass

rules.note: The resolver clause is language-shaped and lives in each language part; this rule holds the shared intent.

rules.rule: A test builds the repository, files and folders it needs in its own temp folder, and never reads an ignored file, another member's output, the checkout's own git folder, or another repository's checkout.
rules.detail: tests.isolation.1 holds that a test inherits nothing from the run that started it. This rule holds what a test may read from the tree around it: its own package's checked-in testdata and nothing a run writes. A test that needs a git repository makes one in its temp folder. A test that needs a built binary gets it from the package's shared setup (tests.runners.5). A test that needs another repository declares it and fetches it once in setup, or it is an opt-in member that skips with the exact command (tests.admission.5). A test that reads the checkout's own git folder fails in an exported tree and passes in a clone, which is two answers for one tree.
rules.why: Two tests of one project needed the checkout's own git folder, so every exported tree carried a failure that had to be explained away; four tests of another fleet needed sibling checkouts and failed rather than skipped, so a fresh clone was red.
rules.review_question: What does this test read outside its own temp folder and testdata, and would it pass in an exported tree with no git folder?

rules.rule: Default tiers never change shared machine state, a test launches its own browser and database and never attaches to the person's, and no script kills a process by name; an opt-in tier that must touch the service manager does so only under names hashed from its own root and proves its cleanup, and a privileged system test seals the host first and proves the seal.
rules.detail: Shared machine state is the service manager, the terminal multiplexer, the real home, the real git config, the person's browser and profile, and any process the test did not start. In the default tiers a scan against a machine-writer list (launchctl, systemctl, tmux, git config --global, the real home, a kill or pkill by name) fails, fakes of those programs sit on the test's PATH, and the isolate helper (tests.isolation.1) gives each test a temp home as a backstop. A test that needs a browser or a database starts its own on a temp profile or a temp data folder. An opt-in integration tier (declared as in tests.admission.5) may register units with the service manager only under names that carry a hash of its own root; its cleanup removes them and then lists what is left under that hash and fails if anything remains. A system test that needs a privileged container first seals the host's devices, kernel settings and cgroups from the container, and a check run before and after proves the seal held.
rules.why: A test that registers a service, edits the real git config, drives the person's browser or kills a process by name damages the host it runs on; one repo's integration tests need root and write under a system folder. An opt-in tier that must touch the host is held to names it owns and a cleanup it proves, so a failed run leaves nothing behind.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the machine-writer scan of the same family as tests.isolation.7, with its own list file, over default-tier tests. Plant: a test running git config --global against the real home fails; a script that runs pkill by name fails. Control: a fake on PATH passes

the opt-in tier's cleanup lists every unit carrying its root's hash after the run and fails on any; a seal check reads the container's device, kernel-setting and cgroup access before and after a privileged run.
