rules.rule: Each journey declares what it exercises, and a change selects the journeys whose declared inputs it touches; every command, route or page has a journey.
rules.detail: End-to-end journeys of a CLI or a daemon (the built binary run script-style, an install and start under the init system, a request and its answer) and browser journeys declare their inputs: commands, routes, packages, config files, build inputs, source paths. A change selects the journeys whose declared inputs it touches or whose inputs depend on what it touched. The journey map is a file; the command tree (CLI) and the route table (daemon) are the complete list, and a test fails when a leaf command or route has no journey, a journey has no declared inputs, a journey sits in no entry or a glob matches nothing. A flow that spans CLI, daemon and page has one cross-program journey, run when any touched program changes; its declared programs list is the selector's cross-repo input. A consumer contract comes first, so a journey covers only what the contract cannot see. Unplaced paths pick all (tests.selection.2); the plan is printed and carries a hash and a freshness date per map entry. Every cross-service flow has a journey, run when any program it touches changes.
rules.why: Operator direction: end-to-end tests must be scoped. One repo's browser reach map selected 7 of 41 journey files for a one-card change; none of the repos declares inputs per journey, and the land step runs the whole acceptance suite.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. journey map file plus a test that every leaf command and route has a journey and every journey declares inputs; selector tests with a planted failing journey behind a changed command. Plant: a command with no journey fails, a journey with no declared inputs fails, and a planted journey behind a changed command is selected. Control: a complete map passes

rules.rule: A journey that needs a virtual machine, a container runtime or a device is a journeys member at release or on demand, skipped with its reason where the host lacks the runtime and listed every run; a container leg for a second platform is a release member, and the long or costly set is on demand.

This rule places the journeys that need a machine the gate's host may not have: at release where the host has the runtime, on demand for the long set (gates.command.26), and never at push. A platform the project claims is proved by a run on it (gates.command.16); a container leg is one way to run one.

rules.rule: Each journey declares a stated risk naming what a cheaper test cannot see, an owner and its place in a capped list; the cap is an alarm and not a limit.

rules.rule: A program that writes users' files is killed at many points of a write and recovered in a crash-injection run at release, with a short run at push.
rules.detail: The release run kills the program at a stated number of points across each write path and checks that every recovery leaves the old file or the new one and never a half. The push run kills at a smaller number of points chosen to cover every path once, and takes seconds. A program that writes no user file has no crash-injection member. The number of points is data on the member, and a path added to the write code adds its points in the same change.
rules.why: A torn write is found only by the kill that lands in it, and a run long enough to find them all does not belong in a push; the release already runs everything a release alone proves.
rules.review_question: Does this program write a user's file, and does a run kill it at points across that write and check the recovery?
open: Planned check: the member table holds a crash-injection member in the release tier and a short one at push for a program whose write paths are listed in data. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A screen is held to one golden width read by a person, and at the narrower widths to properties: no line wider than the screen, nothing cut off, the same rows in the same order.
rules.detail: The golden at the standard width is the oracle a person approved. At each narrower width a check runs the same command and asserts the three properties on its output, so a width adds a few lines of data and no golden file. A property that fails prints the width, the row and the measure. The widths are data on the check, and a screen that is new adds its rows to the standard golden only. A column a table leaves out and marks is not cut off only when the width forces it out: the lowest of the table's drop order, in that order, never the first column, and no more than the width leaves no room for.
rules.why: Three goldens of the same screen at three widths triple the review of every change and say the same thing three times; the properties catch the same breakage and never need a hand read.
rules.review_question: Is this screen's narrow-width behaviour held by properties, and does only the standard width have a golden?
open: Planned check: a narrow-width member at push that runs the screens at the stated widths and asserts the three properties. The member is unbuilt; the rule stays a review question until it exists.

rules.rule: The long crash-injection run at release is 400 kill points and 100 recoveries spread over several child processes, each with its own root; a program that writes only its own records takes atomic-write tests instead and is exempt from the crash members.
rules.detail: tests.journeys.7 holds that a program which writes users' files is killed and recovered at release with a short run at push. This rule holds the long run's size and shape. The points are split across children so the run uses the pool (gates.command.27) and each child writes under its own root, so a kill in one cannot touch another's files. A program whose files are its own records (a cache, a journal) proves atomic writes (cli.commands.23) and lists no crash member.
rules.why: The crash run of one project is 400 and 100 by ruling; run in one child it is a serial member that sets the release time.
rules.review_question: How many children run this release's crash points, does each have its own root, and does this program write a user's files or only its own records?
open: Planned check: the crash member's report carries the child count and the points per child. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: Each tier's wall time is recorded per run with the load beside it where the system gives one, and re-measured at each release, never on a timer.
rules.detail: The runner writes a times file per run with tier, seconds and the load, and per-package elapsed time from the test JSON; a schema test fails a summary without time and load. A timeout prints the load. The load is the load average where the system keeps one (go-proc load.Read). Where it keeps none (Windows: load.ErrNoAverage) the program records the CPU time of the run's own process tree (proc.Usage with proc.JoinTree) and says that is the figure, never an invented average.
rules.why: Whole suite 4 to 66 s wall on five repos under load, and the top three packages are 63 to 89 percent of the time in every repo (one sample). Own measure: 7 of 60 sampled bugs were time or load budgets.

checks.note: v1 class shared-code. runner writes a times file per run with tier, seconds and the load (the load average where the system gives one, else the tree's CPU time); schema test fails a summary without time or load. Plant: a summary without load fails the schema. Control: a summary with time and load passes

rules.rule: A tier's floor is its best time on a quiet host, written with its date, machine and load; the budget is the floor times 1.5; a target such as about one minute is never a budget, and a project's budget is its own.
rules.detail: tests.measures.2 holds that a budget is a ceiling with a measured floor and is raised only with a new floor. This rule holds how the floor is taken and how far the budget sits above it. A floor measured on a loaded host is not a floor, and every number from a study of a busy host is a target until a quiet run is made. The margin is one number for every project, 1.5, so a report that prints the floor and the budget can be read without the file. A run over its budget on a busy host is unjudged, never green, and says so in its first lines (tests.measures.9).
rules.why: Every measured push of one project broke its 180 second budget and passed through the loaded-host clause printed at the bottom where nobody read it; another fleet had no budget at all, and a commit hook took 218 to 241 seconds unseen.
rules.review_question: Where is this tier's floor written, with what date, machine and load, and is the budget 1.5 times it?
open: Planned check: the budgets file holds a floor row with date, machine and load for each tier and the budget equals the floor times 1.5, held by a test over the file. No tool key is bound yet; the floors are measured by gragas#648.

rules.rule: A test that takes over a third of its timeout when the host is idle is a finding, before it ever fails.
rules.detail: A timeout is sized for a loaded host and a test that uses a third of it when idle uses all of it at load three. The finding names the test, its idle time and its timeout, and is fixed by making the test faster (tests.runners.5, tests.runners.8) or by splitting it, never by raising the timeout alone. The tier report lists the tests over the line.
rules.why: One test took 9.5 seconds idle against a 30 second limit and went red at load 27; another's module took 565 milliseconds idle against a 60 second budget and still timed out nine times, and the tickets stayed open 21 to 23 days.
rules.review_question: How long does this test take on an idle host, what is its timeout, and is the first over a third of the second?
open: Planned check: the runner reads per-test times from the test tool's output and lists each over a third of its timeout. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: A timing assertion on a shared host is off the blocking path: it is judged against a reference taken in the same run and only on undisturbed samples, and a reading that cannot be judged gives no verdict for a bounded time, three tips of the main branch or 24 hours, and then locks.
rules.detail: tests.flakes.4 holds that a test asserts counted work and judges timing only on an undisturbed machine or as a ratio. This rule holds what happens when the machine is never undisturbed. The reading is inconclusive, not red, and the run is green for everything else. Inconclusive readings are counted, and after three tips of the main branch or 24 hours without a judged sample the member locks landing until someone measures on a quiet host. A rule that turns one inconclusive reading into a lock holds landing for a host it cannot control.
rules.why: One fleet's timing specs put 11 of 44 land logs red in one day and locked landings twice, and a rule that turned an all-inconclusive budget into a lock held landing for 8 hours 2 minutes.
rules.review_question: Is this timing judged against a reference from the same run, what happens to an inconclusive reading, and after how many does it lock?
open: Planned check: the budget member records each inconclusive reading with the load and counts them against the bound. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: Each tier has a whole-suite budget, a selected-run budget where selection is on, and each package a budget, written in one file; a budget is a ceiling with a measured floor, raised only with a new floor measurement in the same change, and a budget that is passed or a package whose time rises tree after tree fails or is flagged.
rules.detail: Each budget line holds the ceiling and the floor it was set from (the measured time, the date, the machine and its load). Lowering a ceiling needs nothing. Raising one is refused unless the same change replaces the floor with a new measurement on the stated machine, and the new ceiling stays within the stated margin of the new floor. A count that grows on purpose (tests, packages) is a register, not a ratchet. A slow file is split or declared. Test count is reported beside seconds. The web starting values are 15 s selected and 60 s whole for the first tier, 60 s and 3 minutes, 5 and 10 minutes, and 15 minutes. A ratchet on the count of packages over 5 s is the Go growth check. The fail-closed path (an unplaced path selects everything) may run over the tier's budget; it runs and records the time and is never refused or trimmed.
rules.why: A suite written by agents cannot grow unnoticed to hours. One repo's browser journeys alone are 35 minutes serial for one family (not re-timed).

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. budget file with a ceiling and a measured floor per tier (whole, and selected where selection is on) and per package; raising a ceiling is refused unless the same change carries a new floor measurement; a ratchet on packages over 5 s. Plant: raising a budget with the old floor is refused, and a test package slowed past the ratchet fails. Control: an unchanged budget passes, and a raised ceiling with a new floor measured in the same change passes

rules.rule: Report the code-to-test change share by test level, and the deletion candidates: tests with no failure in a stated window, identical coverage or a covered path that also has a stronger test; deleting one is a commit with a stated reason.
rules.detail: The change share per path class per release is a trigger for what to run and what to fix. Deletion stays a visible act. The reports are built from failure history and per-test coverage.

rules.rule: Coverage is measured per changed file and reported at the slowest tier, and is never a threshold in the inner loop.
rules.detail: The record keeps the coverage figure with no floor; packages without tests count as zero percent. No land tier adds a coverage threshold, and a gate scan bans a fail-under line in the Makefile or workflows. Packages without tests count as 0% in the record.
rules.why: Practice; one repo reports without a threshold. Low value, kept so the cheap scan closes the row.

Plant: a Makefile line with a coverage threshold fails. Control: -cover only passes

rules.rule: A time limit stated as a percentage or as a small number of seconds is judged on the median of at least three runs per side, with the base and the head run on the same machine in one window.
rules.detail: A small-seconds limit means a limit of a few seconds; a percentage or such a limit needs the median of three runs per side.
rules.why: On our host on 4 Nov the same tree read 55 s and 67 s plain, and 93 s and 130 s with the race detector across runs: 22 percent and 40 percent between runs of one tree, so one run per side could not tell a regression from noise.

rules.rule: A performance ceiling comes from the 99th percentile of at least twenty runs times a stated margin, with the machine's load written beside each timing.
rules.why: A ceiling set from one run is noise; the method is a number method, not a check.

rules.rule: Tests have a declared size class bounding what each may touch, and small tests are kept from the network, disk outside temp and the clock.
rules.detail: The class comes from a build tag or the test name. A tracer reports what each test touched. Go has no runner sandbox for this, so the class is reported and nothing enforces it by construction.

rules.rule: A tier that passes its budget only under the loaded-host clause is a finding, not a pass, and the clause prints at the top of the report where the reader looks.
rules.detail: The budget is the tier's measured floor on a quiet host times a stated margin (tests.measures.2; this repository states 1.5). A run on a busy host that is over the budget is not judged, and its report says so in its first lines and counts the run as unjudged, not as green. The tier is judged on the next quiet-host run, and a tier whose last quiet-host run was over the budget fails on budget. A run that is only green because the host was busy is never recorded as the floor.
rules.why: Every measured push run broke its 180 second budget (206 to 301 seconds) and passed only through the clause that excuses a busy host, so the budget never pushed the heaviest member out of the tier.
rules.review_question: Did this tier pass its budget on a quiet host, or only because the host was busy?

rules.rule: Unit tests run in the gate from one runner, uncached, over the whole tree, or where selection is on for the packages that changed.
rules.detail: The default is every unit test of every package with the result cache off (tests.selection.1); a repo runs only the changed packages only when it has turned selection on.
rules.why: A test that is not in the gate does not exist for the agent; unit tests are the fastest tier.

checks.note: the gate's rule table names the unit-test step for every program, run over the whole tree uncached, or fed by the selector (tests.selection.1) where selection is on. Plant: a program with no unit-test step in the gate list fails; a cached unit-test run with selection off fails. Control: a program with the step passes

rules.rule: The package whose tests read the whole tree reads it once through one shared snapshot and scans in parallel, and it may run without the race detector at push when an on-demand race member covers it.
rules.detail: Every project has one package of tests that read every file: names scans, repository rules, layout checks. It runs on every change whatever changed, so it sets a floor for every push and makes selection pointless for itself. Its tests share one read of the tree taken in the package's setup (tests.runners.5) and scan that snapshot in parallel (tests.runners.4). It checks text, not concurrency, so under the race detector it is 7 to 40 times slower for nothing; tests.runners.6 keeps the detector on at push for the light packages, and this package is the one exception, covered by the on-demand race run.
rules.why: It was the slowest package in every project of one fleet, 7 to 40 times slower under the race detector: 47 seconds to 334 seconds in one, and one test from 4.5 seconds to 72.8 seconds in another.
rules.review_question: Does this tree-reading package take one snapshot in setup and scan it in parallel, and which race member covers it if it runs without the detector at push?

rules.rule: The gate's own tests run in the test member, parallel and built once, and never as a serial step of their own on every push.
rules.detail: A gate has tests: of its runner, its scripts, its plants (gates.plants.12). They are tests like any other and belong in the test member, where they run beside the rest and share the package's setup. A self-test step that runs each gate once more, or a sweep that runs each gate twice, is the suite run again in series, and it sets the push time.
rules.why: Self-tests set the push time in three repositories of one fleet, 126 of 189 seconds in one service and 221 of 254 seconds in another; the gate's tests were one project's slowest package, 126 seconds, for the same reason.
rules.review_question: Where do this gate's own tests run, and does any member run them again as a step of its own?

Left to build: a tool key in a preset that checks the members file has no member whose command is the gate's own test suite outside the test member, so the row can be added without raising the baselines of checks-unresolved, checks-without-fix and advisory-with-checks.

rules.rule: A change to the test runner's pool, isolation or worker settings is proved on the whole suite in the shared pool, on every host the project claims, before it lands.
rules.detail: Isolation off, a shared pool, a worker count: each changes what every test sees, and a test that passes alone can fail only there. The change's proof is the whole suite under the new setting on each claimed platform (gates.command.16), run where the other gates run, not on a quiet machine. A selected run proves nothing for a setting that touches every test.
rules.why: One fleet set isolation off on a shared pool; four specs went red only there, one at 31 seconds against 6 seconds alone, and two changes were held off the main branch for 4 hours 23 minutes.
rules.review_question: Does this change touch the runner's pool, isolation or workers, and was the whole suite run under it on every claimed host?
open: Planned check: a change to the runner config file is a protected path whose verdict names the whole-suite run on each platform. No tool key is bound yet.

rules.rule: Test and browser workers per run equal cores divided by concurrent slots, with the slot count read from the job tool and never hard-coded, applied only inside a slot.
rules.why: On the current host 15 cores and two heavy slots give 7 workers per run; a hard-coded number oversubscribes one run and starves another.

rules.rule: The test runner configuration is one shared preset, and race, leak and shuffle flags are set once in the shared fragment.
rules.why: One preset is the only place a flag is set once; the reference practice has one preset for every program.

rules.rule: A test runs in parallel with the others of its package by default, and a test that runs alone says why in its own code.
rules.detail: A test that needs its own process state (an environment variable, the working folder, a global) is the exception, and it carries a comment naming the state it needs. A test that only needs a variable for a child process sets it on that child's environment and stays parallel. The cases of a long table test are parallel subtests when each has its own temp folder. A package whose tests all run one at a time is a finding in the tier report, with the share of its wall time. This rule holds the tests; gates.command.17 to .20 hold the members around them. The shuffle seed (tests.isolation.10) still prints, and a test that fails only in parallel is a bug ticket, never a retry (tests.flakes.1).
rules.why: One push kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy because two packages ran 152 and 101 tests one after another; making them parallel removes the longest member of the tier without dropping a test.

sources.says: Parallel signals that this test is to be run in parallel with (and only with) other parallel tests.

rules.review_question: Does this test run in parallel, and if it runs alone, does its code say which process state it needs?

Control: a parallel test, and a serial one with its reason, are not. Held by TestThePresetShowsASerialTestRedAndOneWithItsReasonGreen in internal/preset_parallel_test.go.
The shared preset enables tparallel, which reports a parallel parent over a subtest that is not. Plant: a half-parallel test is reported. Control: a fully parallel one is not. Same test.

rules.rule: Expensive setup (a build, a clone, a started program) runs once per package, in TestMain or a once, and never once per test or per case.
rules.detail: A case that needs a different input to the same built program reuses the build and changes the input. A case that must have its own build says so in its code. The setup writes nothing into the tree under test. This is about how many times the work is done; tests.isolation.3 holds how the shared fixture is reached (through a helper with its own temp folder and no fixed port), and both hold together.
rules.why: One test built the landing judge and ran the landing script four times, 38 to 47 seconds of every push, to prove four things that one build could show.

rules.rule: The race detector runs at push over the light packages, and the heavy race run is on demand; the race detector is not turned off at push.
rules.detail: The light packages run with the race detector on in the push tier, because a race there costs a few seconds of wall time and is found at the earliest moment. The heavy race run (the packages whose race build takes minutes) leaves every tier and runs when the owner asks for it, or when the hub asks the owner first. A change that adds shared state across goroutines to a heavy package asks for that run in its pull request. Turning the race detector off at push is not taken: it saves about 17 seconds of wall time today and about none once members run together.
rules.why: The heavy race tests took 6 minutes 38 seconds of a release and found no race; the light race run costs 17 seconds of wall time and keeps every race visible at push.

sources.says: The cost of race detection varies by program, but for a typical program, memory usage may increase by 5-10x and execution time by 2-20x.

rules.review_question: Is the race detector on for this package at push, and if the package is heavy, has its race run been asked for in this change?
open: Planned check: the gate's member table names the race flag for the light members and no heavy race member in any tier. The members change in gate/members.yaml, a protected path with its own verdict, and is the work of gragas#638's follow-up tickets.

rules.rule: A project that turns the race detector off at push names who runs it on the main branch each day, and an issue opens on a red.
rules.detail: The name is a person, a scheduled job or an agent, written in the project's test guide, and the run is daily on the default branch. A red opens an issue with the failing package and no one waits for the next day to read it. This project keeps the detector on at push (tests.runners.6), so the rule binds a project that takes the other road; a daily run that the guide asks for and nobody runs is the failure it prevents.
rules.why: In one project the daily race run its docs asked for was not happening, and its main branch failed the race detector on a data race in test code.

rules.rule: A test that waits out real time (a timeout, a retry delay, a poll) runs on a fake clock, and a real sleep in a test is a finding with its reason beside it.
rules.detail: The code under test takes its clock as an input, or the test runs it inside a bubble whose time package is fake, so a wait of seconds takes no wall time. A test that must observe real time, such as one of the clock adapter itself, says so in its code. The wait is not shortened by setting a smaller timeout in the test, as that tests another number.
rules.why: A test that waits out real time takes that time on every run however many cores it has; a fake clock takes none, and a ruling applies it with the other time recommendations.

sources.says: Within a bubble, the time package uses a fake clock.

rules.review_question: Does this test sleep or wait on a timer, and could its clock be fake?

rules.rule: A module's whole suite is one invocation of the test tool per tier, so the runner spreads its packages over the CPUs, and a per-package timeout lives in that invocation's flags, named in the members file.
rules.detail: Two batches of one module run the second after the first and the CPUs idle between them. One invocation over the whole module lets the test tool schedule every package at once. A second invocation for a cover profile is the same suite run twice; one run gives the verdict and the profile. A second module in the same repository (a web folder, a tools module) is its own member with its own folder. The timeout that applies to each package is a flag of the invocation and the members file names it, so the number is in one place.
rules.why: One project ran its tests as two batches, 135 seconds, where one batch takes 51 seconds; another ran its Go tests then its web tests in series; a third ran the test tool twice, the second time for a cover profile sent nowhere.
rules.review_question: How many times does this tier invoke the test tool for this module, and where is the per-package timeout written?

rules.rule: A repo whose full suite fits its push budget runs it whole and uncached at every push, and a full run always satisfies the gate; where a repo turns selection on, a program picks the tests from what changed, prints what it skipped, and runs global checks whole.
rules.detail: Whole and uncached means every test of every package, with any result cache off (in Go `-count=1`), because a cached pass is a claim about a run that did not happen. A repo turns selection on by a declared setting in its gate config, with the measured whole-suite time that passed the push budget; without that setting the selection rules (tests.selection.2 to 15) do not bind and a selected run does not satisfy the gate. Where selection is on: it is by package in Go and by recorded reads in TypeScript; global checks (types, lint configuration, structure, size, vulnerability scan, tidiness) are never affected-only unless the tool is sound under caching: the rule table carries a scope field and the runner refuses an affected-only run of a global check. The plan prints the global list and the gate fails if one is missing from the run. The plan data is a protected path. Tests of the selector plant a failing package behind a changed one, and an unknown path selects everything (tests.selection.2).
rules.why: Selection is a tool for a suite too slow to run whole, and its only failure mode is a missed dependency. A full uncached run has no such failure and is the claim every target makes, so it is the default, and the selection rules are kept for the day a suite outgrows its budget.

checks.note: v1 class our-cli. the gate's push step runs the whole suite uncached unless the gate config declares selection on with a measured whole-suite time; a cached or partial run without that setting fails the gate. Plant: a push step that runs only the changed packages with no selection setting fails; a cached test result at push fails. Control: a whole uncached run passes

v1 class our-cli. where selection is on, the selector library lifted from our CLI repo's package selector; the plan prints the global checks and the gate fails if one is absent. Plant: a plan that omits the vet step for a small change fails, and a failing package behind a changed one is selected. Control: the full plan passes

v1 class shared-code. where selection is on, a rule table with a scope field; the runner refuses the affected option on a global-scope check. Plant: the affected option on the type check is refused, and a cross-file type error is caught by the whole run. Control: a global check run whole passes

One pass runs the suite once per deletion, so it is a separate job outside the release time, run by dispatch at the release step and not on a schedule. The result prints the corpus size, because a smaller corpus is the known way round. It has run on script tests only, never on a browser grid.
rules.why: Selection has one failure mode, a missed dependency, and the oracle is the only check on it. Decision 18's "each skip proved" is unproved until the oracle runs; it learns dependencies from deletions only.

rules.rule: Applies only where selection is on: a full no-cache run backstops selection at least every third release, the tag records whether it ran selected or in full, and a red locks further releases.
rules.detail: A repo with no selection runs whole at every push and records nothing here. At most two releases pass since the last full run (decision 27). On a red the bad range is bisected, a lock file stops further releases until the miss is fixed or reverted, and each miss becomes a permanent fixture. rules.rule: One schema library holds the model, JSON Schema, types, DDL and API contracts are generated from it and held by regenerate-and-diff, no second schema library is a dependency, and what the model exports parses back to the same value.
rules.detail: The model is the one source. Every other shape (the JSON Schema files, the TypeScript types, the SQL DDL, the HTTP and tool contracts) is generated from it, committed, and regenerated and diffed by the gate; a hand edit to a generated file fails. The live database schema is checked against the DDL the model generates, never used to generate the model or the types. A landed migration is never edited; new SQL is appended and held to the generated DDL. The manifest names one schema library; a second one, or a query builder that owns its own schema, fails the manifest check. A round-trip test exports each model shape and parses it back to an equal value. The checks are engine-free.
rules.why: One model that generates every other shape is the strongest guard against a type, a table and a contract drifting apart over years, and regenerate-and-diff makes it mechanical. Naming the model as the source, and checking the live schema against it, leaves no second place where the truth can start.

Plant: a hand edit to a generated type file fails; a column added in the database and not in the model fails. Control: a model change with its regenerated files in the same change passes

rules.rule: A function exported from a module declares its return type.

rules.why: A declared return type is the contract the next reader builds on, and it stops an inferred type drifting under a refactor in a file the caller never sees.

rules.rule: Time enters through one clock port, instants are one branded type, and Date is constructed only in the clock adapter and the file reader.
rules.detail: Code that needs the time takes the clock port as a parameter; `new Date()`, `Date.now()` and `performance.now()` appear only in the clock adapter, and `new Date(value)` only there and in the adapter that reads file times. Every other module carries the branded instant type, never a `Date` or a bare number. Tests use the fake clock. The two allowed paths are listed in one place. Biome form: a GritQL plugin for a `Date` construction or `Date.now()` call, with an `overrides` entry for the two listed paths. ESLint form: `no-restricted-syntax` on the same calls with the same path list.
rules.why: A clock port is what makes every time-dependent test deterministic; a direct read of the clock is a test that passes today and fails in another timezone or at midnight.

The lint is `eslint-plugin-i18next` `no-literal-string` in jsx-text-only mode plus attribute lists on components and templates; strings in frontmatter and script that reach the page are caught by `no-restricted-syntax` on assignments to `textContent`, `innerText`, `title` and `placeholder` with a string literal; a syntax-tree scanner is the second net. Server-owned display text that is not an error renders through a marker part that is marked and counted. Where a builder has no notices, errors go to the lifecycle banner as messages. Template element `<h1>` and `<script>` in `.astro` and `.tsx`; lint mode `mode: "jsx-text-only"`; plants `el.textContent = "Something went wrong"`; control `t("dash.title")` as a JSX expression.
rules.why: One site holds 981 literals, another 1,844, about 8,400 sites in all; the scanner's verdicts agreed on 80 of 80 judged cases on the web. There is no zero target for old files.

checks.note: `eslint-plugin-i18next` `no-literal-string` (jsx-text-only plus attribute lists) and `no-restricted-syntax` on literal assignment to textContent, innerText, title and placeholder, with bulk suppressions for old files. Plant: a sentence in an h1 and `el.textContent = "Something went wrong"` each fail. Control: `{t("dash.title")}` passes

rules.rule: Numbers, sizes, durations, relative times, dates, times, money and lists come from one formatter with one locale rule, golden-tested against a table that the Go side also runs; the Intl constructors appear only inside it.
rules.detail: View files may not use `toFixed`, `toLocale*String`, `Intl.NumberFormat`, `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.PluralRules`, `Math.pow`, `** 10`, `>> 10`, `/ 1024` or `/ 1e9`; only the formatter module may (ESLint `no-restricted-properties` and `no-restricted-syntax`). No currency-symbol concatenation. The shared golden table runs in the TypeScript and the Go formatter tests (190 of 190 in trial). Named formats live in a data file. Pure logic with a stateable invariant (a formatter, a parser) has a property test; no property-test library is picked, so one enters through the supply-chain rule. Golden data file: `formats.json`; property tests use `fast-check`. Plant: `bytes.toFixed(1) + " GB"`.

rules.rule: Every story renders in a real browser with the accessibility engine at error; for a design system that is a push member, and for an application it runs at land.

A design system's stories are its product, so they render at push, where 474 stories with the engine took 44 seconds. An application's stories are many and the render runs at land, with the plays (web.cycle.3). A story the engine skips carries an owner and an expiry (gates.exemptions.4).
rules.why: One fleet's design system shipped two versions with its stories unrun, and its consumer opened seven contrast tickets in eight days.

rules.rule: At push a small browser smoke set runs: the journeys that prove the page loads and the main path works, beside the other members at no wall cost; the member declares the network and its platform, and a skip is red at land.
rules.detail: The smoke set is a handful of journeys, chosen for what a cheaper test cannot see (tests.journeys.4), and it runs in the pool beside the build and the tests, so it adds nothing to the wall time when it is shorter than the longest member. The member carries net and os fields (gates.command.30); on a builder's machine with no browser it prints SKIPPED, and at land that skip is red. The full suite is a release member (web.cycle.6).
rules.why: Ten journeys of one project, 17.4 seconds, run beside its site check at no wall cost; browser gates in a no-network sandbox of another fleet failed 49 of 49 blocks with a network error nobody read as a skip.

rules.rule: At release the full browser suite runs sharded across the pool's workers, with the shards balanced by each journey's recorded duration and never by file count, and both browser engines run until the grid is green and balanced.
rules.detail: A shard by file puts the slow journeys in one shard and the suite waits for it. The runner records each journey's duration and the next run balances by it. The worker count is the pool's (gates.command.27); more shards on a loaded host only add contention. Both engines run at release until the grid has been green and the shards balanced; then the owner decides on the green numbers which engines stay. A release does not carry a known red journey; a tolerated red is a listed entry with an owner and an expiry (gates.exemptions.4, tests.flakes.6).
rules.why: One project's slowest shard fell from 1,573 seconds to about 1,261 when balanced by duration, and its grid was red three of three releases.

rules.rule: A browser journey waits on a condition through the runner's auto-wait and never on a sleep; a fixed budget scales by a printed load factor; and the page's own timers run on the runner's fake clock.
rules.detail: tests.runners.8 and tests.isolation.6 hold that no test waits out real time. In a browser the runner waits for the element to be ready before it acts, so a journey that sleeps is waiting twice. A budget that must be fixed (a page load) is multiplied by a factor from the host's load and the factor prints, so a red under load is read as one. The page's own timers (a poll, a toast, a debounce) run on the runner's clock, so a wait of seconds takes none.
rules.why: Fixed 10 and 15 second browser budgets of one fleet ran out at load 65, and a 5 second idle wait of one project was paid twice per journey.

sources.says: It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action.
Utilizing Clock functionality allows developers to manipulate and control time within tests

rules.rule: A journey's teardown removes every route handler it added, so a poll in flight cannot fail the next journey, and an action re-resolves its locator after the component's ready mark.
rules.detail: A route handler left on the page answers a poll that fires after the journey ended, and the failure lands on whichever journey runs next. The teardown fixture unroutes all handlers and waits for the ones in flight. A locator held across a re-render points at an element that is gone; the runner re-resolves a locator each time it acts, so the action waits for the component's ready mark and then locates.
rules.why: A poll left routed after one journey failed the next in one fleet, and a held element handle failed on the re-render.

sources.says: Removes all routes created with page.route() and page.routeFromHAR().

rules.rule: A project styles through tokens from the token document as CSS custom properties, with one declared scoping mechanism: CSS Modules, or one utility-class framework whose theme is generated from the token document and holds no colour, size or font of its own. A second mechanism or utility framework is banned, and a colour, size or font not from the tokens fails under either mechanism.
rules.detail: The mechanism is the project's declared parameter (web.tokens.13); tokens are the invariant. Under CSS Modules a stylesheet lint allows only token variables for colour, size and font, and a utility-class framework in the dependencies fails. Under a utility framework the rest of this detail applies. A mechanism added later states its own lint for the same invariant; the rule does not change. Class-variant and class-merge helpers (`cva`, `clsx`, `tailwind-merge`) are allowed. A colour, size or font that is not from the theme in a class string fails (`bg-[#fff]`, `p-[13px]`, `[color:red]`); the default palette is cleared. Layout-only arbitrary values pass from a lint-checked allow-list data file. Inline style is banned. The theme file is generated and compared (generate-then-check), and a stylesheet on it allows only token variables. A new brand token is added to the brand layer with a canary value. Class-string lint covers framework templates and embedded script strings. Migrating a site's old CSS is per-repository adoption work, not a foundation rule. Lint plugin: `eslint-plugin-better-tailwindcss` with `no-restricted-classes` (arbitrary-value regex `\[.+\]`), `no-unknown-classes` and `no-conflicting-classes`; the default palette is cleared with `--color-*: initial`. Inline style: html-validate `no-inline-style` (template stack); the component-stack ban is react.components.4. Works on `.tsx` and `.astro` class strings. A calc width such as `w-[calc(100%-var(--sidebar))]` passes only from the allow-list. Layout-only arbitrary values such as `grid-cols-[...]` also pass only from the allow-list. The theme file is checked with `companion gen --check` and the `@theme` block allows only `var(--token)` values; the dependency check is `companion deps` over `package.json`, with `cva`, `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` off the ban list.
rules.why: No project used it at first; proposed to carry the earlier lint requirement and widened by decision 29 to cover both frameworks. The targets style two ways over the same tokens, so the mechanism is a parameter and the tokens are what the rule holds.

rules.rule: Browser targets are declared once and read by the bundler, the style lint and the script lint; a feature outside them fails.
rules.detail: One targets file (a browser list or a Baseline year) is read by the bundler, the Stylelint baseline plugin, the ESLint CSS baseline rule and a script compatibility rule. The targets file is a `browserslist` file or a Baseline year, and the passing twin is a widely-available feature.

rules.rule: No colour literal appears outside the generated token file, in CSS, markup or script, in any colour notation.
rules.detail: Covers hex, named colours, `rgb`, `rgba`, `hsl`, `hsla`, `hwb`, `lab`, `lch`, `oklab`, `oklch`, `color` and `color-mix`, in stylesheets, embedded style blocks and script strings, class names included (no raw palette classes). Inline `style` is banned. Hex and token values live only in the token files and the per-brand token files. Current hits are fixed in the same change; there is no baseline. Stylelint 17 runs over `.css`, `<style>` blocks of `.astro` (through `postcss-html`) and CSS in `.tsx`, with `ignoreFiles` set to the generated token file only. The colour functions are `rgb rgba hsl hsla hwb lab lch oklab oklch color color-mix`. Script strings are caught by `no-restricted-syntax` on string literals that are a `#` and 3 to 8 of `[0-9a-f]`, nothing else; inline style by html-validate `no-inline-style` on templates, and on components by the React style-prop ban, react.components.4.
rules.why: A regex that matched only hex and five functions reported zero literals and missed named colours and four more functions, so zero was zero of the shapes it looked for. Both sites were at zero; one palette file holds 42 distinct hex values inside token definitions, which the rule allows.

checks.note: Stylelint 17 core rules over CSS, embedded style blocks and CSS in components: `color-no-hex`, `color-named: never`, `function-disallowed-list` for the colour functions, ignoring only the generated token file; ESLint `no-restricted-syntax` on string literals that match a hex or a colour function, plus `no-restricted-properties` on the style prop and the HTML validator's no-inline-style rule. Plant: a hex, a named colour, `oklch()`, `color-mix()` and `rgb()` each in a stylesheet, an embedded style block and a script string must fail. Control: the same value inside the generated token file passes

open: Not planted: SVG colour attributes (`fill="#fff"`), `hsl()`, `hwb()`, `lab()`, `color()`; they sit in the same disallowed-list.
Stylelint 18 is blocked by two plugin peers; stay on 17.16.

rules.rule: Spacing, font size and radius come from a scale, and a literal that repeats a scale step is refused; arbitrary layout-only values pass only from an allow-list.
rules.detail: Hand CSS: the value of `padding*`, `margin*`, `gap`, `font-size` and `border-radius` must be a token variable; `px` is banned where a rem scale applies. Utility classes: the theme drops the default scale, and numeric steps not in the token scale are banned (the framework accepts any number as a step, so `p-13` is valid without a ban). Layout-only arbitrary values (a grid template, a calc width, a max width) pass only from a data file of allowed values. Legacy type sizes and arbitrary pixel sizes fail. Brand values arbitrary in a class string are zero. Utility side: the theme drops the default scale with `--spacing-*: initial` and `better-tailwindcss/no-restricted-classes` bans numeric steps outside the token scale. The allowed value form is `var(--space-*|--text-*|--radius-*)`.
rules.why: One site holds 1,172 spacing, 502 type-size and 241 radius literals as a baseline; none is traced to a fault on its own, so this is a rule held by the aim, not by a fault.

checks.note: Stylelint `declaration-property-value-allowed-list` (or stylelint-declaration-strict-value) on the properties above, `unit-disallowed-list` for px, and a utility-class lint rule with a negative-list regex banning numeric steps outside the token scale. Plant: `padding: 13px` and `p-13` fail; `padding: var(--space-3)` and `p-3` pass (when 3 is a token step). Control: a token-scale value passes

open: Depends on a scale that does not exist yet; the scale is derived from the data, and px versus rem is open.

Baseline for existing literals: Stylelint `--suppress` (experimental) or a px ratchet already held at 453 in one site. The reference allowed no baseline (current hits fixed in the same change); the two positions conflict and the baseline wins until the scale exists.
A regex without a negative list flagged the clean `p-3`.
Proposed for lack of a source (decision 47); the v1 evidence was: A: baseline counts only; no fault traced to a raw px alone

rules.rule: `!important` and `outline: none` each need a stated reason, and an outline is never removed without a visible focus ring in its place.
rules.detail: The focus ring is a token applied on `:focus-visible` and never hidden. An allowed use carries a reason comment (`reportDescriptionlessDisables`). Debt is held by a count baseline. Stylelint writes `stylelint-suppressions.json`; `--prune` must run in the same change as a fix. The outline entry is `outline` mapped to `["none","0"]`; both rules also fired in `.astro` `<style>` blocks. The utility form of outline removal is `outline-none`.
rules.why: The counts are 9 `!important` and 102 `outline: none` in one site; hiding the keyboard position leaves a keyboard user with no way to see where they are.

checks.note: Stylelint 17.16 core `declaration-no-important` and `declaration-property-value-disallowed-list` for `outline: none` and `0`, with `reportDescriptionlessDisables` so an allowed use needs a reason; debt through Stylelint's `--suppress` file. Plant: `color: red !important` with no reason fails; with a description passes; `outline: none` fails. Control: a described exception passes

open: Stylelint suppressions are experimental; slack after a fix is the weak spot (a stale entry exits 0, where ESLint's exits 2), so the prune step must run in the same change as a fix.

rules.rule: Every text and status pair passes a contrast of 4.5 to 1, and 3 to 1 for large text and parts, on every ground it may sit on, in both modes, by a pure test computed from the tokens.
rules.detail: WCAG AA in both themes for every foreground and background token pair. The test iterates the token document, so a new role is covered; it also computes APCA Lc and prints it beside the ratio. It runs on any change to the token source. The generator ships the test, and the terminal side generates its own contrast test from the same table.
rules.why: Measured faults: a muted role at 4.29 and 4.49 on light, good 4.32, attention 4.24, white on the dark `bad` role 2.77; the Go test covers 4 of 9 colours. Colour contrast is 89.1 percent of axe WCAG failures in generated pages.
